## Travel Insurance for Schengen Visa: Requirements, Coverage and How to Get It

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/asigurare-viza-schengen
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-11

Descriere: Exact requirements for Schengen visa travel insurance: minimum €30,000 medical cover, what the policy must include, how much it costs, and what embassies check.

Răspuns scurt: For a short-stay Schengen visa, travel insurance is mandatory and must provide a minimum of €30,000 medical cover, be valid for the entire duration of your trip and cover all Schengen countries. It must include emergency medical expenses, medical repatriation and transport in case of death. Without this insurance, the visa is automatically refused.

Romania joined the Schengen Area in 2025 — but non-EU citizens (Moldovans, Ukrainians, Russians and others) who want to enter the EU still need travel insurance when applying for a Schengen visa. Romanians applying for long-stay visas (study, work) also need it. Here is everything you need to know so your application is not refused because of the wrong document.

What the Schengen rules say about insurance

Regulation (EC) No 810/2009 (the Visa Code) requires that every applicant for a short-stay Schengen visa must provide proof of medical insurance covering:


Minimum €30,000 cover (or the equivalent in another currency)

Validity for the entire planned stay

Geographic scope covering all Schengen states (if the itinerary includes more than one country)

Mandatory content: emergency medical expenses, medical repatriation, transport in case of death


Without these elements, the visa is refused automatically — regardless of the rest of your documentation.

What the policy must include

Mandatory (verified by the embassy):


Emergency medical expenses (hospitalisation, surgery, medication)

Medical transport (ambulance, repatriation)

Repatriation in case of death

Minimum €30,000 cover


Recommended but not mandatory for the visa:


Trip cancellation

Lost baggage

Personal liability


Watch out for exclusions: cheap policies often exclude adventure sports, pre-existing conditions and accidents under the influence of alcohol. Read the conditions carefully, not just the insured sum.

What documents you receive

Your insurer will issue an electronic policy (PDF) containing:


Name of the insured

Cover period

Insured amount

Geographic territory

Policy number and insurer details


This is what you submit to the embassy — not a receipt or a confirmation email, but the actual policy document. Some embassies also ask for a Schengen Certificate (a short document confirming the policy meets Schengen requirements). Check what the specific embassy you are applying to will accept before you buy.

How much it costs

Prices vary based on age, duration and provider:

Duration Under 50 50–65 years Over 65 years
1 week €8–12 €15–25 €30–60
2 weeks €12–20 €25–40 €50–90
1 month €20–40 €40–70 €80–150

Indicative prices for standard €30,000 cover

Annual multi-trip policy (if you travel frequently): €50–150 per year, covering all trips up to 30–45 days per journey. Worth it from 3–4 trips a year.

Note that the prices above are starting points. Some providers charge more for high-risk destinations, certain nationalities, or if you want to add baggage or cancellation cover. Always compare the total price with all the options you actually need.

Where to buy it

Schengen insurance can be purchased:


Online directly from the insurer — fastest option, you receive the policy within minutes

Through insurance comparison platforms — you compare multiple providers side by side

At a bank or post office — slower and usually fewer options


Important: buy the policy AFTER you know the exact dates of your trip (entry and exit dates from the Schengen area). The policy must cover precisely the period declared in your visa application. A policy bought for the wrong dates means an automatic refusal.

EKTA — a practical option for Schengen insurance

EKTA is one of the better-known providers for Schengen-compliant travel insurance. The policy is issued instantly online, is available in English (which most embassies accept), and clearly states the required Schengen coverage on the document itself. It covers the mandatory €30,000 minimum and includes medical repatriation and death transport.

You apply, pay, and download the PDF in under five minutes.

Common mistakes that get visa applications refused

Sum below €30,000. Some providers sell policies with €15,000 cover — acceptable in some countries, but insufficient under the Schengen Regulation. Always check the insured amount before purchasing.

Limited geographic scope. An insurance valid "only in Germany" is rejected if your itinerary includes France. You need a policy valid "in all Schengen countries" or "Europe." Check the geographic territory listed on the policy document.

Policy expired on the application date. The embassy verifies that the policy covers exactly the trip period — not just that a policy exists. A policy bought for the wrong dates means refusal.

Using the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC). The EHIC covers emergency treatment in public hospitals within the EU — but it is not the same as travel insurance and embassies do not accept it as a substitute. You need a private travel insurance policy.

Using national health insurance only. Your home country's public health insurance (such as Romania's CNAS) covers treatment at home, not abroad. Embassies do not accept it as proof of Schengen insurance.

Policy not in English (or the required language). Some embassies — particularly for France, Germany and the Netherlands — require the policy in English or with a certified translation. Check before you buy.

Waiting until the last moment. Processing times at embassies can be 2–8 weeks. If your insurance expires before your appointment, you will need to renew it. Buy the policy after you receive your appointment date and check that it covers the entire stay.

Insurance for non-EU nationals: country-specific notes

The Schengen Visa Code applies uniformly across all 29 Schengen states, but individual embassies sometimes have stricter local requirements:

French embassy: Requires the Schengen certificate to explicitly mention "Schengen territory." Most digital insurers include this automatically.

German embassy: Strongly prefers policies from companies listed on the embassy's approved provider list — though legally any policy meeting the regulation is valid.

Dutch embassy: Known for rejecting policies that do not clearly state €30,000 on the document itself (not hidden in the terms and conditions).

Italian embassy: Generally the most flexible — standard online policies are accepted without additional documentation.

If in doubt, contact the embassy directly and ask what format they accept before purchasing.

What about long-stay visas (type D)?

Long-stay Schengen visas (for study, work, or family reunification) often require insurance with higher cover and longer validity — sometimes €60,000 or more, or private health insurance equivalent to the local system. The requirements vary significantly by destination country and visa type. Check the specific requirements at the embassy for the country you are applying to.

Annual multi-trip insurance: when it makes sense

If you travel three or more times a year:

Single-trip (per journey) Annual multi-trip
€8–20 per trip €50–150 per year
Covers one trip only Covers all trips (30–45 days max per trip)
Buy before each trip Buy once, covered all year
Better for infrequent travellers Better from 3+ trips/year

For people who travel regularly — students, business travellers, frequent tourists — an annual policy typically pays for itself by the third trip.

What happens if your trip is cancelled after you buy insurance?

If your Schengen visa is refused, most policies allow a full or partial refund of the premium if you can prove the refusal (by showing the official rejection letter from the embassy). Check the refund conditions before purchasing — they vary by provider.

If your trip is cancelled for other reasons (illness, family emergency), you may be covered under the cancellation section of a more comprehensive policy. Basic Schengen-compliance policies often do not include cancellation — you would need a standard or premium travel insurance for that.

Before you apply: quick checklist


Policy sum: minimum €30,000

Policy valid for the exact dates of your Schengen stay

Geographic scope: all Schengen countries (or "Europe")

Covers: emergency medical expenses, medical repatriation, transport in case of death

Document: official policy PDF (not a booking confirmation or receipt)

Language: in English or with certified translation (check embassy requirements)

Schengen certificate included (if required by the embassy you are applying to)


Five minutes of checking against this list before you buy can save your entire visa application.

Related guides

If you are planning your trip and need more than just visa insurance, these guides cover the next steps:

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Do EU citizens need Schengen travel insurance?
R: EU citizens travelling within the EU do not need Schengen visa insurance for tourism or business. Schengen visa insurance is required for non-EU nationals (Moldovans, Ukrainians, Russians, etc.) applying for a short-stay Schengen visa, and for anyone applying for a long-stay visa (study, work, family reunification).

Î: What do embassies check in the insurance policy?
R: Embassies verify: the minimum cover amount (€30,000), the validity period (must cover the entire planned stay), geographic scope (all Schengen countries, not just one), and that the policy includes emergency medical expenses, repatriation and death transport. Some embassies also require the policy in English or with a certified translation.

Î: How much does Schengen visa insurance cost?
R: A standard Schengen policy with €30,000 cover for two weeks costs between €8 and €20, depending on age, provider and destination. The price increases with age and duration. This is a small amount compared to the real cost of medical care abroad.

Î: Can the same insurance cover multiple trips?
R: Yes, with an annual multi-trip policy, which covers all journeys within a year, ideal if you travel frequently. A single-trip policy covers one journey only, and is cheaper if you travel once a year. For a multiple-entry visa, the insurance must cover at least the first trip.

Î: Does Schengen insurance cover routine doctor visits?
R: No. Travel insurance covers unforeseen medical EMERGENCIES — accidents, acute illness, emergency hospitalisation. It does not cover routine check-ups, planned consultations or treatment for pre-existing conditions (in general). Always read the exclusions before buying.

Î: What happens if my trip is extended beyond the policy dates?
R: If you stay longer than the dates on your policy, you are uninsured for the additional period. You can extend some policies online before they expire. Always contact your insurer if your return is delayed — many have a 24/7 helpline for exactly this situation.

## European Health Insurance Card vs Travel Insurance: What Actually Covers You

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/card-european-vs-asigurare-calatorie
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-25
Actualizat: 2026-07-25

Descriere: The EHIC is free but does not cover repatriation, private clinics, or trip cancellation. See exactly what each covers, where the gaps are, and when you need both.

Răspuns scurt: The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is free and gives you access to the public healthcare system in EU countries — but it does NOT cover medical repatriation, private hospitals, mountain rescue, or trip cancellation. For complete protection you need a private travel insurance policy alongside the card. The ideal setup: EHIC for public hospital emergencies in the EU, travel insurance for everything the EHIC does not cover.

Many travellers assume that because the European Health Insurance Card is free and official-looking, it provides comprehensive coverage. It does not — and the gap between what the card covers and what actually happens during a medical emergency abroad can mean a bill of tens of thousands of euros. Here is exactly what each document does and does not cover.

What the EHIC actually is

The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC, also called CEASS in Romanian) is a document issued free of charge by your national health insurance authority. In Romania, you apply through CNAS at cardeuropean.ro — the card is free and valid for up to 24 months.

What it gives you: the right to necessary medical treatment during a temporary stay in another EU member state, the EEA (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway), Switzerland, and the UK — under the same conditions as local residents.

The word "necessary" is important. It means treatment for an acute problem that arises during your trip — not treatment you travelled specifically to receive, and not anything beyond what the local public system provides.

What the EHIC covers — and does not cover

EHIC Private travel insurance
Price Free €12–50/week
Geographic coverage EU / EEA / CH / UK only Worldwide
Hospitals covered Public only Public + private
Medical repatriation ❌ Never ✅
Trip cancellation ❌ ✅ (optional add-on)
Lost or stolen luggage ❌ ✅
Winter sports accidents ❌ ✅ (with add-on)
Emergency dentistry ✅ Public dentists only ✅
Turkey, USA, Egypt, Asia ❌ Not valid ✅
Private hospital ❌ ✅
Mountain rescue ❌ ✅
Flight delay compensation ❌ ✅

The gaps that cost people the most

Medical repatriation — the most expensive gap

If you are seriously ill or injured abroad and need to be transported home, the EHIC does not contribute a single euro. A medical air ambulance from Western Europe back to Romania costs €15,000–30,000. From the USA or Asia, considerably more. This cost falls entirely on your family unless you have a private policy.

Travel insurance covers repatriation completely, including accompanying family members if needed.

Private hospitals — the gap you hit in tourist areas

In many popular tourist destinations, the conveniently located clinics near beach resorts and ski slopes are private. In Rhodes, Crete, Antalya, and similar tourist-heavy areas, the nearest hospital may well be private — and the EHIC does not cover private treatment anywhere.

When you arrive at a hospital abroad, ask specifically whether they are part of the public system before receiving treatment. If they are private and you only have the EHIC, you will pay out of pocket.

Mountain and ski resort accidents

If you ski in France, Austria, or Bulgaria, the first-aid infrastructure on most ski slopes operates privately. The EHIC covers none of it. A helicopter rescue from a ski slope in the Alps can cost €3,000–8,000. A standard winter sports extension to your travel insurance costs €5–15 extra and covers it completely.

The same logic applies to water sports, quad biking, paragliding, and any activity where accidents happen in private medical facilities.

The UK — no longer covered the same way

Since Brexit, the UK is technically still in the EHIC scheme (bilaterally with most EU countries), but the coverage is more limited and less predictable than within the EU. For full protection in the UK, a private travel insurance policy is the safer option.

Real costs of medical emergencies abroad — without insurance

These are actual cost ranges for medical situations that travellers encounter:

Situation Location Cost without insurance
Broken arm (treatment + cast) Italy (private clinic) €800–2,500
Appendicitis (surgery + 3 nights) Germany (public) €0 with EHIC
Appendicitis (surgery + 3 nights) Turkey (private) €3,000–8,000
Medical repatriation by air Spain → Romania €12,000–25,000
Cardiac event (ICU, 5 nights) USA €50,000–150,000
Ski accident + helicopter rescue France €4,000–10,000
Scooter accident Greece (private clinic) €2,000–6,000
Food poisoning (hospitalisation, 2 nights) Egypt €1,500–4,000

The EHIC covers the Germany appendicitis scenario reasonably well — public hospital, EU country. It covers nothing in Turkey, Greece (private), France (rescue), USA, or Egypt.

How much does travel insurance cost

For comparison with the potential costs above:

Destination 7 days 14 days Recommended coverage
Europe (EU/Schengen) €12–25 €20–40 €30,000
Turkey €15–30 €25–50 €30,000
United Kingdom €15–30 €25–50 €30,000
USA / Canada €35–70 €60–120 €100,000
Asia / worldwide €25–50 €40–80 €50,000

Indicative prices for adults 18–65, individual policy, medical cover + baggage + repatriation. Winter sports add €5–15. Over-65s: prices increase 50–100%.

Annual multi-trip policy: €120–250/year, covers all journeys (typically with a cap of 30–45 days per trip). Worth it from 3+ trips per year.

The seven most common mistakes travellers make

1. "I have the EHIC, I'm covered"

False. The EHIC covers only public hospitals in the EU. An ambulance in Germany, repatriation from Portugal, or any treatment in Turkey costs thousands of euros with no EHIC contribution.

2. "My credit card includes travel insurance"

Sometimes partially true. Many Gold and Platinum cards include travel insurance benefits, but with low coverage limits (€10,000–25,000), requirements to have paid the flight with that specific card, and significant exclusions for pre-existing conditions. Check your card's terms document — the coverage is often insufficient for serious situations.

3. "I'm only going for a 3-day city break, I don't need it"

Trip duration does not affect the probability of an accident. A broken wrist on cobblestones in Prague or food poisoning in Istanbul can happen on day one. A 3-day policy for Europe costs €5–8.

4. "I'll buy it at the airport before the flight"

You can, but airport insurance desks have significantly higher prices (commission-based) and you risk forgetting. Buy online 2–3 days before departure — it takes five minutes and costs less.

5. "I'm driving to Greece, I don't need travel insurance"

Yes, you do. Your car insurance (RCA/CASCO) covers the vehicle. Travel insurance covers you — your health, your luggage, and your ability to cancel and recover costs if something goes wrong. They are entirely different products.

6. "I won't declare my pre-existing condition — they'll never know"

This is the most dangerous mistake. If you have a medical emergency related to an undeclared pre-existing condition, the insurer can legally refuse the claim — and they have access to medical databases. Declare everything. The additional premium is small (€5–15 extra) and the difference in claim acceptance is enormous.

7. "I'll go to the hospital first, then claim later"

Wrong. Call the insurer's 24/7 emergency line first. They will direct you to network hospitals (where payment is handled directly between the insurer and hospital) and pre-authorise treatment. If you walk into a private hospital without prior authorisation, you may pay out of pocket and face complications with reimbursement.

The right approach: use both

The practical recommendation is not to choose between the EHIC and travel insurance — it is to use both:

Get the EHIC free from CNAS (apply at cardeuropean.ro, valid 24 months). Keep it in your wallet on every trip. It supplements your insurance and can cover public hospital treatment in EU countries at no cost to either you or your insurer.

Buy travel insurance for every trip outside Romania — EU or non-EU. The cost is small relative to what it protects. For an EU city break, you need €12–20. For Turkey or the UK, €15–30. For the USA, €35–70.

The EHIC is the floor. Travel insurance is the ceiling. You want both.

What to look for in a travel insurance policy

When comparing policies, check specifically:

Medical cover amount: minimum €30,000 for EU/Schengen (required for Schengen visa), €50,000+ for worldwide, €100,000+ for USA/Canada.

Repatriation: must be explicitly listed, with no sub-limit that would make it effectively useless.

Pre-existing conditions: does the policy cover them if declared? What is the additional premium?

Activities: are your planned activities covered? Skiing, scuba diving, cycling, and water sports require explicit confirmation.

Cancellation: is trip cancellation included or an add-on? What situations trigger it?

Direct payment vs reimbursement: policies that pay the hospital directly (rather than reimbursing you later) are significantly easier to use in a crisis.

For Schengen visa applications specifically, the insurance requirements are stricter — read the complete guide: travel insurance for Schengen visa — exact requirements .

For the full travel insurance guide covering all policy types, costs, and how to choose: travel insurance guide 2026 .

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is the European Health Insurance Card free?
R: Yes, completely free. It is issued by your national health insurance authority (in Romania, through CNAS at cardeuropean.ro). It is valid for up to 24 months and can be renewed. Apply at least two weeks before departure to ensure you receive it in time.

Î: Does the EHIC cover medical repatriation?
R: No, never. The EHIC does not cover repatriation under any circumstances. A medical air ambulance from Western Europe to Romania can cost €15,000–30,000. Without private travel insurance, that cost falls entirely on your family.

Î: Does the EHIC work at private hospitals?
R: No. The EHIC only covers providers within the public healthcare system. On ski slopes, most first-aid centres are private — the card does not cover them. In tourist-heavy areas of Greece, Spain, or Italy, many conveniently located clinics are private and the EHIC is not accepted.

Î: If I have the EHIC, do I still need travel insurance?
R: Yes, for complete protection. The EHIC covers basic public healthcare in the EU, but not repatriation, private hospitals, mountain rescue, trip cancellation, or lost baggage. Travel insurance covers exactly these gaps — and costs €12–25 for a week in Europe.

Î: Does the EHIC work outside the EU?
R: Only within the EU, the European Economic Area (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway), Switzerland, and the United Kingdom. In Turkey, Egypt, the USA, or Asia, the EHIC is not valid — private travel insurance is your only protection.

Î: Does credit card travel insurance replace a proper policy?
R: Rarely. Many premium credit cards (Gold, Platinum, Visa Infinite) include travel insurance as a benefit, but with important limitations: typically lower coverage amounts (€10,000–25,000), requirements to have paid the trip with that card, and exclusions for pre-existing conditions. Check your card's terms — it may supplement but usually should not replace a dedicated policy.

Î: What does travel insurance NOT cover?
R: Standard exclusions: undeclared pre-existing conditions, accidents under the influence of alcohol or drugs, extreme sports (without a specific add-on), planned medical treatment abroad, travel to conflict zones (MAE level 4 warning), and pandemics (with some insurers). Always read the general conditions before purchasing.

## EHIC vs Travel Insurance 2026: What Each Actually Covers

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/ehic-vs-travel-insurance
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-07
Actualizat: 2026-08-23
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/card-european-vs-asigurare-calatorie

Descriere: The EHIC is free but doesn't cover repatriation, private clinics, or mountain rescue. Real costs, country-by-country rules, and when you need both.

Răspuns scurt: The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is free and gives you access to state healthcare in EU/EEA countries on the same terms as locals, but it does NOT cover medical repatriation (€15,000-30,000), private clinics, mountain rescue (€3,500-10,000), trip cancellation, or lost baggage. It doesn't work at all outside the EU (Turkey, USA, Asia). Private travel insurance (from $0.99/day with EKTA or €9-14/week with European insurers) covers exactly these gaps. The right strategy is both: EHIC (free) + private insurance = complete protection for under €15 per week.

Many travellers assume that their European Health Insurance Card means they're fully covered abroad. It's the most expensive misconception in travel: the EHIC and travel insurance cover fundamentally different things, and the gap between them can mean a bill of tens of thousands of euros.

This guide explains exactly what each covers, where each leaves you exposed, what the difference costs in real money, and why the right strategy is "both" — not "one or the other."


What the EHIC actually is

The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is a free document issued by your country's national health insurance authority. It entitles you to medically necessary healthcare during a temporary stay in another EU/EEA country — on the same terms as local residents.

What "same terms as locals" really means

This is the key phrase most people misunderstand. "Same as locals" doesn't mean "free" — it means you pay what they pay:


In France: a 20% co-payment on consultations + €18/day "forfait journalier" for hospital stays. You pay the same with your EHIC.

In Germany: €10 emergency department fee at hospital presentation. The EHIC puts you on equal footing, but doesn't eliminate the co-payment.

In Spain: emergency treatment is free in the public system. The EHIC works well here.

In Italy: genuine emergencies are free, but non-urgent consultations carry a "ticket sanitario" (co-payment) of €25-50.

In Greece: emergency treatment is free, but quality varies significantly between tourist islands and urban centres.

In the UK: the EHIC/GHIC works, and NHS emergency care is free for everyone. But specialist appointments have waiting times of weeks.


The takeaway: the EHIC doesn't make you VIP — it makes you equal to locals in the public system. With all its strengths and limitations.

Where the EHIC works

Works ✅ Doesn't work ❌
All 27 EU member states Turkey
Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway (EEA) Egypt, Tunisia, Morocco
Switzerland USA, Canada
United Kingdom (via GHIC reciprocal) Thailand, Bali, Japan
UAE, Dubai
Any country outside EU/EEA

Full EU list: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden.


What the EHIC does NOT cover — and what the gap costs

These situations are never covered by the EHIC, regardless of circumstances:

1. Medical repatriation — €15,000-250,000

Medical repatriation means organised transport back to your home country when you can't travel normally (serious fracture, major accident, illness requiring ongoing treatment at home). The EHIC doesn't cover a single euro of this.

Real repatriation costs in 2026:

Route Transport type Estimated cost
Western Europe → home country Ground ambulance €3,000-8,000
Western Europe → home country Air ambulance €15,000-30,000
Spain/Portugal → Northern Europe Air ambulance €20,000-35,000
Europe → USA Medicalised flight $120,000-250,000
Asia → Europe Medicalised flight $150,000-300,000
Medical escort on commercial flight Escort + business class tickets €5,000-15,000

Real example: a tourist breaks their femur skiing in Austria. The operation in Austria is covered (partially) by the EHIC. But the medicalised transport back home — the air ambulance, medical equipment, medical staff — costs €18,000-25,000. Without insurance, the family pays in full.

2. Private clinics and doctors — variable costs

The EHIC covers only providers within the public healthcare system. The problem: in many tourist situations, accessing the public system isn't practical.

Where you're forced into private care:


Ski resorts: medical centres on the slopes are almost always private. First aid + helicopter transport = private bill

Summer beach resorts: clinics in resort towns (Crete, Costa del Sol, Algarve) are predominantly private

Cruise ships: the ship's doctor is private; the hospital at the port of call is probably private

Greek islands: on many small islands, the only option is a private clinic. The nearest public hospital may be on another island entirely

Rural areas: in many tourist areas, the nearest public hospital can be 50+ km away


Cost example: consultation + X-ray at a private clinic on an Austrian ski slope: €200-500. At a public hospital in Innsbruck (with EHIC): €10 co-payment. But getting from the slope to Innsbruck already involves a transport bill.

3. Mountain rescue and search & rescue — €2,000-10,000

Search and rescue operations — including helicopters, ski patrol, mountain rescue teams — are not covered by the EHIC. At all.

Rescue costs by country in 2026:

Country Helicopter rescue Ski patrol (on-piste) Ambulance
Switzerland CHF 4,500 ( €4,700) average (Rega) CHF 800-2,000 CHF 700-2,100
France €2,000-6,000 ~€300 (stretcher/sled) €400-800
Austria €3,500-10,000 €500-1,500 €400-900
Italy €2,500-8,000 €400-1,200 €300-700
Germany €3,000-7,000 €500-1,000 €500-1,000

Switzerland example: you crash on a slope at Zermatt. The helicopter takes you to the hospital in Visp — bill of ~CHF 4,500. Swiss mandatory health insurance covers 50%, capped at CHF 5,000/year — but only for Swiss residents. As a tourist with your EHIC? You pay the full amount.

The France exception: public mountain rescue (PGHM — Peloton de Gendarmerie de Haute Montagne) is free in France for life-saving rescue — but only if life is in danger and you're on public land. On-piste (the resort's private domain), the resort's ski patrol charges €300-2,000. And a private helicopter is billed at €2,500/hour.

4. Trip cancellation and travel disruption — zero coverage

The EHIC is a health card — it has nothing to do with your trip itself. If your flight is cancelled, your luggage is lost, or you need to cancel your holiday for medical reasons, the EHIC covers nothing.

What travel insurance covers (and the EHIC doesn't):

Situation EHIC coverage Insurance coverage
Flight cancellation by airline ❌ ✅ Reimbursement + accommodation
Lost baggage ❌ ✅ Up to €1,000-2,000
Delayed baggage (> 4-6 hours) ❌ ✅ €100-300 for essential items
Trip cancellation (personal illness/family) ❌ ✅ Reimbursement of prepaid costs
Personal liability (you cause damage on holiday) ❌ ✅ Up to €50,000-100,000
Legal assistance abroad ❌ ✅ Legal support

5. Dental care — minimal coverage

The EHIC covers emergency dental care in the public system only — and only "immediate medical necessity" (antibiotics, emergency extraction). A temporary crown, an implant, or root canal treatment is not considered an emergency. And private dental clinics (which are the majority in most EU countries) don't accept the EHIC.

Cost example: dental emergency (abscess) on holiday: €150-500 at a private clinic. With EHIC, at a public hospital: €0-30 co-payment. But finding a public dentist who takes emergencies at 10pm on a Saturday in Santorini isn't realistic.

Common EHIC mistakes that cost travellers money

1. "I have the EHIC, so I'm fully covered"

The most dangerous myth. The EHIC covers at most 30-40% of situations you might face on holiday. Repatriation, private clinics, and mountain rescue — the most expensive ones — are completely excluded.

2. Not checking the expiry date

The EHIC is valid for 2 years (in most countries). If it's expired, it's as if you don't have one — the hospital won't accept it. Check before every trip , not at the airport.

3. Travelling outside the EU with only the EHIC

The EHIC doesn't work at all in Turkey, Egypt, the USA, or Asia. If you go to these countries with only the EHIC, you effectively have zero medical protection.

4. Assuming "necessary" means everything

"Medically necessary care" doesn't mean any visit to a doctor. Routine consultations, check-ups, and treatments that can be postponed until you return home are NOT considered "necessary" and can be refused.

5. Not carrying the physical card

Some hospitals don't accept photos of the card or screenshots. Carry the physical card in your wallet, not just on your phone.

6. Not knowing the co-payment system

If France charges a 20% co-payment on consultations, you pay 20% — even with the EHIC. Research the co-payment system of your destination country before you travel.

7. Applying too late

The card is delivered by post in 7-15 working days (varies by country). If you apply 3 days before departure, it won't arrive in time. You can request a Provisional Replacement Certificate (PRC), but it's an emergency solution, not a comfortable one.


How to avoid a rejected insurance claim

Travel insurance claim rejection rates run at approximately 30-35%. The most common reasons and how to avoid them:

Rejection reasons and prevention

Rejection reason Frequency How to avoid
Missing documentation ~40% of rejections Keep ALL original receipts, prescriptions, medical reports. Photograph everything.
Undeclared pre-existing conditions ~25% of rejections Declare ANY chronic condition when buying the policy — even if well-controlled.
Activity not covered ~15% of rejections Check whether your activity (skiing, diving) is included or needs an add-on.
Exceeded deadline ~10% of rejections File the claim within the specified period (usually 30-90 days from the incident).
Didn't contact insurer in time ~10% of rejections Call the 24/7 helpline BEFORE going to the doctor (if the situation allows).

Successful claim checklist


Call the insurer's 24/7 helpline — first thing, if possible. They can direct you to a partner hospital (they pay directly, no advance from your pocket)

Keep EVERYTHING: original receipts, prescriptions, medical reports, flight tickets, hotel receipts, taxi/ambulance receipts

Photograph all documents — digital backup on phone and cloud

Police report — for theft, road accidents, or lost baggage. Without a police report, baggage claims are almost automatically rejected

Detailed medical certificate from the treating doctor — must state the diagnosis, treatment provided, and that it was an emergency

File the claim within the deadline (30-90 days) — with ALL documentation

The verdict: 3 rules for complete protection

Rule 1: Get your EHIC now. It's free, takes 5 minutes online, and is valid for 2 years. Even if you have no holiday planned, have the card ready for any EU trip.

Rule 2: Buy travel insurance for every trip. €9-15 per week is nothing compared to a potential €5,000-30,000 bill. And it's your only protection outside the EU.

Rule 3: Read the policy before you leave. Check: does it cover your activities (skiing, diving)? Does it include repatriation? What's the medical coverage limit? What are the exclusions? 5 minutes of reading can save you from a rejected claim.

The protection formula: EHIC (free) + private insurance (€9-15/week) = complete protection for under €15. Without the EHIC, you lose the free basic coverage. Without private insurance, you're exposed on repatriation, private clinics, mountain rescue, and trip cancellation — exactly where the costs are catastrophic.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is the EHIC card free?
R: Yes. The EHIC is issued free of charge by your country's national health insurance authority. In most EU countries, you can apply online and receive it within 7-15 working days. It's valid for up to 2 years but does not renew automatically — you must reapply before it expires. Apply at least 2-3 weeks before your trip.

Î: Does the EHIC cover medical repatriation?
R: No, never. Medical repatriation (organised transport back to your home country when you can't travel normally) is completely excluded from the EHIC. An air ambulance within Europe costs €15,000-30,000, while a medicalised flight from the US or Asia can reach €120,000-250,000. Without private insurance, the family pays in full.

Î: Does the EHIC work at private clinics?
R: No. The EHIC covers only providers within the public healthcare system. At ski resorts, most first-aid centres on the slopes are private. In tourist areas, the nearest clinic is often private. On small Greek islands, the only medical facility may be a private clinic. In all these situations, the EHIC is useless — you either pay out of pocket or need private insurance.

Î: If I have the EHIC, do I still need travel insurance?
R: Yes, for complete protection. The EHIC covers basic public healthcare on the same terms as locals (including co-payments). Private travel insurance covers exactly the EHIC's gaps: repatriation, private clinics, mountain rescue, trip cancellation, lost baggage, and personal liability. The two complement each other — they don't replace each other.

Î: Does the EHIC work outside the EU?
R: Only in the EU (27 states), plus the European Economic Area (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway), Switzerland, and the UK (via the GHIC reciprocal arrangement). It does NOT work in Turkey, Egypt, the USA, Canada, Asia, South America, or Australia — there, private travel insurance is your only medical protection.

Î: What happens if I need a helicopter rescue while skiing and only have the EHIC?
R: You pay out of pocket. In Switzerland, a Rega helicopter rescue costs an average of CHF 4,500 (~€4,700). In France, an on-piste helicopter costs €2,000-6,000. In Austria, helicopter mountain rescue costs €3,500-10,000. The EHIC covers none of this. Travel insurance with a 'winter sports' add-on pays in full.

Î: How much does travel insurance cost that covers what the EHIC doesn't?
R: From $0.99/day with EKTA (Start plan, $50,000 coverage) to $5.90/day (Max+ plan, $500,000 coverage). European insurers typically charge €9-15 per week for standard coverage. Annual multi-trip policies cost €20-170/year depending on coverage level — cheaper than two individual policies if you travel 2+ times per year.

Î: Can I use the EHIC for planned dental treatment abroad?
R: No. The EHIC covers only medically necessary emergency dental treatment in the public system (abscess, dental fracture). Planned treatments (crowns, implants, cosmetic dentistry) require a separate S2 form and prior authorisation from your national health authority.

Î: My EHIC expired — can I still use it?
R: No. An expired EHIC is treated as if you don't have one — the hospital will not accept it. Check the expiry date before every trip, not at the airport. If your card has expired and you can't get a new one in time, your national health authority can issue a Provisional Replacement Certificate (PRC) valid for 90 days.

## Emergencies Abroad 2026: What to Do When Things Go Wrong — Step-by-Step Guide

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/emergencies-abroad-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-29
Actualizat: 2026-07-29
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/urgente-in-strainatate-ghid-2026

Descriere: Medical emergency, theft, lost passport, missed flight, natural disaster — exact steps for every travel emergency, who to call first, and how travel insurance handles each scenario.

Răspuns scurt: In any serious emergency abroad: (1) Call 112 (EU) or the local emergency number for immediate danger. (2) Call your travel insurer's 24/7 line for medical emergencies — they organise everything including hospital and repatriation. (3) Contact your country's embassy or consulate for passport loss or legal problems. The single most common mistake: going directly to a private hospital without calling the insurer first — this can invalidate reimbursement. Save your insurer's emergency number in your phone before departure.

The scenarios in this guide are not hypothetical. Medical emergencies happen to fit, young travellers on first trips. Passports disappear. Flights are missed. Natural disasters redirect carefully planned itineraries. The difference between a bad experience that becomes a story you tell later and a genuine crisis is almost always the same thing: knowing what to do in the first 30 minutes.

This guide covers every major travel emergency in sequence — what to do first, who to call, and how to protect yourself financially.


Before any emergency: the five things to do before departure

These five actions take 20 minutes total and make every scenario below significantly easier to handle:

1. Save your insurer's emergency number in your phone
It is on your policy document, in the insurer's app, and on the back of any physical insurance card. Save it as a contact called "TRAVEL EMERGENCY" — capital letters so it appears first when you start typing in a moment of stress.

2. Photograph your passport and email it to yourself
Both sides. Email to yourself and to one trusted person at home. If your passport is lost or stolen, this photo is your primary evidence of identity at the consulate. Without it, the process takes significantly longer.

3. Note the address and phone number of your country's embassy in your destination
Search "[your country] embassy in [destination]" — the result is always the official government website. Save the address and emergency phone number. Embassies have after-hours emergency lines for genuine crises (passport loss, arrest, medical repatriation).

4. Save your bank's international fraud line
The number on the back of each card. If your cards are stolen, you call this number to block them before the thief uses them. Bolt or Uber apps, Google Pay, and Apple Pay are also worth setting up as backup payment methods.

5. Share your itinerary
Email your accommodation details, flight numbers, and rough daily plans to a trusted person at home. If you cannot be reached for 48 hours, they know where to start looking.


Medical emergency abroad

A medical emergency is the highest-stakes scenario. The decisions made in the first hour determine both outcomes and costs.

Immediate danger to life

Call 112 (universal EU emergency number) — or the local equivalent:


Turkey: 112

UK: 999 or 112

USA/Canada: 911

Australia: 000

Morocco: 15 (medical), 19 (police)


112 works from any mobile phone, even without a SIM card, credit, or data. If your phone is dead, ask anyone nearby to call.

Non-life-threatening medical situation

Call your insurer's emergency line first. This is critical and counterintuitive: the instinct is to go to the nearest hospital. But:


The insurer directs you to a network partner hospital where they pay directly — you pay nothing out of pocket

If you go to a non-partner private hospital without pre-authorisation, the insurer can refuse or reduce reimbursement

The insurer's emergency operator speaks multiple languages and can also communicate with the hospital on your behalf


What to say when you call:


Your name and policy number (in the insurer's app before departure)

Your location — as precise as possible

Your symptoms or situation

Your phone number in case you lose connection


The insurer then:


Directs you to the nearest appropriate facility

Contacts the hospital and pre-authorises treatment

Arranges payment directly with the hospital

Assigns a case manager who monitors your situation


If you pay out of pocket (partner hospital not available)

Keep every document:


Medical report or discharge summary

All receipts for treatment, medication, tests

Prescription copies

Taxi receipts to and from the hospital

Hotel receipts if your stay was extended due to illness


Submit a reimbursement claim on return. Most insurers have an online claims portal. Reimbursement typically arrives within 14–30 days.

Medical repatriation

If you are seriously ill or injured and need to return home for treatment, your insurer organises this:


Air ambulance (if required): €15,000–80,000 — covered in full

Commercial flight with medical escort: covered

A family member's flight to accompany you: covered by most comprehensive policies


Do not try to arrange repatriation yourself — the insurer has specialist logistics teams for this. Call them, describe the situation, and let them manage it.

What the EHIC covers (and does not)

The European Health Insurance Card gives you access to public hospitals in EU countries under the same conditions as local residents. It does NOT cover:


Private hospitals (where most tourist-area urgent care happens)

Medical repatriation

Non-EU destinations (Turkey, UK, USA, Asia, etc.)


For non-EU destinations, travel insurance is your only protection. For EU destinations, travel insurance covers the gaps the EHIC leaves. See the full comparison: EHIC vs travel insurance .


Passport lost or stolen abroad

Losing your passport abroad is stressful but solvable. The process is well-established.

Step-by-step: lost or stolen passport

Step 1 — File a police report (within hours)

For a stolen passport: go to the nearest police station and file a theft report. For a lost passport: file a loss report. You need this document for:


Applying for an Emergency Travel Document

Travel insurance claims

Proving the original passport is no longer usable (prevents fraudulent use)


In most EU countries, you can file a police report online. In Turkey: Jandarma (rural) or Polis (urban), both reachable via 155.

Step 2 — Contact your country's embassy or consulate

Find the nearest location before you travel (saved from your pre-departure preparation). Call their emergency line — most embassies have 24/7 emergency services for genuine passport loss situations.

For Romanian citizens abroad: the Consular Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs operates a permanent emergency line. Contact via mae.ro → "Cetățeni români în dificultate."

For UK citizens: contact the FCDO on +44 207 008 5000 (24/7).

For US citizens: contact the nearest US Embassy or +1 202 501 4444.

Step 3 — Apply for an Emergency Travel Document

Bring to the embassy:


Police report

Two passport-size photos (available at local photo shops, pharmacies, or printing services)

Proof of your original passport — the photo on your phone counts

Proof of your travel plans (flight booking)

Payment for the document fee (€50–80 approximately)


Processing time: typically 24–48 hours in normal circumstances. In acute situations, some embassies issue same-day documents.

Step 4 — Replace your travel insurance documentation

If your physical insurance card was also stolen, access your policy digitally (most insurers have apps). Contact the insurer and they will resend documentation by email.

Preventing passport theft

The best prevention: keep your passport at the hotel safe and carry only a photo of it and your national ID for daily use. Most EU countries accept national ID for identification within the EU — you only need the physical passport at the airport or at accommodation check-in.


Phone and wallet stolen

Theft of phone and/or wallet is the most statistically common travel emergency, especially in high-tourist areas (metro stations, outdoor markets, beach areas).

Immediate steps (within the first hour)

Block your cards immediately:


Revolut: one tap in the app (from a borrowed phone) → freeze card

Bank card: call the international fraud line (saved before departure)

PayPal, Apple Pay, Google Pay: log in and suspend from any browser


Change passwords: if your phone is taken unlocked, the thief has access to your email, banking apps, and social media. Change email password first (via another device) — this locks out everything connected to it.

File a police report: required for insurance claims and for blocking the stolen phone via IMEI (the IMEI number is on the original box if you have it, or on the SIM slot area of most phones — take a photo before travel).

Lock your phone remotely:


iPhone: iCloud.com → Find My → Mark as Lost

Android: myaccount.google.com → Find My Device → Lock


This prevents access to the phone even if the passcode is bypassed.

Practical access to money after card theft


Google Pay / Apple Pay on a borrowed phone: if you set up digital wallets before travel, you can pay using a borrowed phone logged into your account

Western Union or MoneyGram: someone at home can transfer money — you collect with ID at a local outlet

Your country's embassy: some embassies can provide emergency funds or facilitate transfers for genuinely stranded citizens


Does travel insurance cover phone theft?

Many standard travel insurance policies include a baggage/personal effects section that covers stolen items — typically with a maximum claim per item (€200–500 for phones) and a policy excess. You need the police report and evidence of ownership (receipt, or the phone's serial number). File the claim on return.


Missing your flight or connection

Missing a flight has two completely different causes with completely different remedies.

Missed because of the airline (delay, cancellation, overbooking)

The airline is responsible. Under EU Regulation 261/2004:


Re-routing to your destination on the next available flight at no cost

Meals and refreshments during the wait

Hotel accommodation if overnight stay required

Compensation of €250–600 depending on distance (for delays over 3 hours at final destination)


Do not buy a new ticket yourself — ask the airline to rebook you. Full details: EU261 flight delay and cancellation rights .

Missed because of you (overslept, traffic, misjudged time)

The airline is not responsible. Your options:


Contact the airline immediately — some will waive fees for documented emergencies (hospital certificate, police report)

Buy a new ticket — check all airlines on the route, not just the original one

Check your travel insurance — some policies cover missed departures if the cause was a covered event (accident en route to airport, medical emergency)


AirHelp can assess whether any compensation is owed if the miss was caused by a prior airline delay: check eligibility .

Missed connection on a single booking

If you miss a connection because the first flight was delayed and both flights are on the same booking, the airline rebooks you automatically and owes you care (meals, hotel if overnight) and potentially compensation. Do not buy a new ticket — go to the airline's service desk.

If you had two separate bookings: you are on your own for the second flight.


Natural disaster or civil unrest at your destination

Before the situation develops: monitoring

UK FCDO: travel.fco.gov.uk — regularly updated travel advisories per country with specific risk ratings.

US State Department: travel.state.gov — similar system, updated in real time during crises.

Romanian MAE: mae.ro → "Atenționări de călătorie" — advisories for Romanian citizens.

Subscribe to email alerts from your government's foreign affairs ministry — they send updates when the situation in a destination changes.

If you are caught in a developing emergency

Register with your embassy: many embassies have registration systems for citizens abroad — useful for being contacted and evacuated in a crisis. Some countries mandate this for high-risk destinations.

Follow official government advice: not social media rumours. In a genuine crisis, the FCDO, State Department, or equivalent is your authoritative source.

Contact your insurer: travel insurance typically covers emergency evacuation in cases of natural disaster, civil unrest, or terrorist incident — this is a separate benefit from medical evacuation. Check your policy for "catastrophe evacuation" or "political evacuation" language.

If evacuation is announced: follow official routes and timings. Do not improvise. Embassies coordinate evacuation logistics and will contact registered citizens.

If you can't return on your original flight

Airlines typically waive rebooking fees during declared disasters or government-ordered evacuations. Document everything. Your travel insurance covers additional accommodation and transport costs when your return is disrupted by a covered event.


Legal trouble abroad

Minor incidents (fine, minor dispute)

Contact your hotel for local guidance — staff in tourist hotels deal with these regularly and often speak the language. Most minor incidents (overstayed parking, minor traffic violation, noise complaint) are resolved directly with local authorities.

Arrest or detention

Contact your embassy immediately. This is the embassy's primary consular function. They cannot get you released, but they can:


Ensure you are treated according to local law and international standards

Provide a list of local lawyers

Contact your family at home

Monitor your case


Do not sign any document in a language you do not understand before consulting a lawyer. You have the right to consular access in virtually every country.

Your insurer may cover legal costs: some travel insurance policies include a legal liability or legal expenses section — check your policy for this.


Accident or injury (not medical emergency level)

If you are involved in a road accident, fall, or injury that requires documentation:


Document everything: photos of the scene, the other party's details (if applicable), witness contacts

File a police report even for minor incidents — required for insurance claims

Seek medical assessment even if you feel fine — some injuries manifest hours later, and having a medical record from the day of the incident protects your insurance claim

Contact your insurer and your travel insurance within 24–48 hours



The travel emergency kit: what to prepare before departure

On your phone (offline, in photos or notes app):


Photo of passport (front and back)

Photo of travel insurance policy document and policy number

Travel insurer's 24/7 emergency number

Your home country's embassy address and phone in each destination country

Your bank's international fraud line (each card)

Your flight booking references and airline contact numbers

Accommodation booking references and addresses


Physical backup (in a different bag from your main wallet):


One bank card (keep one card physically separate from the rest)

€100–200 cash (different from your main wallet)

Printed copy of your travel insurance with emergency number


Apps to install before departure:


Your insurer's app (policy accessible offline)

Your bank app (instant card blocking)

Revolut or Wise (instant freeze, digital payments from any device)

Google Maps with offline maps downloaded for your destination

Find My (iPhone) or Google Find My Device activated

Country / Region Police Medical General emergency

Important: 112 works in the EU from any mobile phone regardless of network, credit, or SIM. Even a phone with no SIM card can call 112.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: What is the emergency number in Europe?
R: 112 is the universal emergency number across all EU member states and most European countries — it works for police, ambulance, and fire brigade. It functions from any mobile phone, even without a SIM card or credit. Outside the EU, emergency numbers vary: Turkey 112 (also works), USA/Canada 911, UK 999 or 112, Australia 000. Save these before departure.

Î: Should I go straight to hospital or call my insurer first?
R: For life-threatening emergencies: call 112 immediately, then call your insurer. For non-life-threatening medical situations: call your insurer first. They direct you to a partner hospital where the insurer pays directly, avoiding the need for you to pay out of pocket and claim reimbursement later. Walking into a private hospital without pre-authorisation can result in the insurer refusing to reimburse — always call first when time permits.

Î: What do I do if my passport is lost or stolen abroad?
R: Step 1: File a police report immediately — you need this document for everything that follows. Step 2: Contact your country's embassy or consulate — they can issue an Emergency Travel Document (ETD) within 24–48 hours in most cases. Step 3: Contact your travel insurer if the loss was due to theft — some policies cover emergency document costs. Always keep a photo of your passport on your phone and emailed to yourself before departure.

Î: What is an Emergency Travel Document and how quickly can I get one?
R: An Emergency Travel Document (ETD) is a temporary passport issued by your country's embassy or consulate abroad, valid for a single journey home. Processing time: typically 24–48 hours with a police report and proof of identity (even a photo of your passport on your phone). Cost: approximately €50–80 depending on the issuing country. You need: police report, passport photo (can be taken at local photo shops), and proof of your original passport (your phone photo counts).

Î: Does travel insurance cover medical evacuation?
R: Yes — this is one of the most important coverage elements. Medical evacuation (transport by air ambulance with medical personnel) can cost €15,000–80,000 without insurance, depending on the destination. Travel insurance covers this in full as part of the repatriation benefit. Always confirm that 'medical repatriation' is explicitly listed in your policy — it is standard in most comprehensive policies but absent in some basic ones.

Î: What if I miss my flight due to an emergency?
R: Contact the airline immediately — many will waive rebooking fees for documented medical emergencies. Keep all medical certificates and police reports. Travel insurance covers the cost of a new flight if you miss your connection or departure due to a covered emergency. For delays caused by the airline itself (mechanical issues, crew shortages), EU261/2004 applies — see the flight delay rights guide.

Î: What numbers should I save in my phone before travelling?
R: Save: (1) Your travel insurer's 24/7 emergency line — printed on your policy and/or the company's app. (2) Your home country's embassy or consulate in your destination country — find it on your foreign ministry's website. (3) Your bank's international fraud line — on the back of each card. (4) Local emergency number of your destination (112 in EU, 911 in USA). (5) A trusted contact at home who knows your itinerary.

## Travel Insurance Guide 2026: What It Covers, What It Costs and 7 Mistakes to Avoid

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/ghid-asigurare-calatorie
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-25
Actualizat: 2026-07-25
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/ghid-asigurare-calatorie-2026

Descriere: Everything you need to know about travel insurance in 2026. What it covers, what it does not, real prices by destination, the difference from the EHIC, and the most common mistakes.

Răspuns scurt: A standard travel insurance policy for one week in Europe costs €12–25 per person (€30,000 medical cover, repatriation, baggage). For non-EU destinations (Turkey, UK, USA) prices rise to €20–70/week. The European Health Insurance Card is NOT a substitute — it covers only emergencies in public EU hospitals and does not cover repatriation, trip cancellation, or sports accidents. A single night of hospitalisation in Italy costs €500–3,000 without insurance.

A medical emergency abroad without insurance is not just stressful — it is potentially financially devastating. A single night of hospitalisation in a private Italian clinic costs €500–3,000. Repatriation from Western Europe runs €15,000–30,000. From the USA, considerably more. A week's travel insurance for Europe costs €12–25. The maths are straightforward; the only question is which policy to choose and what to check before buying.

What travel insurance covers

A standard policy combines several types of cover in one document:

Emergency medical expenses

The core of any travel insurance policy. Covers hospitalisation, surgery, medication, emergency dental treatment, and doctor's fees for unforeseen illness or injury that occurs during your trip.

The insured sum matters significantly: minimum €30,000 for Europe and Schengen (required for Schengen visa applications), minimum €50,000–100,000 for destinations outside the EU, and €100,000+ for the USA and Canada. The cost difference between €30,000 and €100,000 cover is usually €3–8 — always take the higher sum.

Medical repatriation

If you are seriously ill or injured and need to return home by medical air ambulance or accompanied by a medical team, repatriation is covered. This is the cover that most travellers underestimate — a medical flight from Spain to your home country costs €12,000–25,000. The EHIC covers none of it.

Most policies also cover the repatriation of a travelling companion if you need someone to accompany you home.

Death transport

If the worst happens, the cost of transporting remains to your home country (€5,000–15,000) is covered by the policy, sparing your family an additional financial burden.

Lost, stolen or damaged luggage

Compensation for baggage lost, stolen or damaged during your trip. Standard limits: €500–1,500. Important: high-value items (phones, laptops, cameras, jewellery) have separate sub-limits, usually €200–300 per item. If you travel with expensive electronics, check whether you need additional cover.

Trip cancellation and interruption

Reimbursement if you cancel before departure or cut your trip short due to covered reasons — typically: acute illness (documented by a doctor), death of an immediate family member, a serious accident, or a legal summons. Not all standard policies include this — it is often an add-on at €5–10 extra. If you have non-refundable bookings, this cover is worth including. Read the full guide: trip cancellation insurance — when it is worth it .

Flight delay compensation

Daily allowance (usually €30–60/day) if your outbound flight is delayed more than a specified number of hours (typically 6–12 hours). Separate from your rights under EU261/2004 — the regulation covers delays caused by the airline, while the insurance covers costs during the wait regardless of cause. For your EU261 rights: flight delay and cancellation rights .

Winter sports (add-on)

Standard policies cover ordinary activities (swimming, cycling, light hiking). Skiing, snowboarding, surfing, scuba diving, and most adventure sports require a specific winter sports or adventure sports add-on — typically €5–15 extra for the policy duration. Without it, an accident on the slopes is not covered.

What travel insurance does NOT cover

These are the exclusions that cause the most claim refusals. Read this section carefully.

Undeclared pre-existing conditions. If you have diabetes, hypertension, a heart condition, or any chronic illness and do not declare it when purchasing, any emergency related to that condition will not be covered. Insurers have access to medical databases and conduct checks when significant claims are made. Declare everything — the additional premium is small (€5–15) and the alternative is a refused claim on a €30,000 hospital bill.

Accidents under the influence of alcohol or drugs. If you fall off a scooter in Crete after three cocktails, the insurer has the legal right to refuse the claim. This is the most commonly invoked exclusion in claim disputes at tourist destinations. It does not require blood alcohol levels at the time — circumstantial evidence is often sufficient.

Extreme sports without add-on. Paragliding, bungee jumping, kite surfing, mountaineering, cliff diving — not covered by standard policies. If your trip includes these activities, verify or add the cover explicitly.

Planned medical treatment. Cosmetic surgery, elective dental procedures, or any treatment you specifically travelled abroad to receive — not covered. The policy covers unforeseen emergencies, not planned procedures.

Known events. If a hurricane has been named, a strike has been announced, or a conflict has escalated publicly before you buy the policy, costs related to those events are typically not covered. Insurance covers the unforeseen; known risks at purchase time are excluded.

Conflict zones. Travel to countries under a level 4 government travel warning (active armed conflict) is excluded by most standard policies. Specialised war risk cover exists but is significantly more expensive.

Real prices by destination

Destination 7 days 14 days Recommended cover
Europe (EU/Schengen) €12–25 €20–40 €30,000
Turkey €15–30 €25–50 €30,000
United Kingdom €15–30 €25–50 €30,000
USA / Canada €35–70 €60–120 €100,000
Asia / worldwide €25–50 €40–80 €50,000

Indicative prices for adults 18–65, individual policy, medical + baggage + repatriation. Winter sports add €5–15. Over 65s: prices increase 50–100%.

Annual multi-trip policy: €120–250/year, covers all trips within 12 months (with a cap, typically 30–45 days per trip). Worth it from 3+ trips per year — you buy once and travel covered all year.

The EHIC vs travel insurance — the key comparison

The European Health Insurance Card is free and useful, but it is not a substitute for travel insurance:

EHIC Travel insurance
Cost Free €12–70/week
Geographic scope EU/EEA/CH/UK only Worldwide
Hospitals Public only Public + private
Medical repatriation ❌ ✅
Trip cancellation ❌ ✅ (add-on)
Lost baggage ❌ ✅
Winter sports ❌ ✅ (add-on)
Emergency dentistry ✅ Public only ✅
Turkey, USA, Asia ❌ Not valid ✅

Recommended approach: get the EHIC (free, apply at your national health authority) and carry it on every trip. Buy travel insurance as well — the two are complementary, not alternatives. For a detailed comparison: EHIC vs travel insurance .

Seven common mistakes

1. "I have the EHIC, I'm covered"

The single most common and costly misconception. The EHIC covers public hospital emergencies in EU countries. It covers nothing in Turkey, the UK (partially), or anywhere outside the EU. It does not cover repatriation, private clinics, or any of the extras that make the difference in a serious situation.

2. "My credit card includes travel insurance"

Partially true in some cases. Many premium cards include travel insurance benefits — but with limitations that are easy to miss. Coverage amounts are often low (€10,000–25,000), the trip usually needs to have been paid with that specific card, and pre-existing conditions are excluded. Read the actual certificate of insurance from your bank, not the marketing summary.

3. "I'm only going for 3 days, I don't need it"

Trip duration does not affect the probability of an accident. A broken wrist from a cobblestone stumble in Prague or food poisoning in Istanbul can happen on day one. A 3-day European policy costs €5–8. The risk-reward calculation is clear.

4. "I'll buy it at the airport before the flight"

You can, but airport insurance desks charge significantly more (they are commission-based operations with captive customers). Buy online 2–3 days before departure. It takes five minutes, you receive the policy by email instantly, and it costs 20–30% less.

5. "My car insurance covers me driving to Greece"

Your car insurance (third-party liability and comprehensive if you have it) covers the vehicle. Travel insurance covers you — your health, your luggage, your ability to cancel and recover costs. They are entirely separate products covering entirely separate risks.

6. "I won't declare my pre-existing condition — they'll never find out"

They often do, particularly when the claim is significant. Insurers have access to medical records and databases and can conduct investigations when processing large claims. An undeclared hypertension history when the emergency is a cardiac event is grounds for full claim refusal. Declare everything at purchase. The additional premium is almost always a fraction of the alternative risk.

7. "I'll go straight to the hospital, then claim back"

The correct procedure is: call the insurer's 24/7 emergency line first. They will direct you to a network hospital where the insurer pays directly, pre-authorise treatment, and assign a case manager. If you walk into a private hospital without prior authorisation, you may end up paying out of pocket and face a complicated reimbursement process.

In a genuine life-threatening emergency: call 112 (or the local equivalent) first. Then call the insurer. Your life takes priority over procedure.

How to use travel insurance when something goes wrong — step by step

A real scenario: severe food poisoning in Istanbul. What do you do?

Step 1. Call the 24/7 emergency number on your policy card (save it to your phone before departure).

Step 2. The operator asks for your policy number and location, and directs you to the nearest partner hospital or approved facility.

Step 3. At the hospital, show your policy (PDF on your phone is fine). The insurer pays the hospital directly — you pay nothing.

Step 4. If you end up at a non-partner hospital and pay out of pocket: keep every receipt, invoice, and discharge summary in original form.

Step 5. On return, submit the claim online with all documentation. Reimbursement typically arrives within 14–30 days.

What to keep: medical reports, prescription receipts, taxi receipts to the hospital, hotel receipts if your stay was extended due to illness. Anything with a date and amount.

How to choose the right policy — quick checklist

Step 1: Confirm the destination. EU, non-EU, or worldwide? This determines the base price range.

Step 2: Choose the medical cover amount. Minimum €30,000 for Europe (Schengen visa requirement), minimum €50,000–100,000 for non-EU, €100,000+ for the USA. The price difference is small.

Step 3: Check your activities. Skiing, snorkelling, mountain cycling? Add the winter/adventure sports extension.

Step 4: Decide on cancellation cover. Non-refundable flights and hotels? Add trip cancellation. Flexible bookings only? It may not be necessary.

Step 5: Declare pre-existing conditions. Everything chronic — diabetes, hypertension, asthma, cardiac history. Pay the small additional premium.

Step 6: Buy 2–3 days before departure. Online. Five minutes. Policy delivered by email. Done.

For Schengen visa applicants

If you need travel insurance as part of a Schengen visa application, the requirements are specific: minimum €30,000 medical cover, valid for the entire stay, covering all Schengen countries, with repatriation explicitly included. The policy document must be in a format the embassy accepts. Full details: travel insurance for Schengen visa .

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How much does travel insurance cost?
R: Prices vary by destination and duration. Europe 7 days: €12–25. Turkey 7 days: €15–30. USA 7 days: €35–70. Worldwide 14 days: €40–80. For frequent travellers, an annual multi-trip policy (€120–250/year) is more economical from 3+ trips per year.

Î: Is the European Health Insurance Card enough?
R: No. The EHIC covers emergency medical treatment in PUBLIC hospitals in EU countries only, under the same conditions as local residents. It does not cover: medical repatriation (which can cost €10,000–50,000), trip cancellation, lost baggage, winter sports, or private hospitals. It is a useful supplement, not a complete insurance solution.

Î: What does standard travel insurance NOT cover?
R: The most common exclusions: undeclared pre-existing conditions, accidents under the influence of alcohol or drugs, extreme sports (without a specific add-on), planned medical treatment abroad, travel to conflict zones, and pandemics (with some insurers). Always read the general conditions before purchasing.

Î: Can I buy travel insurance after I have already left home?
R: Yes, but with restrictions. Most insurers apply a waiting period of 3–7 days after purchase before the policy is active. If you forgot to buy before departure, purchase immediately — but be aware you are not covered during those first days.

Î: Do I need travel insurance for Turkey?
R: Absolutely yes. Turkey is outside the EU, so the EHIC does not apply. Medical costs at Turkish private hospitals are surprisingly high (€500–2,000/night). Private travel insurance is the only protection you have.

Î: Is travel insurance compulsory?
R: Not legally for most destinations, but it is compulsory for a Schengen short-stay visa (minimum €30,000 medical cover required). For all other destinations it is optional but strongly recommended for any trip where medical costs abroad could be financially catastrophic.

Î: Does credit card travel insurance count?
R: Sometimes partially. Many premium credit cards (Gold, Platinum, Visa Infinite) include travel insurance as a benefit, but typically with lower coverage limits (€10,000–25,000), requirements to have paid the trip with that card, and exclusions for pre-existing conditions. Check your card's terms carefully — it may supplement but usually should not replace a dedicated policy.
