## Ski Travel Insurance 2026: What Is Covered, What Is Not, and How to Choose

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/ski-travel-insurance
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-30
Actualizat: 2026-07-30
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/asigurare-schi-munte

Descriere: Complete guide to ski and winter sports travel insurance in 2026. Piste rescue costs, off-piste cover, equipment insurance, trip cancellation, and the clauses that catch skiers out every season.

Răspuns scurt: Standard travel insurance does NOT cover skiing — it must explicitly state 'winter sports' or 'ski cover' to be valid on the slopes. The most important coverage: piste rescue and mountain rescue (helicopter evacuation costs €3,000–15,000 in the Alps), emergency medical treatment for ski injuries (knee ligament surgery: €15,000–40,000), and piste closure cover. Off-piste skiing requires explicit endorsement — without it, any injury off a marked run invalidates the entire medical claim. Buy ski insurance before departure; purchasing on the mountain after an injury has occurred is not possible.

Skiing sits in an unusual insurance category: the activity is extremely popular, the potential costs of something going wrong are very high, and the specific coverage required is almost universally absent from standard travel insurance. Every winter season, thousands of skiers discover this after an injury — when it is too late to purchase the right coverage.

This guide covers everything specific to ski and winter sports insurance: what the key coverage elements mean in practice, the clauses that routinely catch out experienced skiers, and how to choose a policy that actually covers the holiday you are taking.


Why standard travel insurance is not enough

A standard travel insurance policy is designed for mainstream travel risks: illness, trip cancellation, lost luggage, flight delays. Most standard policies explicitly exclude hazardous or extreme activities — and skiing almost universally falls into this category.

The typical wording in a standard policy exclusions section:

"This policy does not cover claims arising from participation in hazardous activities including but not limited to: skiing, snowboarding, off-piste skiing, ski racing, extreme sports, winter mountaineering..."

The consequence: if you are injured while skiing on a policy that does not include winter sports cover:


Your medical treatment is not covered

Your mountain rescue is not covered

Your extended accommodation due to injury is not covered

You pay everything out of pocket


The fix is simple: choose a policy that explicitly includes winter sports, or add a ski extension to your existing travel insurance. The additional premium for ski cover: typically €8–20 per person per week on top of base travel insurance — the best-value insurance purchase available.


The six key coverage elements for ski insurance

1. Piste rescue and mountain rescue

This is the most immediate cost when something goes wrong. If you fall and cannot ski down, the ski patrol brings you off the mountain — by sled (pulka), snowmobile, or helicopter depending on the severity and location.

Helicopter rescue costs:

Country Approximate cost Notes
France €2,000–8,000 Some costs offset by PGHM (mountain rescue service)
Austria €3,000–12,000 Varies by Bundesland
Switzerland €4,000–15,000 Typically highest in Europe
Italy €2,000–10,000 Varies by region
Romania (Poiana Brașov, Sinaia) €500–2,000 SMURD helicopter, lower cost

In France and Austria, the lift pass levy funds part of the rescue infrastructure — but the helicopter itself and any private medical involvement is billed to the patient. Swiss rescue is typically the most expensive.

What the insurance covers: the full cost of rescue, transport to hospital, and any medical stabilisation during transport.

2. Emergency medical treatment for ski injuries

The most frequent ski injuries by cost:

Injury Typical treatment cost Notes
ACL/knee ligament tear €8,000–25,000 Surgery + physio + follow-up
Fractured wrist €3,000–8,000 Very common in beginners
Shoulder dislocation/fracture €4,000–12,000 Common in falls
Head injury (concussion) €2,000–8,000 Imaging, monitoring
Spinal injury €20,000–100,000+ Rare but catastrophic

ACL tear is the most consequential common ski injury: it requires surgery (often unavoidable), 6–9 months of physiotherapy, and potentially multiple follow-up appointments. The total cost can exceed €25,000 in Western European private hospitals.

What to verify: does the policy cover only emergency stabilisation, or full surgical and rehabilitation costs? Some budget ski policies cover only emergency treatment — leaving the surgery and rehabilitation to be managed on return. A comprehensive policy covers the complete medical episode including follow-up surgery at home if repatriation is required.

3. Medical repatriation

If the injury is serious enough to require treatment at a specialist facility in your home country, medical repatriation is required. This means transport by air ambulance or medically equipped commercial flight, with medical personnel.

Cost: €15,000–60,000 depending on the distance and medical complexity.

A spinal injury in the Alps requiring specialist neurosurgery available only at home: the repatriation alone costs more than most people earn in a year. This is the scenario where insurance exists specifically to protect against.

4. Trip cancellation

If injury prevents you from skiing before the trip starts — a broken leg three weeks before departure, for example — trip cancellation cover reimburses the non-refundable costs: flights, lift passes, accommodation, ski hire.

Important detail: the injury must occur after you have purchased the policy. If you injure your knee before buying the insurance and subsequently cannot travel, it is a pre-existing condition and not covered.

Also covered under trip cancellation: illness of a family member requiring you to cancel, redundancy, jury service, and specific other reasons listed in the policy. Read the cancellation triggers carefully — they vary significantly between policies.

5. Ski equipment cover

Equipment theft and accidental damage to owned ski equipment:

What is typically covered:


Theft from a locked vehicle or secured ski storage

Damage in a collision accident

Loss of equipment (rare, but covered)


What is typically excluded:


Equipment left unattended on a public ski rack (common exclusion)

Normal wear and tear

Damage to hired equipment (covered separately by the hire shop's own damage waiver)


Cover limits: typically €500–1,500 for the full equipment set. High-end equipment (custom boots, race skis, performance helmets) may exceed standard limits — declare and pay for additional cover if needed.

Hired equipment: if you rent skis, boots, and poles at the resort, and they are stolen or damaged while in your care, your liability depends on the hire shop's own terms. Many hire shops offer their own damage waiver at 3–7 EUR/day — worth taking if your travel insurance does not explicitly cover hired equipment.

6. Piste closure and poor snow conditions

Piste closure insurance pays a daily benefit when the ski area reduces operation significantly due to:


Insufficient snow

High wind causing lift closures

Fog reducing visibility below operational limits

Temperature extremes


What it pays: a fixed daily amount (typically €30–50/day) for each day the area is substantially closed. It does not refund your accommodation, flights, or lift pass.

Is it worth buying?


High-altitude resorts with reliable snow (Verbier, Zermatt, Val d'Isère above 2,000m): low risk, probably not worth it

Mid-altitude resorts susceptible to snow variability (many Balkan resorts, lower Austrian/Italian resorts): worth considering

Late-season bookings (March/April): higher risk, worth it

Early-season bookings (November/December): moderate risk



On-piste vs off-piste: the most misunderstood distinction

On-piste: marked and groomed runs within the official ski area boundary, numbered and maintained by the resort. Standard ski insurance covers on-piste skiing.

Off-piste: anything outside the marked run boundary — even 5 metres from the piste edge into ungroomed snow. Including:


Powder fields adjacent to runs but not within the marked boundary

Trees runs ("tree skiing")

Ski touring (ascending and descending outside resort boundaries)

Backcountry skiing

Heliskiing


Why the distinction matters: many intermediate and advanced skiers drift off the edge of marked runs regularly — for a powder turn, to cut through trees to the next run, or simply because the run boundary is not clearly visible in poor visibility. Any injury occurring in this terrain, on a policy without off-piste endorsement, is not covered.

The off-piste endorsement: most ski policies offer this as an optional extra at €5–15 additional premium for the week. If you ski at intermediate to advanced level, add it.

Guided off-piste: some policies distinguish between unguided and guided off-piste skiing — with a qualified local mountain guide, coverage may be available on some policies without the standard off-piste endorsement. Verify specifically.


Snowboarding, ski touring, and other winter activities

Snowboarding

Covered under all ski insurance policies that reference "winter sports" — snowboarding injuries are treated identically to skiing injuries.

Ski touring (ski mountaineering)

Ascending and descending terrain using touring skis and skins, outside the resort boundary. Requires explicit cover — standard ski insurance and standard off-piste endorsements sometimes exclude touring. Look for "ski touring" or "ski mountaineering" in the policy.

Cross-country skiing (Nordic)

Lower risk, lower altitudes, lower rescue costs. Most ski policies cover Nordic skiing, but verify — some budget ski policies are designed only for downhill.

Ice skating, sledging, snowshoeing

These are lower-risk winter activities that many standard travel policies cover without a specific ski endorsement. Check your standard policy before adding ski cover.


Popular ski destinations and specific considerations

The Alps (France, Switzerland, Austria, Italy)

The world's highest-density ski infrastructure and the highest rescue costs. French and Austrian resorts have well-organised mountain rescue (PGHM in France, Bergrettung in Austria) — but the helicopter hours are billed. Swiss insurance requirements are strict and costs are high.

Best approach: comprehensive ski insurance with off-piste endorsement, minimum €500,000 medical cover, explicit mountain rescue.

Romania (Poiana Brașov, Sinaia, Predeal)

Rescue costs are lower — SMURD helicopter rescue typically €500–2,000. Medical treatment in private hospitals: much lower than Western Europe. A standard ski policy is appropriate, but do not skip insurance — the mountains are real and the risks are real. An ACL tear in Poiana Brașov still requires surgery.

For car rental to reach Romanian ski resorts: see hidden fees in car rental and Romania road trip guide .

Bulgaria (Borovets, Bansko, Pamporovo)

Bansko is the largest ski resort in the Balkans, well-developed, with a good rescue infrastructure. Medical treatment costs are lower than Western Europe. Rescue costs: moderate. Standard ski cover is appropriate.

Andorra

Zero VAT means cheap lift passes, ski hire, and equipment — but medical costs are standard European private rates if you end up at a clinic. Ski insurance is as necessary as anywhere.


How to choose: the checklist

Before purchasing ski travel insurance, verify:

Medical and rescue:


Minimum €500,000 medical cover (€1,000,000+ for Alpine destinations and USA)

Mountain/piste rescue explicitly included

Helicopter rescue explicitly included

Medical repatriation included


Activity cover:


Skiing on marked pistes confirmed as covered

Off-piste endorsement (if you ski off-piste)

Snowboarding confirmed (if applicable)

Ski school injuries covered


Financial protection:


Trip cancellation (injury before departure)

Trip interruption (injury during trip, cannot return as planned)

Piste closure benefit (optional but useful for variable-snow resorts)

Equipment cover (owned and/or hired)


Practical:


24/7 emergency assistance line (in English or your language)

Pre-authorisation process understood (call before hospital where possible)

Policy period covers travel days AND skiing days



What ski insurance costs: real pricing

For a 7-day ski holiday in the Alps, per person:

Coverage level Approximate cost
Basic (on-piste, €500k medical) €18–30
Standard (on-piste + off-piste, €1M medical) €28–45
Comprehensive (all above + cancellation + equipment) €40–70
Annual ski policy (unlimited ski trips, 1 year) €80–150

Family policies: typically 2 adults + 2 children at 15–20% less than four separate policies.

For families with children who ski, see: travel insurance for children 2026 — the accompanying parent clause is particularly relevant for skiing accidents involving children.


Before departure: the ski insurance checklist


Policy purchased before departure (not on the mountain)

Winter sports / ski cover explicitly confirmed in the policy

Off-piste endorsement added (if applicable)

Medical limit appropriate for destination

Policy document saved offline on your phone

Insurer's 24/7 emergency number saved as a contact

Policy number written separately from your phone

Understand the pre-authorisation process: call insurer before hospital if time permits

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Does standard travel insurance cover skiing?
R: Almost never. Standard travel insurance treats skiing as a hazardous activity and excludes it from medical and accident coverage unless winter sports cover is explicitly added or the policy specifically states it includes skiing. Always verify before purchase — look for 'winter sports,' 'ski cover,' or 'hazardous activities including skiing' in the policy wording.

Î: How much does mountain rescue cost in the Alps?
R: Helicopter rescue in the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps costs €3,000–15,000 depending on complexity, duration, and whether a doctor flies with the rescue team. In some Alpine countries (France, Austria), rescue costs are partially covered by the piste operator's levy (already included in your lift pass). In Switzerland, costs can be higher. Without insurance, rescue is billed to the individual — payable within 30 days in most cases.

Î: Is off-piste skiing covered?
R: Only with an explicit off-piste endorsement. Most ski insurance policies distinguish between on-piste (marked runs within the ski area boundary) and off-piste (unmarked terrain, backcountry). An injury sustained off-piste on a policy without off-piste cover invalidates the medical claim entirely. If you ski off-piste at any point, even briefly, confirm your policy explicitly covers it.

Î: What is piste closure insurance and is it worth it?
R: Piste closure insurance pays a daily cash benefit (typically €30–50/day) when the ski area closes due to insufficient snow, extreme weather, or other causes outside your control. It does NOT refund your lift pass or accommodation — it pays a fixed sum per day of closure. Worth considering for peak-season bookings in lower-altitude resorts susceptible to snow shortages.

Î: Does ski insurance cover equipment theft?
R: Only if the equipment cover is explicitly included. Most ski policies offer optional equipment cover for skis, boots, poles, and helmet up to a stated limit (typically €500–1,500). Equipment must be properly secured when not in use — left unattended on a ski rack outside a restaurant is often excluded. Hired equipment is usually covered differently from owned equipment.

Î: Can I buy ski insurance after I arrive at the resort?
R: No legitimate insurer will sell you ski insurance after you have already started skiing — the insurable risk has already materialised. Buy before departure. If you are already at the resort and realise you are not covered: stop skiing until you have purchased coverage, then purchase online for the remaining days. Some insurers exclude the first 24 hours after purchase for this reason.

Î: What happens if I am injured and cannot return on my original flight?
R: Ski insurance covers the cost of extending your accommodation and rebooking your flight if a medical situation prevents you from travelling on the original date. This requires a medical certificate from the treating doctor stating that you are not fit to travel. The insurer typically requires pre-authorisation before booking a new flight.

Î: Does ski insurance cover ski lessons?
R: Injury during ski school lessons is covered under standard ski insurance — lessons on marked runs with a qualified instructor are treated as normal on-piste skiing. The exception: any lesson conducted off-piste requires the off-piste endorsement.

## Travel Insurance for Children 2026: Complete Parent's Guide

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/travel-insurance-children
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-08-23
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/asigurare-calatorie-copii

Descriere: Everything parents need to know: real prices, pediatric emergency costs by destination, family vs individual policies, activity coverage, and common mistakes.

Răspuns scurt: Children need their own travel insurance — they're not automatically covered by a parent's policy. A child's policy costs €6-14 per week in Europe (20-30% less than adults), and family packages save an additional 15-25%. Pediatric emergencies abroad cost €500-15,000 without insurance, and medical repatriation €5,000-80,000. For Schengen visas, children also need minimum €30,000 medical coverage. The policy must explicitly include: pediatric care, repatriation, companion accommodation, and any planned activities (skiing, swimming pools).

Travelling with children is one of life's best experiences — and one that deserves careful attention to insurance. A child who falls ill or gets injured abroad generates enormous costs, pediatric emergencies are more unpredictable than for adults, and finding a paediatrician at 10pm on a Saturday on a Greek island is a nightmare no parent wants to face without a 24/7 assistance line.

This guide covers everything parents need to know: real prices, what the policy covers, pediatric medical costs by destination, common childhood travel illnesses, activity coverage, and the mistakes that can cost you thousands.


Why Children Need Separate Insurance

Children are not automatically covered by a parent's travel insurance. Every person — including babies — needs their own insurance document or must be explicitly included in a family policy. If the parent has a policy and the child doesn't, the child is uninsured.

Why Children's Insurance Costs Less

Children (0-17) pay 20-30% less than adults aged 30-45. The reasons:


Statistically fewer serious cardiovascular and orthopaedic emergencies

Fewer pre-existing conditions

Lower risk profile for dangerous activities


The exception: children aged 0-2 may carry a 5-10% surcharge compared to the 3-17 age group, due to greater immune vulnerability (fever, dehydration, allergic reactions to new foods).

Why It's Still Essential

Although children have a lower general medical risk, pediatric emergencies have specific characteristics that make insurance critical:


Unpredictability — children get seriously ill suddenly (40°C fever out of nowhere, allergic reactions, severe gastroenteritis)

Rapid dehydration — small children dehydrate much faster than adults, turning ordinary diarrhoea into a hospitalisation emergency

Need for a paediatrician — a general practitioner at a resort medical centre isn't always qualified for pediatric emergencies. Insurance with a 24/7 line directs you to hospitals with pediatric departments

Companion accommodation — if the child is hospitalised, a parent must stay with them. Who pays for the hotel, food, and rebooking the rest of the family's flights?

Germany (private) €200-500 €800-2,500 €2,400-7,500 €15,000-25,000

Real-world USA scenario: a 4-year-old with high fever and febrile seizures at Disney World. Ambulance + ER + 2-night hospitalisation (pediatric observation) + tests = $25,000-40,000 USD . Without insurance, the family pays in full.

Real-world Greece scenario: a 7-year-old with acute appendicitis on Paros island. Helicopter transfer to a pediatric hospital in Athens: ~€3,500. Surgery at the public hospital: covered by EHIC. Total without insurance: ~€3,500 for transport alone.

Common Childhood Illnesses and Accidents on Holiday

Based on CDC data and travel medicine studies, the most common pediatric travel emergencies are:

Emergency Frequency Higher risk where Typical cost (no insurance)
Gastroenteritis / diarrhoea Very common Turkey, Egypt, Southeast Asia, Latin America €100-500 (consultation + medication)
Fever (viral / infection) Common Everywhere, especially with climate change €150-400 (consultation + tests)
Severe dehydration Common in ages 0-5 Hot destinations + gastroenteritis €300-2,000 (hospitalisation + IV fluids)
Otitis (ear infection) Common (post-pool/sea) Destinations with pools/sea €80-200 (consultation + antibiotics)
Allergic reactions Moderate Destinations with new foods €200-2,000 (depending on severity)
Severe sunburn Common Greece, Spain, Turkey, Egypt €100-500 (if medical treatment needed)
Fractures / sprains Moderate Skiing, amusement parks, hiking €200-1,500 (immobilisation + X-ray)
Drowning / near-drowning Rare but serious Pools, sea €1,000-10,000 (intensive care)
Insect/jellyfish stings Common Greece, Croatia, Thailand €50-300 (if allergic reaction)

Rule of thumb: the family package is almost always cheaper. The only reason to choose individual policies: if family members have different medical conditions that require separate declaration.

Break-even: from ~1.5 trips/year, the annual family policy is cheaper than per-trip policies.

Companion Accommodation — Critical Detail

If your child is hospitalised abroad, a parent must stay with them. The costs that accumulate:


Accommodation (hotel near the hospital): €60-150/night

Meals : €30-50/day

Flight changes for the entire family: €200-500

Flight for the other parent coming from home: €150-400


Potential total for a 5-day hospitalisation: €600-1,500 just for the companion's expenses. A good policy covers these costs in full.

How to check: look for the terms "companion accommodation", "accompanying person", "relative's expenses", or "escort cover" in the policy wording. If it's not mentioned, it's not included.

Skiing and Winter Sports with Children

Skiing with children requires special attention to insurance:

Element Why it matters Check in policy
Mountain rescue on-slope Rescue toboggan: €300-1,500 ✅ "Mountain rescue" included?
Helicopter (if needed) €2,000-10,000 ✅ "Helicopter evacuation"?

Water Parks and Pools

Water parks with large slides are considered "active sport" by some insurers. If you're planning visits to such parks (Aquapark, water slides), check whether your policy covers them.

Hotel swimming pool is considered "calm rest" and is covered as standard.

Organised Excursions and Group Activities

If you book excursions through agencies (GetYourGuide, Viator, local operators), check:


Does the excursion include insurance? — some do, but with minimal coverage

What activities are planned? — a "jeep safari" or "ATV tour" qualifies as active sport

Does your policy cover those activities? — if not, either buy a rider or skip that activity



EHIC (European Health Insurance Card) for Children

Each Child Needs Their Own Card

The child's EHIC is separate from the parent's. Children are not included on an adult's card — each child must have their own card issued in their name.

How to Get the Card for Your Child

The process varies by country, but generally:


Contact your national health insurance provider

Apply for the child's card using their details (not the parent's)

Provide: child's ID or birth certificate + proof of health insurance enrolment

The card arrives by post in 7-15 working days


Cost: free. Validity: typically 2-5 years (varies by country).

What the EHIC Covers for Children (and What It Doesn't)

The same rules apply as for adults — full details in our EHIC vs travel insurance guide :

Covered ✅ Not covered ❌
Emergencies in public EU hospitals Private clinics
Public pediatric consultations Medical repatriation
Medication (with co-payment) Mountain rescue / helicopter
COVID-19 Trip cancellation / baggage
Anything outside the EU (Turkey, USA)

The formula: EHIC (free) + private travel insurance = complete protection for your child.


Ages and Specific Risks — Guide by Age Group

0-2 Years (Babies)

Main risks: dehydration (from heat or gastroenteritis), fever, reactions to new foods, ear infections (otitis after flying/pressure changes).

What matters in the policy:


Coverage from age 0 (or 2 months — EKTA)

Repatriation with companion

Pediatric emergencies (not just general medicine)

Hospitalisation + parent accommodation


Tip: babies under 6 months are more vulnerable to infections. Consult your paediatrician before travelling to tropical countries.

3-6 Years (Preschoolers)

Main risks: gastroenteritis (dirty hands, new foods), allergic reactions (new foods — seafood, nuts), severe sunburn, pool accidents.

What matters in the policy:


Coverage for "calm" activities (pool, beach)

Emergency dental (falls, broken teeth)

Trip cancellation (chickenpox, flu — common at nursery age)


7-12 Years (School Age)

Main risks: fractures and sprains (intense physical activity), insect/jellyfish stings, water park accidents, skiing accidents.

What matters in the policy:


Active sport rider (if you're skiing, horse riding, visiting water parks)

Sports equipment (skis, helmet)

Personal liability (if the child causes an accident on the slope)


13-17 Years (Teenagers)

Main risks: extreme sports (parasailing, ATV, rented scooter), road accidents (bicycle/scooter), risk-taking behaviour.

What matters in the policy:


Extreme sport rider (if the teenager wants parasailing, jet-ski, etc.)

Higher personal liability (teenagers can cause more significant damage)

Scooter/bicycle coverage (check — many policies exclude motorised vehicles)


Warning: renting scooters/ATVs to minors (under 18) is illegal in most EU countries. If a minor drives a scooter and has an accident, insurance may reject the claim.


Camps and School Trips — What to Check

Does the Camp Include Insurance?

Most organised camps include group insurance in the package price. But:


Coverage may be minimal (€10,000-20,000 cap vs €50,000-100,000 on an individual policy)

Adventure activities (skiing, horse riding, climbing) may not be included in the group policy

Repatriation may be missing or limited

Cancellation before the camp may not be covered


What to Do


Ask the organiser for a copy of the group insurance policy

Check: medical cap, covered activities, repatriation included

If insufficient: buy a supplementary individual policy for your child

Save on your child's phone: insurer's emergency number, your phone number, policy details


School Trips Abroad

Schools typically have an obligation to insure students during trips, but coverage may be minimal. Check with the trip coordinator what the group policy covers and supplement with an individual policy if needed.


Schengen Visa Requirements (Non-EU Children)

If you're applying for a Schengen visa for a non-EU child, the requirements are identical to adults:


Minimum €30,000 medical coverage

Valid for the entire duration of stay

Coverage in all Schengen countries being visited

Includes medical emergencies, hospitalisation, repatriation


Embassies check the child's documents separately from the parents'. Each child needs their own proof of insurance coverage.


10 Common Mistakes Parents Make with Travel Insurance

1. "My child is covered on my policy"

No. The child must be explicitly included on the policy or have a separate one. Check the document — if the child's name doesn't appear, they're not covered.

2. Not checking companion coverage

If the child is hospitalised, a parent must stay with them. If the policy doesn't cover companion accommodation and transport, you pay €60-150/night out of pocket.

3. Forgetting the sports rider

You go skiing and the child falls on the slope. Without a winter sports rider, the insurer rejects the claim. The rider cost: €5-15. The cost of mountain rescue without the rider: €500-1,500.

4. No cancellation cover

Children get sick suddenly — chickenpox, flu, ear infection 2 days before departure. Without cancellation cover, you lose all the flight and hotel money (€1,000-3,000 for a family holiday).

5. Missing travel consent documents

You're travelling alone with your child. At the border, an officer asks for a notarised consent letter from the other parent. You don't have one. Consequence: you may not be allowed to travel. Holiday cancelled.

6. Expired EHIC

You have the child's EHIC, but it expired 3 months ago. At the hospital in Barcelona, they won't accept it. You pay the emergency consultation out of pocket (€150-300).

7. Not saving the insurer's emergency number

It's 11pm on Crete, the child has a 40°C fever. You search for the insurer's number — can't find it. You waste precious time. Save it on your phone BEFORE departure , in contacts, and take a screenshot for your home screen.

8. Not declaring the child's allergies

Your child has a nut/seafood/bee sting allergy. You didn't declare it when buying the policy. Severe allergic reaction on holiday. The insurer may reject the claim on grounds of undeclared pre-existing condition.

9. Buying the policy at the airport

Airport counter policies are typically more expensive and with more limited coverage than online ones. And they don't include trip cancellation (logically — you're already at the airport). Buy online, 24-48 hours before departure.

10. Assuming "all-inclusive" means everything

No "all-inclusive" holiday package includes private medical insurance. Not even the most expensive resorts. Travel insurance is separate — it must be purchased separately.


Pre-Departure Checklist — The Complete Family

3-4 Weeks Before


Check each child's passport/ID card (validity!)

Apply for the child's EHIC if you don't have one or it's expired

Get a notarised travel consent letter (if travelling with only one parent)

Buy travel insurance (including sports rider if you're skiing/doing active sports)


1 Week Before


Verify the EHIC has arrived

Save on your phone: insurer's emergency number, policy (PDF/screenshot)

Make copies of EHICs (photo on phone + cloud storage)

Prepare a basic medical kit: pediatric antipyretics, oral rehydration solution, bandages, SPF 50+ sunscreen


On Departure Day


Physical EHIC for each family member — in your wallet

Notarised consent letter (original) — easily accessible (not in checked luggage)

Insurer's emergency number — in your contacts



The Bottom Line: Protection Formula for Families

The real cost: travel insurance for a family of 4 (2A + 2C), 7 days in Europe, costs €28-48 — the equivalent of two pizzas at a restaurant. Without it, a single pediatric emergency can cost €500-25,000 .

The correct formula:


EHIC for each family member (free, 5 minutes online per person)

Private family travel insurance (€28-48/week for 4 people)

Sports rider if you're doing active sports (+ €5-15 per person)

Notarised consent letter if only one parent is travelling with the children


Total complete protection: under €50 per family per week + free EHIC. That's the cheapest peace of mind you can buy for a holiday with children.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Does a child under 2 need travel insurance?
R: Yes. There's no minimum age for travel insurance — babies can have medical emergencies on holiday (fever, dehydration, allergic reactions). EKTA covers from age 0 (2 months). Children aged 0-2 may have a 5-10% premium surcharge due to higher medical vulnerability, but the policy remains very affordable (under €10/week).

Î: Does the EHIC cover children too?
R: Yes, each child can have their own European Health Insurance Card (EHIC), free of charge. But like adults, the EHIC only covers emergencies in PUBLIC hospitals within the EU and does NOT cover repatriation, private clinics, or adventure activities. The child's card is separate from the parent's — children are not automatically included on an adult's card.

Î: How much does travel insurance cost for a child?
R: €6-14 for 7 days in Europe (Schengen). €12-28 for 8-15 days. Children pay 20-30% less than adults. Family packages (2 adults + 2 children) offer an additional 15-25% discount vs individual policies. With EKTA, the price starts at $0.99/day/person (Start plan), regardless of age.

Î: What documents does a child need when travelling with one parent?
R: Requirements vary by country, but many destinations require a notarised consent letter from the absent parent, specifying the destination and travel dates. Some airlines also require this. Check the requirements for your destination well in advance — especially for non-EU travel.

Î: Does summer camp or school trip insurance cover my child?
R: Check with the organiser. Many camps and school trips include group insurance, but coverage may be limited (lower medical caps, no adventure sports rider). If the camp includes skiing, horse riding, or water sports, verify explicitly that the group policy covers those activities. If not, buy a supplementary individual policy.

Î: What happens if my child gets sick and we have to cancel the holiday?
R: A policy with trip cancellation coverage reimburses prepaid costs (flights, hotels, excursions) if your child falls ill before departure and a doctor certifies they can't travel. Children get sick more frequently than adults — cancellation cover is more important for families than any other traveller type.

Î: Does insurance cover activities like swimming pools, water parks, or skiing?
R: It depends on the policy. Swimming pools and beaches are considered 'calm' activities and are covered as standard. Water parks with slides, skiing, horse riding, and water sports may require an 'active sport' or 'winter sport' rider. Check the policy BEFORE departure — a skiing accident without a winter sports rider means a rejected claim.

Î: Can a child under 14 be insured separately from their parents?
R: Yes — a child can have their own travel insurance policy regardless of age. The insurer doesn't require parents to be insured with the same provider. But family packages are usually cheaper than separate policies. With EKTA, you add the child as an 'additional traveller' on the same policy.

## Travel Insurance 2026: complete guide — what it covers, real costs, how to choose & file a claim

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/travel-insurance-europe-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-06
Actualizat: 2026-08-23
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/ghid-asigurare-calatorie

Descriere: Complete travel insurance guide 2026: real prices by provider, what's covered and what's NOT, EHIC vs private insurance, how to file a claim, exclusions and the mistakes that cost thousands.

Răspuns scurt: Travel insurance covers medical emergencies, repatriation, trip cancellation, and lost luggage. A basic 7-day policy for Europe costs €9-14 from Romanian providers (Groupama, Allianz, Omniasig) or from $0.99/day with EKTA. The EHIC (European Health Insurance Card) is free but does NOT cover repatriation, private clinics, or mountain rescue — the difference can be €15,000-30,000. For a Schengen visa, a minimum €30,000 medical coverage is mandatory. 33% of claims are denied — the most common reasons: missing documents, undeclared pre-existing conditions, and uncovered risky activities.

A medical emergency on vacation is the kind of thing that doesn't happen — until it does. And then you discover that a single night of hospitalization in Italy costs €500-3,000, that a helicopter rescue in the Alps costs €3,500+, that medical repatriation to your home country costs €15,000-30,000, and that a travel insurance policy costing €9-14 per week was the only thing standing between you and a devastating bill.

This guide explains everything you need to know — from what each type of policy actually covers, to real costs from European and international providers, to how to file a claim without getting denied, and the mistakes 90% of travelers make.

Why you need travel insurance — the numbers that matter

Many travelers consider travel insurance an optional expense. That's the most expensive illusion you can have. Here's what medical emergencies abroad cost WITHOUT insurance:

Real medical costs, without insurance

Situation Where Cost WITHOUT insurance
One night hospitalization Germany, Italy €500-3,000
Emergency room visit Spain €150-300
Emergency room visit USA $400-2,000
ICU 1 day USA $5,000-15,000
Child hospitalization 2 nights USA $30,000-50,000
Ski helicopter rescue Austria, Switzerland €3,500-18,000
Air ambulance (medical plane) Western Europe → home €15,000-30,000
Emergency surgery France €5,000-25,000
Emergency surgery USA $25,000-100,000+
International medical transport Anywhere → home €10,000-50,000
Emergency dental treatment UK £100-500

The comparison that matters: insurance for 7 days in Europe costs €9-14. A single night of hospitalization in Germany costs €500-3,000. That's 50-300x the price of insurance. It's like refusing to pay €1 for a lottery ticket that guarantees a payout if you have bad luck.

Real scenarios that happen

Scenario 1: Ski accident in Austria. Fall on the slope, broken tibia. Mountain rescue + helicopter transport: ~€3,500. Hospitalization 3 days + surgery: ~€8,000. Repatriation by ambulance: ~€5,000. Total: ~€16,500. With insurance: €0 (the insurer covers everything). Without insurance: you pay the full amount out of pocket.

Scenario 2: Food poisoning in Turkey. Hospitalization 2 nights, IV rehydration, lab tests. At a private clinic: ~€400-800. The EHIC doesn't work (Turkey is not in the EU). Without insurance, you pay everything.

Scenario 3: Acute appendicitis in the USA. Emergency surgery + 3 days hospitalization: $30,000-80,000. Without insurance, it's a life-changing bill. With a €15-20 per week policy, complete coverage.

Scenario 4: Flight cancellation for medical reasons. You test positive 2 days before departure. Flight, hotel, excursions — all lost. With insurance including a cancellation clause: 80-100% reimbursement.

What travel insurance covers — in detail

Standard coverage (present in most policies)

1. Emergency medical expenses


Doctor consultations, ER visits, hospitalization

Emergency surgical procedures

Prescribed medications

Emergency dental treatment (usually with a separate, lower cap — €200-500)

Typical cap: €30,000-500,000 (depends on plan)


2. Medical repatriation


Air ambulance transport to your home country if your medical condition requires it

The most expensive covered risk — without insurance it costs €15,000-30,000 from Western Europe, €30,000-80,000 from the USA

Usually included without a sub-limit (fully covered up to the policy cap)


3. Repatriation in case of death


Transport of mortal remains to the country of origin

Real cost: €3,000-10,000

Included in most policies


4. 24/7 assistance


Emergency phone line

Coordination with local hospitals

Sending medication or equipment if not available locally

Administrative support (contacting embassy, family)


Additional coverage (depends on plan)

5. Trip cancellation


Reimbursement of pre-paid costs (flights, hotels, excursions) if you cancel for covered reasons: illness, accident, death in the family, court summons

Usually 80-100% of costs, up to a cap (€1,000-5,000)

CFAR (Cancel For Any Reason): the most flexible option — cancel for any reason, get 50-75% back. Costs 40-60% more than the standard policy.


6. Trip delay


Covers accommodation and meals if your flight is delayed over 4-12 hours

Usually €100-300 per incident

Check: some policies kick in after 4 hours, others after 12 — huge difference


7. Lost or delayed baggage


Permanent loss: reimbursement up to a cap (€500-2,000)

Delay: covers first-necessity items purchased (€100-300)

Important: keep proof of value (receipts, photos)


8. Third-party liability


If you accidentally cause damage to other people or their property

Usually €50,000-500,000

Example: you accidentally hit someone with a rented bicycle — insurance covers the damages


9. Legal assistance


Coverage for legal costs abroad

Usually €3,000-10,000

Useful if you have a car accident or a legal dispute


10. Sports and activities


"Standard" sports (on-piste skiing, snorkeling, cycling) are usually covered

"Extreme" sports (parasailing, scuba >18m, bungee, mountaineering) require an additional rider

Professional sports are never covered


What insurance does NOT cover — critical exclusions

This is where people lose money. 33% of travel insurance claims are denied. The main exclusions:

Exclusion Why it matters What to do
Pre-existing medical conditions Diabetes, hypertension, asthma — if not declared, any related claim is denied Declare EVERYTHING at purchase, request a waiver
Extreme sports without rider Parasailing, scuba >18m, kite, technical climbing Buy a sports rider for your policy
Activities under the influence of alcohol Accident after a night of drinking = claim denied If you've been drinking, any medical incident becomes an exclusion
Planned/elective treatments Scheduled surgery, cosmetic procedures, routine dental Insurance is for EMERGENCIES, not treatments
Pregnancy (routine) Prenatal consultations are not covered Unexpected complications may be covered (check the policy)
Events already known Named storm before purchase, announced strike Buy insurance BEFORE the risk appears
Conflict/war zones Travel to areas with travel warnings Check the geographic exclusion list
Illegal activities Driving without a license, drugs Obvious, but worth mentioning
Undocumented losses Theft without a police report, luggage without proof Document EVERYTHING (see claim section)

The golden rule: read the exclusions BEFORE buying the policy. Not AFTER you need it.

Single trip vs. annual multi-trip — which is worth it

Single trip policy (per journey)

Best for: if you travel 1-2 times a year.


Coverage only for the duration of one trip

Buy separately for each trip

You can choose different coverage per destination (less for Europe, more for the USA)

Price: €9-80 per trip (depends on destination and duration)


Annual multi-trip policy

Best for: if you travel 2+ times a year.


Unlimited coverage for all trips within the policy year

Per-trip limit: usually 25-45 days (check — if you take a 2-month trip, it won't be fully covered)

Price: €60-250/year (depends on zone and age)


The break-even calculation

Example Single trip (×2) Annual Savings
Allianz, Europe, 30 years old €18 (2×9) ~€23 Annual costs slightly more but covers unlimited trips
Omniasig, Europe, 40 years old ~€24 (2×12) ~€100 Depends on frequency
EKTA Gold, Europe, 7 days ×3 ~$37 (3×12.25) ~$100-150 Annual pays off from 3+ trips

The takeaway: if you take 3+ trips per year, the annual policy is almost always cheaper. For 1-2 trips, calculate per situation. The annual policy also has a psychological benefit: you never have to think about insurance before each trip.

EHIC (European Health Insurance Card) — what it REALLY covers

What is the EHIC

The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is a free document issued by your country's national health service. It gives you the right to medically necessary healthcare during a temporary stay in the EU, EEA (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway), Switzerland, and the UK — under the same conditions as local residents.

How to get your EHIC


Apply online through your national health insurance portal (or in person at your local health insurance office)

Free of charge

Validity: usually 2-5 years (varies by country)

You must be enrolled in your country's public health insurance system

Apply at least 2 weeks before departure


What the EHIC covers — and what it does NOT

Covered by EHIC NOT covered by EHIC
Emergencies at public hospitals in EU/EEA Private clinics and doctors
Medically necessary consultations in the public system Medical repatriation (€15,000-30,000)
Treatment as locals (including local co-pays) Repatriation in case of death
Prescribed medications in the public system Mountain rescue / helicopter (€3,500+)
Planned/elective treatments
Trip cancellation, lost luggage
Third-party liability
ANYTHING outside EU/EEA (Turkey, USA, Asia, Egypt)

Co-pays you still pay EVEN with the EHIC

"Same as locals" does not mean "free." Each country has its own co-payment system:

Country What you pay with EHIC
Germany ~€10/day hospitalization (standard co-pay)
Italy €50-60 for minor emergencies (White/Green code — "ticket di pronto soccorso")
France 20% of hospital costs (ticket modérateur)
Spain €0 for public emergencies (the system is free for emergencies)
Austria Small co-pays on prescriptions
Greece 0-15% co-pay on prescriptions

Where the EHIC does NOT work

The EHIC does not work in: Turkey, USA, Canada, Mexico, Egypt, Tunisia, Morocco, Thailand, Japan, Australia, and any other country outside the EU/EEA/Switzerland/UK. For these destinations, private travel insurance is your ONLY protection.

The correct strategy: EHIC + private insurance

It's not "either-or" — it's "both." They complement each other:


EHIC (free) → covers emergencies at public hospitals in the EU, without complicated administrative procedures

Private insurance (€9-20/week) → covers everything EHIC doesn't: repatriation, private clinics, mountain rescue, cancellation, luggage, and works ANYWHERE in the world


With both, you're fully covered. With only EHIC, you're partially covered. Without either, you're on your own.

How to choose the right insurance — complete checklist

Step 1: Determine your destination and protection type

Destination Minimum you need
Europe (EU) — city break, beach EHIC + basic policy (€30,000 medical)
Europe — skiing, mountains, sports EHIC + policy with sports rider + mountain rescue coverage
UK Standard policy (EHIC works, but with post-Brexit limitations)
Turkey, Egypt, Tunisia Standard/premium policy (no EHIC, private clinics common)
USA, Canada Premium policy with minimum €250,000 coverage (medical costs are astronomical)
Asia, Latin America Standard/premium policy (local costs are low, but repatriation is expensive)
Worldwide Worldwide policy (coverage anywhere)

Step 2: Check the medical coverage

Absolute minimum: €30,000 (required for Schengen visa and sufficient for minor emergencies in the EU).

Recommended for Europe: €50,000-100,000 (covers more serious situations, surgeries, extended hospitalization).

Essential for USA/Canada: €250,000-500,000 (an emergency surgery in the USA costs $25,000-100,000+).

Step 3: Check repatriation coverage

Medical repatriation is THE MOST IMPORTANT element of travel insurance. It's what costs the most without insurance (€15,000-80,000) and what the EHIC never covers.

Check:


Does it include medical repatriation? (must be YES)

Does it include repatriation in case of death? (must be YES)

Is there a sub-limit? (ideally no sub-limit = full coverage)


Step 4: Check exclusions for planned activities

If you're planning:


Skiing/snowboarding: requires winter sports rider + mountain rescue/helicopter coverage

Scuba diving: usually covered up to 18m without a rider; >18m requires a rider

Mountain biking, climbing, parasailing: usually requires an extreme sports rider

Walking, snorkeling, city cycling: usually covered as standard


Step 5: Check cancellation clauses

If you've invested significant amounts in your trip (flights, hotels, excursions):


Standard cancellation: covers cancellation for medical reasons, death in the family, court summons

CFAR (Cancel For Any Reason): covers any reason, including "I changed my mind" — costs 40-60% extra, 50-75% reimbursement

No cancellation coverage: if you cancel, you lose everything you paid


Step 6: Check the deductible

The deductible is the amount you pay before the insurance kicks in. Example: €100 deductible, €500 medical bill → you pay €100, insurance pays €400.


€0 deductible: ideal, but the policy costs more

Percentage deductible (25%): cheap plans have a 25% deductible — on a €10,000 bill, you pay €2,500 out of pocket. NOT ideal.

Fixed deductible (€50-150): acceptable compromise


Tip: EKTA's Start plan has a 25% deductible — the Gold plan (0% deductible) is worth the price difference.

Quick final checklist


Sufficient medical coverage (minimum €30,000, ideally €50,000-100,000)

Medical repatriation included, no sub-limit

0% or small fixed deductible

Planned activities are covered (skiing, sports, scuba)

Cancellation included if your investment is significant

Correct geographic zone (EU vs worldwide)

Baggage and delays included

24/7 emergency line

Duration covers ALL days of the trip


Special types of insurance

Ski and winter sports insurance

Skiing is one of the highest-risk vacation activities for injuries. Without special insurance:


On-slope injury + mountain rescue: €1,000-5,000

Helicopter rescue (Austria/Switzerland): €3,500-18,000

Hospitalization + knee surgery: €5,000-20,000


What your ski policy must include:


On-piste accident coverage

Off-piste coverage (if you plan to — some policies exclude off-piste)

Mountain rescue / search and rescue / helicopter

Lost/stolen ski equipment (usually €500-1,500)

On-slope third-party liability (if you hit someone)


Additional cost: a sports rider typically adds 20-50% to the base policy price.

Insurance during pregnancy

Routine pregnancy (prenatal consultations, routine ultrasounds) is NOT covered by travel insurance. However:


Unexpected complications (premature birth, spontaneous miscarriage) CAN be covered, depending on the policy

Week limit: most policies cover complications up to 24-28 weeks of pregnancy (EKTA covers up to 27 weeks)

Check explicitly: "complications of pregnancy" must be mentioned in the policy


Tip for pregnant travelers: if traveling at >20 weeks, verify that the policy covers pregnancy complications, that you have a letter from your doctor confirming you can travel, and that your destination has access to a maternity ward.

Insurance for pre-existing conditions

Pre-existing conditions (diabetes, hypertension, asthma, cancer in remission, heart problems) are the most common cause of denied claims.

How it works:


When purchasing the policy, declare all existing medical conditions

The insurer evaluates them and either accepts them (with or without an additional premium), or explicitly excludes them

If you do NOT declare and have an incident related to a pre-existing condition, the claim is automatically denied


Pre-existing conditions waiver: some insurers offer a waiver if you purchase the policy within 10-21 days of your first trip payment. EKTA and other international providers have explicit options for pre-existing conditions.

Tip: declare EVERYTHING, even if you think it's not relevant. It's better to pay a slightly higher premium than to have a €20,000 claim denied.

Insurance for travelers over 65


Premiums increase significantly with age (2-3x compared to 30-year-olds)

Some insurers don't cover people over 75-80

Pre-existing conditions are more common, making declaration even more important

EKTA insurance: covers up to advanced ages, check the conditions


Insurance for long trips (backpacking, digital nomads)

If you're traveling for more than 30-45 days:


Single trip policies usually cover a maximum of 90-180 days

Annual policies have a per-trip limit of 25-45 days — not suitable!

Solution: long-stay policy or dedicated travel medical insurance (EKTA, SafetyWing, World Nomads)

Approximate cost: €30-80/month for €100,000-250,000 coverage


Insurance for families

Family packages (2 adults + 2-3 children) are usually 15-20% cheaper than separate individual policies.

What to check additionally:


Are children under 2 included? (usually yes, free or very cheap)

Age limit for children (16, 18, or 21 depends on the insurer)

Accompanying person coverage (if a child is hospitalized, one adult stays with them — who pays for the adult's accommodation?)

Cancellation for child illness (children get sick more often)


Also read: Travel insurance for children — complete guide

How to file a claim — step by step (without getting denied)

33% of travel insurance claims are denied. The main reason: lack of documentation. Here's how to avoid that:

Before an incident: preparation


Save the insurer's emergency number in your phone, in Notes, and on paper. Not just in contacts — if your phone is lost, you need the number.

Save a copy of the policy in email, cloud (Google Drive, iCloud), and printed.

Photograph important documents: passport, insurance card, flight tickets, hotel confirmations. You want these accessible even if your phone disappears.


During an incident: what to do

Step 1: Call the insurer IMMEDIATELY


The 24/7 emergency line, BEFORE going to the doctor if possible

The insurer can direct you to a partner hospital/clinic (direct payment between insurer and hospital, no advance from your pocket)

If it's an absolute emergency, go to the nearest hospital — call the insurer after


Step 2: Document EVERYTHING


Keep ALL original invoices (hospital, medications, taxi, extra hotel)

Request the detailed medical report (diagnosis, treatment, prescriptions)

Photograph everything (invoices, prescriptions, reports, ER wristbands)

For theft: file a police report (MANDATORY — without a police report, the theft claim is automatically denied)

For lost luggage: PIR report from the airline + proof of contents


Step 3: Don't throw anything away


No invoice, no prescription, no receipt

Even the taxi receipt from the airport to the hospital is reimbursable


After an incident: filing the claim


Complete the claim form on the insurer's website (deadline: usually 30-90 days from the incident)

Attach documents: original invoices (or quality scans), medical report, police report (if theft), proof of payment

Translations: some insurers require certified translations of medical documents

Payment: usually within 14-30 business days after claim acceptance


Most common reasons for denial

Reason % of denials How to avoid
Missing documentation ~35% Keep EVERYTHING, photograph, file police report
Undeclared pre-existing condition ~25% Declare ALL conditions at purchase
Uncovered activity (extreme sport) ~15% Check exclusions, buy sports rider
Incident under influence of alcohol ~10% Obvious — but many underestimate
Policy expired/wasn't active ~8% Check dates precisely — include transit days
Late claim filing ~7% File within the deadline (30-90 days)

Insurance by destination — what you need to know

Europe (EU/EEA)


EHIC works — emergencies at public hospitals are covered

Private insurance complements EHIC: repatriation, private clinics, mountain rescue

Basic policy (€30,000) is sufficient for city breaks

For skiing/mountains: sports rider + mountain rescue mandatory

Turkey


EHIC does NOT work — Turkey is not an EU member

Private insurance is your ONLY protection

Private clinics dominate (especially in resorts) — without insurance, you pay full price

Emergency consultation at a private clinic: €50-200

Private clinic hospitalization: €200-800/day

USA and Canada


The most expensive destination in the world for medical emergencies

One ICU night: $5,000-15,000

Emergency surgery: $25,000-100,000+

Ambulance: $1,000-3,000 (yes, you pay for the ambulance)

Minimum recommended insurance: €250,000-500,000

Schengen visa — insurance requirements

If you're a non-EU citizen and need a Schengen visa (short-stay), travel insurance is mandatory . Requirements (EU Regulation 810/2009):


Minimum medical coverage: €30,000

Validity: entire duration of stay + a few extra days (buffer)

Geographic coverage: all Schengen countries visited

Must include: medical emergencies, hospitalization, medical repatriation, repatriation in case of death

No deductible at some embassies (check specific requirements)


Schengen-approved policy from EKTA — accepted by all Schengen embassies, issued instantly online.

Embassies verify each policy individually — a policy that doesn't meet the requirements leads to a visa refusal.

10 common mistakes (and how to avoid them)



Traveling without insurance because you have an EHIC. The EHIC doesn't cover repatriation, private clinics, and doesn't work outside the EU. A few euros per day covers you completely.


Not declaring pre-existing conditions. Any claim related to an undeclared condition is automatically denied. Declare EVERYTHING.


Not reading the exclusions. You buy a policy, go parasailing, get injured — and discover that extreme sports aren't covered. Read BEFORE.


Not calling the insurer before going to the doctor. If you call first, the insurer can send you to a partner hospital (no advance payment). If you go directly, you pay out of pocket and file a claim later (more complicated, slower).


Not keeping original invoices. Without invoices, the claim is denied. Photograph EVERYTHING, keep EVERYTHING.


Buying the CHEAPEST policy without checking the deductible. A 25% deductible on a €10,000 bill = you pay €2,500 out of pocket. The price difference for a 0% deductible is a few euros per day.


Not filing a police report for theft. Without a report, the theft/loss claim is automatically denied. For airport baggage theft: PIR report from the airline + police report.


Buying insurance AFTER booking everything. Some cancellation policies have a deadline — they must be purchased within 10-21 days of the first trip payment. Buy early.


Assuming your policy covers scooter/motorcycle. Most policies do NOT cover scooter accidents if you don't have a valid motorcycle license. In Southeast Asia, this is a very common trap.


Ignoring transit days. Your policy must cover ALL days, including transit days. If your flight is on the 15th and the policy starts on the 16th, the flight day is not covered.


How to buy — step by step

Option 1: Direct from the insurer (online)


Go to the insurer's website (EKTA, Allianz, Omniasig, Groupama)

Enter: destination, dates, number of people, age

Choose the plan (basic/standard/premium)

Pay online (card, transfer)

Receive the policy via email, instantly


Buy from EKTA — from $0.99/day

Option 2: Online comparison site


Go to an insurance comparison site

Enter your details

Compare offers from multiple insurers

Choose and buy directly


Option 3: Insurance agent / broker


Visit a local agent or call

Explain where you're going and what you're doing

The agent recommends the right policy

Useful if you have pre-existing conditions or special needs


What to have with you during your trip


Printed policy (some hospitals/clinics require the physical policy, not on your phone)

Digital copy (in email + cloud)

Insurer's emergency number (in your phone, in notes, on paper)

EHIC (if going to EU/EEA)

Passport / ID (the document associated with the policy)


Travel insurance vs. bank card insurance

Many premium cards (Revolut Metal, N26 Metal, Visa Gold/Platinum cards) include some form of travel insurance. But be careful:

Aspect Dedicated travel insurance Premium card insurance
Medical coverage €30,000-500,000 Usually €10,000-50,000
Repatriation Yes, usually without sub-limit Sometimes included, sometimes not
Trip cancellation Optional, €1,000-5,000 Usually €1,000-2,500
Luggage €500-2,000 €500-1,000
Sports With additional rider Usually only "standard" sports
Conditions Dedicated policy, clear documentation Automatic activation if you paid for the trip with the card
Claims Direct with insurer, clear deadline Through the bank, may be slower

The bottom line: card insurance is a nice-to-have bonus, but rarely replaces a dedicated policy. Check what your card actually covers BEFORE relying on it.

Questions people Google (and direct answers)

Can I buy insurance AFTER I've departed?
Yes, from some providers (EKTA allows purchase in the first days of travel). But it's more expensive and you may have a waiting period (24-72h during which the policy isn't active). Ideal: buy BEFORE.

Does insurance cover COVID?
Yes, with most providers in 2026 (EKTA explicitly covers COVID — treatment + isolation up to 15 days). Check the specific policy.

Does insurance cover incidents if I've been drinking?
No. Incidents under the influence of alcohol are excluded by virtually all insurers. If the medical report mentions alcohol, the claim is denied.

What happens if the hospital requires an advance payment?
Call the insurer — they can usually arrange direct payment with the hospital (guarantee of payment). If you pay out of pocket, keep the invoices and file a claim afterward.

Does insurance cover a companion?
Some premium policies cover the accommodation and transport of a companion if you're hospitalized (e.g., a parent staying with a child). Check explicitly for "accommodation of accompanying person."

Can I file a claim WITHOUT original invoices?
Very difficult. Most insurers require originals or certified copies. Quality scans/photos are accepted by some. Rule: keep EVERYTHING.

Does insurance work if I travel to a country with a travel warning?
It depends. Many policies exclude areas with a level 4 warning (Do Not Travel). Check the exclusion list and your country's travel advisories before departure.

What it costs WITHOUT insurance — real stories

European skier in Austria, ski accident (2024): Femur fracture on the slope in St. Anton. Rescue helicopter: €4,200. Surgery + 5 days hospitalization: €12,000. Medical transport home: €6,500. Total: €22,700. Had EHIC but NOT private insurance — EHIC didn't cover the helicopter (private) or repatriation. Paid out of pocket.

Family in Turkey (2025): 4-year-old child with food poisoning in Antalya. Hospitalization 3 nights at a private clinic + IV treatment. Total: €2,100. EHIC doesn't work in Turkey. Without insurance, they paid everything.

Couple in the USA (2024): Acute appendicitis in New York. Laparoscopic surgery + 2 nights hospitalization. Bill: $47,000. They had EKTA Max+ insurance ($500,000 coverage, 0% deductible). They paid $0.

The difference between these 3 scenarios: €9-14 for a week of insurance. That's all that stands between you and a life-changing bill.

When you DON'T need travel insurance

Let's be fair — there are situations where insurance is less critical:


Domestic travel (within your own country): you have national health coverage, ambulance is free, hospitalization is free

Short city break (2-3 days) in an EU country with EHIC: the financial risk is limited if you're not doing sports

You already have verified premium card insurance: if the coverage is sufficient and includes repatriation


But even in these cases, the price of a basic policy (€3-5/day) is so small that it's hard to justify not having one. It's the peace of mind you buy for the price of a coffee.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is travel insurance mandatory?
R: Not legally mandatory for most EU destinations if you're an EU citizen. However, for a Schengen visa (non-EU citizens), a medical policy with a minimum €30,000 coverage is required. Even when not mandatory, going without means risking bills of thousands of euros — a single night of hospitalization in Germany costs €500-3,000, and medical repatriation €15,000-30,000.

Î: How much does travel insurance cost for 7 days in Europe?
R: €9-14 from Romanian insurers (Groupama €9, Allianz €9, Omniasig €9, Generali €11, Asirom €14) for €30,000-50,000 coverage. Alternatively, EKTA offers plans from $0.99/day (Start) to $5.90/day (Max+). An annual multi-trip policy costs about €23/year from Allianz or €60-170/year from Omniasig.

Î: What does travel insurance NOT cover?
R: The most common exclusions: pre-existing medical conditions (unless declared and accepted), extreme sports without an additional rider, incidents under the influence of alcohol/drugs, planned/elective treatments, pregnancy (routine — unexpected complications may be covered), conflict zones/war, and events already known before purchase (named storm, announced strike).

Î: Does the EHIC (European Health Insurance Card) replace travel insurance?
R: No. The EHIC only covers emergencies at PUBLIC hospitals in the EU/EEA, under the same conditions as locals (including local co-pays). It does NOT cover: medical repatriation (€15,000-30,000), private clinics, mountain rescue/helicopter (€3,500+), trip cancellation, or lost luggage. And it doesn't work AT ALL outside the EU (Turkey, USA, Asia). The right strategy: EHIC (free) + private insurance = complete protection.

Î: How do I file a travel insurance claim?
R: 1) Call the insurer's 24/7 emergency line BEFORE going to the doctor (if possible). 2) Keep ALL documents: original invoices, prescriptions, medical reports, cancelled flight tickets, receipts. 3) Take photos of everything. 4) Complete the claim form within the deadline (usually 30-90 days from the incident). 5) Submit original or scanned documents, with translation if required. 33% of claims are denied — the main reason is missing documentation.

Î: Is annual multi-trip insurance worth it?
R: If you take 2+ trips per year, yes. Allianz MultiTravel: ~€23/year (vs ~€9 per trip = €18 for 2 trips). Omniasig annual: €60-170/year. EKTA annual: proportionally cheaper. The break-even is usually at 1.5-2 trips per year. Note: annual policies usually have a per-trip limit of 25-45 days.
