## Travel Insurance 2026: Complete Guide — What It Covers, Real Costs & 7 Mistakes to Avoid

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/travel-insurance-guide-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-31
Actualizat: 2026-07-31
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/ghid-asigurare-calatorie-2026

Descriere: Travel insurance 2026 complete guide. What it covers, what it excludes, how to choose the right policy, and when the European Health Card is not enough.

Răspuns scurt: A standard travel insurance policy for one week in Europe costs €12–25 per person (€30,000 medical cover, repatriation, baggage). For non-EU destinations (Turkey, UK, USA) prices rise to €20–50/week. The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is NOT sufficient — it only covers emergencies in public hospitals, not repatriation, trip cancellation, or sports injuries. A single night of hospitalisation in Germany or Italy can cost €500–3,000 without insurance.

Most people buy travel insurance in 3 minutes as an afterthought at checkout, or skip it entirely because "nothing's going to happen." Then something does happen — a fracture on Rome's cobblestones, a stomach bug in Turkey, a flight cancelled 12 hours before departure — and the reality of uninsured costs becomes very clear, very fast.

This guide covers everything you actually need to know: what travel insurance covers (and the exclusions that cause most claim denials), how much it costs per destination in 2026, how it compares to the European Health Insurance Card, and the 7 mistakes that cost travellers thousands of euros every year.

What Is Travel Insurance and Why Does It Matter in 2026?

Travel insurance is a short-term policy that protects you financially against unexpected events during — and in some cases before — a trip abroad. Unlike car insurance or home insurance (which are often legally required), travel insurance is typically optional, which is why so many people skip it.

The risk calculation has changed in 2026. Post-pandemic travel patterns, more extreme weather disruptions, increased flight cancellations, and rising medical costs across Europe and beyond mean the expected cost of being uninsured is higher than it was five years ago.

What a good travel insurance policy covers:


Medical emergencies abroad — the core, and the most expensive risk

Emergency medical repatriation — flying you home when you can't travel commercially

Trip cancellation — recovering non-refundable costs if you can't depart

Trip interruption — returning home early due to an emergency

Lost, stolen, or damaged baggage — replacement costs

Flight delay — additional expenses caused by significant delays

Personal liability — if you accidentally injure someone or damage property


What varies by policy (read before you buy):


Pre-existing medical conditions (requires declaration and may cost more)

Winter sports and extreme activities

Electronics and high-value items (often sublimits)

Travel to countries with government-issued "do not travel" warnings


What's Actually Covered — Section by Section

Medical Emergencies

The core of any travel policy. Covers hospital treatment, surgery, medications, doctor visits, and in some cases dental emergency treatment, when you need urgent care abroad.

Minimum cover you should accept:


€30,000 for travel within the EU/Schengen area (Schengen visa requirement)

€50,000–100,000 for Turkey, UK, or non-EU European countries

€100,000+ for the USA, Canada, or Australia (American medical bills are astronomical — a single ER visit with tests regularly exceeds $10,000)


Real-world cost examples:


Broken leg in Germany: surgery + 3-night hospital stay = €8,000–15,000

Appendix removed in Italy: €5,000–12,000

Heart attack in Turkey, private hospital: €10,000–30,000

ICU admission in the USA: €5,000–15,000 per day


Without insurance, these costs are paid out of pocket.

Medical Repatriation

If you're seriously ill or injured and cannot travel commercially, you may need a medical evacuation flight back home. This is separate from (and in addition to) the cost of treatment.

Air ambulance from Western Europe: €10,000–30,000
Air ambulance from the USA or Asia: €40,000–100,000+

The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) does NOT cover repatriation. This is the single biggest gap that makes "I have the European card, I'm fine" a dangerous assumption.

Emergency Medical Repatriation of Remains

In the worst case scenario, the cost of returning remains to Romania from abroad: €5,000–15,000, varying by distance and country. Travel insurance covers this entirely, avoiding a devastating additional financial burden on grieving families.

Baggage Loss, Theft, and Damage

Covers the cost of replacing luggage lost by airlines or stolen during the trip. Standard limits: €500–1,500 total.

Important sublimits to check:


Electronics (phones, laptops): often capped at €200–300 per item

Jewellery and watches: often excluded or capped very low

Cash: usually capped at €150–300


If you travel with expensive electronics, check the sublimits carefully — or consider specialist gadget insurance separately.

Trip Cancellation

Covers non-refundable pre-paid costs (flights, hotels, tours, cruises) if you're forced to cancel your trip for a covered reason BEFORE departure.

Covered reasons (standard):


Sudden illness or injury (documented by a doctor)

Death of a close family member

Serious accident

Court summons or jury duty

Redundancy (some policies)

Natural disaster at destination (some policies)


NOT covered:


Changing your mind

Work commitments

An event you knew about when you bought the policy

Fear of travel or pandemic anxiety (without a government travel ban)


For maximum protection, some insurers offer CFAR (Cancel For Any Reason) add-ons — typically at 40–50% extra premium, covering 75% of your costs if you cancel for any reason whatsoever. Worth considering for expensive bookings with non-refundable deposits.

Flight Delay

Covers additional expenses caused by significant delays (usually 4–12 hours, depending on policy): meals, accommodation, transport. Note: this is separate from EU261 compensation (which the airline owes you) — insurance covers expenses the airline doesn't.

Personal Liability

Covers legal costs and damages if you accidentally injure someone or damage their property. Typically €500,000–2,000,000 coverage. Useful but rarely claimed — included in most standard policies.

Real Prices by Destination — 2026

These prices are based on a healthy adult aged 18–65, single trip, standard cover (medical + baggage + repatriation + cancellation). Winter sports, USA, and age 65+ increase premiums significantly.

Destination 7 days 14 days Recommended medical cover
Europe (EU/Schengen) €12–25 €20–40 €30,000 minimum
Turkey €15–30 €25–50 €50,000
United Kingdom (post-Brexit) €15–30 €25–50 €50,000
Egypt, Tunisia, Morocco €18–35 €30–55 €50,000
USA / Canada €35–70 €60–120 €100,000+
Asia (Thailand, Bali, Vietnam) €25–50 €40–80 €75,000+
Worldwide (multi-destination) €40–80 €65–130 €75,000+

Annual MultiTravel policy: €120–250/year, covering all trips (typically with a maximum 30–45 days per individual trip). Break-even point: approximately 3 trips per year. If you travel 5+ times per year, an annual policy is almost always cheaper than buying per trip.

Age premiums: Over 65 increases premiums by 50–100%. Over 75, many standard insurers won't cover at all — specialist senior travel insurance exists for this.

European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) vs. Travel Insurance

This is the single biggest misconception in European travel. The EHIC is not travel insurance. Here's the precise comparison:

European Health Card (EHIC) Private Travel Insurance
Cost Free (apply at CAS/NHS) €12–80/week
Geographic coverage EU + EEA only Worldwide
Hospitals covered Public hospitals only Public + private
Medical repatriation ❌ Not covered ✅ Included
Trip cancellation ❌ Not covered ✅ Included
Lost/stolen baggage ❌ Not covered ✅ Included
Winter sports ❌ Not covered ✅ With add-on
Turkey, UK, USA ❌ Not valid ✅ Covered
Dental emergency ✅ At public dentists only ✅ Included
Flight delays ❌ Not covered ✅ Included

The correct strategy: Get the EHIC (it's free, takes a few days) and use it as a secondary backup within the EU — some insurers reduce your premium slightly if you have it. But never rely on it as your primary protection.

What's NOT Covered — The Exclusions That Cause Most Claim Denials

Insurance companies are required to cover what they promise — and they're also legally allowed to exclude what they clearly specify. These are the most common exclusion-related claim denials:

1. Undeclared Pre-Existing Conditions

If you have diabetes, hypertension, asthma, a heart condition, or any chronic illness and you don't declare it at the time of purchase, any emergency related to that condition will be denied. Period.

What to do: Declare everything. The premium surcharge is usually small (€5–20 extra), and it's far less than the cost of a denied claim.

2. Accidents Under the Influence of Alcohol

Fell off a scooter in Bali after 3 cocktails? The insurer has the legal right to deny the claim. This is the most commonly invoked exclusion for denials. Insurers are explicit about this in their conditions.

3. Sports Without the Add-On

Standard policies cover everyday activities: swimming, cycling, light hiking, snorkelling. They exclude: skiing, snowboarding, surfing, scuba diving (beyond recreational), bungee jumping, paragliding, and most "extreme" activities. Adding the winter sports or adventure sports rider: €5–20 extra. Without it, a ski accident means you pay everything yourself.

4. Planned Medical Procedures

If you travel specifically to get medical treatment abroad (dental tourism, cosmetic surgery, planned procedures), this is entirely excluded from standard travel insurance. These are elective choices, not emergencies.

5. Conflict Zones

Travel to countries under government "do not travel" advisories (FCO Level 4, MAE Level 4) is typically excluded. This includes active war zones and some high-risk areas.

6. Pandemics (Policy-Dependent)

Coverage for pandemic-related cancellations or medical costs varies widely by insurer and policy. Some cover COVID-19 as a standard illness; others exclude it entirely. Read the specific policy wording.

7 Mistakes Travellers Make — and How to Avoid Them

Mistake 1: "I have the European card — I'm covered"

As detailed above: the EHIC covers only public hospitals in EU countries. It doesn't cover repatriation, baggage, cancellation, or any trip to Turkey, UK, or outside the EU. Thousands of travellers discover this gap in an emergency.

Mistake 2: "My bank card has travel insurance"

Some premium bank cards (Gold, Platinum) include travel cover — but with critical limitations: medical cover of only €10,000–25,000 (often insufficient), conditions requiring you to have paid the flight with that specific card, activation requirements, and sometimes shorter maximum trip durations. Call your bank before assuming you're covered. Get the details in writing.

Mistake 3: "I'm only going for a city break — 3 days, nothing can happen"

Duration doesn't reduce risk. A broken ankle on Barcelona's cobblestones, an allergic reaction in Amsterdam, or food poisoning in Prague can happen in 3 hours. Three-day insurance for Europe costs €5–8. The ratio is clear.

Mistake 4: "I'll buy insurance at the airport"

Airport insurance is typically 40–60% more expensive than buying online. Insurance agents at airports operate with high commission structures. Buy online, ideally the same day you make your first non-refundable booking.

Mistake 5: "I'm driving to Greece — I don't need it"

Your car insurance (third-party liability) covers the vehicle. Travel insurance covers YOU: your health, your baggage, your trip costs. They are entirely separate products. Romanian drivers in Greece without travel insurance are exposed to the same medical cost risk as everyone else.

Mistake 6: "I'll figure out the hospital and claim back later"

Wrong approach — and it can invalidate your claim. If you need emergency medical treatment abroad, call your insurer's 24/7 emergency line first (the number is on your policy card). They will direct you to network hospitals where payment is direct, and they will authorise treatment. Going directly to a private hospital without prior authorisation may result in the insurer refusing reimbursement.

Mistake 7: "I'll buy it a few days before, just in case"

Trip cancellation cover works in reverse: you buy it as close as possible to when you make your non-refundable bookings. If you book a €800 non-refundable hotel in February and only buy insurance in April, you've been unprotected for two months. Buy insurance immediately after the first non-refundable cost.

How to Choose the Right Policy in 5 Minutes

A practical decision tree for most travellers:

Step 1: Where are you going?


EU/Schengen: minimum €30,000 medical cover

Turkey, UK, non-EU Europe: minimum €50,000

USA, Canada, Australia: minimum €100,000

Asia, South America, Africa: minimum €75,000


Step 2: What activities?


Skiing, snowboarding, winter sports: add sports rider

Scuba diving, paragliding, extreme sports: add adventure rider

Standard sightseeing, hiking, beaches: no add-on needed


Step 3: Do you have pre-existing conditions?


Yes: declare them at purchase — don't skip this


Step 4: How much have you paid non-refundably?


Under €300: basic policy is fine

€300–1,000: standard policy with cancellation cover

€1,000+: comprehensive policy, consider CFAR add-on


Step 5: How often do you travel?


1–2 trips per year: single trip policies

3+ trips per year: annual MultiTravel policy


What to Do When You Need to Make a Claim

The process matters as much as having the policy:

1. Call the 24/7 emergency line immediately (printed on your policy card). Don't go to a hospital first — call the insurer first for emergencies.

2. Get documentation of everything:


Medical: doctor's report, diagnosis, all invoices and receipts

Baggage: airline's Property Irregularity Report (PIR) and baggage claim reference

Cancellation: doctor's note, death certificate, official documents depending on reason


3. Keep ALL receipts. Every meal, taxi, pharmacy purchase, phone call made because of the insured event.

4. File the claim as soon as you're home. Most policies require claims within 30–60 days of the incident. Don't wait.

5. If your claim is denied: You have the right to appeal. Insurers must provide the specific reason for denial. If they've denied a legitimate claim incorrectly, the Financial Supervisory Authority (ASF in Romania) handles insurance complaints.

Travel Insurance and EU261 — How They Work Together

These two protections cover different things and complement each other:


EU261 (see our full guide): the airline owes you €250–€600 when THEY cancel or significantly delay your flight. This is separate from insurance — it's a legal obligation on the airline.

Travel insurance : covers YOUR costs when a disruption causes knock-on effects the airline doesn't cover — cancelled hotel nights, non-refundable excursions, additional transport.


The best protection is both: EU261 for the airline's legal obligation, and travel insurance for everything else.

If your flight is cancelled and the airline cites "extraordinary circumstances" (weather, ATC strike) — which means NO EU261 compensation applies — your travel insurance trip cancellation/interruption cover becomes your primary protection.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How much does travel insurance cost?
R: Prices vary by destination and duration: Europe 7 days: €12–25 per person; Turkey 7 days: €15–30; USA 7 days: €35–70; worldwide 14 days: €40–80. For frequent travellers, an annual MultiTravel policy (€120–250/year) covering all trips is better value if you travel 3+ times per year.

Î: Is the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) enough?
R: No. The EHIC only covers medical emergencies in PUBLIC hospitals in EU/EEA countries, under the same conditions as local residents. It does NOT cover: medical repatriation (can cost €10,000–50,000), trip cancellation, lost baggage, sports injuries, or treatment in private hospitals. It's a useful backup — not a substitute for travel insurance.

Î: What does standard travel insurance NOT cover?
R: The most common exclusions: undeclared pre-existing conditions, accidents under the influence of alcohol or drugs, extreme sports without the specific add-on, planned medical procedures abroad, travel to conflict zones (MAE/FCO Level 4 warnings), and pandemics (varies by insurer). Always read the policy conditions before buying.

Î: Can I buy insurance after I've already left home?
R: Yes, but with restrictions. Most insurers apply a 3–7 day waiting period after purchase before cover activates. If you've already left and buy now, you won't be covered for the first few days. The best practice: buy before departure, ideally the same day you book your first non-refundable component.

Î: Do I need travel insurance for Turkey?
R: Yes, absolutely. Turkey is outside the EU, so the European Health Card doesn't work there. Private hospital costs in Turkey are surprisingly high (€500–2,000/night), and Turkish hospitals often require advance payment or proof of insurance before treating. Medical repatriation to Romania from Turkey: €8,000–20,000 without insurance.

Î: My bank card includes travel insurance — is that enough?
R: Possibly, but check the details carefully. Many premium bank cards (Gold, Platinum, Black) include travel cover, but with lower limits (€10,000–25,000 medical cover vs the recommended €30,000+) and restrictive conditions (the flight must be paid with that card, or you must activate the coverage before travel). Call your bank and confirm the exact terms.

Î: What's the difference between travel insurance and trip cancellation insurance?
R: Standard travel insurance covers what happens DURING the trip: medical emergencies, lost baggage, delays, repatriation. Trip cancellation insurance covers BEFORE departure: if you can't travel (illness, family emergency) and want to recover non-refundable costs. The best policies combine both. Read our dedicated guide on trip cancellation cover.

Î: Do I need travel insurance for skiing?
R: Yes — and you need the winter sports add-on specifically. Standard policies cover everyday activities (swimming, cycling, light hiking) but exclude skiing, snowboarding, and snow sports. A ski insurance add-on typically costs €5–15 extra and is essential: mountain rescue in Austria or France alone can cost €2,000–10,000.

## Travel Scams in Europe 2026: The 15 Most Common Tricks and How to Protect Yourself

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/travel-scams-europe-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-14
Actualizat: 2026-07-14
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/scam-uri-inselatorii-vacanta-2026

Descriere: Every tourist scam you'll encounter in Europe in 2026 — from ATM skimming and taxi tricks to fake petitions and restaurant traps. City-by-city breakdown with real prevention tips.

Răspuns scurt: The most common travel scams in Europe in 2026: ATM skimming (use indoor bank ATMs only), taxi meter tricks (use Bolt/Uber instead), restaurants without prices on the menu (always ask before ordering), forced friendship bracelets in Paris and Rome, fake petitions that cover pickpocketing, and Dynamic Currency Conversion at ATMs (always choose local currency, never your home currency). Travel insurance covering theft costs €15-25/week and is essential.

Why tourists fall for scams (and why you won't)

Travel scams work because tourists are in an unfamiliar environment, relaxed (guard down), pressed for time, and often too polite to say a firm "no." Scammers count on exactly this combination. The good news: once you know the playbook, these schemes are laughably transparent. This guide covers every major scam category with specific examples from cities you'll likely visit.

At the ATM — skimming and hidden fees

Card skimming — the invisible threat

A near-invisible device fitted over the card slot copies your magnetic stripe data while a pinhole camera or fake keypad records your PIN. Result: your card is cloned within hours.

Where it's common: street ATMs in tourist zones — Rome , Barcelona , Prague, Athens , Istanbul .

How to protect yourself:


Use ATMs inside bank branches only — never street-facing machines

Wiggle the card slot before inserting — skimmers are loosely attached and will move

Cover the keypad with your hand when entering your PIN

Enable instant push notifications on your banking app — you'll see any unauthorized transaction immediately

Use Revolut or Wise for travel spending — instant card freeze if compromised, plus zero foreign exchange fees


Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) — the legal scam

The ATM asks: "Would you like to be charged in your home currency?" If you say YES, the ATM operator's bank does the conversion at a rate 3-8% worse than your own bank would charge. That's €30-80 lost on every €1,000 you spend.

The rule: ALWAYS choose local currency (EUR, GBP, TRY — whatever the country uses). At POS terminals too — if the waiter asks "in pounds or euros?" choose the local currency. Your bank's exchange rate is always better.

The maths: on a €500 holiday, DCC costs you €15-40 in unnecessary fees. Revolut and Wise charge 0% — that's the price of a nice dinner saved by pressing the right button.

At the taxi rank — rigged meters and scenic routes

The "broken" meter

Driver says the meter "isn't working" and proposes a flat rate — typically 3-5x the real fare. Or the meter works but runs suspiciously fast.

Where it's common: airports (especially Athens , Istanbul , Rome Ciampino, Prague), central train stations.

The fix: Bolt or Uber . Price fixed before the ride, GPS-tracked route, card payment, accountability through the app. It eliminates taxi scams entirely. If you must take a street taxi, insist on the meter. If it "doesn't work," get out.

Tip: at airports, ONLY use taxis from the official rank — never drivers who approach you inside the terminal.

The scenic route

Driver takes the "long way" to inflate the fare. Common with tourists who don't know the city layout.

The fix: open Google Maps on your phone with the route displayed. The driver sees you're tracking and takes the direct route. Download offline maps before your trip so this works without data.

At the restaurant — menus without prices

The "special recommendation"

Waiter enthusiastically recommends the "catch of the day" or "chef's special" without mentioning the price. At the bill: €40-80 per portion.

Where it's common: tourist squares in Rome (Piazza Navona, Campo de' Fiori), Venice, Dubrovnik (Stradun), Greek islands.

The fix:


ALWAYS ask the price before ordering, especially for recommendations

Don't sit at restaurants without prices on the menu

Check Google reviews first — tourist trap restaurants have terrible ratings

Walk one block away from the main attraction — prices drop 30-50% and food quality improves


Book dining experiences through GetYourGuide — food tours and cooking classes have fixed prices and genuine local food.

Coperto, service charge, and surprise fees

In Italy, "coperto" (cover charge, €2-4/person) is legal and normal — it covers bread, oil, and the table setting. What's NOT normal: a 15-20% service charge added automatically without being mentioned. In the UK, 12.5% service charge is standard and usually noted on the menu.

The fix: check the bill before paying. If service charge is already included, don't tip on top.

On the street — classic cons

The friendship bracelet (Paris, Rome, Barcelona)

Someone ties a bracelet on your wrist "for free" or "for good luck," then demands €10-20. If you refuse, they become aggressive or call accomplices.

Where: Sacré-Cœur in Paris, Colosseum in Rome , La Rambla in Barcelona .

The fix: hands in pockets in crowded tourist areas. If someone approaches, a firm "No, thank you" and keep walking. Don't stop, don't engage, don't feel guilty.

The fake petition (Paris, Rome, Milan)

Groups of young people ask you to sign a petition "for the deaf" or "against drugs." While you're signing, an accomplice checks your pockets. Or after signing, they demand a €20 "donation."

The fix: never stop and never sign anything on the street. "No" and walk.

The three-cup shuffle / shell game (Barcelona, Prague)

A man with three cups and a ball. It looks easy. Accomplices in the "crowd" win to make it look genuine. You play, you lose — always. It's mathematically rigged.

The fix: don't play. Walk away. It's illegal in most countries but operates because tourists keep playing.

Distraction theft (everywhere)

Someone asks for directions / asks the time / spills something on you / "trips" into you. Meanwhile, an accomplice takes your wallet or phone.

The fix: phone and wallet in front pockets . Backpack on your front in crowded areas. If a stranger touches you, immediately check your belongings.

Online — booking scams

Fake accommodation websites

Clone sites mimicking Booking.com or Airbnb with impossibly low prices, requesting payment via bank transfer.

The fix: check the URL (booking.com, not book1ng.com). Pay ONLY through the platform, never via direct bank transfer. If a price is too good to be real, it isn't real.

Fake attraction tickets

Unauthorized websites selling tickets to the Colosseum, Sagrada Familia , or flights at below-face-value prices.

The fix: buy tickets only from official attraction websites or authorized platforms like GetYourGuide (which includes free cancellation). For flights, use trusted search engines.

Scam map — city by city

City Common scams
Paris Bracelets at Sacré-Cœur, fake petitions, "gold ring" found on ground
Rome Gladiators demanding money for photos, restaurant traps at Piazza Navona, airport taxi
Barcelona Three-cup game on La Rambla, pickpockets on metro, fake "police" checking wallets
Prague Rigged taxis from airport, exchange offices with fake rates
Istanbul "Friendly" men inviting you to a bar (bill: €200+), shoe shiners
Athens Taxi without meter from airport, Plaka restaurants with double prices
Dubrovnik Cruise-day price inflation, fake "skip the line" sellers

7 golden rules against scams

1. If someone approaches you on the street with an offer, it's a scam. Nobody gives free things to strangers out of kindness.

2. Bolt/Uber instead of taxis. Fixed price, GPS route, card payment. Zero arguments.

3. ATMs inside bank branches only. And always choose the local currency.

4. Check prices BEFORE ordering. At restaurants, taxis, and excursions.

5. Phone and wallet in front pockets. Backpack on your front in crowds.

6. Never sign anything on the street. Ever.

7. Travel insurance with theft coverage. If it happens, you're financially covered. A week's policy costs less than what a single scam could take from you. Full insurance guide .

8. Use an eSIM instead of buying a local SIM from a street vendor. SIM swap scams (where your number is hijacked) are growing. An eSIM installed from home is impossible to physically tamper with.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: What are the most common tourist scams in Europe?
R: Top 5: rigged taxi meters (or 'broken' meters with inflated flat rates), ATM skimming devices that clone your card, restaurants without prices that present inflated bills, street sellers forcing bracelets/roses then demanding payment, and the 'helpful stranger' who distracts you while an accomplice picks your pocket.

Î: How do I avoid ATM skimming in Europe?
R: Use ATMs inside bank branches only — never street ATMs in tourist areas. Wiggle the card slot before inserting (skimmers are loosely attached). Cover the keypad when entering your PIN. Enable instant transaction notifications on your banking app. Use Revolut or Wise for travel spending — they have instant freeze if compromised.

Î: Is Uber/Bolt safe to use in Europe?
R: Yes, and it's the single best defence against taxi scams. Price is fixed before the ride, route is GPS-tracked, payment is on card (no cash disputes), and you have a direct complaint channel in the app. Bolt and Uber work in most major European cities.

## Trip Cancellation Insurance 2026: What It Covers, When It Is Worth It and How to Claim

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/trip-cancellation-insurance
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-30
Actualizat: 2026-07-30
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/asigurare-anulare-calatorie

Descriere: Trip cancellation insurance: what is covered and excluded, how much it costs, difference from standard travel insurance, Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR), claims process and common mistakes.

Răspuns scurt: Trip cancellation insurance covers non-refundable travel costs (flights, hotels, cruises, excursions) if you are forced to cancel due to a covered reason: sudden illness documented by a doctor, death or serious illness of a close family member, a home emergency requiring your presence, or a legal summons. It does NOT cover changing your mind, fear of travelling, or events already known when you bought the policy. It is worth buying whenever your total non-refundable bookings exceed €500–600 — the policy typically costs 5–8% of that amount.

You booked your holiday four months ahead: a non-refundable flight for €350, a non-refundable resort stay for €800, a cruise deposit of €600. Total at risk: €1,750. Three weeks before departure, you break your ankle. How do you recover your money?

If you have trip cancellation insurance with medical coverage: you file the claim, submit the medical certificate, and receive the non-refundable amounts back.

Without insurance: you lose the money.

Trip cancellation insurance exists specifically for this scenario — but it works quite differently from what most people assume when they first encounter it.


What is and what is not covered: the essential distinction

The fundamental principle: trip cancellation insurance covers giving up a planned trip due to circumstances outside your control, unforeseeable, and documentable . It is not a universal refund option.

What standard policies cover

Medical reasons:


Sudden acute illness making you unfit to travel — diagnosed and documented by a doctor with an explicit recommendation not to travel

Accident requiring hospitalisation or medically advised immobility

Serious illness or death of a spouse, child, or parent

Pregnancy complications arising after the booking was made

Acute worsening of a declared pre-existing chronic condition (must have been disclosed at purchase)


Non-medical reasons:


Death of a close family member included in or related to the policy

Major home emergency (fire, flood, burglary) requiring your presence

Legal summons or court proceedings preventing travel

Involuntary redundancy or job loss (in some premium policies)

Visa refusal for a destination requiring one (in some policies)

Passport stolen in the weeks before departure with insufficient time to replace


What is almost never covered

Changing your mind — you no longer want to travel, you found something better to do, or you simply do not feel like going. No standard policy covers this. (CFAR addresses this need — see below.)

Fear of travelling — general travel anxiety, fear of turbulence, fear of terrorism that has not materialised — these are not documentable medical conditions.

Events already known at purchase — if a strike, natural disaster, or geopolitical situation was already public before you bought the policy, it was a known risk and is excluded.

Pandemics already declared — COVID-19 demonstrated that standard policies exclude widely declared epidemics. Some post-2020 policies explicitly include pandemic coverage — check the wording.

Voluntary work reasons — you resigned, chose not to take holiday from work, or preferred another commitment. Some policies cover employer-mandated travel refusal; most do not cover voluntary work decisions.


When is trip cancellation insurance worth buying?

Simple calculation: if your total non-refundable bookings exceed the cost of the insurance by 10–15 times, the insurance is economically rational.

Situation Amount at risk Policy cost Worth it?
Low-cost flight €80, flexible hotel ~€80 €15–20 Marginal
Flight €250 + non-refundable hotel €350 ~€600 €25–40 ✅ Yes
All-inclusive package €1,500/person ~€1,500 €50–80 ✅ Clearly yes
Cruise €2,000/person ~€2,000 €70–120 ✅ Essential
Flexible fares + free-cancellation hotel ~€0 at risk — ❌ Not needed
Concert/event tickets + flights Ticket value Depends ✅ If significant

Practical rule: if your total non-refundable bookings exceed €500 , trip cancellation insurance is almost always financially rational. The premium typically costs 5–8% of the at-risk amount — the expected value calculation works clearly in the insurance's favour whenever a genuine covered event occurs.


How much it costs: real pricing

Non-refundable booking value Standard CFAR premium
€500 €25–40 €60–100
€1,000 €50–80 €100–200
€2,000 €100–160 €200–400
€5,000 €250–400 €500–1,000

Comprehensive policy (medical emergencies + cancellation + baggage): €15–30/week for European travel. For most travellers, this is the right product — it provides complete protection rather than only the cancellation component.


CFAR: Cancel For Any Reason insurance

CFAR is the premium tier of cancellation insurance: cancel for any reason, with no documentation required, and recover 50–75% of your non-refundable costs .

Typical CFAR conditions:


Must be purchased within 14–21 days of your first booking (the window closes quickly)

Cancellation must be made at least 48–72 hours before departure

You recover 50–75% (not 100%) of non-refundable amounts

Costs 2–3 times more than standard cancellation insurance


When CFAR is worth the premium:


Large non-refundable bookings booked far in advance (cruise deposits, expensive packages)

Uncertainty about whether the trip will actually happen (early pregnancy, uncertain work situation)

Long lead times (6–12 months between booking and travel — anything can change)

Personal preference for flexibility over cost optimisation


CFAR example: you book a €3,000 cruise in January for August. You buy CFAR immediately (cost: ~€240). In May, a family situation changes your plans. You cancel — and recover €1,500–2,250 (50–75%). Without CFAR and without a covered medical reason: you keep €0–750 depending on the cruise line's cancellation schedule.


Cancellation penalties by booking type

Understanding the penalties tells you exactly what you stand to lose — and therefore whether insurance is worth buying.

Airlines

Airline Cancellation policy Amount at risk
Ryanair (standard fare) Non-refundable 100% of ticket
Ryanair (Flexi Plus) Partially flexible ~50%
Wizz Air (standard) Non-refundable 100% of ticket
Wizz Air (WIZZ Flex) Credit only No cash refund
British Airways (Light) Non-refundable 100%
British Airways (Flex) Refundable with fee €50–100 fee
Lufthansa (Economy Light) Non-refundable 100%

Hotels


Flexible / Free cancellation rates: at-risk amount = €0 (cancellable until 24–48h before check-in)

Non-refundable / Early booking rates: 100% non-refundable from the moment of booking

All-inclusive resort packages: typically escalating penalties as check-in date approaches


Cruises — the harshest penalties

Days before sailing Typical penalty
90+ days 0–25% (or deposit only)
60–89 days 25–50%
30–59 days 50–75%
15–29 days 75–90%
Under 15 days 100% — no refund

At €2,000 per person, an illness 10 days before sailing costs the full amount for two people: €4,000. Trip cancellation insurance on the same booking costs €140–240. The expected-value calculation is not difficult.

See: first Mediterranean cruise guide and how much does a cruise cost for the full cruise planning context.


The claims process: step by step

Step 1 — Notify the insurer immediately (within 24–48 hours)
Contact the insurer as soon as you know you cannot travel. Notification deadlines are strict — missing them can invalidate the claim entirely.

Step 2 — Try to recover money directly first
Insurers require evidence that you attempted to recover costs directly from the airline and hotel. The unrecovered amount is what insurance covers. If you had a refundable booking and did not request the refund, insurance will not pay that portion.

Step 3 — Collect documentation
For medical reasons:


Medical certificate with a specific diagnosis and explicit recommendation not to travel

Hospital records, prescriptions, test results

"General malaise" or "fatigue" is not sufficient — the diagnosis must be specific and the contraindication for travel explicit


For other reasons:


Death certificate (if family bereavement)

Legal document (court summons, redundancy notice)

Police or fire department report (if home emergency)

Visa refusal letter (if applicable)


Step 4 — Submit the complete claim
Complete the insurer's form, attach all documentation, submit. Processing time: typically 5–30 business days.

The most common reasons claims are rejected:


Diagnosis too vague on the medical certificate

Pre-existing condition not declared at purchase — invalidates the entire claim

Notification after the policy's stated deadline

Claim includes amounts that were recoverable directly (e.g. a refundable hotel that was not refunded)

The illness or condition began before the policy was purchased



Trip cancellation vs flexible fares: the strategic decision

Before buying cancellation insurance, assess what you actually have at risk:

If your bookings are... Do you need cancellation insurance?
Predominantly free-cancellation Probably not — at-risk amount is minimal
Mix of flexible and non-refundable Yes, for the non-refundable portion
Predominantly non-refundable Yes — essential
Cruise or expensive package Yes — always

The cost-efficient approach: book with free cancellation where possible (hotels on Booking.com with the Flexible rate, flexible airline fares), and buy cancellation insurance only for the non-refundable amounts. Total cost is often lower than buying premium flexible fares for everything.


Trip cancellation vs medical travel insurance: what covers what

Coverage Medical travel insurance Trip cancellation Comprehensive policy
Medical emergencies during trip ✅ ❌ ✅
Medical repatriation ✅ ❌ ✅
Cancellation before departure ❌ ✅ ✅
Trip interruption (return early) ❌ ✅ (some) ✅
Flight delay expenses ✅ (some) ❌ ✅
Lost or stolen baggage ✅ (some) ❌ ✅
EHIC complement (non-EU) N/A N/A ✅

Recommendation: a comprehensive policy combining all three elements is almost always better value than buying them separately or relying on partial coverage from a credit card benefit.

For the EHIC comparison in EU destinations: EHIC vs travel insurance . For the complete guide to all travel insurance coverage: travel insurance guide 2026 .


When to buy: the timing window

Buy immediately after your first non-refundable booking. Not a week before departure.

Four reasons timing matters:



Waiting period: 24–72 hours after purchase before the policy is active. Fall ill on the day you buy and you are not covered.


CFAR window closes: the Cancel For Any Reason option is only available within 14–21 days of your first booking. Miss this and CFAR is no longer purchasable.


Known events excluded: if a strike, pandemic, or political situation is already publicly announced before you buy, it is a known risk and not covered.


Pre-purchase illness excluded: any condition that develops before the policy is purchased cannot be used as a cancellation reason.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: What is the difference between trip cancellation insurance and standard travel insurance?
R: Standard travel insurance covers what happens DURING your trip: medical emergencies, lost luggage, flight delays, repatriation. Trip cancellation insurance covers what happens BEFORE departure: you cannot travel and want to recover the money you have already paid. Comprehensive policies combine both — medical cover, cancellation, baggage, and delays — in a single product. This is usually the better option for most travellers.

Î: Can I buy trip cancellation insurance after booking?
R: Yes, any time before departure — but with important caveats. There is typically a 24–72 hour waiting period after purchase before the policy activates. If you fall ill on the day you buy, you are not covered. For Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR) options, you must buy within 14–21 days of your first booking. The rule: buy immediately after your first non-refundable reservation.

Î: Does trip cancellation insurance cover pre-existing medical conditions?
R: Partially, depending on the policy. If you have a stable chronic condition and suffer an unexpected acute worsening documented by a doctor, many policies cover this. If you choose not to travel due to a pre-existing condition without a specific acute medical event, it is typically not covered. Always declare existing conditions at purchase — non-disclosure can invalidate the entire claim.

Î: Is trip cancellation different from when an airline cancels my flight?
R: Completely different scenarios. If the airline cancels your flight, it is legally required to refund you or reroute you under EU261/2004 — your insurance is not involved. Trip cancellation insurance activates when YOU cancel for a personal reason (illness, family emergency). These are separate entitlements. See: flight delay and cancellation rights EU261.

Î: How much does trip cancellation insurance cost?
R: Standard trip cancellation insurance costs approximately 5–8% of the total non-refundable booking value. For €1,000 of non-refundable bookings: €50–80. For €3,000: €150–240. A comprehensive policy covering medical emergencies, cancellation, and baggage costs €15–30/week for European travel — less than a restaurant meal.

Î: What is Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR) insurance?
R: CFAR allows you to cancel for any reason — no medical certificate, no documentation — and recover 50–75% of your non-refundable costs. It must be purchased within 14–21 days of your first booking (after this window, it is not available). It costs 2–3 times more than standard cancellation insurance. Worth it for large non-refundable bookings (cruises, expensive packages) where you want complete flexibility.

Î: Do cruise passengers need trip cancellation insurance?
R: Yes — cruise lines have the most severe cancellation penalties in the travel industry: typically 100% forfeiture with less than 15 days before sailing. On a €2,000/person cruise, an unexpected illness 10 days before departure means losing the entire amount. Trip cancellation insurance is practically mandatory for cruise bookings.

Î: Does the insurance from my credit card cover trip cancellation?
R: Premium credit cards (Visa Infinite, Mastercard Platinum, Amex Gold) sometimes include trip cancellation benefits — typically covering €1,000–5,000 per claim with specific conditions (the trip must be paid with that card). Read your cardholder agreement carefully before buying a separate policy. If your non-refundable bookings exceed the card's limit, supplement with a dedicated policy.

## Is Turkey Safe to Visit in 2026? Antalya, Istanbul and the Coast — Honest Guide

URL: https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/turkey-2026-safety-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: asigurari
Publicat: 2026-07-29
Actualizat: 2026-07-29
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/vacanta-turcia-2026-siguranta

Descriere: Current safety situation in Turkey for tourists in 2026, which regions to avoid, what travel advisories say, and essential practical advice for Antalya, Istanbul and the Aegean coast.

Răspuns scurt: Turkey's tourist areas — Antalya, Istanbul, the Aegean coast (Bodrum, Marmaris, Fethiye) — are considered safe for visitors in 2026 by UK, EU, and US government travel advisories. The regions to avoid are in southeastern Turkey, near the borders with Syria, Iraq, and Iran — approximately 1,200–1,700 km from the main tourist destinations. An eSIM is essential (buy before arrival — provider websites are blocked inside Turkey). Travel insurance is mandatory — the EHIC does not apply in Turkey.

Turkey generates more travel anxiety searches than almost any other popular destination. The question "Is Turkey safe?" appears thousands of times a day from prospective visitors, driven by a combination of regional news, social media amplification, and genuine uncertainty. This guide gives you the factual answer based on current government advisories and the practical reality on the ground.

What the travel advisories actually say

Before anything else: the authoritative sources. Every government with a significant number of citizens travelling to Turkey publishes regularly updated travel advice. Here is what they say as of July 2026:

UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO):


Advises against all travel to areas within 10 km of the Syrian border (Hatay province) and to areas of southeastern Turkey near the Iraqi border

Does NOT advise against travel to Antalya, Istanbul, Izmir, Bodrum, Marmaris, Fethiye, or other main tourist areas

Standard precautions recommended for terrorism risk in major cities


US State Department:


Level 2 (Exercise Increased Caution) for Turkey as a whole

"Do Not Travel" for specific southeastern provinces near Syrian, Iraqi, and Iranian borders

No specific warning for coastal tourist areas


EU member states:


Similar split assessment: avoid southeast, normal precautions for tourist areas


The key point: no major Western government advises against travel to Turkey's tourist destinations. The risk alerts are geographically specific and clearly separated from the Mediterranean coast and Istanbul.

The geography that matters

Turkey is a large country — 784,000 km², comparable to the combined area of France and Germany. The southeastern provinces where conflict risk exists are separated from the tourist coast by enormous distances:

Tourist destination Distance to Syrian border Distance to Iraqi border
Antalya ~1,200 km ~1,500 km
Istanbul ~1,700 km ~2,000 km
Bodrum ~1,400 km ~1,700 km
Marmaris ~1,350 km ~1,650 km
Cappadocia ~900 km ~1,100 km

For context: 1,200 km is the distance from London to Warsaw, or from Rome to Copenhagen. Events in southeastern Turkey are physically disconnected from where tourists spend their time in the same way events in one part of a large continent are disconnected from another.

Tourist areas: current situation

Antalya and the Turkish Riviera

Antalya is Turkey's most popular tourist destination and the anchor of the Turkish Riviera — the Mediterranean coastal strip that includes Kemer, Side, Alanya, and Belek. The area hosts millions of European tourists annually, with large resort hotels operated by international chains (Rixos, Titanic, Delphin, Club Med, and others).

Current situation: fully operational. International charter flights from across Europe continue to serve Antalya Airport (AYT), which handles over 35 million passengers per year. No travel advisory targets this region specifically.

The resort area reality: Antalya's major hotels are effectively self-contained holiday environments — all-inclusive properties with private beaches, multiple pools, entertainment programmes, and on-site facilities. For many visitors, the geopolitical context of the broader region becomes abstract when the day consists of moving between the beach and the buffet.

Istanbul

Istanbul is Turkey's largest city, its cultural capital, and one of the world's great urban destinations. The city of 16 million people spans two continents across the Bosphorus Strait.

Key attractions operating normally: Hagia Sophia (now a mosque — dress modestly for entry, non-Muslims welcome), Topkapi Palace, the Blue Mosque (Sultan Ahmed Mosque), the Grand Bazaar, the Spice Market, the Bosphorus cruise, Galata Tower, and the Dolmabahçe Palace.

Safety in practice: Istanbul is a safe city by international standards for most of its urban area. The tourist districts (Sultanahmet, Beyoğlu, Karaköy) are heavily visited and policed. Standard urban precautions apply: watch for pickpockets in crowded areas, use Uber/Bolt rather than unlicensed taxis, and be alert to tourist-specific scams (see below).

Bodrum, Marmaris, Fethiye — the Aegean coast

Turkey's Aegean coast attracts a different type of visitor — more sailing, more upmarket, and geographically opposite to the risk areas. Bodrum is the centre of Turkey's luxury tourism scene; Marmaris is a large resort town popular with British tourists; Fethiye and the surrounding area (Ölüdeniz, Kayaköy, the Turquoise Coast) offer some of the most beautiful scenery in the Mediterranean.

All operate normally with no specific travel advisory concerns.

Essential practical differences from EU travel

eSIM: buy before you land (critical)

Turkey is not in the EU. Your EU free roaming allowance does not apply. Without a local data solution, you will be charged by your home carrier at non-EU roaming rates — typically €10–15 per gigabyte. A week of moderate data use could cost €50–100 in roaming charges.

The solution: buy a Turkey eSIM before departure. A 5 GB / 30-day plan costs approximately $10–15 on Airalo.

The critical warning: since 2025, Turkish authorities have blocked access to major eSIM provider websites from within Turkey. If you arrive without an eSIM and try to buy one in your hotel room, you will find the websites inaccessible. The eSIM must be purchased and installed before landing.

Installation: install the eSIM at home before departure. It sits dormant on your phone and activates automatically when you land and connect to a partner network. See the full installation guide: how to install an eSIM 2026 .

Provider recommendation: Airalo has the widest network coverage options for Turkey (typically Turk Telekom or Turkcell). Compare with Saily and Yesim for your specific plan size: best eSIM by destination 2026 .

Travel insurance: mandatory, not optional

Turkey is outside the EU. The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is completely invalid — Turkey has no bilateral healthcare agreement with EU member states. Without private travel insurance, you have no medical coverage at all.

The cost of treatment without insurance:


Emergency doctor visit at a private clinic: €100–300

Night in a private hospital: €500–2,000

Surgery: €3,000–15,000

Medical evacuation by air to home country: €15,000–40,000


Turkish private hospitals in tourist areas are generally good — modern facilities, English-speaking staff, and prompt care. The quality exists; the cost without insurance is the risk.

Travel insurance for Turkey costs €15–25 for a week. The math does not require explanation.

What to verify in your policy:


Minimum €30,000 medical cover (standard for Schengen visa; appropriate for Turkey too)

Medical evacuation explicitly covered

24/7 emergency assistance line

Coverage for water sports and activities if relevant to your trip


e-Visa: apply before departure

Most Western nationalities require an e-Visa for Turkey, obtained at evisa.gov.tr.

Who needs it: UK citizens, US citizens, Australian and New Zealand citizens, Canadians, and most non-EU nationalities. Some EU citizens can enter without a visa — check your specific nationality at the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs website.

The process: apply at evisa.gov.tr, pay by card (approximately $50–60 depending on nationality), receive approval by email (typically within minutes to a few hours). Print or save the e-Visa on your phone — you need to show it at passport control along with your passport.

Validity: typically 180 days from issue, maximum 90-day stay. Multiple entry in most cases.

Apply before you travel — doing it at the airport or upon arrival is possible at some airports but slower and occasionally problematic.

Passport, not ID card

Turkey requires a valid passport from all visitors — national ID cards are not accepted. Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months beyond your entry date. If your passport expires in less than 6 months from when you plan to enter Turkey, renew it before travelling.

Turkey-specific scams to know

Istanbul in particular has well-documented tourist scams that have operated for decades. Knowing them makes them easy to avoid.

The friendly bar invitation: a local (or someone posing as one) strikes up a genuinely pleasant conversation, invites you for drinks at "his friend's bar," and escorts you somewhere. The bill arrives at €150–400 for drinks you may not have ordered. The establishment will have enforcers to ensure payment. Solution: politely decline any unsolicited invitation to go somewhere specific.

The shoe shine "drop": a shoe shiner apparently accidentally drops his brush in front of you. When you pick it up and return it, he insists on shining your shoes as a thank you. The "service" costs €10–20. Solution: do not pick up the brush.

Unlicensed taxis: taxis that approach you at tourist sites or airports often charge 3–5x the legitimate rate. Use Uber or Bolt — available in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, and Antalya. Fare shown before the trip, GPS-tracked, card payment. Eliminates all taxi fraud.

Currency exchange by hand: anyone offering to change money on the street. Never. Always use bank ATMs (not standalone machines on tourist streets) or official exchange bureaux inside commercial premises.

Grand Bazaar pricing: this is not a scam — it is the culture. Prices in the Grand Bazaar are starting points for negotiation. Accepting the first price offered means significantly overpaying. Starting at 50% of the stated price and meeting around 60–70% is standard practice. This applies to bazaars throughout Turkey.

What to eat and drink in Turkey

Turkish cuisine is one of the world's great food traditions, and eating well in Turkey is inexpensive by European standards.

Must-try:


Kahvaltı (Turkish breakfast): an extraordinary spread of small dishes — cheeses, olives, honey, clotted cream, tomatoes, cucumbers, eggs, bread, and unlimited tea. €4–8/person at a local breakfast café. The most generous breakfast tradition in Europe.

Kebab (the real version): Adana kebab (spiced minced lamb on a flat skewer), İskender (döner over pide with tomato sauce and butter), Şiş (cubed lamb or chicken). €5–10 at a local lokanta.

Meze: small plates served with rakı (anise spirit) or beer — hummus, eggplant dishes, stuffed grape leaves, fresh cheese, böreks. The full meze experience at a good meyhane (Turkish tavern): €15–25/person with drinks.

Pide: Turkish flatbread baked with toppings in a wood-fired oven. A boat-shaped pide with cheese and egg costs €4–6.

Turkish tea (çay): served in small tulip-shaped glasses everywhere, always, and always free in shops where you are browsing.


Tap water: do not drink tap water in Turkey. Bottled water is cheap (€0.50 for a large bottle) and universally available.

Alcohol: Turkey is a Muslim-majority country but alcohol is widely available in tourist areas, restaurants, and supermarkets. Avoid drinking visibly in non-tourist areas and near mosques.

Before you go: the Turkey preparation checklist


Valid passport (6 months validity beyond entry date)

e-Visa obtained at evisa.gov.tr

eSIM purchased and installed (Airalo, Saily, or Yesim) — before departure

Travel insurance purchased — minimum €30,000 medical cover, evacuation included

Emergency contacts saved: your insurer's 24/7 line, Romanian/EU embassy in Ankara (+90 312 xxx xxxx), your airline

Check mae.ro or your country's travel advisory 48 hours before departure

Revolut or Wise card for card payments (avoid foreign transaction fees)

Local cash: withdraw TRY from ATMs on arrival (not airport exchange bureaux)

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is Antalya safe in 2026?
R: Yes. Antalya is on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, approximately 1,200 km from the Syrian and Iraqi borders. UK, EU, and US travel advisories do not advise against travel to Antalya, Kemer, Side, Alanya, or Belek. The resort areas operate normally with full international tourist flows.

Î: Which regions of Turkey should I avoid?
R: All major government advisories (UK FCDO, US State Department, EU member state foreign ministries) advise against all travel or all but essential travel to southeastern Turkey: the provinces bordering Syria (Hatay, Gaziantep, Kilis), Iraq (Sirnak, Hakkari, Şırnak), and Iran (Van, Ağrı, Kars). These areas are 800–1,700 km from the main tourist destinations.

Î: Is Istanbul safe in 2026?
R: Yes, with normal urban precautions. Istanbul operates normally as a major global city and tourism hub. Hagia Sophia, Topkapi Palace, the Grand Bazaar, and the Bosphorus are all open and fully functioning. Standard advice: use Uber or Bolt rather than unlicensed taxis, watch for the 'friendly bar' scam (a 'local' invites you for drinks, bill arrives at €200+), and be alert to pickpockets in crowded tourist areas.

Î: Do I need an e-Visa for Turkey?
R: Most Western nationalities need an e-Visa. UK, US, Australian, and most EU citizens need to apply at evisa.gov.tr before departure. Cost: typically $50–60 USD, valid for 180 days with a maximum 90-day stay. EU citizens from some countries may enter without a visa — check your specific nationality. The e-Visa application takes 5–10 minutes and is processed within minutes to hours.

Î: Do I need an eSIM for Turkey?
R: Yes, strongly recommended — and it must be purchased BEFORE you arrive. Turkey is outside the EU, so your EU roaming allowance does not apply; carrier roaming typically costs €10–15/GB. A 5 GB / 30-day Turkey eSIM costs approximately $10–15 on Airalo. Critically: since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to major eSIM provider websites (Airalo, Saily, Holafly) from within Turkey. You cannot purchase after arrival.

Î: Does the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) work in Turkey?
R: No. Turkey is not an EU member and has no bilateral healthcare agreement with the EU. The EHIC is completely invalid in Turkey. Private travel insurance is your only medical protection. A single night in a private Turkish hospital can cost €500–2,000+. Travel insurance for Turkey costs €15–25 for a week.

Î: What currency should I use in Turkey?
R: Turkish lira (TRY) is the official currency. In major tourist areas (Antalya, Istanbul, resort hotels), euros and US dollars are widely accepted, often at competitive rates. In bazaars and local shops, Turkish lira is preferred and you will get better prices. Withdraw TRY from local ATMs (not at the airport — rates there are poor). Use Revolut or Wise for card payments to avoid foreign transaction fees.
