3. Tbilisi — 365 days visa-free and prices that feel impossible

€700–1,000/month | 30–50 Mbps | Coworking from €60/month

Georgia offers something genuinely unusual: 95 nationalities can enter and stay for up to 365 days visa-free. For non-EU nomads, this is an enormous advantage. For EU citizens, it is a bonus destination with extraordinary value.

Monthly budget: 1-bedroom apartment (Vera, Vake): €300–450. Khinkali (Georgian dumplings): €0.50 each. Natural Georgian wine at a bistro: €4–6/glass.

Unique advantages: natural wine culture (Georgia is one of the world's oldest wine regions — qvevri clay-vessel wine is extraordinary), Caucasian mountain scenery 30 minutes from the centre, and a food tradition that genuinely surprises first-time visitors.

Drawbacks: slower and less consistent internet than Western European capitals, less polished urban infrastructure.


4. Budapest — thermal baths between video calls

€1,000–1,500/month | 100+ Mbps | Coworking from €100/month

Budapest offers a rare balance: Eastern European prices with Western European infrastructure and cultural richness. Excellent coworking spaces, fast internet, and a café culture built for long laptop sessions — the Hungarian Kávéház tradition means lingering is expected and welcomed.

Monthly budget: 1-bedroom apartment (Erzsébet, Józsefváros): €500–700. Goulash soup (the national comfort food): €4–5. Craft beer at a ruin bar: €2.50.

The secret advantage: Széchenyi thermal baths as a lunch break. €25 entry, outdoor thermal pools at 36°C, one hour of complete disconnection in the middle of a working day. Few other nomad bases offer this specific kind of reset.

See: Things to do in Budapest .


5. Athens — history as your working backdrop

€1,100–1,600/month | 50–100 Mbps | Coworking from €100/month

Athens has undergone a visible renaissance — creative neighbourhoods (Koukaki, Exarcheia), coworking spaces on rooftops with Acropolis views, and a food scene that has genuinely surprised global food writers. Less mature as a nomad destination than Lisbon, which means better prices and a less crowded community.

Monthly budget: 1-bedroom apartment (Koukaki, Neos Kosmos): €550–800. Souvlaki: €3–4. Monthly metro + bus pass: €30.

Athens' key advantage: ferries to the Greek islands depart from Piraeus port, 30 minutes away. Hydra in 90 minutes, Santorini in 8 hours. Weekend island resets are genuinely accessible.

See: Things to do in Athens and Greece 2026 holiday guide .


6. Split — Adriatic from your desk

€1,200–1,700/month | 50–100 Mbps | Coworking from €120/month

Split became a serious nomad destination after 2020 and in 2026 is fully established. Diocletian's Palace — a 3rd-century Roman palace in which 3,000 people live — is your neighbourhood. Work mornings, sail to Hvar or Brač in the afternoons.

Monthly budget: 1-bedroom apartment (Manus, Varo): €600–900. Seafood risotto: €10–15. Ferry to Hvar: €8.

Critical seasonality: Spring (May–June) and autumn (September–October) are excellent. Summer (July–August) is overcrowded and prices triple. Winter is quiet and very affordable.


7. Lisbon — Europe's nomad capital

€1,200–1,800/month | 100+ Mbps | Coworking from €150/month

Lisbon became the reference nomad destination in Europe within a few years, for good reasons: 300 days of sun annually, the largest international nomad community in Europe, excellent coworking (Second Home, Heden, B.create), and an atmosphere that blends authentic Portuguese life with significant tech influence.

Monthly budget: 1-bedroom apartment (Mouraria, Anjos): €900–1,300. Full meal with wine at a local tasca: €8–12. Pastel de nata: €1.20. Coworking subscription: €150–250.

Community: the densest concentration of digital nomads in Europe. Weekly meetups and networking events. If you want to meet other nomads, it takes about one week.

Portugal D8 digital nomad visa: for non-EU nationals. Requirements: proof of income of minimum €3,500/month, health insurance, clean criminal record. One of the best-regarded nomad visas globally.

See: Portugal holiday guide 2026 .


8. Vienna — maximum quality, maximum cost

€1,800–2,500/month | 100+ Mbps | Coworking from €200/month

Vienna consistently ranks #1 globally for quality of life (Mercer, EIU). Impeccable public transport, UNESCO-recognised café culture (Kaffeehäuser tradition), and a functional orderliness that lets you focus on work without mental overhead.

Monthly budget: 1-bedroom apartment (Mariahilf, Neubau): €900–1,300. Wiener Schnitzel: €12–18. Monthly Wiener Linien transport pass: €51.

Who Vienna is for: nomads with higher income who prioritise quality over cost savings. And as a periodic base for 1–2 months — Vienna is hard to equal for sheer life quality.

See: Things to do in Vienna .


The 183-day tax trap — what nobody tells you

This is the topic absent from Instagram nomad guides that can cause real financial consequences.

The rule: spending more than 183 days in a single country in a calendar year may make you a tax resident there — even if you pay taxes at home.

What this means in practice:


7 months in Portugal while paying taxes in Romania or Germany → Portuguese tax authorities can argue you are a Portuguese tax resident

France and Germany actively pursue fiscal residency claims against digital nomads

Portugal specifically has the NHR (Non-Habitual Resident) regime — advantageous but requiring registration


The practical solution:


Stay no more than 5 months consecutively in any single destination

Rotate between 2–3 bases per year

Maintain your primary life connections in your home country (bank, doctor, property)

Consult an international tax specialist if your income exceeds €40,000/year


This is not tax evasion — it is the legal use of freedom of movement rights. Documentation matters.

What nobody tells you about nomad life

The loneliness is real. The first 2–3 weeks in a new city are often isolating. Invest actively in meeting people — coworking spaces are the fastest path to community.

Productivity is variable. Some nomads report working more effectively away from home distractions. Others find the novelty of new environments pulls their focus. A fixed work schedule regardless of destination is the most reliable foundation.

The real cost is higher than the listed cost. Add to monthly rent: setup costs (deposit + first month), moving logistics, coworking (cheap apartments often have poor internet), restaurant overspending in the first 2 weeks before you find the local spots, and the "tourist tax" on central restaurants.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Do I need a digital nomad visa for Europe?
R: EU/EEA citizens: no. Free movement and residence rights cover all 27 EU member states — no visa, no work permit, no formalities. Non-EU citizens (UK, US, Australian, Canadian): several countries offer specific digital nomad visas — Portugal D8 (min €3,500/month income), Croatia (€2,300/month), Greece, Spain and Estonia. Without one, most non-EU nationals can stay 90 days in Schengen on a tourist entry.

Î: What is the 183-day tax trap?
R: Spending more than 183 days in a single country in one calendar year may make you a tax resident there — even if you pay taxes at home. France, Germany and Belgium actively pursue fiscal residency claims. The practical solution: rotate between 2–3 bases, staying under 5 months in each. Consult an international tax specialist if your income exceeds €40,000/year.

Î: What internet speed do I need for remote work?
R: Email and Slack: 10 Mbps is sufficient. HD video calls (Zoom, Teams): 25+ Mbps. 4K video or simultaneous streaming: 50+ Mbps. All cities in our list exceed 30 Mbps at good coworking spaces. Bucharest and Lisbon have 100–300+ Mbps guaranteed at premium coworking venues.

Î: What is the cheapest European city for digital nomads?
R: Tirana, Albania: €600–900/month all-in. Tbilisi, Georgia: €700–1,000/month. Bucharest, Romania: €800–1,200/month. Among EU capitals specifically, Bucharest is by far the cheapest, significantly below Bratislava, Sofia or Budapest.

Î: What insurance do I need as a digital nomad?
R: Annual multi-trip insurance: €120–250/year covering all trips with a maximum 30–45 days per individual stay. Significantly cheaper than buying individual policies for each trip. For longer stays (2+ months in one place), look for expat-specific policies or long-stay travel insurance — standard annual multi-trip policies cap individual trips at 30–45 days.

Î: Which digital nomad visa in Europe is the best?
R: Portugal's D8 visa is generally considered the best: clear income requirement (€3,500/month), path to residency and eventually citizenship, stable country, great quality of life. Estonia's e-Residency + digital nomad visa combination is interesting for those wanting EU business registration. Croatia's visa is gaining popularity for its relatively simple requirements (€2,300/month income).

Î: eSIM or local SIM — what works better for nomads?
R: An eSIM with a European multi-country plan (30–40 countries) is the ideal nomad solution: no SIM swapping when crossing borders, your regular number stays active, and one plan covers your entire rotation. Within the EU/EEA, EU free roaming on your home plan is a valid free alternative for EU residents. For non-EU destinations (Georgia, Albania, UK), an eSIM is the economical choice.

Î: Coworking or apartment with good internet — which is more cost-effective?
R: Depends on your working style. Central apartment with fibre internet (€400–800/month) + occasional café days is cheaper overall. Coworking (€80–200/month) adds community, clear work-life separation, and networking. Most experienced nomads combine: coworking 3 days/week for focus and community, apartment the rest. The apartment-only approach works best if you can verify the internet speed before signing.

## Dubrovnik 2026: Game of Thrones, Medieval Walls & Hidden Beaches — Complete Guide

URL: https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/dubrovnik-city-break-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: city-breaks
Publicat: 2026-07-13
Actualizat: 2026-07-13
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/city-break-dubrovnik-2026

Descriere: Everything you need for a Dubrovnik city break in 2026. Walking the walls, Game of Thrones tours, best beaches, day trips, budget tips, and how to avoid the crowds.

Răspuns scurt: A 3-4 day Dubrovnik trip costs €350-800 per person depending on season and style. The city walls (€35, 2 hours, don't miss), a Game of Thrones walking tour (€25-40 via GetYourGuide, 2 hours), and the island of Lokrum (€15 return ferry, Iron Throne replica) are the top three experiences. Croatia uses the euro since 2023. Visit May-June or September to avoid cruise ship crowds — in peak summer, Dubrovnik limits Old Town visitors to 4,000 at a time.

Why Dubrovnik is special

There are beautiful coastal cities all over Europe. What makes Dubrovnik different is the scale of preservation. The Old Town — enclosed within 1,940 metres of medieval walls, with terracotta rooftops cascading toward impossible-blue water — looks essentially the same as it did 500 years ago. UNESCO listed it in 1979. HBO chose it as King's Landing. And unlike many tourist-heavy historic cities, Dubrovnik is small enough to feel intimate rather than overwhelming.

The catch? Dubrovnik knows it's special, and prices reflect it. This is Croatia's most expensive destination. But with smart timing (avoid peak summer) and local knowledge (eat away from Stradun), it's entirely manageable on a moderate budget.



The big three: walls, GoT, and Lokrum

1. Walking the city walls — Dubrovnik's #1 experience

The medieval walls encircle the entire Old Town — 1,940 metres, up to 25 metres high, with towers and bastions offering views over the terracotta rooftops and the Adriatic. Walking the complete circuit takes 1.5-2 hours.

Ticket: €35 (or included in Dubrovnik Pass). Enter from Ploče Gate (east side) — it's quieter than the main Pile Gate entrance and you walk the most photogenic section first.

When to go: At opening time (8:00 AM in summer) or after 5:00 PM. Midday is brutally hot and packed with cruise ship passengers. Bring water, a hat, and sunscreen — there's almost no shade.

2. Game of Thrones walking tour

Dubrovnik was the primary filming location for King's Landing from Season 2 to Season 8. A guided walking tour (2 hours, from €25 on GetYourGuide) takes you to the real locations with side-by-side comparisons on a tablet.

Key filming locations you'll visit:

Pile Gate: where Joffrey was pelted with dung during the riot scene. Jesuit Staircase: Cersei's Walk of Shame (the staircase in the south of the Old Town). Lovrijenac Fortress: the Red Keep exterior (separate entry €15, or free with walls ticket). Minčeta Tower: the House of the Undying from Season 2.

Even if you've never watched the show, the tour is worthwhile — the guides are excellent local historians who use GoT as a framework for telling Dubrovnik's real history.

3. Lokrum Island — the Iron Throne and tropical gardens

A 15-minute ferry from the Old Town port (€15 return, boats every 30 minutes). Lokrum served as Qarth in Season 2, and HBO donated a replica of the Iron Throne to the island — it sits in the Benedictine monastery courtyard.

Beyond GoT: Lokrum has a botanical garden planted by Maximilian of Habsburg in the 1860s, the "Dead Sea" (a small saltwater lake perfect for swimming), peacocks roaming freely, and rocky beaches with crystal-clear water. Budget 2-3 hours.



Beyond the big three: what else to see

Stradun (Placa)

The limestone-paved main street that runs through the Old Town like a spine. Onofrio's Large Fountain at one end, the Clock Tower at the other. In the evening, the entire city promenades here with gelato. It's the simplest and most timeless pleasure Dubrovnik offers.

Cable car to Mount Srđ

Four-minute ride to 412 metres for a panoramic view of the city, walls, islands, and open sea. €27 return. There's a restaurant at the top and the Homeland War Museum (telling the story of the 1991-92 siege, when this mountain was the front line). Best time: sunset.

Sea kayaking along the walls

Seeing the walls from sea level is a completely different perspective. Three-hour guided kayak tours (€40-50) take you along the walls, into sea caves, and to a swimming stop at Betina Beach. Most tours include snorkelling gear. Book a morning departure for calmer water.

Buža Bar

Not a bar so much as a hole in the city wall leading to a cliff-edge platform with tables perched above the water. Two locations (Buža I and Buža II); Buža II has the better view. Beer: €5. The sunset from here — walls behind you, open Adriatic ahead — is arguably better than any formal viewpoint.

Best beaches

Banje Beach: 5 minutes' walk east of Ploče Gate. The most convenient beach to the Old Town. Pebbly, with loungers available (€30/day for a sun bed, or free if you bring a towel). The view of the walls from the water is extraordinary.

Sveti Jakov: 15 minutes' walk from the Old Town (or take a bus to Sveti Jakov stop). Steeper access but far less crowded, with the same crystal water and a better panorama.

Lokrum beaches: Rocky platforms and small pebble coves on the island. The water clarity is absurd — you can see 10-15 metres down. Bring water shoes.

Lapad Beach: 20 minutes by bus from the Old Town. Sandy, family-friendly, with cafés and facilities. Where locals go when they want to avoid tourist beaches.

Where to eat (away from the tourist traps)

Stradun restaurants are overpriced. Walk one street parallel (Prijeko street is one, but it's nearly as touristy). Better: head to the residential streets behind the cathedral.

Konoba Dalmatino: Hidden in a back alley, one of the best restaurants in the Old Town. Black risotto €15, grilled fish €18. Reserve for dinner.

Pizzeria Tabasco: Locals' favourite. Pizza from €7, pasta from €9. Unpretentious, consistent, quick.

Dubravka 1836: Restaurant by Pile Gate with a terrace overlooking Lovrijenac. The view alone is worth it. Mains €15-25.

Pekara bakeries: Throughout the Old Town. Burek with cheese €3, fresh bread €1. Best quick breakfast.

Budget: 3 nights, per person

Category Budget Mid-range Comfort
Flights £80-150 £120-200 £180-300
Accommodation 3 nights €180 €300 €500
City walls + Lokrum €50 €50 €50
GoT tour €25 €40 €150 (private)
Food (3 days) €60 €120 €200
Cable car + kayak — €70 €70

Total ~€415 ~€720 ~€1,170

Practical tips

Currency: Euro (Croatia adopted it January 1, 2023). Card payments accepted nearly everywhere.

Visitor limits: The Old Town has a 4,000 simultaneous visitor cap. In peak summer (July-August), entry can be temporarily restricted at busy times (10:00 AM - 2:00 PM). Go early or late.

Cruise ship strategy: Check the port schedule online. On days with 3+ ships, 8,000-15,000 day-trippers flood the Old Town. Plan your walls walk and Old Town exploration on lighter days, and use cruise-heavy days for beaches, Lokrum, or kayaking.

Water: Tap water is safe and excellent. Bring a reusable bottle — buying water at tourist spots costs €3-4.

Getting there: Direct flights from London (easyJet, BA, Jet2) and other European cities in summer. From outside Europe, connect via Zagreb, Munich, or Istanbul.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is Dubrovnik worth visiting in 2026?
R: Absolutely — but timing matters. Dubrovnik in May-June or September-October is magical: uncrowded, warm, and affordable. In July-August it's beautiful but packed (4,000 person limit in Old Town) and expensive. The medieval walls, crystal-clear water, and Game of Thrones locations make it unlike anywhere else in Europe.

Î: How much does a Game of Thrones tour cost?
R: Walking tours of GoT filming locations start at €25 per person on GetYourGuide (2 hours, English-speaking guide). Extended tours including Lokrum Island (where you can sit on the Iron Throne) cost €35-50. Private tours for groups run €150-200. All tours include photo comparisons with actual scenes from the show.

Î: How expensive is Dubrovnik?
R: Dubrovnik is Croatia's most expensive city, but still cheaper than Western European equivalents. Budget lunch: €8-12. Restaurant dinner: €20-30. Beer on Stradun: €5. City walls ticket: €35. Accommodation ranges from €60/night (apartment in Lapad) to €200+ (Old Town boutique hotel). Eating and drinking one street away from the main drag saves 30%.

Î: When do cruise ships arrive in Dubrovnik?
R: Most cruise ships dock between 8:00 AM and 2:00 PM, disgorging 2,000-5,000 passengers each. If your visit overlaps with cruise ship days, hit the Old Town early (before 8:00 AM) or late (after 5:00 PM). Check the Dubrovnik Port Authority website for the daily cruise schedule — and avoid days with 3+ ships.

## Europe Holiday with Kids 2026: 10 Best Family Destinations with Real Costs

URL: https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/europe-holiday-with-kids-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: city-breaks
Publicat: 2026-07-30
Actualizat: 2026-07-30
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/vacanta-cu-copiii-europa-2026

Descriere: Best European holiday destinations for families in 2026. Real budgets, age-by-age recommendations, all-inclusive vs hotel, and the one rule that saves every family trip.

Răspuns scurt: The best European destinations for families with children in 2026: Antalya all-inclusive (€1,300–2,300 total for 2 adults + 2 children, 7 nights with flights), Crete (shallow water beaches perfect under age 6), Barcelona (Aquarium + Park Güell + beach), Budapest (thermal pools with slides), Vienna (Schönbrunn Zoo + Prater), MSC cruise (children under 12 free on most sailings), and Zakynthos or Corfu for island beaches. The single rule that saves every family holiday: one major attraction in the morning, pool or beach in the afternoon. More than this and the holiday becomes an exhausted march.

Travelling with children transforms every decision: the beach is no longer just scenic, it needs shallow water and no currents. The city break is no longer about finding the right restaurant, it is about finding the right pacing. The hotel is no longer about the view, it is about whether there are pool floats and whether the breakfast includes something other than local cuisine a five-year-old will refuse.

This guide is written from the reality of family travel — what each destination actually looks like with children at different ages, how to budget honestly, and the one scheduling rule that makes or breaks a family holiday.


Matching destination to age group

0–3 years: predictability, warm water, short flights

Infants and toddlers need routine. A successful holiday at this age is one where the sleep schedule is not completely disrupted, food is accessible, and there are a few quiet hours for the adults.

What works: Antalya all-inclusive (structured, diverse food, separate paddling pools), Crete or Rhodes (ultra-shallow beaches). Maximum flight time: 3–4 hours.

What does not work: intensive city breaks (Paris, Vienna with 10+ km walking), cruises (too much variability), remote destinations with limited medical facilities.

3–7 years: waterparks, animals, wonder

The golden age for family holidays. Everything is new, energy is unlimited, enthusiasm is genuine. Waterslides, dolphins, castles, theme parks — all work spectacularly.

What works: Antalya (waterpark), Crete (beaches + animals), Budapest (Széchenyi thermal pools with slides), Vienna (Schönbrunn Zoo).

8–12 years: adventure, discovery, some context

Children begin to understand history, can walk further, and can appreciate more variety. City breaks become manageable with good pacing.

What works: Barcelona (Sagrada Família + Aquarium + beach), London (interactive museums), MSC cruise (freedom on board), Prague (castle + submarine museum).

12–17 years: real experiences, less "for children"

Teenagers want authentic experiences — not children's clubs and energetic entertainment teams. Diving, water sports, cultural city breaks, open-air concerts.

What works: Dubrovnik (sea kayaking, city walls), Athens (Acropolis with real context), Greek islands (surfing, windsurfing, diving), Vienna (Naschmarkt + galleries).


The 10 best family destinations — complete with costs

1. Antalya, Turkey — unbeatable value for families

Antalya is the destination I recommend as a first instinct for almost any family with children under 12: Turkish all-inclusive hotels are built around families. Daily entertainment teams, children's clubs with structured programmes, waterparks with slides for all age groups, separate paddling pools for under-fives, and a sandy beach with gradual entry that stays at waist height for fifty metres.

What is included in AI: hotel waterpark (generally impressive), evening shows, beach sports, mini-golf, theatre, billiards, unlimited food and drinks. You need not leave the resort if you prefer not to.

Activities outside the hotel: Land of Legends theme park (€40/person — Turkey's largest), Antalya Aquarium (€25 adults, €15 children — the world's longest underwater tunnel), "Pirates of the Mediterranean" boat trip (€25–35, waterslides from the boat, swimming stops).

2. Crete — perfect beaches and Greece's most complete island

Crete is the most versatile Mediterranean destination for families. The island is 260 km long — turquoise lagoons with pink sand, mountains with spectacular gorges, and one of the world's most significant archaeological sites (the Palace of Knossos, 3,700 years old).

Why it works for young children: Elafonisi and Balos are lagoons with warm 20–25 cm water for hundreds of metres. No currents, no significant waves, no danger — a two-year-old plays in turquoise water on pink sand while you watch without anxiety.

Activities for children: CretAquarium Thalassocosmos (€10 adults, €6 children — one of the Mediterranean's largest), Dinosauria Park Gournes (€8/person), Palace of Knossos (€15 adults, free under 6 — told well, it fascinates children over 6+), boat trips to Balos lagoon (€20–25/person).

Family budget (2+2, 7 nights): €1,400–2,600 with flights depending on hotel category.

Best age: any age — Crete has something for every family configuration.

Read: Greece 2026 holiday guide .


3. Barcelona — urban beach + Gaudí + world-class aquarium

Barcelona works better for families than Rome, Paris, or Amsterdam because it combines a beach (Barceloneta — 20 minutes from the centre by metro) with cultural activities and a pace that does not exhaust children.

Essential activities for children: Aquarium Barcelona (€25 adults, €18 children — underwater tunnel, sharks, ocean sunfish), Park Güell (€10 with timed entry — the mosaics fascinate from age 3 upwards), Tibidabo (retro fairground on a mountaintop overlooking the city and sea, €25–35), IMAX at the Aquarium (3D, included with the ticket).

Practical tip: avoid July–August for families — 35°C in the city and maximum crowds. May–June or September: 24–28°C, half the queues, 20% lower prices.

Family budget (2+2, 5 nights): €1,600–2,800 with flights.

Pickpocket alert: Barcelona is Europe's most active city for pickpocketing. Crossbody bags for adults, children carry nothing of value. Read: travel scams in Europe 2026 .

4. Budapest — thermal pools with slides at one-third of Vienna's price

Budapest is the guaranteed surprise for families — a city break with excellent tourist infrastructure, prices 40% below Western Europe, and two activities that work perfectly with children: thermal pools with slides and architecture so spectacular it requires no explanation.

Széchenyi Thermal Baths: outdoor pools at 36–38°C, slides for children and adults, Olympic-size outdoor basin. €25 adults, €15 children. You spend 4–5 hours without thinking about anything else.

Activities for children: the Parliament building (tour adaptable for children over 8), Fishermen's Bastion (fairytale architecture free to enter), Danube Promenade (the Little Prince statue — universally loved by children), and Városliget City Park with lake and ice rink in winter.

Family budget (2+2, 4 nights): €800–1,400 with flights.

Read: Things to do in Budapest .


5. Vienna — the world's oldest zoo and the most beautiful imperial park

Vienna does not appear on typical "family destinations" lists, but works exceptionally well for families with children aged 5–14, particularly in combination with Schönbrunn and the Prater.

Schönbrunn Zoo: the world's oldest zoo (1752), with 700 species. Giant pandas, gorillas, penguins, and one of Europe's most beautiful botanical gardens as the backdrop. €22 adults, €10 children.

The Prater and Wiener Riesenrad: the 1897 Giant Ferris Wheel (€14, sees all of Vienna), and the Wurstelprater — a retro amusement park with 250 attractions. Entry to the Prater itself is free; you pay per attraction.

Naturhistorisches Museum: dinosaurs, meteorites, the 30,000-year-old Venus of Willendorf — a genuinely spectacular collection with short queues.

Family budget (2+2, 4 nights): €1,200–2,200 with flights.

Read: Things to do in Vienna .


6. MSC Mediterranean Cruise — children free, non-stop activities

A cruise with children sounds complicated in theory. In practice, it is one of the most efficient family holiday formats: you unpack once, food is included and varied, children have their own daily programme at the kids' club, and you see 4–5 destinations without organising anything.

MSC and children free: on most MSC Mediterranean itineraries, children under 12 sail without a supplement in the cabin. A family of four pays effectively for two adults.

Children's clubs on board: MSC offers Mini Club (ages 3–6), Junior Club (7–11), Teen Club (12–17) — all included in the price, with multilingual entertainment teams, daily activities, and supervised care.

Why it works so well with children: child is happy at kids' club → you are free at the pool → dinner together as a family → wake up in a new port. Repeat for 7 days.

7. Greek Islands — Zakynthos and Corfu for families

Not Santorini (difficult terrain, no beach) and not Mykonos (expensive and not designed for families) — for family holidays in the Greek islands, Zakynthos and Corfu are the correct choices.

Zakynthos: Navagio Beach (the shipwreck — accessible by boat, €20) is one of Greece's iconic images. The east coast beaches (Tsilivi, Kalamaki) have calm, shallow, sandy water. Bonus: loggerhead sea turtles nesting on the beach — responsibly organised observation trips (€20/person).

Corfu: as green as Ireland, as Mediterranean as Greece. Paleokastritsa — one of Europe's most beautiful bays, with turquoise water and yachts anchored in the cove. Best explored by rental car.

Read: Greece 2026 holiday guide .


8. London — free museums that beat any theme park

The Natural History Museum is free, has life-size dinosaur reconstructions and a meteorite collection. The Science Museum is free with a interactive flight simulator. The British Museum is free and has Egyptian mummies.

No European destination offers more free high-quality content for children aged 5–14 than London.

What costs money: London Zoo (€30/person), London Eye (€36/person — expensive but worth it with children), Harry Potter Studio Tour (€55/person, 30 km from central London — book months in advance).

Note: London is outside the EU since Brexit. Passport required (national ID insufficient for most non-EU nationals), travel insurance essential.

Family budget (2+2, 4 nights): €1,200–2,200 with flights.


9. Prague — Europe's most compact and safest city break

Prague is arguably the easiest European city break with children aged 7–14: compact (everything within 20–30 minutes on foot), safe, with excellent public transport, and with highlights that do not require lengthy historical explanations to impress.

Prague Castle and St Vitus Cathedral: the world's largest castle complex by area. Children over 7 are invariably impressed by the scale and the Gothic cathedral.

Underground Prague: the military museum with a real submarine (€6/person), the medieval underground passages in Vinohrady, and the Gothic cellars beneath the Old Town. Prague is a city with three levels — above ground, underground, and on the river (rowboats on the Vltava).

Family budget (2+2, 4 nights): €900–1,500 with flights.

Read: Things to do in Prague .


10. Romania — cheapest and most authentic family adventure

A road trip with children through Transylvania is a holiday they will talk about at school for months: Bran Castle (is Dracula real or not?), Peles Castle (a fairy-tale palace with 160 rooms), a bear spotted at the roadside near Predeal, and traditional food at a mountain guesthouse.

Family budget (2+2, 7 nights, everything included): €800–1,400 — the most affordable in the top ten.

Essential practical advice for families

The one-activity rule

One attraction in the morning, pool or beach in the afternoon, relaxed evening. How many family holidays have become an exhausted forced march at 35°C with a five-year-old crying at every corner? A family holiday is not a cultural tour — it is recovery for the whole family. Internalise this rule before departure.

Flights with children

Seats must be reserved on Wizz Air and Ryanair — without reservation, your child may be seated separately. €4–8/seat per segment is the cheapest safety cost in the entire holiday.

Boarding: families with children under 5 or with pushchairs typically board first at most airlines — check the specific policy before travel.

Hand luggage for families: rolled clothing (not folded), nappies in the first accessible compartment, tablet with offline downloads, snacks, and — critically — one change of clothes for each child in the hand luggage, not the hold bag . Turbulence and airsickness are real.

Travel insurance for families

A family policy (2 adults + dependent children) costs €30–60/week — cheaper than four separate policies. Essential checks: (1) trip cancellation included (children get ill the night before departure), (2) accompanying parent covered if child is hospitalised, (3) minimum €30,000 medical coverage.

Read the complete guide: travel insurance for children 2026 .

eSIM for the family

One eSIM with hotspot activated covers the whole family. €10–15 once instead of 4 × roaming charges. Mandatory for Turkey and UK. See: best eSIM by destination 2026 .

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: What is the cheapest European holiday destination for families?
R: Antalya, Turkey — all-inclusive hotels consistently offer the best value for families: €1,300–1,800 total for 2 adults + 2 children, 7 nights with flights. Children under 12 typically receive 30–70% discounts at most hotels. All-inclusive eliminates the cost and stress of meals entirely.

Î: Is an all-inclusive or hotel with breakfast better for families?
R: All-inclusive wins clearly for children under 8: it eliminates meal anxiety (there is always something a picky eater will accept in an AI buffet), removes financial surprises, and means you never have to search for a child-friendly restaurant each evening. For children over 10, a hotel with breakfast opens up more authentic local eating experiences.

Î: Which European destinations have the best beaches for young children?
R: Crete (Elafonisi and Balos lagoons — shallow turquoise water for hundreds of metres, no currents), Zakynthos east coast (Tsilivi, Kalamaki — calm, shallow, sandy), Corfu (Paleokastritsa), and Antalya (sandy beach with gradual entry). Avoid beaches with pebbles, steep drop-offs, or strong currents for children under 5.

Î: Should I book a cruise or a resort holiday for a family?
R: Depends on the children's ages. Under 3: resort is simpler — routine matters and the constant movement of a cruise is disruptive. Ages 3–17: cruise is often the better choice — you unpack once, children have structured programmes at the kids' club, and you see 4–5 destinations without any logistics. MSC offers children under 12 free on most sailings.

Î: What is the best age to start travelling with children?
R: There is no wrong age, but the experience differs significantly. Under 18 months: short flights only (2–3 hours), beach or pool resort format. Ages 2–5: any beach destination works well. Ages 6–12: city breaks become viable with careful activity pacing. Ages 12–17: adventure activities, diving, cultural immersion — almost any destination works.

Î: How much does a European family holiday cost?
R: Budget range for 2 adults + 2 children, 7 nights: Budapest or Romania €800–1,400 (most affordable), Antalya AI €1,300–2,300, Crete or Greek islands €1,400–2,600, Barcelona or Vienna €1,200–2,200, London €1,200–2,200, MSC cruise €1,800–3,200. These figures include flights, accommodation, food, and 2–3 paid activities.

Î: Do children need their own travel insurance?
R: Yes — children are not automatically covered by a parent's policy. They must be named on the policy or included under a defined family policy. Family travel insurance policies covering 2 adults and dependent children typically cost €30–60/week — cheaper than four separate policies. See the full guide: travel insurance for children 2026.

Î: Do children need a passport for European travel?
R: EU children can travel within the EU using a national ID card where applicable. For Turkey, the UK, and all non-EU destinations, a passport is required. Children under the age when national ID is issued (varies by country) will always need a passport for international travel. Plan renewals carefully — children's passports have shorter validity periods than adult passports.

## Florence 2026: The Complete Guide — Uffizi, Duomo, David, Oltrarno & the Secrets Most Visitors Never Find

URL: https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/florence-complete-guide-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: city-breaks
Publicat: 2026-07-31
Actualizat: 2026-07-31

Descriere: Florence 2026 complete guide. Uffizi and David tickets, Duomo dome booking, best neighbourhoods, budget tips and what to skip in the most-visited city in Italy.

Răspuns scurt: Florence (Firenze) is the city where the Renaissance was born and where more great art is concentrated per square kilometre than anywhere else on Earth. The historic centre is UNESCO World Heritage. Essential must-sees: Uffizi Gallery (Botticelli, Leonardo, Raphael — €25, book weeks ahead), Brunelleschi's Dome climb (463 steps, world's largest masonry dome — €30 Brunelleschi Pass, book in advance), Michelangelo's David at the Accademia (€16), and the Bargello (Italy's greatest Renaissance sculpture collection, almost no queue). Best kept secret: the Oltrarno neighbourhood across the Arno — artisan workshops, Brancacci Chapel, Bardini Garden — where Florentines actually live. Best time: April–June and September–October.

Florence stops you mid-stride. You turn a corner on a street that seems like any other and the Duomo fills the sky in front of you, appearing with no warning, impossible in its scale and beauty. You step into a church that looks unremarkable from the outside and find a Botticelli altarpiece lit by afternoon sun, with no one else in the room. This happens repeatedly in Florence, and it never stops being remarkable.

The city of roughly 360,000 people packs the most concentrated collection of Renaissance art and architecture on Earth into a compact historic centre that most visitors cover on foot. It is also a city that rewards depth: the same places look completely different depending on whether you know the story behind them. The Dome is beautiful from the outside. It becomes extraordinary when you understand that its builder invented the methods of its construction as he went, keeping them secret from everyone, including his own co-superintendent, in case he died or was replaced.

This guide covers everything: the major sites with the detail they deserve, the hidden places most visitors never find, the food you should eat, and the practical information that makes the difference between a frustrating visit and an unforgettable one.


When to Visit — The Honest Seasonal Guide

April–June: The best months for a first visit. Temperatures 18–26°C, wildflowers in the Tuscan countryside, the city's rose gardens in bloom (Giardino delle Rose above the Oltrarno is extraordinary in May), and crowds manageable outside of Easter weekend. Book the Uffizi and Dome 2–3 weeks ahead.

September–October: The second golden window. Temperatures 20–28°C in September, vineyard harvests beginning in October (the smell of fermenting Chianti fills the Oltrarno in October), tourists thinning after mid-September. The truffle season starts in San Miniato (white truffle, October–December) — some of the best pasta dishes of the year appear on menus.

July–August: Beautiful but intense. 30–38°C, crowded queues at every major site, museums and galleries packed by 10:00. The Dome sells out 6 weeks ahead. If you visit in August, book everything the moment you confirm dates, and schedule outdoor sightseeing for early morning.

November–March: Cold (5–12°C), many Tuscan day-trip destinations closed, but the city itself is atmospheric and completely navigable. The Uffizi and Accademia are almost walk-in accessible. The Christmas markets around Piazza Santa Croce are genuinely good.


The Neighbourhoods — How Florence Is Divided

Florence's historic centre is more compact than almost any major European capital. Santa Maria Novella station to the Uffizi is 15 minutes on foot. The Duomo to Piazzale Michelangelo is 30 minutes. Most visitors never need public transport.

Centro Storico — The Renaissance Core

The area between the Duomo, the Uffizi, Piazza della Repubblica, and Piazza Santa Croce. The streets here — Via dei Calzaiuoli, Via Porta Rossa, Borgo degli Albizi — are medieval in layout and contain the densest concentration of art and architecture.

The problem with staying too close to the Duomo: restaurants and cafés within 200 metres of the Duomo and Uffizi charge tourist prices for mediocre food. Walk two streets in any direction and the quality improves sharply.

San Lorenzo and the Mercato Centrale

North of the Duomo, the San Lorenzo market area is Florence's most local-feeling central neighbourhood. The Mercato Centrale (the iron-and-glass covered market, open from 07:00) has the best fresh produce, charcuterie, and cheese in the city. The upstairs food hall (open until midnight) is excellent for quick affordable lunches. The Sant'Ambrogio market, 10 minutes east, is even more local.

Santa Croce

The eastern quadrant of the historic centre, centring on the Basilica di Santa Croce — the "Pantheon of Florence," where Michelangelo, Galileo, Machiavelli, and Ghiberti are buried. The neighbourhood around it, particularly Via dei Benci and the streets toward the Arno, is where many locals eat and drink — less touristic than the Duomo area.

The Oltrarno — Where Florence Actually Lives

"Oltrarno" means "beyond the Arno" — the neighbourhood south of the river, reached by crossing the Ponte Vecchio or any of the other bridges. This is Florence for anyone who wants to go beyond the brochure. Artisan workshops producing leather goods, bookbinding, gilded frames, furniture restoration, and custom jewellery line the streets. The bars and restaurants on Piazza Santo Spirito are full of students and professionals, not tourists.

Sub-areas: San Frediano (the most working-class, most authentic, gentrifying slowly — Borgo San Frediano named one of Europe's coolest streets recently); San Niccolò (quieter, more residential, medieval gate Torre San Niccolò open for evening climbs in summer); Piazza Santo Spirito (the neighbourhood's social centre, morning market on weekdays, excellent nightlife).

The Oltrarno holds: Palazzo Pitti (five museums), Boboli Gardens, Bardini Garden, Forte di Belvedere, Brancacci Chapel, Piazzale Michelangelo, San Miniato al Monte. Cross the Arno and spend at least a full afternoon here.


The Major Sites — With the Detail They Deserve

The Duomo Complex — A Story of Genius, Rivalry, and Secrecy

The complex of Santa Maria del Fiore — cathedral, dome, bell tower (Campanile di Giotto), Baptistery, and the Opera del Duomo museum — is the heart of Florence and one of the most extraordinary concentrations of architecture and art from any period.

The Cathedral (free entry): Construction began in 1296 under Arnolfo di Cambio, continued under Giotto (who designed the bell tower) and Francesco Talenti, and concluded with Brunelleschi's dome in 1436 — a building project of 140 years. The white Carrara marble, green Prato serpentine, and red Maremma marble of the polychrome facade (completed 1887 in Gothic style that matches the original intent) create a surface that changes character entirely under different light conditions.

Brunelleschi's Dome — the whole story:

In 1418, after 122 years of construction, the cathedral had a vast octagonal hole where the dome should be. The problem: the opening was 42 metres wide, the planned dome was to rise 55 metres above the drum, and there was no known technique for building it without wooden centring — temporary scaffolding that normally supports an arch or dome during construction. But no tree in Europe was tall enough to span 42 metres, and even if the timber could be sourced, the weight would be unsustainable.

Filippo Brunelleschi, a goldsmith who had never built anything of significance, entered the competition for the dome commission. His fellow competitor was Lorenzo Ghiberti — the most celebrated Florentine artist of the moment, who had already beaten Brunelleschi in the 1401 competition for the Baptistery bronze doors (a loss that stung Brunelleschi so deeply he left Florence for Rome with his friend Donatello, where they spent years studying ancient Roman construction).

Brunelleschi won the dome commission, but the Opera del Duomo (the building authority) didn't fully trust him. They appointed Ghiberti as co-superintendent — a calculated insult to both men. The two rivals were forced to work together. Brunelleschi's response was to keep his methods completely secret: he told workers only what they needed for the next step, never revealing the overall plan, apparently fearing that if his techniques were known, the authorities might replace him.

His solution was a double shell — two domes, one inside the other, self-supporting through interlocking masonry rather than wooden centring. The inner dome provides structural integrity; the outer dome gives the dramatic silhouette visible from across Tuscany. The brickwork follows a herringbone pattern (a technique he invented or adapted) that distributes stress around the circular form. He built custom cranes and hoisting machinery to lift materials to the construction level, since the traditional method of workers carrying materials up ladders was impossible at this scale.

When Brunelleschi feigned illness in 1434 and refused to come to the site, everything stopped. Ghiberti, who had been present for 14 years without understanding the method, couldn't continue. (Some historians believe Ghiberti engineered Brunelleschi's arrest on a guild technicality the same year — a moment of bureaucratic revenge.) The authorities reinstated Brunelleschi immediately.

Ghiberti's assistant, the architect Giovanni da Prato, was so incensed by Brunelleschi's success that he wrote a sonnet calling Brunelleschi "a miserable and imbecile beast" and a "dark, deep wellspring of ignorance" and promised to kill himself if Brunelleschi's plan succeeded. The plan succeeded. Da Prato did not follow through.

The dome was consecrated on 25 March 1436 — the Feast of the Annunciation — by Pope Eugenius IV. Brunelleschi died ten years later, in 1446, and was buried in the cathedral crypt with his "divine intellect" commemorated on a memorial plaque. This was extraordinary — before him, the crypt was reserved for saints.

The dome climb (463 steps): You ascend between the two shells of the dome — the narrow staircase runs through the masonry, and at points you can see Vasari and Zuccari's Last Judgement fresco (painted 1572–1579, covering 3,600 m²) from the inside at close range. The view from the lantern at the top: Florence spread across the valley of the Arno, the Tuscan hills, and the red-tile roofscape below. Book the time slot well in advance — this sells out faster than any other Florence attraction.

Baptistery and the Gates of Paradise:

The Baptistery of San Giovanni (opposite the cathedral's main entrance) is one of Florence's oldest buildings — the exterior octagonal structure dates from the 11th–12th centuries, though the site has been a place of worship since Roman times.

Its three sets of bronze doors are Florence's greatest public artwork. The north doors were cast by Lorenzo Ghiberti after his famous 1401 competition victory. The east doors — made by Ghiberti between 1425 and 1452 after he won a second commission — were described by Michelangelo as "so beautiful they deserve to be the Gates of Paradise." The name stuck.

What's on display on the Baptistery today are high-quality copies. The originals were removed to prevent further weathering and are in the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo — where you can examine them at eye level, close enough to see the individual figures in each gilded panel.

Museo dell'Opera del Duomo: The museum that holds the originals of Ghiberti's Gates of Paradise, a Pietà by Michelangelo (the Pietà Bandini — an unfinished work he was making for his own tomb, which he broke in frustration and a student later repaired), Donatello's wooden Magdalene, and Luca della Robbia's original Cantoria (marble choir gallery with singing children). This museum is one of the great art repositories of Florence, and it's dramatically less crowded than the Uffizi or Accademia. Included in the Brunelleschi Pass.

Ticket options (2026):


Cathedral only: Free (queues for security)

Brunelleschi Pass (dome + baptistery + bell tower + crypt + museum): €30 , valid 72 hours

Giotto Pass (everything except dome): €20

Official booking: duomo.firenze.it


Uffizi Gallery — One of the World's Great Art Museums

The Uffizi (Galleria degli Uffizi) houses the Medici family's art collection — assembled over 200 years by the most powerful patrons in Renaissance history. What this means in practice: an unbroken sequence of masterpieces from Cimabue and Giotto in the 13th century through Botticelli, Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Raphael in the 15th and 16th, and on to Titian, Caravaggio, and Rembrandt. There are approximately 3,000 works in the collection; around 1,500 are on permanent display.

Room 10–14 — Botticelli: The rooms that most visitors come specifically to see. The Birth of Venus (1484–1486) and Primavera (1477–1482) are the Uffizi's most famous works, and genuinely extraordinary on a scale that reproduction doesn't prepare you for. The Birth of Venus is nearly 3 metres wide; the figure of Venus emerges from the foam of the sea with an expression that has been analysed for 500 years without definitive interpretation. Primavera — the allegory of spring — contains nine figures, each identifiable through mythological iconography, set against a dark grove. The orange-gold of the citrus fruits, the blue of Mercury's cloak, the translucent gauze of the Graces: Botticelli painted this for Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, probably to hang in a room where it would be studied for meaning, not merely admired for beauty.

Room 15 — Leonardo da Vinci: The Annunciation (1472–1475) and the unfinished Adoration of the Magi (1481). The Annunciation was painted when Leonardo was approximately 20, still working in Verrocchio's workshop — the figure of the angel Gabriel has already the characteristic softness of atmosphere that defines Leonardo's mature style.

Michelangelo's Doni Tondo (Room 35): The only completed panel painting by Michelangelo. The Holy Family in a circular frame (tondo), with young St John the Baptist and a group of nude male figures in the background. The colours are shocking — acidic green, electric orange — anticipating Mannerism by a generation. Michelangelo and the patron Agnolo Doni famously argued about the price after delivery.

Caravaggio (Rooms 90–93): Medusa on a shield (a self-portrait), Bacchus (possibly another self-portrait, the fruit slightly overripe), Sacrifice of Isaac, and the extraordinary Boy Being Bitten by a Lizard — in which the pain and shock on the boy's face is rendered with a psychological realism that no painter before Caravaggio had achieved.

The Uffizi terrace: Walk through the corridor connecting the west and east wings and emerge onto a loggia overlooking Piazza della Signoria and the Duomo — a panorama of Florence from a gallery window, free, no extra ticket, available during museum hours.

Practical: Entry €25–29 (prices vary by season). Book online at uffizi.it or via GetYourGuide weeks ahead in summer. Start with Room 2 (Cimabue and Giotto — the revolution that preceded the Renaissance) and work forward chronologically. Allow 2.5–3 hours minimum; 4–5 hours for a comprehensive visit. The museum is slightly east of the main tourist cluster — the piazza outside is quieter than the Duomo area and one of Florence's most beautiful public spaces.

Galleria dell'Accademia — Michelangelo's David

The Accademia Gallery was founded in 1784 by Grand Duke Pietro Leopoldo to teach art students from originals. The collection of 15th and 16th century paintings is genuinely good — but everyone comes for David.

Michelangelo's David (1501–1504): 5.17 metres tall, carved from a single block of Carrara marble that had been quarried in 1464 and abandoned for 35 years (because another sculptor had made a preliminary cut that was considered a ruinous mistake — Michelangelo used that cut for the legs). Michelangelo was 26 years old when he received the commission. He worked for two years in near-secrecy; the finished statue was unveiled in 1504 and moved to its original position outside Palazzo Vecchio, where it stood until 1873 (the version outside the Palazzo today is a copy; the original came to the Accademia for conservation).

The proportions are intentionally distorted: David's hands and head are larger than anatomically correct, because the statue was originally intended for a high position on Florence Cathedral's buttresses, where it would be seen from below. Michelangelo corrected for the distortion that viewing angle would create.

The expression — the slightly dilated left eye, the tensed jaw, the veins in the hand — depicts the moment before the confrontation with Goliath, not after. This is new: previous Davids (Donatello's, Verrocchio's) showed the victor after victory. Michelangelo shows the instant of highest psychological tension before the first stone is thrown.

The Prisoners (Prigioni): In the corridor leading to David, four unfinished sculptures — figures apparently struggling to emerge from the marble. These were made for the tomb of Pope Julius II (a project that consumed decades of Michelangelo's life and was never completed). They appear to be fighting the stone; the effect is of extraordinary physical and psychological tension. Michelangelo either left them unfinished deliberately or ran out of time. Either way, they are among his most moving works.

New (2026): Combined ticket Accademia + Bargello: €26, valid 48 hours. Highly recommended — see the two most important sculpture collections in Florence together.

Practical: Entry €16. Book at uffizi.it (Accademia tickets are on the same platform). Open Tuesday–Sunday. Queue without a ticket in summer can be 2 hours.

The Bargello — Italy's Greatest Renaissance Sculpture Museum

The most underrated major museum in Florence. Built in 1255 as Florence's first government building (the bargello was the chief of police, hence the name), converted to a prison in the 16th century, opened as a museum in 1865. Almost no tourists come here directly — they come to the Uffizi and Accademia. The Bargello opens at 08:15 and is quiet for the first 90 minutes every day.

What's here:

Donatello's bronze David (c.1440–1450): The first freestanding life-size nude sculpture since antiquity. David in a wide-brimmed hat, standing on Goliath's severed head, with an expression that is ambiguous, unsettling, and unlike anything sculpture had attempted since ancient Greece. Commissioned by Cosimo de' Medici for his private courtyard — this was a private object, not a public monument. The bronze casting alone was a technical achievement of the highest order for its time.

Michelangelo's Bacchus (1496–1497): One of his earliest surviving large sculptures, made for the Roman banker Jacopo Galli. A drunk Bacchus, slightly swaying, with a glazed expression and a cup of wine. Behind him, a small satyr stealing grapes from under his arm. The Romans who commissioned it wanted an antique work; they considered it so successful that some believed it actually was ancient.

The 1401 competition panels: Both Brunelleschi's and Ghiberti's bronze trial panels for the Baptistery door commission — both depicting the Sacrifice of Isaac — are in the Bargello, side by side. This is rare: you can examine the two competing submissions that changed the history of Renaissance art, in the same room, at the same time.

Cellini's Perseus model (1545–1554): The small-scale wax and bronze model Cellini made for the Perseus that stands in the Loggia dei Lanzi in Piazza della Signoria (the finished version is too large and too far away to examine properly). The Bargello model lets you see the extraordinary detail of Cellini's work close up.

Practical: Entry €10. Via del Proconsolo 4 (5 minutes from the Uffizi). Open 08:15–13:50 (Tuesday–Saturday, first and third Sunday, second and fourth Monday of each month — check before visiting). Combined with Accademia: €26.

Piazza della Signoria and the Loggia dei Lanzi

Florence's main civic square has been the political heart of the city since the 13th century. The Palazzo Vecchio (the medieval fortress-palace, now the city hall and a museum) anchors the piazza; a copy of Michelangelo's David stands outside the entrance where the original stood until 1873.

The Loggia dei Lanzi — the open-air sculpture gallery on the south side of the piazza — displays some of the most significant large-scale Renaissance bronzes in existence in the open air, for free. Cellini's Perseus Holding the Head of Medusa (1545–1554) and Giambologna's Rape of the Sabine Women (1583) are the highlights. The Perseus in particular — the culmination of Cellini's career, cast in one spectacular pour after repeated earlier failures — is here for anyone to walk up and look at, without a ticket, any time the piazza is open.

Palazzo Vecchio Museum: Entry approximately €19. Includes the Hall of the Five Hundred (the largest room in any palace of the Italian Renaissance, covered in frescoes by Vasari — but concealing, according to some scholars, a lost Leonardo da Vinci mural on the wall behind Vasari's paintings), the Study of Francesco I (a tiny jewel-box room entirely decorated in Mannerist panels), and the tower (Torre di Arnolfo) for panoramic views.


The Oltrarno — Florence's Other Half

Cross any bridge over the Arno and you're in a different city. The Oltrarno is where Florentines actually live, work, and eat — artisan workshops have operated here continuously since the Middle Ages, and unlike the centro storico, the Oltrarno has maintained a functioning neighbourhood rather than becoming entirely tourist-oriented.

Palazzo Pitti and Boboli Gardens

The Medici's principal residence from 1550, the Palazzo Pitti is a vast Renaissance palace containing five separate museums — the Palatine Gallery (the Medici's private art collection, with Raphael, Titian, Caravaggio, and Rubens hung wall-to-wall in the original rooms), the Royal Apartments, the Gallery of Modern Art, the Silver Museum, and the Carriage Museum.

The Boboli Gardens behind the palace — 45,000 m² of terraced Medici gardens with grottoes, fountains, sculptures, and views toward the city — are separately ticketed at €10–13 (or combined with Pitti at €22). A genuine respite from the city, best in the late afternoon.

Brancacci Chapel — The Sistine Chapel of the Early Renaissance

Inside the Church of Santa Maria del Carmine in San Frediano, the Brancacci Chapel contains frescoes painted between 1424 and 1427 by Masaccio, with later additions by Masolino and Filippino Lippi. Only 30 visitors are allowed in the chapel at a time.

Masaccio was approximately 22 years old when he began these paintings, and he died at 27 — but the Brancacci Chapel frescoes are among the most important works in the history of Western art. For the first time in painting, figures have weight, cast shadows, occupy space convincingly, and display facial expressions of genuine emotional complexity. The Tribute Money — in which Christ, the Apostles, and the tax collector interact in a landscape with actual atmospheric perspective — influenced Botticelli, Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Raphael directly. Michelangelo came to copy the Brancacci Chapel figures and had his nose broken by a fellow student he'd insulted over his sketches. The nose remained crooked for the rest of his life.

Entry: €10. Limited capacity — book in advance (cappellabrancacci.it) to guarantee a slot. Closed Tuesdays.

Bardini Garden — The Best View in Florence

On Costa San Giorgio, above the San Niccolò neighbourhood: the Bardini Garden is a Baroque-style terraced garden in a hillside position that gives continuous views toward the Duomo, the Arno, and the city. Unlike the crowded Boboli Gardens, Bardini is quiet — there are rarely more than a few dozen visitors at a time. In spring (typically late April to mid-May), the wisteria tunnel — a 100-metre pergola of century-old wisteria — blooms in dense purple and lilac cascades. The perfume is extraordinary. Entry: €10.

The Caffetteria delle Oblate: For a free Duomo view, enter the Oblate public library on Via dell'Oriuolo (near the Duomo, behind the cathedral's south side), take the stairs to the rooftop café. Order a coffee (€3) and look directly at the dome from the terrace. Almost no tourists know this exists. No ticket, no booking, open during library hours.

San Miniato al Monte

A 12th-century Romanesque church on a hilltop above the Oltrarno — one of the finest examples of Romanesque architecture in Tuscany, with an inlaid marble facade in white and green and extraordinary floor mosaics inside. The walk up from the Arno takes approximately 30 minutes (via the Rampe del Poggi from Piazzale Michelangelo, or directly uphill from San Niccolò).

The view from the church terrace is different from Piazzale Michelangelo (from which most people photograph Florence) — quieter, higher, with the Chianti hills visible to the south. The Benedictine monks who still inhabit the adjacent monastery sing Vespers at 17:30 daily. Arriving for Vespers means you hear the plainchant in a medieval space with no amplification while the late-afternoon light turns the city below to copper and gold. Free entry.


What Florence's Best Visitors Do Differently

Skip the Firenze Card. Unless you're planning to visit more than 8–10 museums in 72 hours, the card (€85+) is rarely cost-effective. Calculate your specific museum list and buy individual tickets.

The Uffizi before 09:00. The museum opens at 08:15 on weekdays. Visitors with booked first-entry slots see the Botticelli rooms almost alone. By 10:30, those same rooms are impenetrably crowded.

Avoid restaurants within 200 metres of the Duomo and Uffizi. This rule is reliable. Two streets in any direction in the Oltrarno, Sant'Ambrogio, or San Lorenzo area gives you local prices and quality. Specific streets: Borgo San Jacopo (Oltrarno), Via dei Serragli (San Frediano), Via dei Macci (Sant'Ambrogio).

The Bargello at opening. 08:15, first Sunday of the month when entry is free, is remarkable — you'll have Donatello's David and Michelangelo's Bacchus almost to yourself.

Eat lunch at Trattoria Mario. Via Rosina 2, near Mercato Centrale. Open since 1953, no reservations, communal tables, cash only, the menu changes daily. Arrive at 12:00 when it opens — by 12:30 there's a queue outside. Full meal with wine: €15–18.

Walk across Ponte Vecchio at 07:00. The bridge (built 1345, the only Florentine bridge the Germans didn't destroy in 1944) is lined with goldsmiths' shops — a function it has served since the 16th century, when the Medici ordered the original butchers and tanners to be evicted for reasons of smell. In the early morning before the shops open, you have it to yourself.

The Vasari Corridor: Built in 1565 for Cosimo I de' Medici to walk from the Palazzo Vecchio to Palazzo Pitti without descending to street level, the Corridor runs above the Ponte Vecchio shops and through the Uffizi. It was reopened for visits in 2024 after extensive renovation. Timed tickets required — check uffizi.it for current availability.


Food and Wine in Florence

What to Eat

Lampredotto: The fourth stomach of a cow, slow-braised, sliced thin, served in a semelle roll with salsa verde and optional spicy sauce. Florence's working-class street food, sold from trippaio carts for €4–5. Find it near Mercato Centrale, Mercato Sant'Ambrogio (the more local market, excellent for breakfast), and Piazza dei Cimatori near Piazza della Signoria.

Bistecca alla Fiorentina: The definitive Tuscan dish. A T-bone from Chianina IGP cattle (the huge white breed of the Val di Chiana valley south of Arezzo), grilled over hardwood embers to rare, finished with coarse salt and Tuscan olive oil. Minimum 1 kg, usually 1.2–1.5 kg, priced by weight (€50–65/kg in 2026). For two people. Non-negotiably rare — requesting well-done is a refusal. Trattoria dall'Oste (Via Luigi Alamanni) and Buca Lapi (Via del Trebbio) are the reliable addresses.

Pappa al pomodoro: Tuscan bread-and-tomato soup — stale bread rehydrated with fresh tomatoes, olive oil, and basil. Humble, extraordinary in quality. The bread Tuscans use is salt-free (unsalted bread has been a Tuscan tradition since the 12th century — there are different explanations including a salt trade tax — which means it goes stale faster and is perfectly designed for bread-based cooking).

Ribollita: Winter bread soup — cannellini beans, cavolo nero (black kale), carrots, celery, stale bread, olive oil. Literally "re-boiled" (the next day's reheated leftover soup is considered better than the first day's). Not a summer dish — order it October–March.

Crostini di fegatini: Chicken liver pâté on toasted bread, typically with capers and anchovies. The most common Tuscan antipasto. Good anywhere; extraordinary when the liver is fresh.

Peposo: Beef slow-cooked in Chianti with extraordinary quantities of whole black peppercorns. The origin story: Brunelleschi's kilnmen — the tile workers who fired the bricks for the Dome's construction — made this dish in their kilns using the cheapest cuts of meat and the cheapest wine, slow-cooking it for hours in the residual heat. Brunelleschi ate it on the building site.

Cantucci con vin santo: The Tuscan dessert ritual — twice-baked almond biscuits dipped in vin santo (a sweet amber dessert wine made from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia grapes). Never dip cantucci in espresso. Never skip the dipping. Vin santo comes in a small glass; dip and wait for the biscotto to soften slightly before eating.

Gelato: Florence has dozens of excellent gelaterie. Signals of quality: natural colours (pistachio is pale grey-green, not electric green), stored in metal containers with lids rather than displayed in towering peaks, a short seasonal menu. Gelateria dei Neri (Via dei Neri, near Santa Croce) and Sbrino (Via dei Serragli, Oltrarno) are consistently mentioned by locals.

Wine

Chianti Classico DOCG: The wine of the hills between Florence and Siena, made primarily from Sangiovese. The Gallo Nero (Black Rooster) seal on the bottle neck guarantees it's from the specific Chianti Classico zone. House Chianti at restaurants: €5–8 per quarter-litre. A bottle of good Chianti Classico: €25–40.

Brunello di Montalcino: Tuscany's most prestigious red, from the hills around Montalcino (90 minutes south). 100% Sangiovese Grosso, aged minimum 5 years before release. €60–150 per bottle at restaurants.

Vernaccia di San Gimignano: The white wine of San Gimignano (a day-trip destination from Florence). Dry, slightly mineral, perfect with lampredotto or white-fleshed fish.

Wine windows (buchette del vino): Small openings in the walls of Renaissance palazzi, used from the 16th century for selling wine directly from palazzo cellars to street buyers. They were revived during COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020 and many continue operating. Look for them in the Oltrarno — Babae on Via Santo Spirito has one.

Where to Eat

Trattoria Mario (Via Rosina 2): Open since 1953. Communal tables, no reservations, daily changing menu, cash only, lunch only. The most honest value in Florence. Arrive at 12:00 when it opens. Budget €15–18 for a full lunch with wine.

Buca dell'Orafo (Vicolo de' Girolami 28): Near the Ponte Vecchio. Old-school Florentine — ribollita, bistecca, pasta with wild boar ragù. Dinner reservations needed.

Trattoria Sostanza (Via del Porcellana 25, Oltrarno): The oldest trattoria in Florence (opened 1869, still family-run). Famous for its burro pasta (pasta with butter, in a manner that is richer than it sounds) and its butter-fried artichokes.

Fuori Porta (Via del Monte alle Croci 10, San Niccolò): The best wine bar in Florence for an Oltrarno afternoon — hundreds of Tuscan and Italian labels, excellent crostini and cheese plates, an outdoor terrace.


Day Trips from Florence

Siena (1h15 by bus or car)

Medieval rival of Florence, with one of the most beautiful main squares in the world — Piazza del Campo, the shell-shaped brick square where the Palio horse race takes place twice yearly (2 July and 16 August — if these dates align with your visit, attend, because the Palio is one of Europe's most intense sporting and cultural events). The Duomo of Siena has striped marble interior and a floor of inlaid marble panels — extraordinary. Direct bus from Sita Nord station in Florence: approximately €8 return.

Pisa (1h by train)

Primarily the Piazza dei Miracoli — the Cathedral, Baptistery, and Leaning Tower (currently 3.97 degrees off vertical after stabilisation work). Entry to the tower: €20, 300 steps, advance booking essential. The tower is better than you expect from the photos. The baptistery has extraordinary acoustics — ask a guide to demonstrate. Train: €9–13 return.

Chianti Countryside

The wine-producing hills between Florence and Siena — Greve in Chianti, Panzano, Radda, Castellina. Best by car, though cycling is possible on the quieter roads. Wine tastings at Castello di Brolio (the estate that codified the Chianti Classico blend in the 19th century, spectacular castle, guided tastings from €15), Antinori nel Chianti Classico (the ultra-modern winery buried in a hillside, extraordinary architecture, tasting from €25).

San Gimignano (1h20 by bus)

The medieval hill town of towers — in the Middle Ages, wealthy families competed by building towers (there were once 72; 14 survive, up to 54 metres). The interior of the Duomo has an extraordinary Last Judgement fresco cycle, and the town is small enough to cover on foot in 2–3 hours. Best visited early morning before the tour buses arrive at 10:00.


Getting To and Around Florence

Airports: Florence Amerigo Vespucci (FLR), 5 km from the city — small but well-connected. Pisa International (PSA) — 80 minutes by train, a viable alternative with more Ryanair and Wizz Air connections. Bologna Guglielmo Marconi (BLQ) — 90 minutes by train, useful for broader flight options.

From Bucharest: Direct flights to Pisa with Wizz Air from €50 return, and to Bologna or Rome (with onward train). Florence itself has limited direct budget connections; the Pisa or Bologna combination works well.

Train from Rome: High-speed Frecciarossa Roma Termini → Firenze SMN: 1h30, €25–60 depending on booking lead time.

In the city: Walk everywhere. Florence's historic centre is 2 km across. ZTL (restricted traffic zone) covers almost all of the historic centre — cars without special permits (hotels can arrange this) cannot enter. Taxis are available but rarely necessary for in-city movement. Trams run to the train station and suburbs but don't serve the main tourist areas.

Shoes: The cobblestone streets of Florence — the irregular sampietrini that pave every piazza and alley — are hard on thin soles and can be genuinely slippery after rain. Proper walking shoes are not optional.

Practical Tips

Book the Dome first. Before anything else. It sells out faster than the Uffizi.

The Brunelleschi Pass requires a timed entry for the dome. When you book, select your dome time slot — this is the anchor around which you schedule everything else. The other elements of the pass can be used flexibly within 72 hours.

Coperto (€2–3/person) is standard and legal at Florentine restaurants. Not a scam.

Restaurant hours: Most trattorias serve lunch 12:00–14:30 and dinner 19:30–22:00. Arriving at 19:30 means tourist competition; arriving at 20:30 means you eat alongside Florentines.

Dress code for churches: Covered shoulders and knees required at the Duomo, Santa Croce, Santa Maria Novella, and most churches. Shawls and cover-ups sold near entrances.

Gelato tip: Avoid any gelateria with fluorescent-coloured, towering peaks of gelato. These are tourist product, not real gelato. Natural colours, metal containers with lids, shorter menu.

Water: Tap water in Florence is safe and excellent (from the Apennine spring system). Ask for acqua del rubinetto (tap water) at restaurants. Free drinking fountains throughout the city.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How many days do you need in Florence?
R: Two full days is the absolute minimum to cover the Uffizi, the Duomo dome climb, Michelangelo's David, and the Ponte Vecchio. Three to four days lets you add the Oltrarno, the Bargello, Brancacci Chapel, Boboli Gardens, and a day trip to Siena, Pisa, or the Chianti countryside. A week allows you to genuinely understand the city. One day is enough for a single highlight — but not enough to understand what makes Florence extraordinary.

Î: How far in advance should I book Florence museums?
R: For July–August: Uffizi and Brunelleschi Dome climb should be booked 4–6 weeks ahead. The Dome sells out first — book the moment your dates are confirmed. David at the Accademia: 2–3 weeks ahead in peak season. For April–June and September–October: 2 weeks ahead for Uffizi and Dome, 1 week for Accademia. The Bargello almost never sells out — walk in any morning.

Î: What is the Brunelleschi Pass and is it worth it?
R: The Brunelleschi Pass (€30, valid 72 hours) covers the dome climb, Baptistery, Bell Tower, Crypt of Santa Reparata, and the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo. It is worth it — the Opera del Duomo museum alone (Ghiberti's original Gates of Paradise, Michelangelo's Pietà Bandini) would justify €15 on its own. The Giotto Pass (€20, excludes the dome) is worth it only if heights aren't your thing. The cathedral itself is free.

Î: What is the Bargello and why do most tourists miss it?
R: The Bargello Museum (Via del Proconsolo 4) is Italy's greatest Renaissance sculpture museum — and Florence's most underrated major site. It houses Donatello's bronze David (the first life-size nude sculpture since antiquity, 1440s), a second David by Michelangelo (Tondo Pitti), works by Verrocchio (Leonardo's teacher), Cellini's Perseus model, and extraordinary bronze reliefs by both Ghiberti and Brunelleschi from the 1401 Baptistery door competition. Entry: €10. It opens at 08:15 and is almost always quiet in the morning — the opposite of the Uffizi.

Î: What is the Oltrarno and why should I go?
R: The Oltrarno ('beyond the Arno') is the neighbourhood south of the Arno river, separated from the historic centre by the Ponte Vecchio and other bridges. It's where Florentines actually live — artisan workshops producing leather, bookbinding, goldsmithy, and furniture restoration; local wine bars; Palazzo Pitti with five museums and Boboli Gardens; the Brancacci Chapel (Masaccio's frescoes, the 'Sistine Chapel of the early Renaissance'); Bardini Garden (the best view of the Duomo in the city); and San Miniato al Monte. Cross the Arno and spend an afternoon here.

Î: What is lampredotto and should I try it?
R: Lampredotto is Florence's quintessential working-class street food — the fourth stomach of a cow (the abomasum), slow-braised until tender, sliced thin, and served in a crusty roll (semelle) with salsa verde (parsley, capers, anchovies) and optional spicy sauce. It's been sold from trippaio carts in Florence for centuries. It costs €4–5. Most visitors are apprehensive; most who try it are surprised. Find it at carts near Mercato Centrale, Mercato Sant'Ambrogio, and Piazza dei Cimatori.

Î: What is Bistecca alla Fiorentina?
R: A T-bone steak (minimum 1 kg, usually 1.2–1.5 kg) from Chianina IGP cattle — the large white breed of the Val di Chiana — grilled over hardwood embers and served rare, finished with coarse salt, pepper, and Tuscan olive oil. It is always priced by weight (approximately €50–65/kg in 2026) and intended for two people to share. If you ask for it well-done, the chef will refuse. This is not rudeness — it is the definition of the dish.

Î: What are Florence's best hidden viewpoints?
R: Three better than Piazzale Michelangelo (where every tour bus goes): the Bardini Garden terrace (€10 garden entry, views of the Duomo and Arno without crowds); the Caffetteria delle Oblate rooftop (a café inside the Oblate public library, free to enter, extraordinary Duomo view from the terrace, €3 for coffee); and San Miniato al Monte (a 12th-century Romanesque church 30 minutes' walk uphill from the Arno, free entry, most peaceful elevated view in the city — arrive for Vespers at 17:30 if you can).

## Formula 1 in Europe 2026: How to Attend a Grand Prix — Tickets, Budget & Best Races

URL: https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/formula-1-europe-grand-prix-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: city-breaks
Publicat: 2026-07-31
Actualizat: 2026-07-31
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/formula-1-europa-2026-grand-prix

Descriere: How to attend a European F1 Grand Prix in 2026. Best races, ticket prices, real budget, accommodation strategy and what to expect at your first GP weekend.

Răspuns scurt: The most accessible European Grand Prix for fans in Central and Eastern Europe is the Hungarian Grand Prix at Hungaroring (Budapest) — 1h20 by flight or 8h by car from Bucharest, with General Admission weekend tickets from €100–150. Other accessible European races: Italian GP at Monza (from €120 GA), Spanish GP at Barcelona (from €150), Austrian GP at Red Bull Ring (from €180). Total weekend budget (ticket + travel + accommodation): €400–1,200 per person depending on race and ticket category. The 2026 season introduces the first major technical regulation change since 2022 — new hybrid power units, active aerodynamics, and lighter cars that make every race unpredictable.

Television doesn't convey what Formula 1 actually is at a circuit. Watching a modern Formula 1 car pass at 300 km/h from 10 metres is a visceral physical experience — the speed, the downforce washing over you, the sound that resonates in your chest — that has no equivalent on a screen. A Grand Prix weekend is also a festival: 100,000+ people from dozens of countries, three days of activities from practice sessions to concerts, and a shared intensity that even non-fans find compelling.

From most European capitals, attending a Grand Prix is logistically simpler than most people assume. This guide covers the 2026 European calendar, which races to prioritise, exactly how to buy tickets, and what the realistic total cost looks like.

The 2026 Season — Why This Year Is Special

The 2026 Formula 1 season is the most technically significant in years. New regulations have fundamentally changed what the cars are and how they perform:

New power units: The 2026 engine regulations mandate a roughly 50/50 split between the internal combustion engine and the electric motor — up from approximately 80/20 in recent seasons. The total power output increases substantially, but the electric motor now plays a far more dominant role, particularly out of slow corners.

Active aerodynamics: Both front and rear wings now feature deployable elements that adjust automatically based on speed and corner type. This represents a completely new aerodynamic philosophy — cars will look and behave differently from their 2025 predecessors.

Manufacturer shake-up: 2026 sees new engine suppliers entering the sport. The competitive order from previous seasons is not guaranteed to continue. Teams that struggled in 2023–2025 may suddenly be competitive; dominant teams may face unexpected challenges.

What this means for spectators: Unpredictability. Multi-year regulation stability (like 2022–2025) tends to consolidate around one or two dominant teams. The 2026 reset creates a season where the championship battle may genuinely be open, overtaking patterns will be different, and each race weekend holds unusual interest even for veteran fans.


The European Calendar — 2026 Races

The European portion of the F1 calendar typically runs May through October, forming the dense core of the season. Key 2026 European rounds:
