The Five Best European GPs — Detailed Guide

1. Hungarian Grand Prix — Hungaroring, Budapest

The case for it: For fans in Central and Eastern Europe, Hungaroring is the obvious starting point. Budapest is 8 hours by car from Bucharest, 1h20 by direct flight (Wizz Air, from €30 return). The circuit is 19 km from the city centre. Tickets are among the most affordable on the calendar. And the Hungaroring's natural amphitheatre layout means you can see a substantial portion of the circuit from the GA hill sections without paying grandstand prices.

The circuit: A 4.381 km technical circuit with 14 corners, low-speed and high-downforce. Not the fastest or most dramatic, but extremely competitive — overtaking is difficult, meaning race strategy and pit stop execution matter enormously. The on-track action is actually more interesting than at faster circuits because position changes require genuine skill rather than just raw speed.

Ticket options:

Type Price What you get
General Admission (weekend) €100–150 Access to hill sections with 60-70% circuit visibility
Grandstand K (Turn 3) €200–280 Fixed seat, good view of challenging hairpin
Grandstand B (Start/Finish) €300–450 Full pit lane and start view
Premium grandstands €400–600 Best views, some with hospitality

Accommodation: Stay in Budapest city centre (not at the circuit — options are extremely limited). Hotel prices increase 50–100% for GP weekend — book 3–4 months ahead. The suburban rail to the circuit (30 minutes, €3) is faster than driving on race day.

City break combination: Budapest has enough to fill 2 full days alongside the GP weekend. The thermal baths, Parliament building, ruin bars, and Danube cruise make it an excellent combination.

👉 Full Budapest guide: Things to Do in Budapest

Flights: Direct Bucharest → Budapest from €30 return (Wizz Air). Book 6–8 weeks ahead.


2. Italian Grand Prix — Monza

The case for it: Monza has the most intense atmosphere of any Grand Prix on the calendar. The Parco di Monza is Italy's fastest circuit — cars reach 340+ km/h on the main straight — and the tifosi (Ferrari fans) turn it into something between a rock concert and a religious event. If Ferrari scores points, the post-race atmosphere on the track (fans flood the pit straight legally after the chequered flag) is extraordinary.

The circuit: 5.793 km, designed in 1922, the oldest purpose-built racing facility still in active use. The Lesmo curves, Ascari chicane, and the Parabolica at the far end of the track are iconic. The high-speed nature of Monza means that aerodynamic efficiency matters most — teams bring low-downforce setups that look visually different from other races.

Ticket options:

Type Price What you get
General Admission (weekend) €120–180 Access to specified GA areas — less good than Hungaroring GA
Grandstand Parabolica €250–380 The last corner — watch cars brake from 340 to 80 km/h
Grandstand Tribune Centrale €350–550 Pit straight and start/finish
Tribune K (Curva Grande) €200–300 Fastest section of the circuit

Recommendation: The Parabolica grandstand (last corner) is outstanding value at Monza. You watch cars brake from 340 km/h to 80 km/h, then accelerate through the fastest corner on the circuit. The braking point is one of the most dramatic moments in motorsport repeated 53 times per race.

Getting there: Flights from Bucharest to Milan (Malpensa or Bergamo Orio al Serio) from €45 return (Wizz Air/Ryanair). From Milan, the suburban S8 train to Monza takes 20 minutes (€2.80) from Garibaldi station. Circuit shuttle buses run from Monza station during GP week.

Accommodation: Milan city centre (not Monza — hotel options are very limited). Expect hotel prices to triple for GP weekend in September. Book 4–5 months ahead. Hotels in Bergamo (30 minutes by S8 from Garibaldi via Bergamo airport) are a good alternative.

The post-race invasion: After the chequered flag, Monza has a unique tradition: spectators are allowed onto the pit straight to celebrate. If Ferrari has had a good race, the scene — 50,000+ people in red filling the circuit, standing on the track that's been driven by Schumacher, Senna, and Fangio — is unlike anything else in sport.


3. Austrian Grand Prix — Red Bull Ring, Spielberg

The case for it: The Red Bull Ring sits in a natural bowl in the Styrian Alps — the circuit climbs through the mountains with extraordinary backdrop scenery. The GA experience here rivals anywhere on the calendar: the hills give views of a significant proportion of the circuit, and the camping culture creates a festival atmosphere over the full weekend. The circuit is also relatively short (4.318 km) with high overtaking potential, making the racing itself exciting.

The atmosphere: Dominated by Dutch fans (Max Verstappen's home-away-from-home given Red Bull's Austrian identity). A sea of orange — surprisingly good-humoured and festive, with organised fan areas and camping villages.

Getting there: Fly to Vienna (1h15 from Bucharest, Wizz Air from €40 return) or Graz (45 minutes closer to the circuit). Car rental from either airport: a 2-hour scenic drive through the Styrian countryside. This is one race where renting a car genuinely adds to the experience — the Grossglockner High Alpine Road is 90 minutes from the circuit and one of Europe's great mountain drives.

👉 Car rental: GetRentacar

Weather note: The Styrian Alps create unpredictable weather — sunshine at the start/finish line, rain at Turn 9, hail 20 minutes later. Bring a waterproof layer. The 2023 Austrian GP had multiple weather interruptions. This also makes the racing more interesting.


4. British Grand Prix — Silverstone

The case for it: Silverstone is the home of British motorsport and the largest Grand Prix crowd in Europe — typically 150,000+ across the weekend. The circuit itself is one of the fastest, with Copse, Maggotts, Becketts, and Chapel creating a sequence of ultra-high-speed corners that rewards pure aerodynamic excellence. The British crowd is knowledgeable, passionate, and enthusiastic about all teams — not just home favourites.

Ticket prices: Higher than the Central European races — GA weekend from £130, grandstands from £200–600. The Wing (pit straight complex) is the premium experience.

Getting there: Fly to London (Heathrow, Luton, or Stansted), then rail to Milton Keynes Central (1h15 from Euston) + shuttle bus to the circuit. For fans already in the UK, driving is practical. For Central European fans, this is the most expensive GP on the list in total trip cost.

Book early: Silverstone consistently sells out popular grandstands 6+ months in advance.


5. Belgian Grand Prix — Spa-Francorchamps

The case for it: Spa is considered by many drivers and fans to be the greatest circuit in Formula 1. The 7.004 km layout through the Ardennes forest includes Eau Rouge/Raidillon (the uphill blind corner sequence after the first chicane), Pouhon, Stavelot, and Blanchimont — corners that expose the full capability of a modern F1 car. Racing in the rain at Spa, which happens with reasonable frequency, is sometimes the most dramatic spectacle in the sport.

Weather: Belgium in late July is genuinely unpredictable. Rain ponchos are essential, not optional. Wet weather at Spa creates some of the most dramatic racing conditions in motorsport — the combination of the circuit's gradient changes, the mix of high-speed and low-speed corners, and the variable weather across different parts of the circuit makes for extraordinary racing.

Getting there: Fly to Brussels or Cologne/Bonn, then drive (~1.5h to Spa). The circuit is in the Ardennes — a beautiful area with villages, spa towns (Spa city itself, from which the circuit takes its name), and excellent Belgian food and beer.


How to Buy F1 Tickets — Avoiding the Scams

Formula 1 tickets are among the most frequently counterfeited sporting event tickets in Europe. The modern ticketing system uses digital tickets with unique QR codes verified against your name and ID at the gate — meaning a ticket bought from an unauthorised secondary seller won't scan correctly.

Official channels only:


formula1.com — official F1 tickets page with links to all circuit ticketing

Individual circuit websites (hungaroring.hu, monzanet.it, etc.) — same inventory, sometimes with circuit-specific packages

Official F1 hospitality — for Paddock Club and premium experiences


What to avoid:


Viagogo, StubHub, and general secondary market sites — tickets may be invalid, prices are always inflated (2–5×), and you have no recourse if the ticket doesn't scan

Social media sellers — fake tickets are indistinguishable from real ones until you're at the gate

"Too good to be true" prices — GA tickets for Monza at €40 are fake. There is no legitimate reason for tickets to be below face value at a major GP


The resale test: Formula 1's official resale platform (if available for your race) allows ticket resale at face value or up to a defined maximum. Anything above this on unofficial platforms is grey-market at best, fraudulent at worst.


General Admission vs Grandstand — Making the Right Choice

This is the most consequential ticket decision for first-time attendees.

When GA is the right choice

Hungaroring: The hill sections (particularly the main straight hill and the final sector hill) give views of 60–70% of the circuit from a single spot. GA here is genuinely superior to some grandstand positions for overall race watching.

Red Bull Ring: The bowl shape of the circuit means GA spectators on the outer banking can see the majority of the circuit. The camping culture means GA is the full Red Bull Ring experience.

Spa: The GA area includes access to the legendary Eau Rouge section — watching F1 cars take Eau Rouge flat-out from a few metres away is one of the most visceral experiences in motorsport.

When grandstand is the right choice

Monza: The flat, forest-lined circuit layout severely limits GA views. Grandstands are the only way to watch a substantial portion of the race.

Barcelona: GA at Catalunya is restricted and has limited views of key sections. Grandstands add significantly to the experience.

Silverstone: GA exists but the best views (Club corner, Copse) require being in specific areas early. Grandstands for The Wing complex give the full atmosphere.

Monaco: No GA exists. Grandstands from €500; without one, you watch from public vantage points with very limited views. Monaco is primarily an atmosphere and social event rather than a racing spectacle.


The Full Weekend — What Happens When

Friday — Free Practice (FP1 and FP2)

Two 60-minute sessions where teams test setups and gather data. The atmosphere is relaxed — no pressure, drivers can try experimental setups. This is the best day to explore the circuit, find your GA spots, and watch without the crowd intensity of race day. Friday is often the most underrated day — prices are lower for Friday-only tickets, the circuit is accessible, and you get 2 hours of F1 cars on track.

In 2026, some race weekends use Sprint format (Sprint Qualifying Saturday + Sprint race Sunday) — check the format for your specific race.

Saturday — Qualifying

The day that determines the grid. A one-lap shootout across three sessions (Q1, Q2, Q3) where each driver's best lap determines their starting position. Q3 — the top 10 fight for pole position — is typically 15 minutes of the most concentrated, tension-filled motorsport of the weekend. The crowd reaction to a pole position lap is the sharpest collective emotion of the weekend.

Sunday — Race Day

The main event. Arrive early (gates typically open 4–5 hours before the race) to claim GA positions if you don't have a fixed grandstand seat. The grid walk, national anthem, and the formation lap build the atmosphere to an almost overwhelming intensity before lights out.

Race start: the most visually dramatic moment of any GP. Twenty cars going from a standing start to 200 km/h in under 4 seconds, funnelling into the first braking zone, creates a moment of chaos and spectacle that no screen can replicate.

Practical Tips for Your First Grand Prix

Ear protection is non-negotiable. Even with 2026's revised power units (which have a different sound character from the V8 era), modern F1 cars at 10 metres produce levels that will cause discomfort or hearing damage without protection. Disposable foam earplugs (€1–2) work fine; proper motorsport headphones allow you to hear commentary while protecting your ears.

Download the F1 app before leaving home. The official F1 app (subscription required) streams live race radio from all team-driver combinations, plus live timing with tyre strategies visible. At the circuit, following strategy on your phone while watching on track transforms the experience — you understand why a car pits when it does, which driver is on fresh tyres, who's on a different strategy.

Arrive Friday, stay Sunday. A single-day (Sunday only) GP ticket misses the best parts. Practice sessions show you things race day doesn't — experimental setups, driver development, and a relaxed atmosphere. If budget forces a choice, Sunday + Saturday (qualifying) is the minimum meaningful experience.

Never drive to the circuit on race day. Parking fills 3–4 hours before the race, and post-race traffic can mean 3+ hours to exit a car park that's 2 km from the circuit. Train (Hungaroring, Monza, Barcelona) or shuttle bus is always faster. Check the specific circuit's recommended transport before you go.

Water and food inside the circuit. Food and drink inside F1 circuits is expensive (€6–10 for a beer, €12–15 for basic food). Most circuits allow you to bring in a sealed water bottle and some food. Check the specific circuit's bag policy and bring accordingly.

Combine the race with a city break. Every European GP venue has a major city nearby. Hungaroring + Budapest, Monza + Milan, Red Bull Ring + Vienna, Spa + Brussels — the GP weekend is 3 days, and the surrounding area fills a 5-day trip naturally.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How much do Formula 1 tickets cost?
R: General Admission (GA, no fixed seat): €100–200 for a full weekend (Friday–Sunday) at most European races. Grandstand seats: €200–600. Premium grandstands (pit straight, Turn 1): €400–1,200. Paddock Club (hospitality, track access): €3,000–6,000. Monaco is the most expensive (no GA, grandstands from €500). Hungaroring and Red Bull Ring are among the most affordable on the calendar.

Î: Where do I buy official F1 tickets?
R: Directly from formula1.com or the individual circuit websites (hungaroring.hu, monzanet.it, circuitcat.com, formula1.at for Red Bull Ring). Do NOT buy from unauthorised resale sites — fake tickets are common at major GPs and you will be refused entry. Formula 1 now uses digital tickets with unique QR codes verified against your name at the gate.

Î: General Admission or grandstand — which is better?
R: GA is excellent at circuits with natural geography — Hungaroring and Red Bull Ring have hills from which you can see 60–70% of the track without a fixed seat, and the atmosphere is festival-like. At Monza and Barcelona, grandstands are worth the premium as the flat circuit layout limits GA viewing. For your first GP, Hungaroring GA is the best introduction: cheap, social, great sightlines from the hills.

Î: What is the best European Grand Prix for a first-time attendee?
R: Hungarian GP (Hungaroring, Budapest): closest to Central/Eastern Europe, most affordable tickets, compact circuit where you see a large percentage of the race, and you can combine it with a Budapest city break. Monza (Italian GP) has the most intense atmosphere — if Ferrari scores points, the tifosi create an experience unlike anything else in sport. Barcelona is good but hotter and more expensive.

Î: What changed in F1 for the 2026 season?
R: 2026 introduces the largest technical regulation change since 2022. New power units with a 50/50 split between internal combustion and electric motor (previously ~80/20). Active aerodynamics — deployable front and rear wings that adjust automatically. Lighter cars overall. The result: a complete reset of the competitive order, with teams that struggled in 2023–2025 potentially competitive and vice versa. Every race in 2026 has an element of genuine unpredictability that multi-year regulations eliminate.

Î: How far in advance should I buy F1 tickets?
R: Monaco: 6–12 months ahead (sells out almost immediately). Silverstone, Monza, Spa: 4–6 months ahead for preferred grandstands. Hungaroring, Red Bull Ring, Barcelona: 2–3 months ahead is usually fine for GA. For 2026, with the new regulations creating unusual interest, buying 3–4 months ahead for any race is the safe approach.

Î: What should I bring to a Formula 1 race?
R: Ear protection (essential — even the 2026 engines are very loud at close range), sunscreen SPF50+, refillable water bottle (free water at most circuits), comfortable walking shoes (you cover 5–10 km on race weekend), portable phone charger, lightweight rain poncho (mountain circuits like Red Bull Ring change weather quickly), and a cap or hat. Download the official F1 app before arriving — it streams race radio and live timing so you can follow strategy in real time.

## Greece 2026 Holiday Guide: Which Island, Real Costs, When to Go and What to Know

URL: https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/greece-2026-holiday-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: city-breaks
Publicat: 2026-07-29
Actualizat: 2026-07-29
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/grecia-2026-ghid-vacanta

Descriere: Complete guide to a Greece holiday in 2026. Which island suits you, real prices by destination, how to get there, best beaches, car rental tips, and why September beats August.

Răspuns scurt: Greece is Europe's most popular summer destination in 2026, with Crete, Rhodes, Corfu, Santorini and Mykonos leading bookings. A 7-night holiday for two costs €750–3,500 depending on island and season. The sweet spot: Crete or Rhodes in September — same excellent weather, 20–30% lower prices, far fewer crowds. EU citizens need no visa. No eSIM needed (EU free roaming applies). A rental car is essential on large islands like Crete and Rhodes.

Greece in 2026 is not just a destination — it is the destination. Bookings are up sharply across all markets as travellers who tried Dubai or Egypt and found prices and logistics disappointing have redirected to a proven, accessible, spectacular destination that delivers reliably. The result: popular islands are fully booked earlier, and the case for September has never been stronger. Here is everything you need to plan the right trip.

Why Greece works so well as a holiday destination

The case for Greece is not complicated. Within 2–3 hours from most of Europe, you have:


Water that is genuinely turquoise — not "travel brochure turquoise," actual turquoise, visible from the beach

Reliable summer weather from May through October with virtually zero rain

Food that is among the best in the Mediterranean and meaningfully cheaper than Italy or Spain

History layered so densely that a beach day and a Bronze Age palace are often on the same road

Infrastructure that has improved dramatically over the past decade — good roads, reliable ferries, consistent accommodation quality


What Greece cannot offer: city sophistication at the level of Paris or Rome, world-class museums (the National Archaeological Museum in Athens is exceptional, but the islands are not museum destinations), or significant nightlife outside Mykonos and Rhodes Town.

For a beach-centred, culturally enriched, affordable Mediterranean holiday, Greece beats comparable alternatives at almost every price point.

Island by island: which one is right for you

Crete — the one that does everything

Crete is Greece's largest island at 260 km long and feels, in many respects, like a country of its own. It has mountains over 2,400 metres, Europe's longest gorge (Samaria Gorge, 16 km), three distinct regions with different characters, Bronze Age palaces (Knossos, the centre of Minoan civilisation 3,700 years ago), some of the most extraordinary beaches in Europe, and a culinary tradition that many food writers argue is the best in Greece.

The beaches: Elafonisi (pink-tinted sand, shallow turquoise lagoon — genuinely one of the most beautiful beaches on the continent), Balos (accessed by boat or rough road, three shades of blue in one lagoon), Preveli (palm forest, river, beach), Falassarna (wide, sandy, facing west for spectacular sunsets), Vai (unique palm forest beach in the east).

Beyond the beach: the Palace of Knossos (€15 entry, 30 minutes from Heraklion — mandatory), the old Venetian harbours of Chania and Rethymno, the White Mountains, the Archaeological Museum of Heraklion (one of the best in the world), and villages in the inland mountains where little has changed in decades.

Getting there: direct flights from most European cities to Heraklion (HER) or Chania (CHQ). Flight time from London: 3.5 hours. From Amsterdam or Paris: 3.5–4 hours.

Prices (7 nights, 2 people, 2026):


Budget (self-catering apartment, own food): €700–1,100 including flights

Mid-range (3-star B&B hotel, some restaurants): €1,000–1,600 including flights

All-inclusive 4-star: €1,200–2,000 including flights

Luxury: €2,500–5,000+


Best for: families with children, first-time visitors to Greece, travellers who want beach AND culture, food enthusiasts, anyone who wants the most complete Greece experience.

Worst time to visit: the third week of August — extremely crowded and at peak prices. Book early or go September.

Rhodes — the lively one with history

Rhodes has the best medieval old town in Greece — a UNESCO-listed walled city built by the Knights of St. John in the 14th century, with cobbled streets, the Palace of the Grand Master, and a maze of alleyways that somehow still feels inhabited and alive rather than museified.

Beyond the old town: Lindos (a spectacularly situated village with an acropolis above a white-painted hillside above a turquoise bay — the most photographed scene in Rhodes), excellent beaches on the west coast (Faliraki, Tsambika), and the butterfly valley of Petaloudes.

Character: more animated than Crete, with a stronger nightlife scene (Faliraki has one of the liveliest strips in Greece), more package-holiday infrastructure, and a slightly younger crowd on average.

Getting there: direct flights from most European airports to Rhodes (RHO). Flight time from London: 4 hours.

Prices (7 nights, 2 people, 2026): similar to Crete — €800–2,000 including flights depending on accommodation category.

Best for: couples (mix of history and beach), young adults, people who want the Old Town experience alongside beach time.

Car: useful for reaching the south of the island (Prasonisi, Gennadi) — less essential than in Crete given better public transport.

Santorini — the expensive icon

Santorini is the most immediately recognisable Greek island — the caldera, the blue-domed churches of Oia, the white cubic architecture draped over volcanic cliffs 300 metres above the sea. These images are accurate and beautiful. So are the crowds and the prices.

In July and August, Santorini hosts approximately 15,000 cruise passengers per day on an island of 15,000 permanent residents. The main streets of Oia are shoulder-to-shoulder by 4 PM, and the famous sunset spot requires positioning yourself by 5 PM at the latest.

The honest Santorini assessment: it is spectacular, unmistakably beautiful, and genuinely worth visiting — in the right conditions. Those conditions are: September or October (crowds drop dramatically, prices fall 30–40%), arriving by ferry rather than tender (cruise passengers have the least pleasant experience), and staying in Imerovigli or Akrotiri rather than Oia (equally beautiful, significantly less crowded).

What to do: caldera walk from Fira to Oia (9 km, 3–4 hours, free), boat tour of the caldera including hot springs and the volcano (€30–60), wine tasting at one of the volcanic-soil wineries (Santo Wines, Domaine Sigalas), Akrotiri Bronze Age excavation (€12 — a Minoan city preserved under volcanic ash, extraordinary).

What to skip: the cable car in peak season (queue is 45+ minutes — the donkey path or walking path is faster), the "instagrammable" blue dome churches in Oia at any time after 10 AM in summer.

Prices (7 nights, 2 people, high season): €2,000–5,000 — the most expensive Greek island by a significant margin. September: €1,400–3,000.

Best for: couples, honeymoons, special occasions, people with flexibility to go in September.

Mykonos — parties and design hotels

Mykonos is Greece's premium party destination and a design-hotel showcase. It is expensive, it is beautiful in an austere, Cycladic way (whitewashed cubes, windmills, narrow lanes), and it has some of the best beach clubs in Europe (Paradise Beach, Super Paradise).

It is also the island where a cocktail costs €15, a beach umbrella €40/day, and dinner for two at a good restaurant starts at €100. The beauty and the experience are genuine — but the value proposition is poor compared to any other Greek island.

Best for: affluent travellers who specifically want the Mykonos scene, party-focused visitors, people who want the beach club experience and are happy to pay for it.

Not for: families with children, budget travellers, anyone who wants to eat well without spending a fortune.

Corfu — the greenest island

Corfu is the most European-feeling of the major Greek islands, shaped by centuries of Venetian and British occupation into something closer to the Italian Adriatic than the Aegean. Cypress trees, cricket (the British legacy), Venetian fortresses, a UNESCO old town with arcaded streets, and some of the most beautiful sandy bays in Greece (Paleokastritsa, Glyfada, Issos).

Less raw than Crete, less dramatic than Santorini, Corfu delivers consistent quality at mid-range prices with good infrastructure and shorter distances between attractions.

Prices (7 nights, 2 people): €900–1,800 including flights.

Best for: couples and families looking for a balanced, beautiful, uncomplicated holiday.

Zakynthos — the photogenic one

Zakynthos is famous for one image: Navagio Beach (Shipwreck Beach) — a rusting freighter on white pebbles in a turquoise cove, visible from the clifftop above and accessible only by boat. It is genuinely one of the most spectacular natural scenes in Greece and one of the most photographed places on earth.

Beyond Navagio: the Blue Caves sea caves (boat tour, €15–20), Loggerhead turtle nesting beaches (the island is a protected sea turtle habitat — night excursions are organised responsibly), and several excellent beaches on the east and south coasts.

Prices (7 nights, 2 people): €900–1,800 including flights.

Best for: couples, anyone who specifically wants the Navagio experience, beach-focused holidays.

When to go — the month-by-month breakdown

Month Weather Crowds Prices Verdict
May 24–27°C, sea cold (20°C) Low Low Excellent for sightseeing, sea still cool
June 27–30°C, sea 22–24°C Medium Medium Sweet spot — warm enough, manageable
July 30–34°C, sea 25°C High High Peak season, book everything in advance
August 30–35°C, sea 26°C Very high Very high Most expensive and crowded — avoid if possible
September 28–32°C, sea 25°C Medium-low Medium Best overall month — optimal conditions
October 22–26°C, sea 23°C Low Low Good for sightseeing, some closures

September is consistently the best month for Greece — particularly for Santorini, Mykonos, and Rhodes where August crowds are at their most intense. The sea is at its warmest (a full season of sun has heated it to 25–26°C), the weather is outstanding, and prices are 20–30% lower than August peaks.

Getting to Greece

By air: direct flights from London to Athens (3 hours), Heraklion (3.5 hours), Rhodes (4 hours), Corfu (3 hours), Zakynthos (3.5 hours), and Mykonos (3.5 hours). Ryanair, easyJet, Jet2 and charter operators all serve Greek island airports directly from multiple UK and European airports. For best fares: how to find cheap flights .

Between islands: the Greek ferry network is extensive and efficient. From Athens (Piraeus port), ferries reach Santorini in 5–8 hours, Mykonos in 3–5 hours, Crete in 7–9 hours, and Rhodes in 10–16 hours. High-speed ferries (SeaJets, Hellenic Seaways) cut times by 30–40% but cost more. Book ferries at Ferryscanner or directly with operators.

Internal flights: Olympic Air and Sky Express operate domestic flights connecting Athens with island airports. Athens–Heraklion costs €40–80 each way and takes 45 minutes — faster than the ferry for longer routes.

Renting a car in Greece

On Crete and Rhodes, a rental car transforms the holiday. Without one, you are confined to resort areas and expensive organised tours. With one, you reach beaches that most tourists never see — Elafonisi and Balos in Crete, Gennadi and Prasonisi in Rhodes.

Prices (2026): small car, 7 days, summer: €250–500. Book online, 4–6 weeks in advance, for the best prices. Airport collection costs 10–15% more — consider picking up in town.

Insurance: CDW (basic damage waiver) is included in most rentals but with an excess of €500–1,500. A third-party excess waiver from a specialist (€3–7/day) reduces this to zero and is far cheaper than the counter's own upgrade.

Full guide: car rental in Greece 2026 — including the 2026 speed limit changes and the colour-coded parking system.

Practical Greece: what you actually need to know

No visa required for EU/EEA citizens. Enter with a national ID card. Non-EU nationals (including UK citizens post-Brexit) may need to check entry requirements.

No eSIM needed for Greece — EU free roaming applies, so your home mobile plan works without extra charges. If your trip extends to Turkey or other non-EU destinations, see best eSIM by destination 2026 .

Currency: Euro. Cards are widely accepted at hotels, larger restaurants, and shops. Keep some cash for small tavernas, village kiosks, and ferry tickets at smaller ports.

Health: the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) covers emergency treatment at public hospitals. However, it does not cover private clinics (which are common in tourist areas), repatriation, or sports/water activity accidents. A travel insurance policy is recommended — see the comparison: EHIC vs travel insurance .

Language: English is widely spoken in tourist areas. In villages and local tavernas, learning a few words of Greek (kalimera, efharisto) is genuinely appreciated.

Tap water: drinkable in most areas of Crete, Rhodes, and Corfu. On smaller or more arid islands (Santorini, Mykonos), bottled water is recommended — the local water supply is limited and sometimes desalinated.

What to eat and drink

Greek food at its best is exceptional. The problem in heavily touristed areas is that the food is simplified and homogenised for international audiences.

Where to eat well: look for tavernas a few streets back from the main waterfront. In Crete particularly, the inland villages serve the most authentic food at the lowest prices — a full meal with wine costs €12–15/person rather than €25–35.

What to order:


Saganaki — pan-fried cheese, served flaming in some places. Excellent appetiser.

Fresh fish by the kilo — always look at what came in that day, priced per kilo. Ask the waiter to see the fresh catch. Grilled fish at a good taverna is one of the great Mediterranean experiences.

Lamb slow-cooked in a wood oven (especially in Crete) — a village specialty that rarely appears on tourist menus. Ask locals where to find it.

Greek yoghurt with honey — for breakfast at any hour, from any kafeneio. The quality in Greece versus exported Greek yoghurt is genuinely different.

Local wine — Greek wine (Assyrtiko from Santorini, Moschofilero from the Peloponnese, Retsina if you are feeling adventurous) is underrated and good value.


Skip: anything on a menu with photographs, anything a waiter actively invites you into from the street, and any restaurant directly on the most famous squares. These are overpriced without exception.

Experiences worth booking in advance

For the best experiences in Greece, advance booking is essential — especially in summer:


Akrotiri, Santorini (Bronze Age excavation, €12) — buy online, queues at peak season

Palace of Knossos, Crete (€15 or €30 combined ticket) — timed entry recommended

Boat tours in any popular port (caldera in Santorini, Blue Caves in Zakynthos, Balos lagoon in Crete) — sell out weeks ahead in July–August

Sunset spots in Oia, Santorini — arrive by 5 PM at the latest in summer


GetYourGuide has excellent options for boat tours, guided archaeological visits, food tours, and coastal experiences across all major islands — often at lower prices than booking locally:

Related guides


Car rental in Greece 2026 — everything about renting on Greek islands, including the new 2026 traffic rules

Mediterranean cruise guide 2026 — the alternative to staying on one island

Greek islands cruise guide — specifically for cruise itineraries through the Aegean

Travel insurance guide 2026 — what you need beyond the EHIC for Greece

Things to do in Athens — if you are combining a few days in the capital with island time

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Which Greek island is best for families with children?
R: Crete is the best overall family destination — the largest island, varied beaches with safe shallow water, excellent all-inclusive options, good medical infrastructure, and plenty of non-beach activities (Minoan palaces, gorges, markets). Zakynthos and Rhodes are also strong family choices. Avoid Santorini and Mykonos with young children — the terrain is difficult, prices are extreme, and neither island is designed for family tourism.

Î: Is September good for Greece?
R: September is arguably the best month to visit Greece. Weather remains excellent (28–32°C air, 25°C sea temperature), the crowds reduce dramatically, prices drop 20–30% compared to August, and popular sites like Akrotiri in Santorini or the Palace of Knossos in Crete are actually enjoyable rather than overwhelming. The only downside: some seasonal restaurants and bars begin closing from mid-September.

Î: Do I need a visa or eSIM for Greece?
R: EU citizens need no visa — enter with a national ID card. Greece is in the EU, so free roaming applies — use your home mobile plan without extra charges. No eSIM needed for Greece specifically, though an eSIM is useful if your itinerary includes Turkey or other non-EU countries.

Î: Is a rental car necessary in Greece?
R: On large islands: essential. On Crete (250 km long) and Rhodes, the best beaches and villages are only reachable by car. On smaller islands (Mykonos, Paros, Zakynthos), ATVs or scooters are common alternatives. On Santorini and Hydra, cars are impractical or prohibited. See the full guide: car rental in Greece 2026.

Î: What is the cheapest Greek island?
R: For European travellers: Crete and Rhodes consistently offer the best value at the beach resort level — wide choice of all-inclusive hotels, direct flights from most European cities, and competitive prices. Lesbos, Samos, and Kos are cheaper but less frequently served. Santorini and Mykonos are in a category of their own — significantly more expensive than all other islands.

Î: How much does a meal cost in Greece?
R: A full meal at a local taverna (Greek salad + grilled fish or meat + wine) costs €15–25/person. Beach clubs and tourist-facing restaurants on Santorini, Mykonos, and the most popular resort areas charge €30–50/person. The best value: inland tavernas a few streets back from the main waterfront, particularly in Crete and Rhodes, where the food is better and the prices much lower.

Î: Can I do a cruise of the Greek islands instead of staying on one island?
R: Yes, and it is often excellent value. A 7-night Greek island cruise visits Santorini, Mykonos, Crete, and Rhodes or other islands — staying on the ship each night, spending 6–8 hours in each port. Costs: from €450/person for a cabin on MSC or Costa. For a comparison of cruising vs island stay, see the Mediterranean cruise guide.

## Is Romania Expensive? Real Travel Costs in 2026

URL: https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/is-romania-expensive
Limbă: English
Verticală: city-breaks
Publicat: 2026-07-09
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/romania-scumpa-ghid

Descriere: An honest cost breakdown for visiting Romania in 2026 — meals, hotels, transport, and activities with actual prices from someone who lives here.

Răspuns scurt: Romania is one of the most affordable countries in the EU. A comfortable mid-range day in Bucharest costs around €60–80 per person (hotel, meals, transport, one activity). Budget travelers can manage on €30–40/day. Outside the capital, costs drop further — a pension in Transylvania with breakfast runs €25–40 per night for a double room.

Romania keeps showing up on "cheap European destinations" lists, and for good reason — but the conversation usually stops at "it's cheap" without giving you actual numbers. As someone based here, let me walk you through what things really cost so you can plan properly.

The quick answer: yes, Romania is affordable

Romania uses the Romanian leu (RON), and at mid-2026 exchange rates, 1 EUR ≈ 5 RON. This matters because many prices are set in lei, and the conversion consistently works in the visitor's favor.

Compared to Western European prices, Romania runs roughly 40–60% cheaper for most things a tourist encounters: restaurants, hotels, local transport, and attractions. The gap is smaller for imported goods and international hotel chains, but for anything locally produced or operated, the savings are real.

Food and drink — actual prices

This is where Romania shines for budget travelers.

Item Typical price
Espresso / cappuccino €1.50–2.50
Local beer (draft, 500ml) €2–3
Covrigi (street pretzel) €0.30–0.50
Full lunch at a local restaurant €6–10
Three-course dinner, mid-range restaurant €15–25
Fine dining (Bucharest/Cluj) €40–70
Supermarket meal prep (per day) €8–12

Romanian cuisine is hearty and portion sizes are generous. A "meniu de prânz" (lunch menu) at a local restaurant — soup, main course, sometimes dessert — costs €5–8. You'll struggle to spend a lot on food unless you actively seek out high-end restaurants.

Tipping: 10% is standard at sit-down restaurants. Not expected at cafés or bars, but appreciated.

Accommodation — what to expect at each budget

Hotels and guesthouses in Romania are legitimately cheaper than most of the EU, even accounting for recent price increases.

Type Price per night (double room)
Hostel (dorm bed) €10–18
Guesthouse / pension (Transylvania) €25–40
3-star hotel (Bucharest, Cluj) €40–65
4-star hotel (Bucharest, Cluj) €65–110
Boutique / design hotel €80–150
5-star / luxury €120–250

The best value in Romania isn't hotels — it's pensions (guesthouses), especially in Transylvania, Maramureș, and Bucovina. These are family-run, typically include breakfast, and often have better character and hospitality than chain hotels at a fraction of the price. A pension with a hot tub or pool in a mountain village can cost as little as €30–50 per night.

Airbnb is popular in cities, with central apartments in Bucharest or Cluj starting around €30–45 per night.

Getting around

Flights into Romania are cheap from most European cities. Budget airlines (Wizz Air, Ryanair) connect Bucharest, Cluj, Timișoara, and Iași to dozens of European hubs. Expect €30–100 round-trip if you book 4–6 weeks ahead.

Within Romania:

Transport Cost
Metro ride (Bucharest) €0.50
City bus / tram €0.30–0.50
Uber / Bolt (5 km city ride) €2–4
Train (Bucharest → Brașov, 2.5h) €8–14
Rental car (per day) €20–35
Fuel (per liter) €1.50–1.70

For cities, public transport and ride-hailing apps (Bolt is more popular than Uber in Romania) are both cheap and reliable. For exploring the countryside — Transylvania's fortified churches, painted monasteries of Bucovina, or the Transfăgărășan road — a rental car is the clear best option and surprisingly affordable.

Road quality note: main highways and national roads are fine. Some secondary mountain roads are narrow and slow. GPS/Google Maps works well everywhere.

Attractions and activities

Entrance fees in Romania are modest by European standards.

Activity Cost
Museum entrance €2–5
Bran Castle ("Dracula's Castle") €8–10
Peleș Castle (guided tour) €6–12
Salt mine (Turda or Slănic) €5–8
Guided city walking tour €10–15 (or tip-based)
Day trip tour (from Bucharest/Cluj) €30–60
Bear watching tour €30–50

Many churches, fortified citadels, and natural sites are free or cost under €3. The salt mines (Salina Turda is genuinely spectacular) and royal castles are the main paid attractions, and even those are a fraction of what equivalent sites cost in Western Europe.

Sample daily budgets

Here's what a day actually looks like at three budget levels, per person:

Budget (€30–40/day): Hostel dorm or shared guesthouse room, breakfast included, lunch at a local restaurant, supermarket dinner, public transport, one free/cheap attraction.

Mid-range (€60–80/day): Private room in a pension or 3-star hotel, restaurant lunch and dinner, a mix of walking and ride-hailing, one paid attraction or guided tour.

Comfortable (€100–150/day): 4-star hotel, eating at the best local restaurants, rental car or private transfers, multiple attractions, a guided tour or unique experience.

Two people traveling mid-range for 10 days should budget roughly €1,200–1,600 total (flights excluded), covering accommodation, all meals, transport within the country, and activities. That's hard to match anywhere else in the EU.

When to visit for the best value

Peak season is July–August and the Christmas/New Year period. Prices for accommodation in tourist areas (Brașov, Sibiu, Black Sea coast) increase 30–50% during these windows.

The best combination of weather, crowds, and prices is May–June and September–October . Temperatures are pleasant (18–28°C), most attractions are open, and you'll pay off-season rates while enjoying peak-season conditions.

Winter (December–February) is ideal for skiing in Poiana Brașov or Sinaia, Christmas markets in Sibiu and Cluj, and dramatically empty castles. Just pack warm.

A few practical tips

Currency: Always pay in RON, not EUR. Some tourist spots accept euros but at unfavorable rates. ATMs (bancomat) are everywhere in cities; withdraw RON directly.

Language: Romanian is a Romance language — if you speak Italian, French, or Spanish, you'll recognize words. In tourist areas and cities, English is widely spoken, especially by younger Romanians. In rural areas, a few Romanian phrases help enormously and are always appreciated.

Safety: Romania is safe for tourists. Bucharest and major cities have the usual big-city precautions (watch your belongings in crowded places), but violent crime against tourists is extremely rare. The countryside is remarkably safe.

SIM / data: If you're coming from the EU, your mobile data works here at no extra cost (EU roaming). From outside the EU, consider an eSIM — it's cheaper than roaming and takes two minutes to set up.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How much does a meal cost in Romania?
R: A full meal at a local restaurant costs €6–10. A coffee is €1.50–2.50. A three-course dinner at a mid-range restaurant runs €15–25 per person. Fast food is €4–6. Street food like covrigi (pretzels) costs under €1.

Î: Is Bucharest cheaper than other European capitals?
R: Significantly. Bucharest is roughly 40–50% cheaper than Prague, 50–60% cheaper than Vienna, and about half the cost of Barcelona or Rome for equivalent experiences. Only Sofia and Belgrade are comparably cheap among European capitals.

Î: Do I need cash or can I pay by card?
R: Card payments are widely accepted in cities — restaurants, supermarkets, taxis, and most attractions take Visa and Mastercard. In rural areas and small villages, carry some cash (Romanian leu, RON). ATMs are everywhere in cities.

Î: How much should I budget per day in Romania?
R: Budget: €30–40/day (hostel, local food, public transport). Mid-range: €60–80/day (3-star hotel, restaurants, occasional taxi). Comfort: €100–150/day (4-star hotel, car rental, guided tours). These are per-person estimates.

Î: Is it cheaper to visit Romania in winter?
R: Accommodation outside ski resorts is cheaper in the off-season (November–March, excluding Christmas/New Year). However, Romania's best value is actually in spring (April–June) and early autumn (September–October) — pleasant weather, fewer tourists, and no peak-season surcharges.

Î: How much does a rental car cost in Romania?
R: A compact car rents for €20–35 per day including basic insurance. Fuel costs around €1.50–1.70 per liter. Renting a car is the best way to explore Transylvania, Maramureș, and the Danube Delta at your own pace.

## Istanbul City Break 2026: 3-Day Itinerary, Real Costs and Everything You Need to Know

URL: https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/istanbul-city-break-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: city-breaks
Publicat: 2026-07-29
Actualizat: 2026-07-29
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/istanbul-city-break-ghid

Descriere: Complete Istanbul city break guide for 2026. Hagia Sophia, Grand Bazaar, Bosphorus cruise, Turkish hammam, best neighbourhoods, real budget, and the eSIM you must buy before you fly.

Răspuns scurt: A 3-night Istanbul city break costs €250–550 per person all-in (flight + hotel + food + sites). Istanbul is one of Europe's most affordable city break destinations: a full meal costs €5–10, a Bosphorus ferry €1–2, and most major mosques are free. Essential to know before travelling: Turkey is not in the EU, so roaming applies — buy an eSIM before you fly (provider websites are blocked inside Turkey since 2025). Travel insurance is mandatory — the EHIC does not work in Turkey.

Istanbul does not ease you in gently. The moment you step out of the airport — or better, the moment you take the ferry across the Bosphorus for the first time and watch the minarets rising above both the European and Asian skylines simultaneously — you understand why this city has been the hinge of the world for 2,500 years. It is the only city on two continents, and it holds layers of history — Byzantine, Ottoman, secular, modern — with a density that no other European destination can match.

It is also remarkably affordable, relatively safe, and genuinely exhilarating for a first-time visitor.

The one thing you must do before you leave home

Buy your eSIM before departure. This cannot be stated strongly enough.

Turkey is outside the EU. Free roaming does not apply. Your home carrier charges €10–15 per gigabyte in Turkey. A week of normal data use (maps, messages, a few photos uploaded) costs €50–100 in carrier roaming.

The solution — a prepaid Turkey eSIM — costs $10–15 for 5 GB / 30 days on Airalo . But here is the critical detail: since 2025, Turkish authorities have blocked access to eSIM provider websites from within Turkey. If you arrive without one and try to buy it at the hotel, you will find the pages inaccessible.

Buy before you fly. Install at home. It activates automatically when you land. Full installation instructions: how to install an eSIM .

3-Day Istanbul itinerary

Day 1 — Sultanahmet: the old city

Sultanahmet is the historic heart of Istanbul — the peninsula where Constantinople stood, surrounded on three sides by water. The density of significant monuments within walking distance of each other here is unmatched in the world.

Hagia Sophia (Ayasofya)

Built in 537 CE as the greatest cathedral in Christendom, converted to a mosque after the Ottoman conquest in 1453, secularised as a museum under Atatürk, and reconverted to a mosque in 2020. The interior — 55 metres high, 270 metres in circumference, covered in gold mosaics that have survived 1,500 years — is staggering under any description.

Arrival: open from 8:30 AM. Come at opening — by 10 AM the interior is crowded and the experience is diminished. Access during prayer times (five times daily, 20–40 minutes each) is restricted. Entry is free for prayer; tourist access through a separate entrance may carry a charge — verify the current arrangement on the Hagia Sophia's official site before visiting.

Blue Mosque (Sultan Ahmed Mosque)

Directly across the Hippodrome from Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque is named for the 20,000 İznik tiles in varying shades of blue that cover its interior. Its six minarets caused controversy when built in 1616 (only Mecca was meant to have six). Free to enter; closed to tourists during the five daily prayer times (30 minutes each). Dress code enforced at the entrance — shoulders and knees covered, women need a headscarf (provided free at the entrance if needed).

Topkapi Palace

The administrative and residential centre of the Ottoman Empire for four centuries (1465–1856). The complex covers 700,000 square metres and contains the Imperial Council chambers, treasury collections, holy relics, and — most fascinating — the Harem, where the sultan's household and family lived in an interlocking world of power, privacy, and protocol.

Allow 3–4 hours minimum. The Harem requires a separate ticket. Entrance: approximately €20 for the main complex, €15 for the Harem.

The Basilica Cistern (Yerebatan Sarnıcı)

A 6th-century underground water reservoir — 336 columns supporting a cathedral-like space that held 80,000 cubic metres of water for the city above. Atmospheric and slightly surreal. Walk the raised platforms among the columns and find the two Medusa heads used as column bases (one upside down, one sideways — a detail that has generated centuries of speculation). Entry approximately €15. Open daily.

The Hippodrome

The open square in front of the Blue Mosque is the site of the ancient chariot racing track of Constantinople, once seating 100,000 spectators. The Egyptian Obelisk (3,500 years old, moved here from Karnak in 390 CE), the Serpentine Column (from Delphi, 479 BCE), and the Column of Constantine stand on what was once the track's central spine. Free, always open.

Where to eat on Day 1: avoid the tourist-facing restaurants immediately around the Hippodrome and Blue Mosque — quality is poor and prices are high. Walk 3–4 minutes into the streets behind them. Simit (sesame bread ring, €0.50) from street vendors for breakfast. A lokanta (Turkish canteen-style restaurant) for lunch — a full meal with soup, main, and water costs €5–8.

Day 2 — Grand Bazaar, Galata and the Bosphorus

Grand Bazaar (Kapalıçarşı)

One of the world's oldest and largest covered markets, operating continuously since 1461. Over 4,000 shops under 61 covered streets, selling jewellery, carpets, ceramics, leather, spices, textiles, and souvenirs. The scale is disorienting and the experience is genuinely unlike any other market in Europe.

The negotiation culture is real but not aggressive. For souvenirs and handicrafts, starting at 50% of the first price and meeting at 60–70% is typical. For carpets and larger items, prices are more complex — treat any carpet purchase as a multi-hour negotiation and research values beforehand.

Opening hours: Monday to Saturday, 8:30 AM – 7 PM. Closed Sunday.

Spice Bazaar (Mısır Çarşısı)

A smaller, more focused market near the waterfront — primarily spices, teas, Turkish delight (lokum), dried fruits, and nuts. Less overwhelming than the Grand Bazaar and more enjoyable for food lovers. Try the saffron, the pomegranate tea, and the pistachio lokum.

Galata Bridge and the Karaköy waterfront

The Galata Bridge crosses the Golden Horn inlet connecting the old city to the Beyoğlu district. The bridge's lower level is lined with restaurants; the upper level is perpetually occupied by Istanbulites fishing — one of the city's most iconic sights. Walk across toward the Karaköy neighbourhood, which has transformed in the past decade into Istanbul's most dynamic area for food, coffee, and contemporary art.

Galata Tower

The 67-metre stone tower built in 1348 by the Genoese offers a 360-degree panorama of Istanbul — the old city, the Bosphorus, the Asian shore, and the Horn. Entry approximately €30. Best visited in late afternoon when the light on the domes and minarets is at its most dramatic.

Bosphorus cruise

The Bosphorus Strait — 31 km connecting the Black Sea to the Marmara Sea, separating Europe from Asia — is the defining geographical feature of Istanbul and best understood from the water.

Option Duration Price Best for
Public ferry (Istanbulkart) 90 minutes (one way) €1–2 Budget, locals' experience
Short Bosphorus tour 1.5–2 hours €15–25 Tourist-focused, commentary
Full day cruise 5–6 hours €25–40 Reaching the Black Sea entrance
Sunset dinner cruise 2–3 hours €40–70 Romantic, food included

The public ferry from Eminönü to Üsküdar (6 minutes, €1) gives you a Bosphorus crossing for essentially nothing. The longer cruise boats depart from the same Eminönü pier and go significantly further north, passing waterfront palaces, fortresses, and the suspension bridges.

Day 3 — Asian Istanbul and the Turkish hammam

Kadıköy (Asian side)

Take the ferry from Eminönü or Karaköy to Kadıköy (approximately 20 minutes, €1–2). This is the Istanbul that locals actually inhabit — a dense, lively neighbourhood with an extraordinary market, independent bookshops, street art, and some of the best food in the city.

The Kadıköy market (Salı Pazarı and the surrounding streets) is the most vibrant food market in Istanbul — fish from the Bosphorus and Black Sea, cheeses, olives, vegetables, and street food at prices significantly lower than tourist areas. The Moda neighbourhood adjacent to Kadıköy is the most pleasant walking area in the city.

Moda promenade: the coastal path along the southern shore of the Asian peninsula, from Moda's tea gardens to Kalamış marina, is genuinely one of Istanbul's most pleasant walks — particularly at sunset, looking back across the water at the old city.

Turkish hammam

A hammam visit is the most distinctly Istanbul experience available, with a 600-year continuous tradition. The process: enter the warm room (ılıklık) to acclimatise, move to the hot room (sıcaklık) for steam, receive a kese (exfoliating scrub with a rough mitten), then a köpük (soap foam massage). The experience lasts 45–90 minutes.

Recommended hammams for first-timers:


Çemberlitaş Hamamı (Sultanahmet, open since 1584): €40–80, excellent facilities, tourist-friendly, central location. The most visited for a reason.

Süleymaniye Hamamı (near the Süleymaniye Mosque): €30–50, more local atmosphere, less polished but more authentic.

Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı (Karaköy): €80–120, the most beautifully restored hammam in Istanbul — Ottoman architecture preserved at the highest standard. Worth the premium.


Book online to guarantee your time slot and avoid long queues, especially on weekends.


Where to eat in Istanbul: the honest guide

Turkish cuisine is one of the world's great food traditions, and Istanbul is its highest expression. The city's street food and local restaurants offer exceptional quality at prices that seem implausible compared to Western Europe.

Street food worth stopping for:


Simit: sesame-coated bread rings sold from street carts — €0.30–0.50. The city's default breakfast.

Balık ekmek (fish sandwich): grilled mackerel in bread, sold from the boats at Eminönü — €3–4. An Istanbul institution.

Döner kebab: different from the tourist-country version — leaner, on better bread, €3–6 at a local shop.

Turkish breakfast (kahvaltı): multiple small dishes — cheeses, olives, honey, eggs, tomatoes, bread, and unlimited tea — served at breakfast cafés. €5–10/person. The most generous breakfast tradition in Europe.

Lahmacun: thin flatbread with minced meat, herbs, and lemon — €2–3.


Where not to eat: the restaurants with menu displays in 12 languages immediately around Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque. They are priced 3–5x higher than equivalent quality 200 metres away. Walk into the residential streets and look for places where you see Turkish people eating.

Where to eat well:


Karaköy: for coffee, modern Turkish cuisine, and the best meze in the city

Kadıköy: for seafood, local restaurant culture, and the highest value-per-euro ratio in Istanbul

Kapalıçarşı (near the bazaar): Havuzlu Restaurant — one of the oldest in the bazaar, consistent quality for Ottoman-style dishes



Practical Istanbul: what you need to know

Transport: the Istanbulkart (a reusable card, ~€3) covers all public transport — metro, tram, ferry, bus. Single fare: approximately €0.50–1 per trip. The T1 tram runs from Kabataş along the historic peninsula through Sultanahmet to Bağcılar — the most useful line for tourists. Metro M2 connects Taksim to the Grand Bazaar area.

Getting in from the airport:


Istanbul Airport (IST, European side): Havaist bus to Taksim (€10, 45–75 min depending on traffic), or metro to Gayrettepe (€5, 40 min), or taxi (€30–50, use the official metered cabs only)

Sabiha Gökçen Airport (SAW, Asian side): Havabus to Kadıköy (€10, 30–60 min), or taxi to Asian Istanbul areas (€15–25)


Money: withdraw Turkish lira from ATMs (not airport exchange bureaux). Use Revolut or Wise for card payments. Always pay in local currency — refuse DCC. For the complete guide: how to pay abroad without fees .

Safety: Istanbul is safe for tourists. The specific scams to know:


The friendly bar invitation (someone befriends you and takes you to a bar where the bill is €150–400) — decline all unsolicited invitations to go somewhere specific

Unlicensed taxis — use Bolt or the official metered taxis from the airport rank

Shoe shine drop (a shine kit falls near you, then service is expected and charged) — just walk past


e-Visa: UK, US, Canadian, Australian, and many other nationals need an e-Visa (evisa.gov.tr, approximately $50–60, takes 5 minutes). Some EU nationalities enter without a visa — check your specific nationality. Apply before departure.

Safety in context: Turkey's tourist areas are safe. For the full regional safety picture and practical preparation list: Turkey 2026 safety guide .

Travel insurance: mandatory. The EHIC is not valid in Turkey. A single night in a private Istanbul hospital can cost €500–2,000+. Insurance costs €15–25 for a week — see EHIC vs travel insurance for why this matters specifically in Turkey.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How many days do you need in Istanbul?
R: 3 days covers the essentials: Day 1 for Sultanahmet (Hagia Sophia, Blue Mosque, Topkapi Palace, Basilica Cistern), Day 2 for the Grand Bazaar, Galata district and Bosphorus, Day 3 for Kadıköy on the Asian side and a Turkish hammam. 4–5 days lets you add the Prince's Islands, Balat neighbourhood, and more food exploration. Even 2 full days produces a rewarding trip if you prioritise ruthlessly.

Î: Is Istanbul safe for tourists in 2026?
R: Yes. Istanbul is a safe city for tourists. Standard urban precautions apply: watch for pickpockets at the Grand Bazaar and on the T1 tram, use Bolt or Uber rather than unlicensed taxis, and be wary of unsolicited invitations to 'my friend's bar' (a well-documented scam where the bill arrives at €100–200+). The tourist police in Sultanahmet are responsive and helpful.

Î: Do I need a visa for Istanbul?
R: Most Western nationalities (UK, US, Canada, Australia, most EU countries) can enter Turkey without a visa for up to 90 days — but check your specific nationality at the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs website, as requirements vary. Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months from your entry date. National ID cards are NOT accepted in Turkey.

Î: Do I need an eSIM for Istanbul?
R: Yes, strongly recommended — and buy it before you fly. Turkey is not in the EU, so free roaming does not apply. Carrier roaming costs €10–15/GB. A 5 GB Turkey eSIM costs approximately $10–15 on Airalo. Critical: since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to eSIM provider websites from within Turkey. You cannot purchase after arrival — the websites simply do not load.

Î: What is the Museum Pass Istanbul and is it worth it?
R: The Museum Pass Istanbul (approximately €55–65 for 5 days) covers 12 major sites including Topkapi Palace, Hagia Sophia Museum section, Chora Church, Dolmabahçe Palace, and several others. If you plan to visit Topkapi (€20) + Hagia Sophia Museum (entry charges for non-prayer access) + Dolmabahçe (€25+), the pass pays for itself. Valid for 5 consecutive days.

Î: What currency should I use in Istanbul?
R: Turkish lira (TRY). In tourist areas and large restaurants, euros and US dollars are sometimes accepted but at poor rates. Withdraw TRY from ATMs (not at the airport — rates are poor there). Use Revolut or Wise for card payments to avoid foreign transaction fees. Always refuse DCC (Dynamic Currency Conversion) — choose Turkish lira at every terminal. For the full payment guide: how to pay abroad without fees.

Î: What is a Turkish hammam and which one should I choose?
R: A Turkish hammam (bath house) involves a steam room, exfoliating scrub (kese), and soap massage. The experience typically takes 45–90 minutes. For a first visit: Çemberlitaş Hamamı (€40–80, open since 1584, central location), Süleymaniye Hamamı (€30–50, more local atmosphere), or Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı (€80–120, the most beautifully restored). Book online to guarantee a slot.

## Lake Como 2026: The Complete Guide — Bellagio, Varenna, Villas, Ferry & Everything You Need to Know

URL: https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/lake-como-complete-guide-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: city-breaks
Publicat: 2026-07-31
Actualizat: 2026-07-31

Descriere: Lake Como 2026 complete guide. Bellagio vs Varenna vs Menaggio, ferry routes, famous villas, real prices and how to visit without the crowds.

Răspuns scurt: Lake Como (Lago di Como) is a Y-shaped glacial lake in the foothills of the Alps in Lombardy, northern Italy — 46 km long, up to 410 metres deep (the third deepest lake in Europe), surrounded by mountains rising to 2,400 metres. The central triangle of Bellagio, Varenna, and Menaggio is the heart of any Lake Como visit. Best access from Milan: train to Varenna (1 hour from Milano Centrale, €8.70 — gets you directly to the lake and the ferries). Ferry system operated by Navigazione Laghi: central car ferry Bellagio–Varenna–Menaggio every 20–30 minutes; fares increased ~15% for 2026. Villa del Balbianello (Casino Royale, Star Wars filming location): gardens €14, guided tour €25, open mid-March to end of December, closed Monday and Wednesday. Best time: May–June and September–October.

There are lakes more dramatic than Lake Como, and there are Italian landscapes with more concentrated art. But there is no lake in Europe that combines the particular alchemy of Como — Alps rising directly from the water's surface, 18th-century villas in impossible positions on narrow promontories, a ferry system unchanged in principle since the 19th century, and a quality of light on the water at late afternoon that has been attracting painters, writers, and people in love for 200 years.

Pliny the Elder owned a villa here. Virgil and Catullus wrote about it. Napoleon reorganised the administrative territory centred on it. Liszt composed at a lakeside villa. George Clooney bought his house here in 1990. Casino Royale and Star Wars were filmed on its shores. And the Milanese have been taking the train north for a weekend since 1892.

Lake Como is 46 km long, up to 410 metres deep, and surrounded by the Alps. The shape is a Y — a southern branch pointing at Como city in the west and Lecco in the east, meeting at a central junction where Bellagio sits on its promontory, with the upper branch extending north toward Colico. This geography dictates everything: the ferries, the choice of base, the experience of each village.


The Geography — Understanding the Lake Before You Arrive

The key to navigating Lake Como intelligently is understanding the Y shape:

Southern west branch: Como city → Cernobbio → Lenno (Villa del Balbianello) → Tremezzo (Villa Carlotta) → Menaggio

Southern east branch: Lecco → Varenna → Bellano

Central junction: Bellagio (on the promontory between the two upper arms)

Upper branch (north): Menaggio/Varenna → Colico

The famous central triangle — Bellagio, Varenna, Menaggio — sits at this junction and is connected by the car ferry service that runs every 20–30 minutes. This is the heart of the Como experience for most visitors.

Key implication for planning: Como city and Lecco (the two ends of the southern branches) are transport hubs, not the scenery destinations. The scenery and the villas are in the central lake and upper branches. Many visitors make the mistake of spending all their time in Como city and wonder why the photographs don't match reality.


When to Visit

May: The single best month. Wildflowers carpet the hillside terraces. Villa Carlotta's azaleas and rhododendrons bloom in extraordinary colour. Temperatures 18–23°C. Ferry at full summer schedule. Crowds manageable. Accommodation not yet at peak prices.

June: Very good. Warmer (22–27°C). Busier than May but without July–August intensity. Villas all open.

July–August: Hottest and most crowded. Bellagio ferry queues can be 30+ minutes on summer weekends. Accommodation must be booked months ahead. The lake itself is beautiful — water temperature 22–24°C. If you visit, arrive early (first morning ferry) and leave by 15:00 to avoid the peak.

September: The knowing traveller's month. Temperatures 20–26°C. Crowds noticeably reduced after mid-September. Vineyards on the hillsides changing colour. The light in September afternoon is extraordinary on the water.

October: Spectacular autumn colour. Some villas beginning to close or reduce hours. Weather less reliable. Fewer tourists, lower prices.

November–February: Most villas closed. Ferry schedule reduced. Bellagio in winter is a genuine village with real locals and empty piazzas — a completely different experience, legitimately beautiful if you want solitude.


The Villages — What Each One Actually Offers

Bellagio — The Most Famous Village

Bellagio is positioned on the central promontory where the two northern branches of the lake meet — giving it views in three directions simultaneously. The combination of the stepped main street (Salita Serbelloni), the piazza with its lakeview café terraces, and the surrounding gardens makes it the most immediately photogenic village on the lake.

First-time visitors who prioritise iconic scenery: Bellagio is correct, but book 6–8 weeks ahead for summer 2026.

Villa Serbelloni gardens: Owned by the Rockefeller Foundation (which uses the main villa as a retreat for academics and artists), the gardens above the village are the highest viewpoint in Bellagio, with views of all three lake branches simultaneously. Guided tours only, advance booking recommended. Entry: €15. Gardens accessible April–October.

Villa Melzi: Lakefront garden villa built by Francesco Melzi d'Eril (Napoleon's vice-president of the Italian Republic) in 1808. English-style garden, Japanese garden section, and a small museum in the orangerie. Villa Melzi: peaceful, lakefront, exceptional in the early morning before the tours arrive. €10 adults.

The Bellagio reality: Bellagio is genuine and beautiful, but it is also intensely visited. The Salita Serbelloni (the famous stepped street with boutiques) is the most photographed street in Lombardy — and between 11:00 and 16:00 in summer, it is genuinely difficult to move. Solution: arrive on the first morning ferry (typically 07:00 from Varenna), have the piazza and gardens to yourself for 2 hours, and be on a ferry out by 12:00.

Dining in Bellagio: Bellagio's stepped lanes hide candlelit cellars serving risotto al pesce persico. The best restaurants are not the ones visible from the ferry pier. Walk up and inland.

Varenna — The Best-Kept Transport Secret

Varenna: east branch, accessible directly by train from Milan Central — Lecco line, 1 hour, €8.70. Varenna has fewer visitors than Bellagio (the east branch gets less traffic), the Villa Monastero gardens, and the Castello di Vezio above (20-minute walk uphill, €5 — the best panoramic view of the central lake).

This is the single most important logistical secret of Lake Como: Varenna is directly train-accessible from Milan in 1 hour, and you step off the train onto the platform and are immediately at the lake with the ferry pier 100 metres away. No further connection needed, no confusing Como city transit, no extra cost.

Villa Monastero: Villa Monastero, Varenna: the most underrated garden on the eastern shore. The botanical garden runs for over 2 km along the lake's edge. €10 adults. Far fewer crowds than the western shore villas. A former monastery converted to a villa in the 16th century, with a lakefront garden that stretches along the shoreline with more than 100 botanical specimens. Almost no queues compared to Villa del Balbianello.

Castello di Vezio: A medieval castle on the hill above Varenna, accessible by a 20-minute uphill walk. The castle itself is modest but the view from the battlements — the central lake triangle spread below, Bellagio visible directly across, the upper branch extending north — is the finest panoramic view of the lake. Entry: €5. In summer, live falconry demonstrations.

The Varenna character: Quieter, less touristic, more genuinely local than Bellagio. A handful of restaurants, the gardens, the castle, the passegiata along the lakefront. For those who want Bellagio's ferry access without Bellagio's crowds, Varenna is the answer.

Menaggio — The Family-Friendly Western Shore

Directly across from Bellagio on the western shore, Menaggio is connected to Bellagio and Varenna by the same car ferry service and offers the same central lake position without the crowds.

Menaggio: the town center is flat, spacious, and genuinely easier to navigate than Bellagio's steep alleys — a meaningful advantage for families or anyone who prefers level ground. The public Lido di Menaggio is one of the few proper beach clubs on the lake with a pool, sunbeds, and a bar.

The promenade along the lake in Menaggio is one of Como's most pleasant evening walks — gelato, café terraces, views across the water to Bellagio.

Hiking base: Menaggio is the best base for hiking on Lake Como. The Alta Via del Lario trail system connects multiple villages on the western shore with ascents into the mountains above. The Monte Bregagno circuit (1,700 m, full day) is the most demanding; shorter routes to Monte Crocetta or San Bernardo are achievable in 2–3 hours.

Como City — The Transport Hub

Como is a pleasant medium-sized city (85,000 people) with a good historic centre, a Romanesque cathedral (Duomo di Como, begun 1396, notable for the carved Gothic facade), a lakefront piazza (Piazza Cavour), and the Brunate funicular.

What Como is NOT: it is not the scenic lake that photographs show. The southernmost arm of the lake near Como is less dramatic than the central junction around Bellagio. Many visitors who spend all their time in Como leave thinking "the lake isn't as beautiful as I expected" — because they haven't reached the beautiful part.

Como's main value: transport hub. The train station, the bus connections, and the ferry terminal that takes you to the villages. Spend a morning in Como for the cathedral and the funicular, then get on a ferry.

Brunate Funicular: A public funicular (€3.50 each way) from Como lakefront to the village of Brunate, 715 metres above, offering panoramic views of the lake and the Alps. The funicular has run since 1894. From Brunate, hiking trails continue to the Volta lighthouse (a tower commemorating Alessandro Volta, native of Como, inventor of the electric battery — the unit of electrical potential is named after him).


The Villas — Lake Como's Private Heritage Made Public

The lake's extraordinary collection of 18th and 19th-century villas represents the summer retreat culture of Milanese aristocracy, Lombard banking families, and eventually European and American celebrities. Most are privately owned. The select group open to visitors:

Villa del Balbianello — The Most Spectacular

Villa del Balbianello is located next to Lake Como, Italy. Built for Cardinal Angelo Maria Durini at the end of the 18th century, the Villa stands on the tip of a steep promontory overlooking Lake Como, almost opposite Bellagio.

Later owned by explorer Guido Monzino (who led the first all-Italian ascent of Everest in 1973 and mounted polar expeditions from the 1950s through the 1970s), the villa contains his collection of expedition equipment and geographical instruments alongside the 18th-century furnishings. Monzino donated the villa and its contents to FAI (Fondo Ambiente Italiano — Italy's heritage trust) in 1988.

The gardens: Formally terraced on multiple levels, with holm oaks pruned into umbrella shapes, roses, azaleas, and unobstructed views of the lake from three sides of the promontory. Casino Royale (2006) used Villa del Balbianello for the scenes where James Bond recovers with Vesper Lynd after the poker sequence. 007 rests under the Loggia Durini, Vesper beside him, the lake below — the same loggia that appeared in the Star Wars saga four years earlier.

The Star Wars connection: Anakin and Padmé's lakeside retreat in Star Wars: Episode II — Attack of the Clones (2002) was filmed on these same terraces — you can stand on the exact spot of the kiss.

Entry 2026: Gardens only €14, gardens + guided tour €25. Online booking is mandatory. Tickets managed directly by FAI. Closed Mondays and Wednesdays. Open mid-March to end of December.

How to arrive: By boat taxi from Lenno (€5–10, 5 minutes across the small bay) — the cinematic approach that shows you the villa's famous silhouette from the water. Or by a 30-minute footpath from Lenno through the woods. The footpath option is only open Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday.

Insider timing: The tourist mistake here is obvious: arriving without a reservation and being turned away at the gate. Book online. Arrive early — the villa often fills its morning slots before 11:00 in summer.

Villa Carlotta — The Botanical Masterpiece

On the western shore at Tremezzo, 15 minutes by ferry from Bellagio. Villa Carlotta is one of the finest examples of neoclassical architecture on Lake Como, built in the 17th century and expanded in the 18th. The villa houses an impressive collection of sculptures and paintings — but its true star is the garden.

The garden is extraordinary in April–May when the azaleas and rhododendrons (hundreds of varieties) bloom in cascades of pink, red, white, and purple visible from the lake. Also notable: the cactus conservatory, bamboo grove, and tropical fern garden. Sculpture highlights: Canova's Palamedes and Cupid and Psyche reproductions. Entry: €15.

Villa d'Este — The Grand Hotel (Not a Museum)

At Cernobbio, on the western shore near Como. The most famous hotel on Lake Como — once the summer palace of Queen Caroline of Brunswick (wife of King George IV of England), converted to a luxury hotel in 1873 and continuously operating. The floating pool (a pontoon moored on the lake) and the extraordinary gardens are the visual signatures. Villa d'Este is a private hotel (not open to the public as a museum), but you can have coffee, lunch, or dinner on the terrace, or book a room. Rates: from approximately €700 per night.

Villa Monastero (Varenna) — The Underrated Alternative

Villa Monastero, Varenna: the most underrated garden on the eastern shore. The botanical garden runs for over 2km along the lake's edge. Far fewer crowds than the western shore villas. Entry: €10. The villa building itself hosts scientific conferences; the lakefront garden is the attraction.


The Ferry System — Complete Guide 2026

Navigazione Laghi operates all public ferries on Lake Como. Understanding the system before you arrive saves significant time and money.

Three Types of Vessel

Slow ferry (traghetto/battello): Stops at all lake villages, open deck, cheapest, bicycles allowed (€3.50 supplement). The best option for sightseeing and seeing the lake gradually. Como to Bellagio by slow ferry: approximately 2 hours, €12.40.

Hydrofoil (aliscafo): Faster, enclosed, air-conditioned, no bicycles. Direct services between major towns — Como to Bellagio: 45–55 minutes, €18.80. Must purchase tickets before boarding (not on the vessel). Suspends first in high winds.

Car ferry (traghetto auto): The central lake triangle service — Bellagio → Varenna → Cadenabbia → Menaggio and back, continuously from early morning to late evening. The central-lake car ferry runs every 20–30 minutes from 6:00 AM to 10:30 PM. Fares start at €4.60 for short crossings. This is how you move between the three central villages quickly. Bicycles and cars carried.

2026 Fares (Key Routes)

Prices were increased approximately 15% for 2026 compared with the previous year. Always verify current rates on the official fares page before your trip.
