The VPN feature: what it actually does

"VPN included" can mean very different things. Here's what the Saily VPN does and doesn't do.

What the Saily VPN does


Encrypts your data connection on any network (including the eSIM data connection itself)

Protects against packet sniffing on public Wi-Fi (someone on the same network intercepting your data)

Hides your browsing activity from the local network administrator (the hotel, the café, the airport)

Blocks ads on websites — reduces data consumption and improves browsing experience

Blocks malicious domains — protection against phishing on unsecured networks

115+ virtual locations — you can appear to be browsing from another country


What the Saily VPN does NOT do


It's not the full NordVPN client — it lacks advanced threat protection, dedicated IP addresses, obfuscated servers, and split tunnelling

It does not reliably unblock streaming services (Netflix, Hulu, BBC iPlayer) the way a full VPN does

It does not bypass country-level internet restrictions (Turkey's social media restrictions, China's Great Firewall)

It has not been independently audited separately from NordVPN's main product


Who it matters for

It matters a lot if: you regularly use hotel or airport Wi-Fi for banking, work email, or accessing sensitive data. The encryption provided is real protection against man-in-the-middle attacks.

It doesn't matter if: you already have a NordVPN/ExpressVPN/Surfshark subscription and use it on your phone anyway. You don't need Saily's VPN if you're already running one.

Calculated value: if Saily's VPN saves you from a separate VPN subscription (~€3–5/month), you save €36–60/year. On an eSIM plan of $10–15 per trip, that effectively makes Saily free over 3–4 trips.

How to buy and install Saily

Step 1: Check eSIM compatibility

Your phone must support eSIM:

iPhone: XS or newer (2018+). Check: Settings → General → About → look for "EID" = eSIM supported. Or dial *#06# — if EID appears, you're good.

Samsung Galaxy: S20 and newer, Z Fold/Z Flip all versions, A54 and newer (some A models).

Google Pixel: 3 and newer.

Other Android: check Settings → Connections → SIM card manager — if "Add eSIM" appears, your phone supports it.

Note: phones purchased through carriers may have eSIM locked. If you don't see the option, contact your carrier for unlocking.

Step 2: Purchase your plan


Go to saily.com or download the Saily app (iOS / Android)

Select your destination (or regional/global plan)

Choose your data amount and duration

Pay by card — you receive the QR code by email instantly


Step 3: Install at home, on Wi-Fi (critical)

Install before departure — not at the airport, not after landing. Stable home Wi-Fi is the correct environment.

On iPhone:


Settings → Mobile Data → Add eSIM

Tap "Use QR Code"

Scan the QR from the email

Label it (e.g. "Saily Travel")

Keep it as secondary / inactive until needed


On Android (Samsung):


Settings → Connections → SIM card manager → Add eSIM

Scan QR code

Confirm installation

Keep inactive until arrival


Step 4: Activate at your destination

When you land:


Go to SIM settings

Select the Saily eSIM profile

Set it as your data SIM

Enable Data Roaming on the Saily profile

Internet starts within 30–60 seconds


Step 5: Keep your primary SIM active

Your physical SIM stays active for calls, SMS, and bank verification codes. Set: Data → Saily, Calls and SMS → your physical SIM. Both work simultaneously.

Full installation guide: how to install an eSIM step by step .

Installation tips


Screenshot the QR code — if you lose the email, you have a backup

Install 24 hours before departure — gives you time to troubleshoot any issues

Don't delete the eSIM profile after data runs out — you can buy a new plan on the same profile

If it doesn't connect on landing: restart your phone, or toggle the eSIM profile off and back on



The Turkey exception: buy before you land

If your trip includes Turkey — and this applies equally to Saily, Airalo, and Yesim — you must purchase and install your eSIM before arriving.

Since 2025, Turkey's telecommunications authority (BTK) has blocked access to major international eSIM provider websites from within Turkey. If you try to buy after landing in Istanbul or Antalya, saily.com, airalo.com, and yesim.app simply will not load — not on Turkish mobile networks, not on local Wi-Fi.

The eSIM profile installed at home activates normally once you land — the block only affects the purchase/installation process, not the service itself. Once installed, it works perfectly.

If you forgot to buy before departure and you're already in Turkey:


Use a VPN (if you have one) to access the provider's website

Ask someone back home to purchase the plan and send you the QR code via WhatsApp/email

Buy a local physical SIM at the airport (Turkcell, Vodafone TR, Türk Telekom) — ~€15–20 for 10 GB

10 common eSIM mistakes to avoid

1. Buying after landing

Many provider websites don't load without Wi-Fi, and in Turkey they're blocked entirely. Buy and install at home .

2. Not enabling Data Roaming

The most common reason for "my eSIM isn't working": you forgot to enable Data Roaming on the eSIM profile. It's a separate toggle in your settings.

3. Deleting the eSIM profile

If you delete the profile, you need to buy a completely new plan. Deactivate it, don't delete it — you can reuse the same profile with a new plan later.

4. Forgetting to disable data on the physical SIM

If both SIMs have data enabled, your phone may use the physical SIM (with expensive roaming) instead of the eSIM. Explicitly set the eSIM as your data SIM.

5. Buying more data than you need

5 GB is enough for a week of moderate use. Don't buy 20 GB "just in case" — it's money wasted. You can purchase an additional plan at any time if you run out.

6. Ignoring the regional vs per-country difference

A Turkey 5 GB / 30-day plan costs ~$10. A Europe plan (which includes Turkey) for 5 GB / 30 days costs ~$15. If you're visiting only Turkey, choose the country-specific plan.

7. Not using free Wi-Fi

Hotel, restaurant, and airport Wi-Fi is free and doesn't consume your eSIM data. With Saily's VPN enabled, it's also secure. Use Wi-Fi for streaming and downloads; use eSIM data for navigation and messaging on the go.

8. Buying from unknown providers

The eSIM market has some questionable providers. Stick to the verified ones: Saily (NordVPN), Airalo (largest provider), Yesim (established). Don't buy from unknown websites found through Google ads.

9. Ignoring speed

Price isn't everything — an eSIM that costs $5 but runs at 5 Mbps is frustrating. Saily delivers 50–95 Mbps, Airalo 30–70 Mbps, Yesim 18–44 Mbps. If you need stable video calls, speed matters.

10. Not testing before departure

After installation, activate the eSIM profile for a few minutes and verify it connects (it should connect to a partner network in your home country or nearby area). Then deactivate and reactivate at your destination.


The verdict: which eSIM is right for you

There is no universal winner — it depends on how you travel.

Choose Saily if: you want free VPN protection included, unlimited data with the most generous threshold (5 GB/day), a trusted brand (NordVPN), and you're primarily travelling to Europe or popular destinations. Best feature-to-price ratio on the market.

Choose Airalo if: you want the widest variety of plans, you're heading to a less common destination (200+ countries), and you prefer the lowest price on fixed-data plans.

Choose Yesim if: you need a virtual phone number integrated with your eSIM, and you're travelling within Europe long-term.

The universal rule: compare prices for your specific destination across all three websites before purchasing — it takes 5 minutes and saves $2–5 per trip.

What doesn't change regardless of provider: buy the eSIM before departure , install on home Wi-Fi, enable Data Roaming when you land, and keep your regular SIM active for calls and bank verification codes.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is Saily eSIM legitimate and safe?
R: Yes. Saily is developed by Nord Security (the company behind NordVPN), which has been operating since 2012 with tens of millions of subscribers globally. It is not a new or unknown startup — it benefits from Nord's established infrastructure, security expertise, and regulatory compliance across EU and UK markets. Data plans are provided through local network partners in each country. It holds a 4.7★ rating on Trustpilot with over 97,000 reviews.

Î: Does Saily include a real VPN?
R: Saily includes a VPN that encrypts your connection on any network (not just public Wi-Fi), plus a built-in ad blocker and web protection against malicious domains. It is not the full NordVPN product — it lacks some advanced features like Threat Protection, dedicated IP, obfuscated servers, and split tunnelling. For travel purposes (securing public Wi-Fi, blocking ads to save data), the Saily VPN layer is sufficient for most users.

Î: Is Saily cheaper than Airalo?
R: Varies by destination and plan type. For fixed-data plans (5-10 GB), Airalo is often slightly cheaper per gigabyte. But Saily's unlimited plans are significantly better value — $23.99 for 7 days of unlimited data (5 GB/day at full speed) vs $27.00 at Airalo (3 GB/day at full speed). Check both for your specific destination — the difference on standard plans is usually $1-3.

Î: Can I use Saily for multiple countries in one trip?
R: Yes — Saily offers regional plans covering multiple countries simultaneously. The Europe plan covers 35+ European countries under a single plan, eliminating the need to buy separately for each destination. If your trip spans France, Italy, and Croatia, one European plan covers all three. Regional plans are slightly more expensive per GB than country-specific ones but save time and hassle on multi-country trips.

Î: Can I install Saily and Airalo on the same phone?
R: Yes, if your phone supports multiple eSIM profiles (most modern phones do). You can install profiles from different providers for different destinations and activate them individually. Many frequent travellers maintain separate eSIM profiles for their regular destinations and activate the relevant one before each trip.

Î: Does Saily work in Turkey?
R: Yes — but you must purchase and install before arriving. Since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to eSIM provider websites (including Saily, Airalo, and Yesim) from within Turkey. If you try to buy after landing in Istanbul or Antalya, the website will not load. Install the eSIM at home, and it activates automatically when you land.

Î: What phones support eSIM for Saily?
R: Saily works on any eSIM-compatible phone: iPhone XS or newer (2018+), Samsung Galaxy S20 series and newer, Google Pixel 3 and newer, and most Android phones released from 2021 onwards. Check by dialling *#06# on your phone — if an EID number appears, your phone supports eSIM.

Î: What happens when I run out of data on Saily?
R: When your fixed plan's data runs out, you can buy an additional plan directly in the app — it activates immediately without needing a new QR code. On unlimited plans, after exceeding 5 GB in a day, speed drops to ~1 Mbps (sufficient for messaging and basic browsing, but not for video streaming). Full speed resets the next day.

Î: Is Saily Ultra worth it?
R: Saily Ultra is a monthly subscription that bundles eSIM data + NordVPN + NordPass + ClassPass. The Premium plan ($59.99/month) includes 30 GB at full speed, then unlimited at ~1 Mbps, plus all Nord products. It's worth it if you already need NordVPN and travel frequently — otherwise, individual per-trip plans are more cost-effective.

## Alba Iulia 2026: The Complete Guide to Romania's Most Historically Significant City

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/alba-iulia-complete-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-08
Actualizat: 2026-08-08
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/alba-iulia-ghid-complet

Descriere: Complete Alba Iulia guide: Alba Carolina Fortress (free entry), changing of the guard in period costumes, Coronation Cathedral, Union Hall and 2,000 years of history. How to combine Alba Iulia with...

Răspuns scurt: Alba Iulia is the capital of Alba County and Romania's most historically significant city — the site of the Great Union of 1 December 1918, the coronation of Kings Ferdinand and Maria, and the most impressive Vauban-style bastion fortress in South-Eastern Europe. Alba Carolina Fortress (120 hectares, 7 bastions, free entry 9:00–23:00) hosts a daily changing of the guard in period costumes at noon. The perfect day trip from Sibiu (75 km) or Cluj (75 km).

On 1 December 1918, in the Assembly Hall in Alba Iulia, over 100,000 delegates from all Romanian provinces voted for union with the Kingdom of Romania. It was the birth moment of Greater Romania — and has been celebrated as Romania's National Day ever since.

But Alba Iulia is not important solely for 1918. It is the place where the Dacians built fortresses, where the Romans constructed Apulum (the largest Roman settlement in Dacia), where Mihai Viteazul first united the three principalities in 1600, and where King Ferdinand and Queen Maria were crowned in 1922.

And above all these layers of history stands Alba Carolina Fortress — the most representative Vauban-style bastion fortress in Romania and South-Eastern Europe, built at the initiative of Emperor Charles VI of Habsburg, under the supervision of Marshal Eugene of Savoy, between 1715 and 1738.

The fortress covers 120 hectares, has 7 bastions and entry is completely free — one of the most valuable places to visit in Romania without any ticket cost.


Alba Iulia at a Glance — Essential Facts

County: Alba, central Transylvania.

Population: approximately 63,000.

Symbolic importance: Romania's symbolic capital — site of the Great Union (1 December 1918) and royal coronations (1922).

Currency: Romanian Leu (RON).

Distances: Sibiu 75 km (1 hour), Cluj-Napoca 75 km (1 hour), Hunedoara (Corvin Castle) 45 km (45 min).

Visit budget: practically free for the fortress + cathedrals. With museums + guide: 50–100 RON per person.


How to Get to Alba Iulia

From Sibiu (Most Practical)

75 km, 1 hour by car on DN1. Coach: frequent services, ~2 hours, 15–20 RON. Best circuit: Sibiu morning + Alba Iulia midday–evening (changing of the guard at 12:00).

From Cluj-Napoca

75 km, 1 hour by car. Coach or train: ~1.5–2 hours.

From Bucharest

~350 km, ~4 hours by car on A1 + DN1. By train: 5–6 hours. Alternative: flight OTP → CLJ (Cluj, ~1 hour, 50–120 EUR) + car/coach to Alba Iulia (1 hour).


Alba Carolina Fortress — The Seven-Bastion Stronghold

Alba Carolina Fortress is the largest Vauban-style bastion fortress in Romania and South-Eastern Europe — built on the defensive system devised by French military engineer Vauban, the same system used at Versailles and in Louis XIV's fortresses.

Technical facts:


Area: 120 hectares

7 bastions and 6 monumental gates

Wall length: ~12 km

Construction: 1715–1738, initiative of Emperor Charles VI of Habsburg

Overseen by: Eugene of Savoy (who stopped Ottoman expansion in Europe)


Entry — Free 9:00–23:00

Fortress entry is completely free, daily 9:00–23:00. There is no entry ticket for the enclosure, walls, bastions or interior squares. Fees only apply to specific museums inside the fortress.

The 7 Monumental Gates

The fortress has 6 monumental Baroque gates, ornamented with Habsburg reliefs. Gate III (the Main Gate) is the most impressive — with mythological sculptures and imperial coats of arms. It is also the site of the changing of the guard.

Underground Galleries

Beneath the fortress stretches a system of defensive underground galleries accessible during certain periods — communication and storage tunnels from the 18th century.


The Changing of the Guard — The Free Daily Spectacle

The changing of the guard takes place daily at 12:00 during tourist season (May–September), at Gate III of the fortress. The guard consists of soldiers in 18th-century costumes — infantry, cavalry, artillery and commanders — in uniforms specific to the Habsburg army.

The spectacle lasts 20–30 minutes and includes:


Guard parade in front of the fortress

The gate exchange ceremony

Cannon salute (on certain occasions)


At weekends: the changing of the guard may be doubled — check the schedule at the fortress entrance.

Medieval Combat Demonstrations

Every Friday from 19:00, during April–October, there are combat demonstrations with Roman soldiers, Dacian warriors and medieval knights in the fortress centre. The show is free and spectacular — re-enacted with authentic period weapons and costumes.

1 December — Romania's National Day: Alba Iulia is the official venue of the national celebration, with military parade, solemn ceremonies and hundreds of thousands of people. A unique spectacle but maximally crowded.


Guided Tour of Alba Carolina Fortress — History in Period Costumes


What to See Inside the Fortress

Coronation Cathedral (Cathedral of the Reunification)

The Cathedral of the Reunification was built specifically for the coronation of King Ferdinand I and Queen Maria on 15 October 1922 — the first coronation in Greater Romania.

In neo-Brâncovenesc style (inspired by 17th–18th century Romanian princely architecture), with spectacular interior frescoes and the royal crypt (tombs of King Ferdinand and Queen Maria). Free entry.

Roman Catholic Cathedral of St Michael

Transylvania's oldest cathedral, with sections dating from the 11th–12th century, with overlapping Romanesque, Gothic and Baroque elements. Inside lies the tomb of John of Hunedoara (Iancu de Hunedoara) — father of Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary. Free entry.

Union Hall

Union Hall is the room where, on 1 December 1918, the delegates gathered from all Romanian provinces voted the Resolution of Union. Voted enthusiastically by thousands of delegates — the birth certificate of Greater Romania.

Entry to Union Hall: free. Located in the former Military Casino (Palatul Apor).

National Museum of the Union

Museum with 200,000+ exhibits covering the region's history from the Stone Age to modernity — with Roman, medieval artefacts and Union documents. Ticket: ~15–20 RON (~3–4 EUR).


Corvin Castle and Alba Iulia Circuit from Sibiu or Cluj

Corvin Castle in Hunedoara — Transylvania's Largest Gothic Castle

45 km west of Alba Iulia (45 minutes), Corvin Castle is Transylvania's largest Gothic castle — the Huniade/Corvin family residence, construction from the 14th–15th century, with impressive towers, Gothic inner courtyard and the legend that Vlad Dracula was held prisoner here for three years (disputed by historians).

Ticket: 45 RON (~9 EUR). Hours: daily 9:00–17:00 (18:00 in season).

Classic circuit from Sibiu: Sibiu (depart 9:00) → Alba Iulia (10:00–12:00, changing of the guard) → Corvin Castle (14:00–17:00) → return to Sibiu (19:00). A complete day, ~3 hours driving total.


Food and Drink in Alba Iulia

Restaurants in the fortress — several medieval-themed restaurants installed in the fortress's historic buildings. Fantastic atmosphere, mid-range prices (50–100 RON per person).

City centre restaurants — cheaper than the fortress, traditional Romanian cuisine (soup, sarmale, mici).

Wine from the Aiud vineyard region — Alba Iulia is in the heart of the Aiud-Crișana wine zone. Local white wine: 15–25 RON a glass at a restaurant.

Recommended Itinerary — One Day in Alba Iulia

Practical Tips

Parking — free or with a small fee at the fortress gates. Don't drive inside the fortress — pedestrian zone.

Changing of the guard at 12:00 — if planning a single visit, arrive at the fortress 15 minutes before noon and position yourself near Gate III.

1 December — if going on National Day, book accommodation 3–6 months ahead. Hotels in Alba Iulia and Sibiu sell out during this period.

AR App — the fortress has an augmented reality app that lets you visualise virtual soldiers on the walls — download "Cetatea Alba Carolina AR" before visiting.

Evening — the fortress is spectacularly illuminated after dark. An evening walk inside the fortress is one of Transylvania's most beautiful experiences.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Alba Iulia?
R: By car: ~350 km, ~4 hours on the A1 motorway + DN1. By train: InterCity Bucharest Nord → Alba Iulia, ~5–6 hours, 100–140 RON. By coach: 5–7 hours, 70–100 RON. Alternatively, flight OTP → CLJ (Cluj, 50 min, 50–120 EUR) + bus/car Cluj → Alba Iulia (75 km, 1 hour). Alba Iulia works best as a day trip from Sibiu (75 km, 1 hour) or Cluj (75 km, 1 hour).

Î: Is entry to Alba Carolina Fortress free?
R: Yes — entry to the fortress (enclosure, walls, bastions, interior squares) is completely free, 7 days a week, 9:00–23:00. The museums inside the fortress have separate fees: Union Hall (free), National Museum of the Union (10–15 RON), official guide (~30 RON). Park outside the fortress gates and enter on foot.

Î: The Alba Iulia changing of the guard — how does it work?
R: The changing of the guard takes place daily at 12:00 during tourist season (May–September), at Gate III of the fortress. The guard consists of soldiers in 18th-century costumes (infantry, cavalry, artillery, commanders) specific to the Habsburg army. It may be doubled at weekends. In addition, every Friday from 19:00 (April–October) there are combat demonstrations with Roman soldiers, Dacians and medieval knights. Everything is free for spectators.

Î: What is the Union Hall and why is it important?
R: The Union Hall is the room in Palatul Apor in Alba Iulia where, on 1 December 1918, delegates from all Romanian provinces voted for union with the Kingdom of Romania — the birth moment of Greater Romania. It is a place of supreme symbolic importance in Romanian history. Entry is free. Located in the centre of the fortress.

Î: How long do I need for a visit to Alba Iulia?
R: Minimum 3–4 hours for the fortress, cathedrals and Union Hall. A full day if you want to visit the museums with a guide, watch the changing of the guard and explore all 7 bastions and underground galleries. Alba Iulia combines ideally with Corvin Castle in Hunedoara (45 km, 45 min) or Sibiu (75 km, 1 hour) in a one-day circuit.

Î: Can Corvin Castle be visited combined with Alba Iulia?
R: Yes — Corvin Castle in Hunedoara is 45 km from Alba Iulia (45 minutes). The classic circuit: Alba Iulia in the morning + Corvin Castle in the afternoon = a complete day from Sibiu or Cluj. Corvin Castle ticket: 45 RON (~9 EUR), including access to all rooms and towers.

Î: Is Alba Iulia suitable for families with children?
R: Absolutely — the fortress is a historic playground for children. The changing of the guard and the combat demonstrations with Roman soldiers, Dacians and medieval knights (Fridays from 19:00) are spectacular for all ages. There is also a vintage locomotive and open play areas inside the fortress.

Î: What is the best time to visit Alba Iulia?
R: May–September: daily changing of the guard at 12:00 and Friday combat demonstrations. 1 December: Romania's National Day — Alba Iulia is the official venue of the national celebration, with military parade and solemn ceremonies (book accommodation months ahead). Spring and autumn: low prices, few tourists, fortress just as spectacular.

## Belgrade 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to the City That Never Sleeps

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/belgrade-complete-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-07
Actualizat: 2026-08-07
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/belgrad-ghid-complet

Descriere: Complete Belgrade guide: Kalemegdan Fortress, Skadarlija, Temple of Saint Sava, splavs and legendary nightlife. Real prices in dinars and EUR, free public transport since 2025 and everything you ne...

Răspuns scurt: Belgrade is the capital of Serbia and one of Europe's most energetic and affordable cities. Famous for its legendary nightlife (splavs — floating clubs on the Sava and Danube), the Kalemegdan Fortress above the confluence of two rivers and extraordinarily cheap Balkan food, Belgrade offers an unmatched value-for-money proposition in Europe. Direct flights from Bucharest: 45 minutes, from 30–70 EUR return.

Belgrade doesn't explain itself — it's experienced.

It's the only European city where you can drink a beer at a floating river club at 4 AM, eat grilled ćevapi two hours earlier and watch the sunrise from the walls of a Roman fortress that's 2,000 years old. All in the same weekend, all for under 50 euros.

It's not an agreeable city in the conventional tourist sense — it doesn't have Prague's perfect cleanliness or Vienna's elegance. It's raw, noisy, contradictory, with NATO-bombed buildings from 1999 standing abandoned next to communist blocks and brand-new boutique hotels. But it has an energy few European cities still possess — that of a place that has bounced back from wars, sanctions and isolation and chosen to party.


Belgrade at a Glance — Essential Facts

Country: Serbia — not an EU member, not in Schengen.

Population: approximately 1.7 million (metropolitan area) — the largest city in the Balkans after Istanbul.

Currency: Serbian Dinar (RSD). 1 EUR ≈ 117 RSD in 2026. Serbia does not use the euro — you need to exchange currency.

Language: Serbian is the official language (Cyrillic and Latin alphabets). English is well understood in the tourist area and by younger generations.

Public transport: free since 2025 — bus, tram, trolleybus throughout Belgrade.

Visa: EU citizens do not need a visa for Serbia — entry with a valid ID card or passport.

Direct flights from Bucharest: Air Serbia, OTP→BEG, 45–55 minutes.


How to Get from Romania to Belgrade

Direct Flight (45 Minutes — Fastest Option)

Air Serbia operates direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Belgrade (BEG). Duration: 45–55 minutes — one of the shortest international flights in Europe.

Indicative 2026 prices: 30–90 EUR return with 2–6 weeks' advance booking. Sometimes available at 25–30 EUR return on promotion.

Airport → city centre transfer: Bus A1 (free since 2025!) → Slavija Square: 30 minutes. Taxi/Bolt: 12–18 EUR, 20–25 minutes.

By Car (Recommended for Flexibility)

Distance Bucharest → Belgrade: ~400 km, 4–4.5 hours on motorway. Important: Serbia is not in the EU — you need your vehicle documents, a Green Card (international insurance) and ID/passport.

By Coach

FlixBus and Romanian operators offer direct routes Bucharest → Belgrade. Duration: 7–8 hours, prices: 20–40 EUR. The budget option, less comfortable.


The Serbian Dinar — Quick Guide for Tourists

Serbia doesn't use the euro. You'll pay in Serbian dinars (RSD) .

2026 exchange rate: 1 EUR ≈ 117 RSD.

Quick calculation:


500 RSD ≈ 4.30 EUR

1,000 RSD ≈ 8.50 EUR

5,000 RSD ≈ 43 EUR


Where to exchange: local ATMs (best rate, small commission), authorised exchange offices in the centre. Avoid airport exchange (unfavourable rate) and street exchanges (scam risk).

Cards are accepted in most restaurants and hotels, but many small local places and markets are cash-only.


When to Go — Seasonal Guide

Period Temperature Advantages Disadvantages
April – June 16–24°C Perfect for walks, splavs open for the season Sometimes rainy in May
July – August 28–35°C Splavs at full speed, festivals Intense heat, crowded
September – October 15–22°C Best time — pleasant cool, fewer tourists —
November – March 0–10°C Warm kafanas, minimum prices, authentic atmosphere Cold, splavs closed

EXIT Festival (Novi Sad, July) is Serbia's largest music festival — if you're into electronic music or rock, it's worth combining with a Belgrade city break.


What to See in Belgrade

Kalemegdan Fortress — 2,000 Years of Free History

Kalemegdan is Belgrade's soul. The Roman-medieval-Ottoman-Austro-Hungarian fortress rises on a hill 125 metres above the confluence of the Sava and Danube — a vantage point that explains why, throughout history, 40 different armies have conquered and lost this place.

Park and walls access: free, open 24/7. In the evening, at sunset, it's one of Belgrade's most spectacular moments — locals come with supermarket wine and sit on the parapets to watch the sun set over the river confluence.

The Victor Monument (Pobednik) — Ivan Meštrović's 14-metre bronze statue, Belgrade's symbol. It faces west, with its back to the city — according to legend, because the Serbs didn't know who the next enemy would be.

Military Museum: entry ~4 EUR, excellent for historical context.

Nebojša Tower: Ottoman prison where Greek revolutionary poet Rigas Feraios was executed in 1798. Entry ~3 EUR.

Knez Mihailova — The Main Boulevard

The pedestrian street Knez Mihailova (Prince Mihailo) is the spine of central Belgrade — 1.5 km from Republic Square to the Kalemegdan gate. Flanked by neoclassical and eclectic 19th-century buildings, it's full of cafés, shops and street performers. Turkish coffee (kafa) at an authentic local café: 1–1.50 EUR.

Republic Square (Trg Republike) — the city's meeting point, with the equestrian statue of Prince Mihailo. Locals say "see you kod konja" (at the horse) — you can use the expression too; Serbs appreciate it.

Skadarlija — The Bohemian Quarter with Kafanas and Live Music

Skadarlija is the quarter with which Belgrade compares itself to Montmartre — a cobblestone street flanked by kafanas (traditional Serbian taverns) with live tamburica music, aromatic stews and rakija served in small glasses.

The major kafanas: Tri Šešira (Three Hats) and Dva Jelena (Two Deer) — historic, touristy, but authentic in food and music. A full meal with live music and beer: 15–25 EUR. Live music charge: sometimes 3–5 EUR separately — ask before sitting down.

Tip: Skadarlija is more authentic Tuesday–Thursday evening. Weekends attract large tourist groups. For the real local experience, come at lunchtime — kafanas serve daily menus for 4–7 EUR.

Temple of Saint Sava — The World's Largest Orthodox Church

The Temple of Saint Sava is colossal — the second largest by floor area in the world (after the converted Hagia Sophia), with a 70-metre dome visible from kilometres away. Construction began in 1935 and continues today (the interior mosaics were recently completed).

Entry is free. The crypt below (more recently completed, with impressive Byzantine mosaics) is worth 15–20 minutes.

Savamala — The Creative District and Underground Clubs

Savamala is what happened when artists and entrepreneurs took over an abandoned industrial neighbourhood on the Sava riverbank. Today it's the epicentre of Belgrade's alternative culture: art galleries, design studios, hipster cafés, concept restaurants and — most importantly — legendary underground clubs.

Klub Drugstore, Mladost i zdravlje, 20/44 — clubs in former warehouses and factories, electronic music, running Friday–Saturday until morning. Entry: free or 5–10 EUR.

Mikser House — former furniture factory, now a cultural space with cafés, galleries and events. Free during the day.

Alternative Walking Tour Through Savamala and Dorćol — Belgrade's Hipster Side

The Splavs — Belgrade's Unique Riverside Nightlife

The splavs are one of Belgrade's most original experiences — floating structures moored on the banks of the Sava and Danube, operating as restaurants by day and clubs by night.

Ada Huja area (on the Danube) and the Sava zone (below Kalemegdan) are the main clusters.

Two distinct categories:

Restaurant/bar splavs (open from 10:00): Serbian food, water-view terraces, cheap beer, relaxed atmosphere. Prices similar to city centre restaurants. Perfect for lunch or a sunset cocktail.

Club splavs (open after midnight, running until 7:00–8:00 AM): electronic music (techno, house) or turbo-folk (popular Balkan music genre, controversial but authentic). Entry: free to 15 EUR. Minimum spend sometimes required.

Essential tip: Belgraders don't start their evening before midnight. If you arrive at a club at 11 PM, you're one of the first. The peak is 2:00–5:00 AM.


Food and Drink — Belgrade Gastronomy Guide

What You Must Eat

Ćevapi (ćevapčići) — Balkan grilled sausages made from mixed minced meat (beef+pork or beef+lamb), served with flatbread (lepinje), onion and ajvar (red pepper paste). A 10-piece portion: 600–900 RSD (5–8 EUR). Best at a roštilj (grill restaurant), not fast food.

Pljeskavica — the Serbian burger — an enormous flat spiced minced meat patty served in lepinje with toppings. At street stalls: 400–600 RSD (3–5 EUR). At good restaurants: the "punjena" version (stuffed with cheese and kajmak) at 700–1,000 RSD.

Kajmak — fermented milk cream, somewhere between sour cream and butter, served as a side with almost everything. Do not leave Belgrade without tasting fresh kajmak.

Burek — filo pastry pie (a savoury baklava), filled with cheese, meat or spinach, baked in large trays and sold by the slice. At local bakeries: 150–250 RSD (1.30–2.20 EUR) a slice. Classic Belgrade breakfast with yoghurt.

Karađorđeva šnicla — Serbia's national schnitzel, rolled with kajmak and ham. 900–1,400 RSD (7–12 EUR) at a restaurant.

Rakija — The National Drink

Rakija is the drink with which Serbia most strongly identifies — a fruit brandy (plum = šljivovica, quince = dunjevača, apricot = kajsijevača) at 40–65% ABV, consumed at any time of day and in any social context.

At kafanas, rakija is served in small glasses (50 ml) at 150–400 RSD (1.30–3.50 EUR). Serbian hosts will offer you homemade rakija — it's a hospitality gesture; polite refusal is acceptable but honest appreciation of the drink's quality is extremely well received.

Where to Eat

Authentic budget (3–8 EUR/meal):


Roštilji (grill restaurants) in popular neighbourhoods Zemun, Vračar

Bakeries for burek and gibanica at breakfast

Zeleni Venac Market — the central market with fresh produce and food stalls


Mid-range (8–20 EUR/person):


Dva Jelena (Skadarlija) — historic kafana, live music, traditional food

Restoran Šešir Moj (Skadarlija) — authentic atmosphere, full menu

Savamala cafés — for something more contemporary

Practical Tips for Belgrade

Public transport is free — since 2025, all buses, trams and trolleybuses in Belgrade are free. No ticket needed. The BusPlus app shows routes and real-time arrivals.

Taxis: use an app — CarGo (Serbian local app) or Bolt are the safest and cheapest. Street taxis can charge inflated prices for tourists.

ATMs: best rates at Raiffeisen, Banca Intesa or UniCredit ATMs. Withdraw larger amounts at once (fixed fee per withdrawal, not percentage).

Live music charge — at Skadarlija kafanas, live music sometimes means an additional charge of 300–500 RSD per person. Ask BEFORE sitting down.

NATO-bombed buildings — in central Belgrade, some buildings remain undemolished and unreconstruted from the 1999 bombings. Avoid photographing them from close up — there are restrictions and locals can react negatively.


Travel Insurance — Serbia Is Not in the EU

Important: Serbia is not part of the EU. The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is not valid in Serbia. You need travel insurance that specifically covers medical assistance in Serbia.

EKTA Travel Insurance covers Serbia in its global plans — verify at booking that the country is included in your package.


eSIM for Serbia

Serbia has a well-developed 4G/LTE network in the city centre. Local operators: Telekom Srbija, A1, Yettel (former Telenor).


Airalo — Serbia-specific or extended European plans; good coverage

Saily — flexible plan alternative


Roaming from Romania in Serbian networks can be expensive — check your tariffs before travelling, or activate an eSIM.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Belgrade?
R: Air Serbia operates direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Belgrade (BEG). Duration: 45–55 minutes — one of the shortest international flights from Romania. Prices: 30–90 EUR return with early booking. By car: 400 km, approximately 4–4.5 hours. By coach: FlixBus and local operators, 7–8 hours, from 20–40 EUR.

Î: What currency does Serbia use? Can I pay in euros?
R: Serbia is not in the EU and uses the Serbian Dinar (RSD). 1 EUR ≈ 117 RSD in 2026. Euros are occasionally accepted at tourist hotels and restaurants, but the exchange rate is unfavourable. Exchange money at local ATMs (best rate) or authorised exchange offices. Avoid airport exchange.

Î: Is Belgrade safe for tourists?
R: Yes, Belgrade is generally safe for tourists. The city centre (Stari Grad, Knez Mihailova, Kalemegdan) is safe day and night. Watch out for: unlicensed taxis (use CarGo or Bolt apps), street currency exchange scams and the noise specific to weekend nightlife areas. Avoid confrontations in bars — Belgraders are passionate and direct.

Î: What are splavs and how do they work?
R: Splavs (splav = raft in Serbian) are floating clubs and restaurants moored on the banks of the Sava and Danube. Two types: restaurant splavs (open all day, food, relaxed atmosphere) and club splavs (open after midnight, electronic music or turbo-folk, running until 6–8 AM). Club entry: free to 15 EUR depending on the event. Active season: May–September.

Î: How much does food cost in Belgrade?
R: Belgrade is one of Europe's cheapest cities for food. Ćevapi (grilled minced meat) with bread: 3–5 EUR. Pljeskavica (giant Serbian burger): 3–4 EUR. A full meal with beer at a local restaurant: 8–15 EUR. At a kafana in Skadarlija with live music: 15–25 EUR. Local beer (Jelen, Lav): 1.50–2.50 EUR at a bar.

Î: Is public transport free in Belgrade?
R: Yes — since 2025, all public transport in Belgrade (bus, tram, trolleybus) is free for all passengers. No ticket needed. This is one of the most generous urban transport policies in Europe and makes getting around the city extremely convenient.

Î: Is Novi Sad worth a day trip from Belgrade?
R: Absolutely. Novi Sad is 90 km from Belgrade (1 hour by train or bus, 3–5 EUR). The Petrovaradin Fortress, multicultural Old Town and the EXIT festival venue (Serbia's largest music festival, held in July) make Novi Sad an excellent excursion. Easily done in a single day.

Î: What is the best time to visit Belgrade?
R: April–June and September–October: pleasant temperatures (16–24°C), active street life, normal prices. July–August: most lively (splavs in full swing) but also hottest (30–35°C) and most crowded. December–February: cold, but Christmas markets and intimate kafana atmosphere. Belgrade works well year-round — it has no bad season.

## Brașov 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to the Gateway of Transylvania

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/brasov-complete-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-08
Actualizat: 2026-08-08
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/brasov-ghid-complet

Descriere: Complete Brașov guide: Piața Sfatului, the Black Church, Tampa Mountain with the BRAȘOV sign, Bran Castle (Dracula), Peleș Castle and the Libearty Bear Sanctuary. New Ghimbav Airport, real 2026 pri...

Răspuns scurt: Brașov is Romania's most visited city (after Bucharest) and the best base for exploring Transylvania — with an authentic medieval centre surrounded by the Carpathian Mountains, the iconic BRAȘOV sign on Mount Tâmpa, the Black Church (Romania's largest), Bran Castle 30 km away and Peleș Castle 50 km away. It now has its own airport (Brașov-Ghimbav, GHV, opened 2024) with direct connections from several European cities.

Brașov is the city from which you understand why Transylvania has captured Europe's imagination for centuries. Stand in Piața Sfatului — the white limestone paving, the colourful-façaded houses, the Gothic Black Church in the background — and look up. Mount Tâmpa rises abruptly above the rooftops, with the white BRAȘOV letters gleaming in the sunlight, like a declaration that you're somewhere entirely special.

Brașov is a medieval town at the foot of Mount Tâmpa and the gateway to Transylvania — surrounded by the Carpathian Mountains, with an Old Town full of history and character.

It is also the most practical base for exploring the greatest concentration of castles, fortresses and mountain landscapes in Romania: Bran Castle 30 minutes away, Peleș Castle one hour, the Transfăgărășan 1.5 hours, Sighișoara 1.5 hours, Sibiu 2 hours.

An important development for 2026: Brașov-Ghimbav Airport (GHV) is now operational, with direct flights from several European cities — you no longer have to land in Bucharest to reach Transylvania.


Brașov at a Glance — Essential Facts

County: Brașov, southern Transylvania.

Population: approximately 290,000 — Romania's sixth largest city.

Currency: Romanian Leu (RON). 1 EUR ≈ 4.97 RON.

Own airport: Brașov-Ghimbav (GHV) — opened in 2024, with direct flights from several European cities.

Distance from Bucharest: ~170 km, ~2h30 by train or car.

Average budget: 160–270 RON/day (~32–54 EUR) — similar to Sibiu, more affordable than Cluj.


How to Get from Bucharest to Brașov

By Train (Most Recommended)

InterRegio/Rapid Bucharest Nord → Brașov: ~2h30, 60–100 RON (~12–20 EUR). Most comfortable — Brașov's station is in the city centre, 15 minutes' walk from Piața Sfatului.

By Car

~170 km on DN1, ~2h30 under normal conditions. Warning: DN1 on Friday evenings and Sunday evenings can be blocked for hours by traffic to/from the mountains. Leave in the morning or check Waze.

Direct Flight to Brașov-Ghimbav (GHV)

Brașov-Ghimbav Airport is now operational with regular services — check availability of direct flights from your city.


When to Go

Period Temperature Advantages Disadvantages
May – June 15–24°C Ideal, green Tâmpa, few tourists —
July – August 20–28°C Lively, all attractions open Bran + Peleș crowded, book online
September – October 12–22°C Ideal — colours, Transfăgărășan open —
December – March -5–5°C Poiana Brașov — skiing and snowboarding Cold in the centre


What to See in Brașov

Piața Sfatului — The Medieval Heart

Piața Sfatului is the heart of medieval Brașov — a rectangular square with colourful houses, restaurant terraces and the Council House (former town hall) at the centre.

Council House (Casa Sfatului) — the 15th-century Gothic building with central tower, today a history museum. Ticket: ~10 RON (~2 EUR). Exterior access free.

Strada Republicii — Brașov's pedestrian artery, connecting Piața Sfatului to the civic centre, with shops, cafés and a character typical of a university city.

The Black Church — Romania's Largest

The Black Church (Schwarze Kirche) is Romania's largest Gothic church and the largest between Vienna and Istanbul, built in the 14th–15th centuries. It received its name after the great fire of 1689, when smoke blackened the exterior walls.

Entry: ~15 RON (~3 EUR). Hours: Monday–Saturday 10:00–17:00.

Interior: one of the most valuable collections of Anatolian rugs outside Turkey (150+ carpets brought by Saxon merchants), the monumental organ and medieval fresco.

Mount Tâmpa and the BRAȘOV Sign

Tampa cable car: Tuesday–Sunday 9:30–17:00, return ticket 8 EUR/adult.

On foot: 40–45 minutes on the Serpentines trail (follow the red marking from the mountain base).

At the top: panoramic observation platform with complete views of the medieval centre, the Bucegi Mountains and the surrounding valleys. The BRAȘOV sign (Hollywood-style) is visible from below and spectacular up close.

Weavers' Bastion and Medieval Walls

The Weavers' Bastion is the best-preserved medieval bastion in Brașov, today a museum of the city's medieval defences. Ticket: ~10 RON. Wall trail: partially open, free.

Schei Quarter — Beyond the Walls

Schei is Brașov's traditionally Romanian neighbourhood, separated from the Saxon zone by Schei Gate. Here stands the First Romanian School (1495) — the first school teaching in Romanian in Transylvania, today a museum. Ticket: ~10 RON.


Tour: Peleș Castle, Bran Castle and Râșnov Fortress from Brașov

Bran Castle — Dracula's Castle?

Bran Castle is 30 km from Brașov — an impressive medieval fortress built in the 14th century, above a gorge that marked the border between Transylvania and Wallachia.

The Dracula connection: Vlad the Impaler probably visited Bran, but didn't live there. The link to Bram Stoker's novel is tourism marketing, not history. The castle is worth visiting regardless — the labyrinthine architecture with towers, narrow corridors and medieval atmosphere are spectacular.

Ticket: 45 RON (~9 EUR) adult. Fast-pass (skip-the-line): 60 RON (~12 EUR). Hours: daily 9:00–18:00 (May–Sept), 9:00–16:00 (Oct–Apr).

Essential tip: arrive at opening (9:00) or after 16:00 to avoid the maximum crowds between 10:00–15:00.

Peleș Castle — Romania's Most Beautiful Castle

Peleș Castle in Sinaia (50 km from Brașov) is the former summer residence of the Romanian royal family, built in neo-Renaissance German style between 1873–1914.

Tickets are purchased EXCLUSIVELY online, in advance, for a specific time slot. There are no walk-up tickets. Capacity: 500 people per slot.

Online prices: 60–100 RON (~12–20 EUR) depending on the tour chosen.

Peleș MUST be booked in advance — check availability at peles.ro or GetYourGuide with skip-the-line included.


Day Trips from Brașov — The Transylvania Castle Circuit

Râșnov Fortress

15 km from Brașov, Râșnov Fortress is a medieval refuge fortress on a hill, with valley panorama. Ticket: ~25 RON (~5 EUR). Accessible by local cable car or on foot (15 minutes). 2026 note: verify it is open — Râșnov Fortress was temporarily closed for works in 2026.

Libearty Bear Sanctuary — Zărnești

The Libearty Sanctuary shelters over 100 brown bears rescued from captivity across 69 hectares of forest — Europe's largest bear sanctuary.

Ticket: 90 RON (~18 EUR). Online booking mandatory. 20 km from Brașov.

Viscri and the Saxon Villages

Viscri is Romania's best-preserved Saxon village — with the fortified church, white houses and preserved traditions. Promoted by Prince Charles (who bought a house there). 65 km from Brașov.

Poiana Brașov — The Ski Resort

13 km from Brașov's centre, Poiana Brașov is Romania's largest ski resort — with 20 km of slopes, ski lifts and active winter nightlife.


Food and Drink in Brașov

Kürtőskalács (chimney cake) — spiral fried dough with sugar and cinnamon, sold by street vendors on Piața Sfatului. 15–25 RON.

Transylvanian sour soup (Ciorbă ardelenească) — denser and more acidic than Moldovan versions. 20–30 RON.

Mici (grilled meat rolls) and chips — obligatory at a Transylvanian restaurant. 25–40 RON a portion.

Where to Eat

Budget (20–50 RON/meal): restaurants on Strada Republicii or Piața Unirii area.

Mid-range (50–120 RON/person): terrace restaurants on Piața Sfatului (pricier but atmospheric), or places in the Schei quarter (more authentic and cheaper).

Practical Tips

Peleș online booking mandatory — cannot be purchased on the day. Book at peles.ro or GetYourGuide at least 1 week ahead in season.

Bran crowded — if going to Bran Castle in season, arrive at 9:00. Between 10:00 and 15:00, queues can be long even with an online ticket.

DN1 traffic — Friday evenings and Sunday evenings, the Brașov–Bucharest road is a nightmare. Take the train or leave early.

Poiana Brașov in winter — bus 20 from Brașov centre reaches Poiana in 30 minutes, 3 RON. No need for taxi or car.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Brașov?
R: By train: InterRegio/Rapid Bucharest Nord → Brașov, ~2h30, 60–100 RON — the most comfortable option. By car: ~170 km on DN1, ~2h30 (watch out for Friday evening traffic). Direct flight: Brașov-Ghimbav Airport (GHV), opened in 2024, with Wizz Air and Ryanair services from several European cities.

Î: Is Bran Castle really Dracula's Castle?
R: Partially — Bran Castle is associated with Dracula through tourism marketing, not solid historical fact. Vlad the Impaler probably visited Bran, but didn't live there. The castle is impressive for its architecture (14th century) and landscape. Worth visiting for its historical and aesthetic value, not necessarily for the Dracula legend. Ticket: 45 RON (~9 EUR).

Î: Peleș Castle — how do I buy tickets and what are the hours?
R: Peleș Castle tickets are purchased EXCLUSIVELY online, in advance, for a specific time slot. There are no walk-up tickets. Wednesday slots: 10:00–12:45. Thursday–Sunday: 9:15–11:00. Maximum capacity: 500 people per slot. Online price: ~60–100 RON. Book at least 1–2 weeks ahead in season.

Î: The BRAȘOV sign on Mount Tâmpa — how do I get there?
R: Tampa cable car: Tue–Sun, 9:30–17:00 (last ride up), return ticket 8 EUR/adult. On foot: 40–45 minutes on the Serpentines trail or Drumul Stejarilor. At the top: observation platform next to the BRAȘOV sign with panoramic views of the medieval centre and the Bucegi Mountains.

Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Brașov cost?
R: A 3-day/2-night city break costs 220–380 EUR per person (mid-range), including flights from Bucharest, accommodation and castle excursions. Brașov is slightly more expensive than Sibiu: a restaurant dinner 60–120 RON per person (~12–24 EUR), mid-range accommodation 250–400 RON per night (~50–80 EUR), castles 45–100 RON entry.

Î: Is the Libearty Bear Sanctuary worth visiting?
R: Yes — the Libearty Sanctuary in Zărnești (20 km from Brașov) shelters over 100 brown bears rescued from captivity, across 69 hectares of forest — Europe's largest bear sanctuary. Ticket: 90 RON (~18 EUR). Online booking mandatory. It is not a zoo — the bears live semi-wild.

Î: Brașov or Sibiu — which is better?
R: Depends: Sibiu = more authentic, more compact, more cultural, more affordable. Brașov = larger, better connected, more spectacular excursions (Bran, Peleș, Tâmpa), livelier. Brașov is ideal as a base for exploring Transylvania; Sibiu is better for deep cultural immersion. Ideally: visit both.

Î: What is the best season for Brașov?
R: Spring (May–June) and autumn (September–October): ideal — pleasant temperatures, Transfăgărășan open, few tourists. Summer (July–August): most lively, all attractions open, but crowded at castles (book Peleș online weeks ahead). Winter (December–March): Poiana Brașov 13 km away — one of Romania's best ski resorts. Christmas in Brașov — festive markets with atmosphere.

## Bratislava 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to the Capital on the Danube

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/bratislava-complete-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-07
Actualizat: 2026-08-07
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/bratislava-ghid-complet

Descriere: Complete Bratislava guide: Bratislava Castle, Old Town, Blue Church, UFO Bridge and Devín Castle. Real prices, how to get there from Bucharest and why it deserves more than a day trip from Vienna.

Răspuns scurt: Bratislava is the capital of Slovakia, located just 56 minutes by train from Vienna and 2.5 hours from Budapest. Although small (around 475,000 inhabitants), it offers a charming Old Town, an impressive castle above the Danube, a uniquely Blue Church and prices half those of Vienna. It deserves at least 2 days — not just a stopover.

Bratislava suffers from a syndrome that few European destinations share: it is systematically underestimated. Half the tourists who visit do so as a day trip from Vienna, stroll through the Old Town for 3 hours, drink an inexpensive beer and leave with the impression they've "ticked off" Slovakia's capital.

Those who stay a night or two discover something entirely different.

They discover a capital with a medieval centre more compact and authentic than Prague (without the tourist crowds), a Blue Church covered entirely in turquoise unlike anything else in Europe, a white castle above the Danube where you can see Austria and Hungary at the same time, a bridge with a flying-saucer restaurant and, beyond the city, the dramatic ruins of Devín Castle on the cliff where the Danube meets the Morava.

Add to this prices half those of Vienna, a rapidly growing craft beer scene and a relaxed city atmosphere that hasn't yet been overwhelmed by mass tourism.


Bratislava at a Glance — Essential Facts

Country: Slovakia, EU member since 2004, Schengen Area, Eurozone (since 2009).

Population: approximately 475,000 — one of the smallest capitals in the EU.

Currency: Euro (EUR) — no exchange needed.

Language: Slovak is the official language. English is spoken well in the tourist area, especially by younger people. German is understood by many — Austrian influence is historical and strong.

Strategic location: 56 minutes by train from Vienna, 2.5 hours from Budapest, 4 hours from Prague.

Average budget: 50–70 EUR/day (mid-range) — 40–50% cheaper than Vienna.

Old Town: compact, fully walkable end-to-end in 15–20 minutes — one of the smallest historic centres among European capitals.


How to Get from Romania to Bratislava

Option 1 — Fly OTP → Vienna + Train (Recommended)

The most practical route: fly Bucharest (OTP) → Vienna (VIE) with Wizz Air, Ryanair or TAROM (1h50, from 50–120 EUR return), then take the train Vienna Hauptbahnhof → Bratislava Hlavná stanica (56 minutes, 12–15 EUR).

This works perfectly for a combined Bratislava + Vienna city break.

Option 2 — Direct Flight OTP → BTS

There are occasionally direct flights to Bratislava M.R. Štefánik Airport (BTS) — check Wizz Air and Ryanair for your dates. When available, they're convenient: the airport is 9 km from the centre (bus no. 61: 1 EUR, 30 minutes; taxi/Bolt: 10–15 EUR).

Option 3 — By Car

Distance Bucharest → Bratislava: ~1,400 km, 13–15 hours. Good for an extended Central European road trip (Bucharest → Budapest → Bratislava → Vienna → Prague).


When to Go — Seasonal Guide

Period Temperature Advantages Disadvantages
April – June 14–22°C Chestnut blossom on the promenade, few tourists, normal prices Sometimes rainy in May
July – August 22–28°C Most lively, Danube terraces Crowded, higher prices
September – October 12–20°C New wines in the Little Carpathians, autumn atmosphere —
December -2–4°C Renowned Christmas markets, magical atmosphere Cold
January – March -5–5°C Minimum prices, almost no tourists Cold, some reduced hours

Bratislava-specific tip: the Christmas market on the Main Square (Hlavné námestie) and Franciscan Square (Františkánske námestie) is considered one of the most beautiful in Central Europe — smaller and more authentic than Prague or Vienna, without their crowds.


What to See in Bratislava

Bratislava Castle (Bratislavský hrad)

The city's absolute symbol — a white building with four towers rising 80 metres above the Danube, visible from the entire area. Its history begins in the 9th century; the current form (rebuilt after the 1811 fire) dates from the 1950s–1960s.

From the castle terraces, the panorama is unique: westward — Austria, south-east — Hungary, northward — the Little Carpathians, below — the Danube and the UFO Bridge.

Practical details:


Courtyard and terraces (exterior): free, open daily 8:00–22:00

Museum (interior): 14 EUR adults, open Tuesday–Sunday 10:00–18:00

Getting there: 15-minute walk from the Main Square (uphill), or bus no. 203


Tip: the exterior courtyard offers the same panorama as the museum tower — if budget is tight, skip the interior and enjoy the view for free.

Walking Tour of the Old Town and Castle — The Best Introduction

The Old Town (Staré Mesto) — Small but Authentic

Bratislava's Old Town is one of the most compact historic centres among European capitals — you can walk from one end to the other in 15 minutes. That's precisely what gives it its charm: a pedestrian bubble with cobblestone streets, hidden courtyards and Baroque palaces, without the overcrowding of Prague or Vienna.

Main Square (Hlavné námestie) — the Old Town's centre, with the Old Town Hall (14th century), Roland's Palace and the Maximilian Fountain (the oldest in Bratislava, 1572). In the evening, when the lights come on and the terraces fill, it's the most beautiful corner of the city.

St Michael's Gate (Michalská brána) — the only medieval gateway remaining from the city walls, built in the 14th century. The tower has a museum of medieval weapons; tower entry: 5 EUR. The classic Bratislava photograph.

Primate's Palace (Primaciálny palác) — the neoclassical pink palace on Primate's Square, built in 1781, where Napoleon Bonaparte signed the Peace of Pressburg in 1805, after his victory at Austerlitz. Entry: 4 EUR; inside are Flemish tapestries from the 17th century, considered among the most valuable in the world.

St Martin's Cathedral (Katedrála sv. Martina) — the Gothic cathedral from the 14th century at the foot of Castle Hill, where 11 kings and queens of the Kingdom of Hungary were crowned between 1563 and 1830, including Maria Theresa in 1741. Free entry (voluntary donation).

The interactive statues — Bratislava is famous for its quirky street statues: Čumil (the man peering from a manhole, the city's symbol), the Napoleonic Soldier (on a bench), Schöner Náci (a local eccentric character). They're free and highly photographable — selfie with Čumil is mandatory.

The Blue Church (Modrý kostolík)

One of the most unusual and most photographed buildings in Central Europe. Built in 1913 in Art Nouveau Secessionist style by architect Ödön Lechner, the Church of St Elizabeth is covered entirely in shades of blue — exterior façade, towers, mosaics, interior decoration. There is nothing else like it in Europe.

Location: 15 minutes' walk from the Main Square, on Alžbetina ulica.
Entry: free (check opening hours, which vary).

Tip: go early morning (before 9:00) or on a Tuesday–Thursday — weekends attract crowds for photos and sometimes weddings that block access.

Guided Tour with Bratislava Castle Entry Ticket Included

The UFO Bridge (Most SNP)

Built in 1972 in communist-futurist style, the Bridge of the Slovak National Uprising is suspended from a single pylon — and at the top of that pylon sits a restaurant and panoramic terrace shaped like a flying saucer (hence the nickname UFO).

Prices: terrace entry 7.50 EUR; free if you consume at the restaurant (minimum spend is 7.50 EUR — practically the same thing). The view from the top takes in the Castle, the Danube, the Old Town and the communist-era apartment blocks on the opposite bank — a visual combination that explains Bratislava better than any guide.

Hours: daily 10:00–23:00 (restaurant), terrace until midnight.

Devín Castle — Dramatic Ruins on a Cliff

10 km west of Bratislava, at the confluence of the Danube and the Morava, the ruins of Devín Castle rise on a 212-metre cliff — one of Slovakia's oldest fortresses (first records from the 5th century) and one of the most dramatic landscapes in Central Europe.

From the castle cliff you can see three countries simultaneously: Slovakia, Austria and Hungary.

Getting there: bus no. 29 from the Most SNP stop (~30 minutes, 1 EUR) or by bicycle on the Danube cycle path (10 km, a pleasant route).

Entry: 8 EUR adults (May–September) / 6 EUR (October–April).
Hours: Tuesday–Sunday 10:00–17:00 (19:00 in summer).

Slavín Memorial

On Slavín hill, north of the centre, stands the Soviet memorial dedicated to soldiers who fell liberating Bratislava in April 1945. Regardless of historical interpretation, the view from the top is one of the most complete panoramas of the city — and entry is free.


Food and Drink — Practical Guide

What You Must Eat

Bryndzové halušky — Slovakia's national dish. Small potato dumplings with sheep's milk cheese (bryndza) and fried bacon. Extremely filling, extremely tasty. 7–12 EUR a portion.

Kapustnica — acidic sauerkraut soup with smoked sausage and mushrooms, traditionally eaten at Christmas. Available in restaurants in autumn and winter. 4–6 EUR.

Langos (lángos) — fried dough topped with sour cream, grated cheese and garlic — a Hungarian-influenced street food extremely popular at market stalls. 2–4 EUR.

Bryndza — the Slovak national sheep's milk cheese, lighter than feta, with a slightly sour and creamy flavour. Take some home from a supermarket.

Fried cheese (Vyprážaný syr) — breaded and fried Edam cheese, served with tartar sauce. Classic Slovak comfort food. 5–8 EUR.

Where to Eat

Budget (7–14 EUR/person):


Menu dňa (daily menu) — between 11:00–14:00, all restaurants serve a set menu (soup + main course) for 6–9 EUR. Best value for money in the city

Street stalls selling langos on the Main Square

Local canteen-style restaurants away from the tourist centre


Mid-range (14–28 EUR/person):


Modrá Hviezda (Blue Star) — traditional Slovak restaurant at the foot of the castle, complete local menu

Slovak Pub — local craft beer and traditional food in generous portions, friendly atmosphere

Danube promenade restaurants — higher prices, but the river view compensates


What to Drink

Slovak beer — Zlatý Bažant, Corgoň, Smädný Mních. At a bar: 1.50–3 EUR for a 0.5L pint — among the cheapest beer prices in any European capital.

Slovak wine — Slovakia has a serious wine tradition, especially in the Little Carpathians (Modra and Pezinok area, 30–40 km from Bratislava). Excellent local white wine (Welschriesling, Müller-Thurgau): 3–6 EUR a glass at a restaurant.

Borovička — the Slovak national spirit made from juniper berries, similar to gin but more intense. At a bar: 1.50–2.50 EUR a shot.

Recommended Itinerary — 2 Days in Bratislava

Day 1 — Castle, Old Town and UFO


Morning (8:30): walk up to Bratislava Castle (free exterior courtyard) — panorama at sunrise

Lunch: menu dňa at a restaurant near the Main Square (6–9 EUR)

Afternoon: St Michael's Gate, Primate's Palace, statues (Čumil!), St Martin's Cathedral

Evening: UFO Bridge — aperitif at the restaurant with panoramic view, dinner in the Old Town


Day 2 — Blue Church, Devín and Little Carpathians


Morning (9:00): Blue Church (before the crowds)

Lunch: excursion to Devín Castle (bus 29, 30 minutes), picnic or restaurant nearby

Return: walk along the Danube promenade, Slavín Memorial (optional, for panorama)

Evening: craft beer at Slovak Pub, bryndzové halušky for dinner



Bratislava + Vienna — The Perfect Combination

Bratislava and Vienna are so close (56 minutes by train, 12–15 EUR) that combining them in the same city break is the ideal strategy:


Stay in Bratislava (50–60% cheaper accommodation) and make a day trip to Vienna

Or the reverse — stay in Vienna and day-trip to Bratislava (but you lose the price advantage)

Trains Bratislava → Vienna Hauptbahnhof depart frequently (every 1–2 hours)


Bratislava + Budapest is another excellent combination — 2.5 hours by train or coach; worth including if you have 4–5 days.


Practical Tips

The Old Town is entirely walkable — no public transport needed in the centre. The only destinations requiring transport: Devín Castle (bus 29), Slavín Memorial (bus) and the airport.

Bratislava Card — if you plan to visit the castle museum + other museums + use public transport, the 24h (~25 EUR) or 48h card may be worthwhile. Calculate beforehand.

Taxi vs Bolt — as in other capitals, unlicensed taxis outside hotels can be expensive. Bolt and Uber work well in Bratislava at fair prices (5–10 EUR cross-city).


Travel Insurance

Slovakia is in the EU and Schengen. The EHIC covers basic emergencies. EKTA Travel Insurance — comprehensive coverage from 3–8 EUR/day.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Bratislava?
R: The simplest route: fly Bucharest (OTP) → Vienna (VIE) with Wizz Air, Ryanair or TAROM (1h50, from 50–120 EUR return), then take the train Vienna Hauptbahnhof → Bratislava Hlavná stanica (56 minutes, 12–15 EUR). This works perfectly for a combined Bratislava + Vienna city break.

Î: What currency does Slovakia use?
R: Slovakia uses the euro (EUR) since 2009. No currency exchange needed. Cards are accepted almost everywhere in the tourist centre.

Î: Is Bratislava worth more than a day trip from Vienna?
R: Yes, definitely. One day covers the Old Town and Castle — but you miss the Blue Church, Devín Castle, the Slavín Memorial and the city's evening atmosphere. Two days is ideal. Accommodation prices are 50–60% lower than Vienna, making Bratislava an excellent base for visiting Vienna or Budapest too.

Î: What is the UFO Bridge in Bratislava?
R: The UFO Bridge (Most SNP — Bridge of the Slovak National Uprising) is a suspension bridge built in 1972, with a restaurant and panoramic terrace at the top of the pylon, shaped like a flying saucer. Entry to the terrace costs 7.50 EUR, but is free if you consume at the restaurant. It offers one of Bratislava's best views — the Castle, the Danube and the Old Town simultaneously.

Î: What is the Blue Church and is it worth visiting?
R: The Church of St Elizabeth (Modrý kostolík), built in 1913 in Art Nouveau Secessionist style, is covered entirely in blue — façade, towers, interior, mosaics, everything. It is one of the most photogenic and unusual churches in Central Europe. Entry is free, and it is 15 minutes' walk from the Main Square.

Î: How much does a 2-day city break in Bratislava cost?
R: A 2-day/1-night city break costs 150–280 EUR per person (mid-range), including the flight (via Vienna), the Vienna–Bratislava train, accommodation and meals. Local prices are 40–50% lower than Vienna: a restaurant lunch 8–15 EUR, a beer 1.50–3 EUR, a cross-city taxi 5–8 EUR.

Î: Can I visit both Vienna and Bratislava in the same trip?
R: Yes — it's one of the most popular combinations in Central Europe. The two capitals are 56 minutes apart by train (RegioJet, ÖBB: 12–15 EUR). Stay 2 nights in Bratislava (cheaper) and make a day trip to Vienna, or vice versa. Bratislava + Vienna in 4 days is an excellent classic itinerary.

Î: What is the best time to visit Bratislava?
R: April–June and September–October: pleasant temperatures (15–22°C), fewer tourists, normal prices. July–August: most lively, but also more crowded and expensive. December: renowned Christmas markets on the Main Square and Franciscan Square — one of the most beautiful atmospheres in Central Europe. Avoid January–February if you dislike sub-zero temperatures.

## Budva 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Montenegro's Riviera

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/budva-complete-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-08
Actualizat: 2026-08-08
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/budva-ghid-complet

Descriere: Complete Budva guide: Venetian Old Town, Mogren Beach, Sveti Stefan — the fairytale island, legendary nightlife and the Riviera beaches. Real prices, when to go to avoid the crowds and how to combi...

Răspuns scurt: Budva is Montenegro's largest coastal tourism centre — a city with 2,500 years of history, with a Venetian Old Town enclosed by medieval walls, sandy and pebble beaches with intensely blue Adriatic water, and one of the Balkans' most active nightlife scenes. 30 minutes from Kotor. Access from Romania: flight OTP → Tivat (TIV) with Wizz Air (seasonal) or flight to Dubrovnik + transfer.

There is a moment on the Budva Riviera — usually in May or September, when the water temperature is 22°C, the beaches aren't yet crowded and the sun descends behind the mountains as the Old Town lights up — when you understand why Montenegrins say they have created the best place in the world to live.

Budva is not subtle. It is one of the most direct tourist destinations on the Mediterranean: spectacular beaches a few minutes from a Venetian medieval town, hotels in all categories, seafood restaurants at half the price of Dubrovnik, and a nightlife that puts many European cities in the shade.

Budva is Montenegro's top coastal destination — a 2,500-year-old walled town backed by Adriatic beaches, with a Riviera stretching 35 km south toward the Albanian border.

What makes it different from any other Mediterranean resort: 30 minutes north lies UNESCO Kotor, 6 km south lies Sveti Stefan — the fairytale island — and the entire Montenegrin coast has the accessibility and prices of a place that hasn't yet reached full tourist maturity.


Budva at a Glance — Essential Facts

Country: Montenegro — not in the EU, not in Schengen. Uses the euro.

Population: approximately 20,000 permanent residents — 200,000+ at peak season (July–August).

Currency: Euro (EUR) — no currency exchange needed.

Nearest airport: Tivat (TIV) — 20 km, 20–25 minutes. Second: Podgorica (TGD) — 65 km, 1 hour. Third: Dubrovnik (DBV, Croatia) — 90 km, 1.5–2 hours.

Visa: EU citizens do not need a visa for Montenegro — entry with a valid ID card.

Main season: May–October. Budva outside season (November–April) is a quiet small town — some hotels and restaurants are closed.


How to Get from Romania to Budva

Option 1 — Flight OTP → Tivat (Direct, Seasonal)

Wizz Air operates OTP → TIV flights in season (May–September). Duration: ~1h30. Transfer Tivat → Budva: taxi (~15 EUR, 20 min) or local minibus (~5 EUR, 30 min).

Option 2 — Flight OTP → Dubrovnik + Transfer (Year-Round)

Budva is 90 km from Dubrovnik — 1.5–2 hours by car or minibus. Flight OTP → DBV (Wizz Air/Ryanair): year-round, from 50 EUR return. Transfer Dubrovnik → Budva: minibus (~15–20 EUR, 2h), private taxi (~80–100 EUR). Advantage: you can combine Dubrovnik + Kotor + Budva in a single circuit.

Option 3 — By Car

Bucharest → Budva: ~1,000 km, 10–11 hours (via Serbia or Bulgaria). Good for a Balkans road trip: Bucharest → Belgrade → Kotor → Budva → Dubrovnik.


When to Go — Seasonality and Prices

Period Air temp Water temp Accommodation Recommendation
May – June 22–28°C 20–23°C Normal ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Ideal
July – August 28–35°C 24–26°C +50–100% ⚠️ Crowded, reservations essential
September – October 20–27°C 22–24°C -20–30% ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Ideal
November – April 8–16°C 14–18°C -60–70% 🔕 Most places closed

Budva's weather is beautifully stable, accommodation prices are more bearable in shoulder season — and you won't spend hours stuck in traffic.

Sea Dance Festival note: Sea Dance is a 3-day electronic music festival at Jaz Beach, held in July–August, with 20,000+ daily attendees and international acts. If you're a festival fan — separate ticket, accommodation booked months ahead.


Budva's Beaches — Complete Guide

Mogren I and II — The Most Photogenic

Mogren consists of two sand and pebble beaches connected by a short tunnel, approximately 100 metres west of the Old Town. They are surrounded by white-gold limestone cliffs, with water of an intense turquoise.

Mogren II (accessible only through Mogren I) is smaller and more secluded — one of the most beautiful small beaches on the Adriatic. Access: free, 10 minutes' walk from the Old Town. Sunbeds: 10–20 EUR per pair.

Slovenska Plaža — The Main Beach

The 1.5 km long beach in front of the town — the classic zone for beach bars, terraces and water activities. Access is free, with a free section along the entire length. Sunbeds: 15–25 EUR per pair in the organised area.

Bečići — The Most Awarded

3 km south of Budva, Bečići is a 2 km fine-sand beach, awarded the Blue Flag and considered one of the best beaches in the Mediterranean. Sunbeds: 10–15 EUR per pair — the best value in the region. Bus: 1.50–2 EUR.

Jaz Beach — For Quiet and Festivals

2 km west of Budva, Jaz is a larger, quieter beach outside festival season. Host of the Sea Dance Festival in July–August. Access by bus or on foot (~25 minutes).

Sveti Stefan Beach — The Postcard Image

6 km south of Budva, the public beach on the southern coast of Sveti Stefan island is free — sunbeds on the organised section at ~15 EUR per person. The combination of the island's pink rock behind you and the turquoise Adriatic ahead is one of Montenegro's most photographed images.


The Old Town (Stari Grad) — The Medieval Heart

Budva's Stari Grad is surrounded by medieval walls, with narrow cobblestone streets and Venetian houses with red-tiled roofs. Its history goes back to antiquity — an Illyrian and Greek centre that became a Roman, Venetian, Ottoman and Austrian fortress.

The Citadel — the 15th-century fortress at the top of the Old Town, with spectacular views over the beaches and sea. Entry: 5 EUR.

The Ballerina Monument — the bronze statue of a ballerina on the stone at the end of the walls, with Mogren beach behind — Budva's most photographed spot. Free.

Main Square — in the centre of the Old Town, with three churches built side by side: the Roman Catholic Cathedral of Saint John (7th century), the Orthodox Church of the Holy Trinity (1804) and the Chapel of Santa Maria in Punta (840 AD). Free.

The seawall promenade — the pedestrian path along the Old Town walls toward the small Ričardova Glava cove — a direct water access point directly below the walls.


Boat Tour Along Budva's Beaches — The Best Perspective from the Water

Budva Bay Panoramic Tour — All the Beaches in 3.5 Hours


Sveti Stefan — The Luxury Destination You Can See for Free

Sveti Stefan is a small village on an island connected to the mainland by a narrow isthmus, 6 km south of Budva. The island belongs to the Aman Resort — one of the world's most expensive hotel groups (rooms from 1,000 EUR per night).

But you don't need to be an Aman guest to enjoy Sveti Stefan. Three ways to experience it free or cheaply:

1. The road viewpoint — the best viewpoint is from the main road above the island. 10–15 minute stop, possible parking, perfect photograph. Best time: sunset (19:00–20:00 in summer) for golden hour light.

2. The southern public beach — the Sveti Stefan beach on the south side normalised access in 2026, with the public sector available from July.

3. The bus — the Budva–Sveti Stefan bus costs 1.50–2.50 EUR and takes 25–40 minutes. You can go, photograph the viewpoint and return in half a day.


Nightlife — Budva After Dark

Budva's nightlife is layered into three distinct levels:

Level 1 — Bars and lounges in Stari Grad — the most atmospheric. Terraces on the medieval walls, live music, cocktails with sea views. Prices: cocktail 8–15 EUR.

Level 2 — Beach bars on Slovenska Plaža — more relaxed, natural transition from beach to bar without cover charge. Daytime lounges that become social spots in the evening. Beer: 3–5 EUR.

Level 3 — Open-air clubs — Top Hill is Budva's largest summer club, with international DJs, open May–September, entry 15–30 EUR, running until 6 AM. A shuttle bus runs from the main seafront on club nights.

Sea Dance Festival (Jaz Beach, July–August): one of the Balkans' largest electronic festivals, with 20,000+ daily attendees and international acts.


Food and Drink

What to Eat

Fresh fish — at any konoba by the sea. Sea bass, dorada, branzino on the grill with lemon and olive oil. A seafood dinner for two at a good restaurant rarely tops 30–35 EUR. Always ask the price per kg before ordering.

Shrimp buzara — shrimps in garlic and white wine sauce. 12–18 EUR.

Black risotto (crni rižoto) — with cuttlefish ink. Adriatic speciality. 10–15 EUR.

Njeguški cheese and pršut — smoked cheese and ham from the Montenegrin mountains. Classic aperitif with local wine. 6–10 EUR.

Where to Eat

Essential tip: some restaurants in Stari Grad place unrequested bread or appetisers on the table and charge for them on the bill. Ask first or send them back immediately.

Better value — go to restaurants on the promenade between Old Town and Bečići or to konobes in the peripheral neighbourhoods (Partizanski put) for the same menu at 20–30% less.

Local beer — Nikšićko pivo is Montenegro's national beer. At a bar: 3–4.50 EUR a pint.

Local wine — Vranac (robust red) and Krstač (white). 3–6 EUR a glass.


Day Trips from Budva

Kotor (30 minutes, essential)

Kotor is a UNESCO World Heritage bay town, 30 minutes by car from Budva. The fortress walls with 1,350 steps, baroque Perast and Our Lady of the Rocks — all accessible in a single day. Read our complete Kotor guide.

Dubrovnik, Croatia (90 km, 1.5–2h)

The Budva–Dubrovnik road passes through the Verige ferry crossing and continues along the Croatian coast. A full day, 90 km, Montenegro–Croatia border. Guided tours from Budva: 25–40 EUR.

Lovćen National Park and Cetinje (1 hour)

Cetinje is Montenegro's former royal capital and Lovćen National Park holds the Njegoš Mausoleum — Montenegro's most spectacular viewpoint at 1,660 m.

Skadar Lake (1.5 hours)

The Balkans' largest lake, with pelicans, fishing villages and a landscape unlike anything on the coast. Boat tours on the lake: 20–40 EUR.

Practical Tips

Parking in peak season is a serious problem. Paid parking in Budva: 2–4 EUR per hour. Free parking near Hotel Mediteran fills before 10:00 on peak days. If possible, arrive without a car and use local buses.

The Mediteran Express bus runs every 15–30 minutes along the Riviera (Budva–Bečići–Przno–Sveti Stefan). Price: ~1–2 EUR per trip. The most convenient way to explore the coastline.

Unlicensed taxis — taxis without official roof numbers or visible meters frequently overcharge tourists. Verify the meter starts from the 1 EUR base fare. Use Bolt where available or taxis with displayed rates.

Unrequested bread and appetisers — some restaurants in Stari Grad place unordered items on the table and charge them on the bill. Send them back if you don't want them, or ask the price first.

Insurance — Montenegro is not in the EU. EHIC is not valid. You need insurance that explicitly covers Montenegro.
