Kebab varieties you must try

Döner is just the beginning. Istanbul has dozens of regional kebab varieties:


Adana kebab — spicy minced meat on a skewer, from south-eastern Turkey. Served with salad, rice, and lavash bread.

İskender kebab — döner slices over bread with tomato sauce and yoghurt, drizzled with sizzling melted butter. The original is in Bursa (day trip — see below).

Beyti kebab — kebab rolled in lavash with tomato sauce and yoghurt. Elegant and satisfying.

Cağ kebab — horizontal spit kebab from Erzurum. Lamb carved directly from the spit. Best at Hocapaşa Sokak, near Sirkeci.

Tantuni — finely diced beef cooked on a griddle with spices, served in lavash. Fast, cheap, perfect.


Where to eat like a local

Turkish breakfast (kahvaltı) — the most impressive meal: cheeses (7-8 varieties), olives, honey, kaymak (clotted cream), eggs, tomatoes, cucumbers, fresh bread, and endless tea. 200-400 TL (€4-7) per person at a breakfast spot. Van Kahvaltı Evi in Cihangir is the classic.

Local restaurant (lokal lokanta): full meal with kebab/home-cooked food, salad, and drink: 250-500 TL (€5-9). Look for places with window displays of trays — the food is cooked in the morning and served throughout the day. Cheap, fast, and delicious.

Meyhane (tavern): the Turkish social experience — meze (appetisers) + raki (anise spirit) + fish. Full evening: 800-1,500 TL (€15-27) with alcohol. The Nevizade area (off İstiklal) is packed with meyhanes — the atmosphere is electric.

Tourist restaurant: 600-1,500 TL (€11-27). Variable quality — many in Sultanahmet are mediocre at inflated prices. Notable exception: Sultanahmet Köftecisi (legendary meatballs, since 1920).

Drinks

Drink Price (TL) Price (~€)

Tea is Turkey's social currency. Accept every offer of tea — it's how Turks socialise. Refusing tea = refusing friendship.

Organised food tours

The best areas for food tours:


Kadıköy (Asian side) — fish market, baklava, local kebabs. The most authentic tour, away from tourists. 3-4 hours, €35-60, includes 6-10 stops.

Sultanahmet + Eminönü — the classic route: spice bazaar, simit, balık ekmek, sand-brewed Turkish coffee. 2-3 hours, €30-50.

Beyoğlu / Karaköy — the modern version: speciality coffee, meyhanes, pastanes (pastry shops). 3-4 hours, €40-65.


Tip: go on an empty stomach. Seriously — you'll eat a lot.

Istanbul's neighbourhoods — beyond Sultanahmet

Istanbul is a universe of neighbourhoods, each with its own personality. Limiting yourself to Sultanahmet is like visiting only the old town of any city and thinking you've seen the place.

Beyoğlu and İstiklal Caddesi

Istanbul's modern heart. İstiklal is the 1.4 km pedestrian boulevard where everything happens — from the nostalgic red tram (purely decorative, but photogenic) to churches hidden in passages, 19th-century embassies, and the densest concentration of cafés, restaurants, and shops in the city.

Don't miss: Çiçek Pasajı (Flower Passage) — a former flower arcade, now packed with meyhanes with atmosphere. Hazzopulo Passage — less known, equally charming.

Balat

The colourful neighbourhood that conquered Instagram — painted Ottoman wooden houses on steep cobblestone streets. But Balat is much more than a photo backdrop: it was the Jewish quarter (Ahrida Synagogue dates from the 15th century), then Greek, then Armenian. Layers of history are visible in every wall.

When to go: early morning (8-9 AM), before the influencers. Have tea at one of the tiny cafés on the side streets, and explore the Gül Mosque (former Byzantine church) and the Bulgarian Iron Church (Sveti Stefan — the only church in the world built entirely from prefabricated cast iron, shipped up the Danube from Vienna in 1898).

Kadıköy (Asian side)

Cross the Bosphorus by ferry from Eminönü (59 TL / ~€1, 20 minutes, spectacular views) and you arrive in a different world — local markets, streets lined with independent cafés, graffiti, vintage shops, and zero tourists. Kadıköy is where the locals go.

Kadıköy Fish Market is the centre — fresh fish at local prices, seafood, cheeses, and sweets. Kaymakçı Pando for the best kaymak (clotted cream) in Istanbul.

The perfect day combo: ferry Eminönü → Kadıköy + food tour through the market + stroll along the Moda waterfront (the bohemian coastal neighbourhood) + return ferry at sunset.

Moda

The green peninsula south of Kadıköy — seaside promenade with views of the Princes' Islands, independent cafés, vintage shops on Kadife Sokak (Velvet Street), and the artistic atmosphere of a former Levantine quarter. The Moda waterfront walk at sunset is one of Istanbul's top free experiences.

Beşiktaş

The local neighbourhood on the European shore — a fish market (more authentic than the touristy ones), university-area energy, and Dolmabahçe Palace. The area is popular with locals for meyhanes with fresh fish.

Ortaköy

The Ortaköy Mosque "beneath" the Bosphorus Bridge is one of Istanbul's most photographed images. At weekends, the area fills with kumpir stalls (giant loaded baked potato — 350-600 TL), artisan crafts, and waterfront cafés. Relaxed, multicultural, with spectacular views.

Üsküdar (Asian side)

Istanbul's contemplative side — Ottoman mosques, cypress-lined cemeteries, and the perfect view of the historic peninsula from the Asian shore. Salacak is the ideal spot for the classic photo with the Maiden's Tower (Kız Kulesi) in the background.

Cihangir

The bohemian hillside neighbourhood — cafés with Bosphorus views, an expat and artist community, never-ending brunches, and a relaxed atmosphere. It's Istanbul's "Montmartre," but more accessible and more authentic.

The verdict: worth it if you visit Topkapi + Galata + at least one museum (individual total: ~€89, plus you get skip-the-line). If you only visit 1-2 attractions, individual tickets are more economical.

Asian side experiences

The Asian side is the half most tourists ignore — and it's a huge mistake. Crossing the Bosphorus by ferry is not just transport, it's an experience in itself.

Maiden's Tower (Kız Kulesi)

The tower on the tiny islet at the entrance to the Bosphorus — legendary (in Turkish mythology, a sultan locked his daughter here to protect her from a prophecy). Recently restored, it functions as a restaurant and viewpoint. Access boats depart from Üsküdar or Salacak.

Çamlıca Hill

Istanbul's highest point (268 m) — a complete city panorama: the Bosphorus, the Golden Horn, the Princes' Islands, and on clear days, Mount Uludağ 150 km away. Çamlıca Mosque (2019, Turkey's largest) is impressive architecturally. The park and gardens are perfect for a picnic.

Access: bus or taxi from Üsküdar (~60-100 TL / €1-2).

Çengelköy

The Bosphorus village — a fishing village that has preserved its character despite the city's growth. Famous for the kokoreç at Çengelköy Tarihi Kokoreççisi and Çengelköy cucumbers (yes, they have their own cucumber variety). Perfect view of the Bosphorus Bridge from below.

Day trips from Istanbul

Princes' Islands (Adalar)

An archipelago of 9 islands in the Sea of Marmara — car-free, just bicycles, horse carriages (under debate whether they'll be eliminated), and total tranquillity after Istanbul's chaos. Büyükada (Big Island) is the most popular — Victorian wooden houses, fish restaurants, and beaches.

Detail Info
Transport Ferry Kabataş → Büyükada: 137 TL (~€2.50), 75-90 min
Alternative IDO fast ferry: faster but more expensive
Activities Bicycle around the island (50-100 TL/day), beach, fish lunch
Day budget 300-600 TL (€6-11) plus ferry
Best days Tuesday-Thursday — weekends are crowded

Tip: take the 8:30 AM ferry — you have the whole day on the island and avoid queues. Bring food from the market or order fresh fish at local restaurants (200-400 TL for a full meal).

Bursa (former Ottoman capital)

The former capital of the Ottoman Empire (1335-1453), at the foot of Mount Uludağ. Famous for the original iskender kebab (invented here), the Green Mosque (Yeşil Cami), Bursa silk, and the Çekirge thermal baths.

Detail Info
Transport IDO fast ferry Yenikapı → Mudanya: 2 hours + 30-min bus
Alternative Direct bus: 2.5-3 hours
What to see Green Mosque, Ottoman mausoleums, silk market, iskender kebab
Day budget 500-1,000 TL (€9-18) plus transport

Edirne

The second Ottoman capital (1365-1453), at the border with Bulgaria and Greece. The Selimiye Mosque (UNESCO, Mimar Sinan's masterpiece — considered by the architect himself as superior to Hagia Sophia) is the main draw. Plus: Edirne white cheese, fried liver (ciğer), and the traditional oil wrestling festival (Kırkpınar, the world's oldest sporting event — 600+ years).

Detail Info
Transport Bus: 2.5-3 hours
What to see Selimiye Mosque, Health Museum, Old Town
Day budget 400-800 TL (€7-15) plus transport

Cappadocia (2 days)

Further away (1.5-hour internal flight), but on many visitors' lists. The hot air balloon ride at sunrise over the lunar landscape is one of the world's most spectacular experiences.

Detail Info
Transport Internal flight Istanbul → Kayseri/Nevşehir: €30-80
2-day package from Istanbul €250-500 (flight + hotel + tour + optional balloon)
Balloon ride €150-300 separately
What to see Göreme, underground cities, valleys, cave churches

Alternative: if you have 4+ days in Istanbul, take an early morning internal flight, do the day tour, and return in the evening. But 2 days/1 night is the ideal option.

Getting around Istanbul — complete guide

Istanbulkart — essential

The rechargeable card that works on metro, tram, bus, and ferry. It's essential — paying with cash or bank card on transport is much more expensive or impossible.

Detail 2026 Info

Transfer (within 2 hours) Progressive discount on rides 2, 3, 4
City ferry 53-59 TL (~€1)
Princes' Islands ferry 137 TL (~€2.50) — no transfer discount

How to buy: machines at any metro station. Interface has English option. Top up with cash or card. You can use a single Istanbulkart for multiple people (tap multiple times).

Metro and tram

The network is extensive and modern. Main lines:


Tram T1: runs through Sultanahmet — from Kabataş (for the funicular to Taksim) via Eminönü, Sultanahmet, Grand Bazaar, to Bağcılar. The most useful tourist route.

Metro M2: Taksim → Levent (business district). Connected to T1 via funicular F1 (Kabataş → Taksim).

Metro M11: the new line from Istanbul Airport (IST) to the centre. Fast and cheap.

Marmaray: the tunnel under the Bosphorus — Europe-to-Asia crossing in 4 minutes, no traffic. Functional, fast, not scenic but efficient.


Ferries

Istanbul's most beautiful transport — and the most practical for crossing the Bosphorus.

Taxi and ride-hailing

Yellow taxis are everywhere, but scams are common: "broken" meter, long routes, switched banknotes. Use BiTaksi or Bolt — the price is fixed, the route is on GPS, and payment is electronic.

Approximate taxi/Bolt prices:

Taksim → Kadıköy (via Bolt): 250-400 TL (€5-7)

10 insider tips for Istanbul

1. Hagia Sophia at 8:00 AM, not 10:00. The difference is between a magical experience and an hour in a queue. At 8:00 you have the interior almost to yourself — you can sit on the carpet, gaze up at the mosaics, and feel the weight of 1,500 years of history.

2. The ferry > the expensive cruise. The Eminönü → Kadıköy ferry (€1) is just as beautiful as a €25 cruise. No guide, but the same spectacular views. Take it at sunset for maximum effect.

3. Eat on the Asian side. Everything on the European side at tourist prices you'll find on the Asian side at half the price and double the quality. Kadıköy is Istanbul's gastronomic mecca — locals eat here.

4. Bargain everything in the Grand Bazaar — but not food. In the bazaar, the initial price is 2-3x the real price. At restaurants and street food stalls, the listed price is the real price.

5. Avoid the restaurants on Galata Bridge. They're tourist traps — high prices, mediocre quality. Balık ekmek at the Eminönü stands is better and 5x cheaper.

6. Istanbulkart from day one. Without it, you pay double or triple for transport. 165 TL (€3) for the card, 46 TL (~€0.85) per ride — pays for itself from day one.

7. Don't take a taxi from the airport without an app. Airport taxi drivers are notorious for long routes. Bolt or BiTaksi — the price is fixed, the route is on GPS, zero stress.

8. A cheap hammam is NOT a bad hammam. Mihrimah Sultan (€25) or Çinili Üsküdar (€25) are authentic hammams with 0% tourists. The experience is just as good as the €100 ones — just without the perfumed towel and tea served on a silver tray.

9. Spice Bazaar — buy from the back. The entrance shops have big tourist markups. Go out to the street behind the bazaar — same spices, 40-50% cheaper.

10. Accept the tea. Always. Tea is Turkey's social language. It's offered in shops, during bargaining, in conversation — it's a form of politeness and friendship. It costs nothing — the experience is priceless.

Practical information

Documents and entry

Passport required. Turkey is NOT in the EU. Most nationalities (US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia) enter visa-free for up to 90 days. Passport must be valid for 6+ months from the date of entry. National ID cards are NOT accepted — a common mistake.

Money

Currency: Turkish Lira (TRY). €1 ≈ 55 TRY (August 2026). Cards accepted at hotels, restaurants, and mall shops. Cash essential at bazaars, street food stalls, small taxis, and local hammams.

Best rates: Revolut or Wise — 0% conversion fee. Avoid exchange offices in Sultanahmet (rates 5-10% below market). Major bank ATMs offer fair rates.

Connectivity

Turkey is NOT in the EU — free European roaming does NOT apply. Your carrier will charge €3-15/day. An eSIM from Airalo costs €4-5 for 1GB/7 days — dramatically cheaper. Install before departure.

Travel insurance

ESSENTIAL. The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) does NOT work in Turkey — you are not medically covered without private insurance. A hospital visit in Istanbul can cost 500-2,000 TL (€9-36) for a simple consultation, much more for emergencies. Full insurance guide . Recommendation: EKTA — comprehensive coverage, good price.

When to go

Period Temperature Crowds Prices Verdict
March-May 10-22°C Medium Medium ✅ Ideal — pleasant weather, not crowded
June-August 25-33°C Very high High ⚠️ Hot and crowded, but vibrant atmosphere
September-November 12-25°C Medium Medium ✅ Ideal — especially September-October
December-February 3-10°C Low Low 🆗 Cold, but good prices and zero queues

The perfect moment: the second half of September — 22-25°C weather, the summer crowds have left, prices drop, and the light is perfect for photography.

Mosque etiquette

The rules are simple but strict: remove shoes (shoe bags available at the entrance), cover shoulders and knees (both sexes), women cover hair (free scarves at the entrance). During prayers (5 times daily, ~30 min), access is restricted. Don't talk loudly, don't eat, don't drink. Photography is permitted but be discreet.

Tipping

10-15% at restaurants (check if service charge is already included). At hammams: 10-20% of the price. At hotels: 20-50 TL (€0.40-0.90) for the bellboy or cleaner. At taxis: round up.

Istanbul's classic scams

The "friend" who invites you to a bar: a friendly man speaks your language perfectly, invites you to "his bar" for a beer. The bill arrives at €200-500. Politely decline and walk away.

The taxi with a "broken" meter: the driver says the meter isn't working. Use Bolt/BiTaksi or insist on the meter.

The shoeshine man who "drops" his brush: he polishes your shoes "by accident," then demands money. Say no, keep walking.

The "special" price just for you: in the Grand Bazaar, the initial price is 2-3x the real price. Bargain from 50%.

What makes Istanbul different from the rest of Europe

Istanbul is not Europe and not Asia — it's both. This shows in every detail: the rhythm of the day follows prayer times, not office hours; a meal is not an individual act but a social event; "quickly" is not a concept Turks prize; and every transaction — from a tea to a carpet — is an opportunity for conversation.

It's a city that overwhelms on a first visit (the noise, the crowds, the scale) and one you love from the second. Don't try to "tick it off" — let yourself be carried by its rhythm.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How many days do you need in Istanbul?
R: Minimum 3 full days for the essentials: Day 1 — Sultanahmet (Hagia Sophia, Blue Mosque, Basilica Cistern, Topkapi). Day 2 — Bosphorus cruise + Grand Bazaar + Spice Bazaar. Day 3 — Asian side (Kadıköy, Moda) + hammam + shopping. With 4-5 days add Balat, Dolmabahçe Palace, Princes' Islands. With 7 days you explore everything — including day trips to Bursa or Cappadocia.

Î: Do I need a visa for Istanbul?
R: Most nationalities (US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia) can enter Turkey visa-free for up to 90 days. Passport must be valid for 6 months from entry date. National ID cards are NOT accepted — a common mistake.

Î: Which is the best hammam in Istanbul?
R: Depends on budget. Premium: Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı (from €90, spectacularly restored, luxury experience) or Ayasofya Hürrem Sultan (from €110, between Hagia Sophia and Blue Mosque). Classic: Çemberlitaş Hamamı (from €68, built by Mimar Sinan in 1584). Budget: Mihrimah Sultan (from €25, most authentic, cash only) or Çinili Hamam Üsküdar (from €25, local atmosphere on the Asian side).

Î: Is Istanbul safe for tourists?
R: Yes, Istanbul is very safe for tourists. Tourist areas (Sultanahmet, Taksim, Kadıköy) are well-lit and populated. Standard precautions: watch for pickpockets at the Grand Bazaar and on tram T1, bargain on prices (first offer is 2-3x the real price), avoid taxis without meters (use BiTaksi or Bolt), and decline 'friendly' bar invitations — it's Istanbul's most famous scam (the bill arrives at €200+).

Î: How do I get from Istanbul Airport (IST) to the city centre?
R: Metro (M11 line): 30-40 TL (~€0.60), reach Sultanahmet with one transfer in ~60 minutes. Havaist (bus): 170-200 TL (~€3.50), 60-90 minutes to Taksim. Taxi/Bolt: 900-1,200 TL (€16-22), 45-90 minutes depending on traffic. Recommendation: the metro is fastest and cheapest.

Î: What is Museum Pass Istanbul and is it worth it?
R: Museum Pass Istanbul costs €105 and is valid for 5 days covering 13 museums/attractions, including Topkapi Palace with Harem and Galata Tower. It does NOT include Hagia Sophia (€25), Basilica Cistern (1,950 TL), or Dolmabahçe Palace (2,000 TL). Worth it if you visit 3+ included attractions — otherwise individual tickets are more economical.

Î: Does my phone roaming work in Turkey?
R: Turkey is NOT in the EU — free EU roaming does not apply. Your carrier will charge €3-15/day. An eSIM from Airalo costs €4-5 for 1GB/7 days — dramatically cheaper. Install before departure.

## Things to Do in Krakow: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Auschwitz & Insider Tips

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-krakow
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-05
Actualizat: 2026-08-05
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-cracovia

Descriere: Complete Krakow 2026 guide — Wawel Castle, Kazimierz Jewish Quarter, Wieliczka Salt Mine, Auschwitz-Birkenau, Polish food, what's free, and a realistic budget. Europe's cheapest city break.

Răspuns scurt: Krakow deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Wawel Castle (grounds free, exhibitions €10–18), Kazimierz Jewish Quarter, Wieliczka Salt Mine 15km away (€33, must book online), and the Auschwitz-Birkenau day trip (70km, free entry but guided tour strongly recommended). Krakow is Central Europe's most affordable city break — pierogi €6–8, craft beer €2–3, 3-star hotel €30–60/night. Direct flight from Bucharest with Wizz Air, ~2h.

Krakow surprises through contrast. You arrive with modest expectations — "it's in the East, it's cheap, it's fine" — and leave after 3 days convinced you've found one of the most complete city breaks in Europe. A main square (Rynek Główny) that is the largest intact medieval market square in Europe. A Jewish quarter that went from historical tragedy to the most vibrant bar and arts district in Eastern Europe. A salt mine with a cathedral carved entirely from salt at 101 meters underground. And 70 kilometers away, Auschwitz-Birkenau — a visit unlike anything else, one that quietly shifts the way you see certain things.

Krakow is not just cheap. It is one of Europe's richest experiences, at a price that makes any comparison uncomfortable.

Rynek Główny — Europe's Largest Medieval Market Square

The geometric center and soul of Krakow. 200 meters by 200 meters of perfect medieval square — surrounded by palaces, towers, and café terraces, dominated at the center by the Sukiennice (Cloth Hall, 14th century), flanked by the Town Hall Tower (50m, with museum) and St. Mary's Basilica.

It is not a decorative square. It is a living organism — mornings with the flower market, midday with tourists and locals eating in the sun, evenings with occasional concerts and café life. Trams are routed around its edges, making it completely pedestrian.

What it costs:


Entering the square: free, permanent

Sukiennice upper floor (museum): ~€5

Town Hall Tower (Wieża Ratuszowa): ~€4, with panoramic views

Rynek Underground Museum (medieval vaults): ~€10 (free on Tuesdays)

St. Mary's Basilica: €5, with the trumpeter every hour


Insider tip: The trumpeter at St. Mary's Basilica is one of Europe's oldest living traditions — for 700 years, every hour, a musician plays the "hejnał mariacki" (a melody that cuts off abruptly, commemorating the legendary trumpeter killed by a Tatar arrow in 1241). The signal is broadcast live on Polish national radio every day. If you're in the square at noon, look up at the north tower — it deserves 60 seconds of attention.

Wawel Castle — 1,000 Years of Polish History on a Hill

Wawel Castle is not an ordinary castle. It is where Polish kings were crowned and buried for nearly 500 years, the residence of the Jagiellonian dynasty during Poland's golden age (15th–16th centuries), and the country's deepest national identity symbol — all the more so because it survived the Swedish Deluge, Partitions, and Nazi occupation (Hans Frank, the Nazi General Governor of occupied Poland, used Wawel as his luxury residence, which is why it remained intact).

Castle grounds (courtyard, exterior): free , during opening hours. The view over the Vistula and the city below is spectacular.

Exhibitions (separate timed-entry tickets):

Exhibition Adult price
Royal State Rooms ~€12
Crown Treasury + Armoury ~€10
Oriental Art Collection ~€8
Wawel Cathedral ~€6
Royal Crypt (kings' tombs) included with Cathedral
Cathedral Tower (bells) ~€4
Selected Mondays: Free for some exhibitions

Practical note: Daily ticket numbers are limited per exhibition. In summer, the State Rooms sell out in the morning. Book online at wawel.krakow.pl or through GetYourGuide with skip-the-line included.

What not to miss: Wawel Cathedral is one of Poland's most important churches — the crypt holds the tombs of kings, national heroes (including Tadeusz Kościuszko, who also fought in the American Revolutionary War, and Józef Piłsudski), and great poets. The Zygmunt Bell (1520), Poland's largest, rings only on national occasions — if you can't hear it, you can at least climb to see it close up.

Book a guided Wawel Castle tour on GetYourGuide

Kazimierz — The Quarter That Came Back from the Dead

Kazimierz has the most complex story in Krakow, and possibly in Eastern Europe. Founded as a Jewish quarter in 1335 by King Casimir the Great, it was for centuries the heart of Polish-Jewish culture — synagogues, yeshivas, kosher markets, a community of 65,000 Jewish residents.

In 1941, the Nazis forcibly relocated Krakow's Jewish population from Kazimierz into the Podgórze Ghetto, across the Vistula. The vast majority ended up at Auschwitz. The quarter remained empty and decayed for decades.

Then, in the 1990s, something unexpected happened: artists, musicians, and young people rediscovered Kazimierz. The cheap buildings and unique atmosphere attracted the first generation of bohemian cafés, galleries, and Central European restaurants. Spielberg's film Schindler's List (shot partly in Kazimierz and Podgórze) brought international attention. Today, Kazimierz is the district with the most intense nightlife and art scene in Eastern Europe — with intact synagogues and the Jewish cemetery standing among bars and restaurants.

What to visit in Kazimierz:


Remuh Synagogue (oldest in Krakow, 16th century) + medieval Jewish cemetery: ~€3

Old Synagogue (Alte Shul) — oldest Jewish building in Poland, now a museum: ~€7 (free Tuesdays)

Schindler's Factory (museum of Nazi occupation in Krakow, Lipowa Street): ~€8 — one of the best-executed thematic museums in Europe; book 1–2 days ahead

Plac Nowy — the round square with zapiekanka for €2–4, the heart of Kazimierz nightlife; Sunday mornings host a flea market

Street art and murals throughout the district — free, walking


Tip: Plac Nowy after 10 PM is Kazimierz at its most authentic — locals and bemused tourists in front of an enormous zapiekanka, beer in hand, on a car-free square. The kind of evening that costs almost nothing and stays with you for a long time.


Auschwitz-Birkenau — The Visit You Owe Yourself Once

This is the most difficult section in any Krakow guide and, simultaneously, the most important. Auschwitz-Birkenau is not a tourist attraction in the conventional sense. It is the place where 1.1 million people were systematically murdered — 90% of them Jewish, but also Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, and others — in the largest Nazi extermination center in human history.

A visit to Auschwitz changes something. Not dramatically, not immediately visible — but a few days later, you notice you're thinking differently about certain things.

Logistics:

Detail Info
Distance from Krakow 70 km, ~1h30 by organized transport
Entry to the site Free
Guided tour (Apr–Oct, 10 AM–3 PM) Mandatory for group visits
Guided tour price €35–45/person with transport from Krakow
Booking Required — auschwitz.org or GetYourGuide
Recommended visit duration 4–5 hours (Auschwitz I + Birkenau)

Important: Auschwitz I (the original camp, with "Arbeit macht frei" at the entrance) and Birkenau (the extermination camp 3km away, 20 times larger) are two separate sites. Many visitors only see Auschwitz I — do not skip Birkenau, it is where the mass exterminations took place and where the scale of what happened becomes fully comprehensible.

How to get there: The most convenient option is an organized tour from Krakow with transport included. Going independently is possible (bus or train from Krakow, ~2h total travel), but logistics are more complex and you risk queueing for timed entry slots.

Book an Auschwitz-Birkenau day trip from Krakow on GetYourGuide

Code of conduct: Respectful clothing (no shorts, no message T-shirts), silence in marked areas, photography is permitted but no smiling selfies or playful content. The site is solemn and visitors who disrespect the atmosphere are asked to leave.


Wieliczka Salt Mine — A Cathedral at 101 Meters Underground

14 km southeast of Krakow, the Wieliczka Salt Mine has been operational since the 13th century and has been UNESCO World Heritage since 1978 — one of the first 12 sites ever inscribed. But 700 years of history is abstract compared to what you find there.

You descend 380 steps (or take the lift on the way out) into 22 chambers carved entirely from salt. Statues, bas-reliefs, crystal-clear underground lakes. And at 101 meters below ground, St. Kinga's Chapel — a functioning chapel, 12 meters high, with altars, chandeliers, and bas-reliefs all hand-carved from salt by miners over several centuries. It has hosted religious services, concerts, and an underground restaurant. Constant temperature: 15°C regardless of season.

2026 Prices:

Category Price
Adult (Tourist Route) 143 PLN (~€33)
Reduced (students, children 4–16, seniors) 121 PLN (~€28)
Children under 4 Free
Family (2 adults + 2 children) 430 PLN (~€99)
Miners' Route (more adventurous) 143 PLN (~€33)

Booking: Online at bilety.kopalnia.pl or through GetYourGuide. Mandatory in peak season — in summer, tickets sell out 3–5 days ahead. Do not show up without a reservation and expect to enter — the probability of getting in on the day is very low.

Practical tip: Temperature is 15°C constant — bring an extra layer even if it's 35°C outside. The tourist route involves 800+ steps total (descent and walking through tunnels) — comfortable shoes are essential.

How to get there: Minibus 304 from Bohaterów Getta Square in Krakow (€1.50, 30 min), train from the central station ( €1, 20 min), or an organized tour with transport included ( €45–65 with guide).

Tip about Kościuszko Mound: The artificial mound raised in honor of Tadeusz Kościuszko (Polish national hero and American Revolutionary War veteran) offers the best panorama of Krakow — better than any paid tower. A 20-minute walk from the tram stop, completely free.


Food in Krakow — Cheap, Hearty, Delicious

Krakow has one of the most underrated urban food scenes in Europe. It is not sophisticated — it is honest, warm, filling, and astonishingly affordable for what you receive.

The Essential Dishes

Pierogi — dumplings filled with potato and cheese, meat, sauerkraut and mushrooms, or fruit (the sweet version). Poland's national dish, found in every restaurant and milk bar. Price: 25–35 PLN (€6–8) for 10 pieces — a complete portion for one person.

Żurek — sour rye soup with hard-boiled egg and smoked sausage, often served inside a hollowed bread loaf. Poland's defining winter dish, served year-round in Krakow. Price: 20–35 PLN (€5–8) .

Zapiekanka — open-faced baguette with mushrooms, ketchup, and melted cheese, toasted. Krakow's iconic street food, sold at Plac Nowy in Kazimierz. Price: 12–25 PLN (€3–6) — enough for a complete lunch.

Obwarzanek Krakowski — ring-shaped bread with poppy seeds, sesame, or salt, sold from the blue carts on every street corner. A protected designation of origin product (like Champagne). Price: 3–4 PLN (€0.70) .

Bigos — sauerkraut stew with meat and sausage, cooked for days. Polish food with the most complex historical story (first recipes from the 15th century). Price: 25–40 PLN (€6–9) .

Oscypek — smoked sheep's cheese from the Tatra Mountains, sold in Kazimierz and at markets. The best culinary souvenir from Poland. Price: 15–25 PLN (€4–6) each .

Bottiglieria 1881 (Kazimierz): Poland's only 2-Michelin-star restaurant. Tasting menu 980 PLN ( €225). If fine dining interests you, Krakow offers one of the best price-to-quality ratios in Europe at this level.

Bar Mleczny — The Socialist Canteens That Survived

Bar mleczny (literally "milk bar") are communist-era canteens that serve traditional Polish food at incredibly low prices. No décor, no English menus, no waiters — you order at the counter, wait, pick up your tray.

Bar mleczny prices: full meal (soup + main + compote) under €5.

Two recommended: Bar Mleczny Pod Temidą (near the Rynek) and Milkbar Tomasza (ul. Tomasza, city center).

Craft Beer — Poland Surprises

Poland has exploded in craft beer over the last decade. Kazimierz is the movement's center in Krakow — dozens of pubs with local artisan beer.

Craft beer 0.5L price: 12–20 PLN (€3–5) in Kazimierz pubs.
Standard beer 0.5L: 8–12 PLN (€2–3).

Well below Prague or Vienna prices for comparable or superior quality.

The mountain resort of Zakopane at the foot of the Tatras is reachable by bus (~€5 return, 2h) or organized tour. Summer: hiking to Lake Morskie Oko (Poland's most beautiful lake, 2h walk from the car park). Winter: skiing and snowboarding. Cable car to Kasprowy Wierch peak: ~€20 return.

Poland's second largest urban center, with a fascinating industrial history (the former "Manchester of Poland"), some of Europe's best street art murals, and an emerging cultural scene. Far less visited than Krakow — for those who want authentic Poland beyond the tourist circuit.

Poland is in the EU and Schengen. The European Health Insurance Card works but does not cover medical repatriation, dental care, or flight cancellation. A comprehensive policy for a week costs €12–18/person.

Insider Tips — What Locals Know

1. The €0.70 obwarzanek is the local breakfast. Blue carts across the center sell warm Polish bagels all morning. One obwarzanek + a coffee from a bakery = complete breakfast for €1.50. Better than anything in a hotel.

2. The currency is Polish Złoty (PLN), not euros. Poland has not adopted the euro. 1 EUR ≈ 4.30 PLN. Most places accept cards, but cash is often cheaper. Avoid airport exchange offices — Kantor offices in Kazimierz have better rates.

3. Gentlemen's clubs = traps. Men near the Rynek will offer "free entry, first drink free" — these venues have a solid reputation for unexplained card charges and aggressive security. Avoid entirely.

4. The flower/bracelet scam. People in costume around the center offer flowers or bracelets "for free" — once you've taken something, they demand money aggressively. Refuse before anything is placed in your hands.

5. The Salt Mine — bring a jumper. It's 28°C outside and 15°C underground. The 13-degree difference is unpleasant without an extra layer, especially after 2 hours below ground.

6. Kazimierz on Sunday morning is different from Saturday night. Sunday before noon is quiet, authentic, with the flea market and locals out for a walk. Saturday night is loud and crowded. Plan based on what you want.

7. At Auschwitz, Tuesday and Wednesday are quieter. Weekends (Saturday–Sunday) are the most crowded. A Wednesday morning gives you more space and less noise — important for the kind of experience you're seeking there.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Krakow cost?
R: Realistic budget per person: flights round-trip €60–120 (Wizz Air direct from Bucharest), 3 nights accommodation €90–180 (3-star hotel), attractions €80–100 (Wawel + Auschwitz + Wieliczka), food €40–60. Total: €270–460/person. Krakow is 40–50% cheaper than Prague or Vienna for equivalent experiences.

Î: Do I need to book Auschwitz tickets in advance?
R: Yes, mandatory in season (May–September). Entry to Auschwitz-Birkenau is free, but timed slots are limited and sell out 2–3 weeks ahead in summer. Book at auschwitz.org or via GetYourGuide. A guided tour (€35–45) is strongly recommended — the site covers 3km to Birkenau and historical context is essential.

Î: Is Wieliczka Salt Mine worth visiting?
R: Absolutely. The Wieliczka Salt Mine (UNESCO, 14km from Krakow) is one of Europe's most impressive underground attractions — 22 chambers carved entirely in salt, including St. Kinga's Chapel at 101m depth with chandeliers and bas-reliefs all made from salt. Standard tour 2–3h, €33/adult. Book online — in peak season tickets sell out 3–5 days ahead.

Î: What's the best neighborhood in Krakow to stay?
R: Old Town (Stare Miasto, within the ring road) is ideal for a first visit — everything is walkable. Kazimierz (the Jewish Quarter) offers more atmosphere, better restaurants, and prices 20% lower — perfect if you've been to Krakow before. Avoid the area around the central train station — far from attractions and less pleasant at night.

Î: What's the currency in Poland — do they use euros?
R: Poland uses the Polish Złoty (PLN). 1 EUR ≈ 4.30 PLN. Most places accept cards, but cash is sometimes cheaper. Avoid airport exchange offices — Kantor (currency exchange) offices in Kazimierz offer better rates. Never exchange at banks — commissions are high.

## Things to Do in Lisbon: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Alfama, Sintra & Insider Tips

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-lisbon
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-06
Actualizat: 2026-08-06
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-lisabona

Descriere: Complete Lisbon 2026 guide — Alfama, Jerónimos Monastery, Belém, free miradouros, authentic fado, ginjinha, Sintra day trip. Important: Belém Tower closed for restoration in 2026.

Răspuns scurt: Lisbon deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Alfama and the historic neighborhoods (free, with fado in the evening), Jerónimos Monastery in Belém (~€18, book online), free miradouros at sunset, ginjinha at €1.50 a shot (mandatory), and the Sintra day trip (40 min by train, €2.45). Important 2026: Belém Tower is closed for restoration — photographable from outside but interior inaccessible. Lisbon is more expensive than Porto but offers unmatched neighborhood variety and energy.

Lisbon doesn't leave you indifferent. It approaches with quiet intensity — that Atlantic light that makes the blue of azulejos look bluer than it should, the sound of fado coming through an open window in Alfama at 10 PM, the taste of a warm pastel de nata with cinnamon taken from the counter before sitting down anywhere.

It is the capital of an empire that no longer exists, built on seven hills above the Tagus, with neighborhoods that have distinct personalities and that reveal themselves only on a second visit. Alfama is the oldest, with impossibly narrow alleys and laundry on lines strung between windows. Chiado is elegant and literary. Bairro Alto is chaos of young people and bars after midnight. Belém is grand and historical — the place where the expeditions that mapped the world departed.

Lisbon is not the cheapest European capital. Far from it, after decades of tourism growth. But it remains one of the best — because the quality-to-price ratio for food and wine stays exceptional, and the experience of getting lost in Alfama at sunset, glass of vinho verde in hand, with fado drifting from somewhere above, is priceless.

Alfama — Lisbon's Oldest Neighborhood

Alfama is the only Lisbon neighborhood that survived the 1755 earthquake almost intact. The rest of the city was rebuilt from scratch by the Marquis de Pombal — Alfama remained: narrow alleys, houses with patterned azulejos, endless stairs, inner courtyards with sleeping cats and flowerpots on windowsills.

It is the most photographed neighborhood in Lisbon and simultaneously the most authentic — because real people actually live there, it is not a reconstructed stage set.

Miradouro das Portas do Sol and Miradouro de Santa Luzia — two free terraces in the heart of Alfama, with views over the orange rooftops and the Tagus. Sunset at Miradouro da Graça (slightly higher up) is considered the best in Lisbon.

Tram 28 — the historic yellow tram line crossing Alfama, Graça, and Chiado through Lisbon's steepest neighborhoods. It is real public transport, not a tourist attraction. In summer, queues are enormous. Local alternative: bus 737 does the same route without queuing.

Fado in Alfama: in the evenings, some small bars (adegas) have live fado without entry charge — you pay for the drink. It is neighborhood fado, not theater performance. The most authentic way to hear the genre. Look on Rua do Barão or Beco da Cardosa.


Castelo de São Jorge — the Hilltop Fortress

The Moorish castle on Alfama's highest hill, with complete views of Lisbon and the Tagus. Built in the 11th century by the Moors, taken by D. Afonso Henriques in 1147, now a museum and cultural space.

2026 Prices:

Category Price
Adult ~€17
Reduced (students, seniors) ~€8.50
Children under 10 Free
First Sunday of the month Free (online, limited)

Tip: The panorama is the main reason to go. If budget is tight, the free miradouros in Alfama offer similar views without the ticket.


Belém — the Grandeur of the Age of Discovery

Belém is the neighborhood 6 km west of the center on the Tagus bank, from where the Portuguese Age of Discovery expeditions departed — Vasco da Gama, Bartolomeu Dias, Pedro Álvares Cabral. Everything Portugal built with the gold and spices brought from around the world is concentrated here.

Jerónimos Monastery — Portugal's Architectural Jewel

Jerónimos Monastery is Portugal's most important monument and one of the world's architectural masterpieces — the Manueline style (uniquely Portuguese, a maritime Gothic with ropes, armillary spheres, coral, and tropical plants carved in stone) at its absolute perfection.

Built from 1501 with money brought by Vasco da Gama from India, it housed the Hieronymite order and served as a royal mausoleum. The tombs of Vasco da Gama and poet Luís de Camões are in the church.

2026 Prices:

Category Price
Adult (monastery + museum) ~€18
Reduced ~€9
Children under 12 Free
With Lisboa Card Free
Sunday until 2:00 PM Free (online reservation required)

Booking: Mandatory online at patrimoniocultural.gov.pt. Queues of 60–90 minutes without a reservation at 11:00–14:00.

⚠️ Belém Tower — CLOSED in 2026

Belém Tower, built in 1516 at the mouth of the Tagus, is under restoration in 2026 (Portugal's Recovery and Resilience Plan). Reopening is estimated for mid-2026 — check patrimoniocultural.gov.pt before visiting. You can photograph the tower from the riverside promenade and surrounding gardens — the exterior is equally photogenic.

Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) — the 52-meter sculpture with the effigies of the navigators — ~€6 entry , with a lift to the top and panoramic views.

Pastéis de Belém — the original 1837 bakery that invented the pastel de nata recipe. The recipe secret is known only by a handful of employees. The queue is always long but moves fast. One tart: €1.50 at the counter, warm, with cinnamon. If you eat only one pastel de nata in Lisbon, eat this one.


Miradouros — Free Views from the 7 Hills

Lisbon is built on seven hills and has dozens of miradouros (viewing terraces) — some with a kiosk bar, all free. The best:

Miradouro Location Note
Miradouro da Graça Graça Best sunset in Lisbon
Miradouro de Santa Luzia Alfama View of Alfama + Tagus, azulejos on the wall
Miradouro das Portas do Sol Alfama Central, animated, with café
Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara Bairro Alto Panorama toward Castelo de São Jorge
Miradouro da Senhora do Monte Graça Highest viewpoint, fewer tourists

The essential tip: Miradouro da Graça at sunset (6:30–8:00 PM in summer) is Lisbon's definitive free experience. Get a glass of vinho verde from the nearby kiosk (€3–4) and stay 30–45 minutes. It is the view that justifies the flight.


Chiado and Bairro Alto — Cafés, Bookshops and Nights

Chiado is Lisbon's most elegant neighborhood — with Livraria Bertrand from 1732 (the world's oldest operating bookshop), literary cafés, Portuguese design shops, and Rua Garrett where Fernando Pessoa spent half his life at café tables.

Livraria Bertrand (Rua Garrett): free entry, not as visually spectacular as Lello in Porto, but holds the official Guinness record as the world's oldest operating bookshop. Worth a visit.

A Brasileira — the historic café with Pessoa's statue on the terrace. Expensive for what it offers (€4–6 an espresso) but a mandatory photograph stop.

Bairro Alto is the nightlife neighborhood — narrow streets, small bars occupying old houses. Works from 10 PM onward. Not Ibiza — it's Lisbon: people with glasses on the street (legal), music at reasonable volume, mix of locals and tourists. One of the best value nightlife scenes in southern Europe.


Ginjinha — The €1.50 Shot That Defines Lisbon

Ginjinha is the local sour cherry liqueur, served in small shots at tiny standing bars with no seats. Price: €1.50 a shot. Drunk standing at the counter, with or without a small chocolate cup (a hollow dark chocolate shell into which the ginjinha is poured — a local tradition).

A Ginjinha (Largo de São Domingos, near Rossio) — the original bar from 1840, the oldest. Permanent queue, moves quickly. Mandatory.

Sem Rival (Rua das Portas de Santo Antão) — the direct rival, equally good.

Tip: Ginjinha is drunk quickly, without lengthy reflection. It is a ritual, not a tasting.

Tip about Feira da Ladra: The Alfama flea market (Tuesday mornings + all day Saturday) has azulejo objects, coins, old books, ceramics, and souvenirs at negotiable prices. Best place in Lisbon for authentic purchases without tourist markup.


Food in Lisbon — Cheaper Than You Think If You Know Where

The Essential Dishes

Pastel de nata — egg custard tart, slightly caramelized on top, with cinnamon. Eaten warm, at the counter, with a bica (short espresso, €0.70). €1.20–2 at any pastelaria. The 1837 original: Pastéis de Belém in Belém.

Bacalhau — salt cod, Portugal's national ingredient with 365 official recipes. Bacalhau à Brás (with eggs and matchstick potatoes), bacalhau à Gomes de Sá (potatoes, boiled eggs), à Zé do Pipo (with mayonnaise, baked). €12–18 at a traditional restaurant.

Bifana — pork sandwich marinated in garlic and spices. €3–4. The Casas da Bifana in Baixa serve the best.

Caldo verde — kale soup with chorizo, simple, warming, perfect for a cool evening. €4–6.

Amêijoas à Bulhão Pato — clams in garlic, butter, and coriander sauce. Classic seafood starter. €10–14.

Sardines grelhadas (summer) — fresh grilled sardines, the festive summer food of Lisbon (especially during the Santo António Festival, June 13). €10–15 a portion.

Ginjinha — a €1.50 shot, described above. Mandatory.

Rules for Avoiding Surprises

Couvert: The bread, butter, olives, cheese automatically brought to your table are NOT free. Decline with "não, obrigado" if you don't want an extra €2–5 on your bill.

Tap water: Safe and free. At restaurants you can ask for "água da torneira" (tap water) — normal and accepted.

Prato do dia (daily lunch special, Mon–Fri): soup + main + drink. €8–12. Lisbon's best deal.

Approximate food budget

Meal type Cost per person

Bifana (snack) €3–4
Prato do dia at a tasca €8–12
Bacalhau at a restaurant (lunch/dinner) €12–18

Fado — the Soul of Lisbon

Fado is Portugal's national music — a melancholic song form with themes of longing, loss, and saudade (an untranslatable Portuguese concept, a mixture of nostalgia and yearning for something that may never have existed). Lisbon fado is more poetic and theatrical than Porto fado.

Types of experience:

Formal fado houses (Clube de Fado, Mesa de Frades, Sr. Fado): fado performance with 4–6 professional fadistas, food included or optional. €35–60/person with food, €20–35 show only. High quality, theatrical atmosphere. Book 2–3 days ahead.

Alfama adegas (neighborhood fado): a small bar where a fadista sings live without a formal stage. You pay for the drink, fado comes with it. €3–8 for the drink. Most authentic — but quality varies and schedules are unpredictable.

Tip: For guaranteed quality and a complete experience, book a formal fado house through GetYourGuide. For authenticity, go to Alfama in the evening and enter the first bar where you hear music.

Book a fado show in Lisbon on GetYourGuide


Sintra Day Trip — Non-Negotiable

Sintra is 40 minutes by train from Rossio Station (€2.45 return) and is one of the most beautiful destinations in southern Europe — a mountain village with fairy-tale Romantic palaces, pine and eucalyptus forests, and views to the Atlantic on clear days.

What to visit in Sintra:

Pena Palace — a pink-and-yellow fairy-tale castle on the mountain peak, built in 1847 by King Ferdinand II in Romantic eclectic style. One of Portugal's most photographed buildings. €17 adults (park + palace). Online booking mandatory — sells out weeks in advance in season.

Moorish Castle — medieval walls on the mountain, with walking trails and views of Sintra and Pena Palace. €10 adults.

Sintra National Palace — in the center of town, with its enormous kitchen chimneys as emblems. €10 adults. Monday free (partial).

Cabo da Roca — the westernmost point of continental Europe, 140-meter cliffs above the Atlantic. 30 minutes by bus from Sintra. Free (certificate of visit: €2–3).

Train Rossio–Sintra: Rossio Station in Lisbon, CP trains every 15–20 minutes, 40 minutes. €2.45 return — the cheapest way to get there.

Suggested Itinerary — 3 Days in Lisbon

Day 1: Alfama and the Old Center


8:30 — Bica + pastel de nata at a local pastelaria (€2)

11:30 — Castelo de São Jorge (or free miradouro if skipping the ticket)

Insider Tips — What Locals Know

1. Refuse the couvert immediately when seated. Not after you've eaten from it. "Não, obrigado" the moment they bring the bread basket. If you've eaten it, you pay.

2. Tram 28 in summer = ordeal. 45-minute queue in the sun, packed carriage, active pickpockets. Bus 737 or Bolt does the same route in peace.

3. Ginjinha is drunk "com ela." "Com ela" (with it) = with the small dark chocolate cup into which the liqueur is poured. "Sem ela" = without. If you want to look local, order "com ela."

4. Prato do dia disappears at 2 PM. If you arrive at a tasca at 2:15 PM wanting the daily special — it's gone. Lunch is sacred and early in Portugal.

5. Pastéis de Belém vs Manteigaria. The 1837 original in Belém is a pilgrimage. Manteigaria (Chiado) is locals' favourite for the warmest and freshest tarts in the center. No objective winner — depends where you are.

6. Bica costs €0.70 at the counter. If you sit at a table, bica costs €1.20–1.50. Same coffee, same quality — the price is for the chair.

7. Pickpockets target Tram 28 and Alfama. Back pocket, phone in view, rucksack on your front. Not dangerous — simply avoidable with basic awareness.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is the Belém Tower open in 2026?
R: No — Belém Tower is closed for restoration under Portugal's Recovery and Resilience Plan, with reopening expected sometime mid-2026 (date unconfirmed at time of writing). You can photograph the tower from the riverside promenade and surrounding gardens. Jerónimos Monastery, 500 meters away, is open and justifies the Belém trip on its own.

Î: Lisbon or Porto — which should I visit first?
R: Lisbon is the first choice for a first visit to Portugal — larger, more diverse, with multiple distinct neighborhoods (Alfama, Chiado, Bairro Alto, Belém, Parque das Nações), more theatrical fado, and Sintra 40 minutes away. Porto is more authentic, 20–30% cheaper, and has Port wine at source. Ideally you visit both — they're 3 hours apart by train.

Î: What is the couvert in Portuguese restaurants?
R: When you sit down, the waiter automatically brings bread, butter, olives, sometimes cheese or fish paste. These are NOT free — they appear on your bill (€2–5 per person). If you don't want them, decline immediately: 'Não, obrigado.' It's completely normal to refuse.

Î: Is Tram 28 worth it or is it just for tourists?
R: Tram 28 is a real public transport line that crosses Alfama and connects the historic neighborhoods — not a tourist attraction, but the tram locals used for decades. Worth it for atmosphere and the route through steep neighborhoods, but in summer it's packed with tourists. The alternative: bus 737 does the same route faster, with no queue.

Î: Is Sintra worth a day trip?
R: Yes, unconditionally — it's one of the most beautiful day trips in southern Europe. Train from Rossio in 40 minutes (€2.45 return) takes you to Sintra, with Pena Palace (pink and yellow on the mountain, €17), the National Palace (in the town center, €10), the Moorish Castle with mountain walls (€10), and Cabo da Roca — the westernmost point of continental Europe. Book Pena Palace online — it sells out weeks in advance.

## Things to Do in Ljubljana: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Lake Bled & Insider Tips

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-ljubljana
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-05
Actualizat: 2026-08-05
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-ljubljana

Descriere: Complete Ljubljana 2026 guide — Ljubljana Castle, Dragon Bridge, Metelkova, Lake Bled 1h away, Postojna Cave, Slovenian food, what's free. Europe's smallest and most surprising city break.

Răspuns scurt: Ljubljana deserves 2–3 days. Top priorities: Ljubljana Castle (free walk up, funicular €6, excellent views), Dragon Bridge and Prešeren Square (free), Metelkova alternative art district (free during the day), Lake Bled day trip (1h15 by bus, €6) and Postojna Cave (1h, €28). Ljubljana is compact, pedestrian-friendly, and genuinely surprising — an intact medieval center, excellent Slovenian food at accessible prices, and the Alps visible from the city center.

Ljubljana is the city that makes visitors wonder why they didn't come sooner. It isn't famous — it doesn't have a single world-class landmark that justifies a flight on its own, it doesn't appear on the front pages of travel magazines, and many Europeans can't pinpoint Slovenia on a map.

That is precisely what makes it perfect. An intact medieval center with Baroque and Jugendstil buildings, a river with pedestrian banks full of café terraces and bars, a castle on a hill with complete panoramic views, the Alps visible from the center, a surprisingly good food scene blending Austrian, Italian, and Balkan influences, and a pace of life that makes no effort to impress anyone.

Ljubljana is the EU's smallest capital by area after Valletta — and that scale makes it the perfect city break: you don't feel the pressure to "tick off" attractions from an endless list. You walk, stop, eat well, climb to the castle, go to Bled.

Ljubljana Castle — the Hill Above the City

Ljubljana Castle dominates the city from a 376-meter hill — visible from anywhere in the center, 15–20 minutes on foot from Prešeren Square. It was a medieval fortress, a prison, and now a cultural complex with museums, viewing terraces, and a watchtower from which the panorama takes in the city's rooftops, the Ljubljanica river, and on clear days the peaks of the Slovenian Alps.

How to get there:


On foot — path through the hill's forest, 15–20 minutes, free. The route starts near the Central Market

Funicular — 2 minutes, up and down


2026 Prices:

Option Price
Funicular (return) ~€6
Castle Courtyard (without funicular) Free
Full ticket (all museums + tower) ~€16 adult
Reduced ticket (students, seniors) ~€11
Children under 6 Free

What the full ticket includes: Slovenian History Exhibition, Museum of Puppetry, Watchtower (panorama), and Virtual Castle (3D reconstruction of the medieval fortress).

Tip: The watchtower is the highest accessible point — on clear days you can see Lake Bled and Triglav peak (Slovenia's highest mountain, 2,864m). Arrive early morning or at sunset for perfect light.

Tip 2: The castle courtyard is free and has its own good views. If budget is limited, walk up for free, spend time in the courtyard, and skip the museums — the experience remains valuable.

Book a guided Ljubljana Castle tour on GetYourGuide


Dragon Bridge and the Old Town — Free and Spectacular

Dragon Bridge (Zmajski Most) — built in 1901 in Viennese Secession style, with four bronze dragons at the corners that are the city's symbol. Photographed from every angle, free, at any hour. Early morning without tourists it is the most photogenic point in Ljubljana.

Triple Bridge (Tromostovje) — three parallel bridges connecting Prešeren Square to the Old Town. Built between 1842–1932, they mark the central point of Ljubljana. In the evening, illuminated, they are the city's meeting point.

Prešeren Square (Prešernov trg) — the heart of Ljubljana, with the statue of national poet France Prešeren, the pink Franciscan Church, and terrace cafés. Permanently open, completely free, animated throughout the day.

Old Town (Staro Mesto) — west of the river: narrow cobbled alleys, Baroque and Jugendstil buildings, craft workshops, and gostilne (traditional Slovenian restaurants). No ticket, no time limit — just walk.


The Ljubljanica Riverbank — the City's Living Heart

The Ljubljanica riverbank, from Prešeren Square to Vodnik Square, is Ljubljana's long outdoor terrace — bars, restaurants, and café umbrellas opening onto the water. It is where locals come in the evening and where tourists stay longer than planned.

Vodnik Square and the Central Market (Tržnica): Ljubljana's morning market, with vegetables, fruit, flowers, Slovenian honey, cheeses, and traditional charcuterie. Open Monday–Saturday, mornings. Free.

Open Kitchen — the street food market held every Friday (March–October, 10:00–21:00) on the riverbank. Local producers and Ljubljana restaurants present food from across Slovenia and beyond. Prices: €4–10 per portion. One of the best gastronomic experiences with free entry in Europe.


Metelkova — the Former Barracks That Became an Artistic Republic

10 minutes on foot from the center, Metelkova Mesto is a fascinating urban anomaly: a former Yugoslav Army barracks, abandoned in 1991 at Slovenia's independence, illegally occupied in 1993 by a group of artists, and since then transformed into the largest autonomous urban art zone in Europe.

The buildings are entirely covered with graffiti and artistic installations — not decorative murals but complete artworks, layered over 30 years. Cultural organisations, galleries, alternative hostels, and clubs with live music and alternative experiences.

Daytime visit: Free, anytime. Interesting as urban documentary.

Evening (Thursday–Saturday, from 11:00 PM): Metelkova's clubs open — Klub Gromka, Klub Monokel, K4, Menza pri Koritu — alternative music, techno, punk, queer. Entry €5–10. Not for everyone, but authentic — none of these clubs were designed for tourists.

Tip about Kavalir: The small electric bus circulating through the pedestrian zone is completely free — it takes you from Prešeren Square to the Castle and back without paying anything. Effectively, transport in central Ljubljana is free.


Food in Ljubljana — Slovenia Surprises

Slovenian cuisine is the least-known culinary blend in Europe — Austrian influences (schnitzels, grills, dumplings), Italian (pasta, risotto, Adriatic seafood), and Balkan (charcoal grills, meat). The result is a food culture with its own personality, excellent local products, and wines that almost nobody outside Slovenia knows exist.

The Essential Dishes

Kranjska klobasa (Carniolan sausage) — Slovenia's national sausage, with protected designation of origin (like Champagne or Parma). 80% pork + 20% bacon, smoked, served with mustard and horseradish. €7–10 at Klobasarna (the specialist restaurant in Ljubljana, near the Central Market). Without the "Certified" stamp, it's not authentic.

Štruklji — rolled dumplings, filled either sweet (walnut, raisins) or savory (cottage cheese, spinach). Specifically Slovenian, with no direct equivalent in European cuisine. €8–10.

Žlikrofi — tiny dumplings from Idrija, filled with potato and lard, served with mutton sauce (bakalca). Protected designation of origin. €11–13.

Potica — rolled pastry cake with walnut or tarragon, Slovenia's festive dessert. A slice: €3–4 at a bakery or market. The best potica is homemade — if invited somewhere, don't decline.

Bled cream cake (Kremšnita) — the cream cake invented at Hotel Park Bled in 1953. Layers of vanilla cream and whipped cream between pastry sheets. The original costs €6.50 and should be eaten in Bled, not Ljubljana. Ljubljana versions cost €4–5 and are excellent.

Pumpkin seed oil (Bučno olje) — black-green pumpkin seed oil with an intense nutty flavour. Goes on salads, soups, and ice cream. The definitive culinary souvenir from Slovenia — a 250ml bottle costs €5–8 and lasts a long time.

Slovenian wine — Slovenia has three small but excellent wine regions, almost unknown outside the country. Primorska wines (Malvasia, Teran), Podravje (Šipon — a Slovenian Furmint), and Posavje (Cviček, a light red) are significantly cheaper and equally good as their Italian or Austrian counterparts. Wine bar tasting: €12–18 for 4–6 glasses.

Where to Eat Cheaply and Well

Klobasarna — specialised exclusively in kranjska klobasa. The authentic sausage with mustard and a Slovenian beer: €10–12 total. Next to Vodnik Square.

Open Kitchen (Fridays) — quality street food at accessible prices, €4–10 per portion.

Central Market — cheeses, charcuterie, fruit, and prepared food at local prices.

Gostilne (traditional inns) outside the tourist center: full menu (soup + main + dessert) €12–18. Those in the tourist center charge 30–50% more for the same food.

Approximate food budget

Meal type Cost per person

Day Trips from Ljubljana — Slovenia Around You

Lake Bled — 1h15 by bus

Lake Bled is Slovenia's signature image: a glacially formed lake with a small island in the center on which a white church is built, a medieval castle on a 130-meter cliff above the water, and the Slovenian Alps as background. The photograph is real — it isn't edited and doesn't disappoint in person.

How to get there:


Bus from Ljubljana (bus station): ~€6 return, 1h15, frequent

Train to Lesce-Bled + local bus: similar price and duration

Rental car: 50 km, 50 minutes


What to do at Bled:

Activity Price
The lake itself (walking the shore) Free
Pletna (traditional boat to the island) ~€18 return
Entry to island church ~€8
Bled Castle ~€15 adult
Original kremšnita at Hotel Park €6.50
Kayak or SUP on the lake €15–25/hour

Tip: Early morning (7:00–9:00 AM), the lake is in mist and nearly without tourists — this is the golden moment. At midday in summer, the shore is overcrowded. Take the first bus and you're an hour ahead of the organised tour wave.

Book a Lake Bled day trip from Ljubljana on GetYourGuide

Postojna Cave + Predjama Castle — 1h by bus

Postojna Cave is Slovenia's second most visited site (after Lake Bled) — 24 km of underground galleries formed over 2 million years, with stalactites, stalagmites, and colonies of proteus (a blind amphibian endemic to Balkan caves, nicknamed "the cave dragon").

The tour includes an electric train ride through the cave (3 km) + walking through spectacular chambers. Temperature: 10°C constant — bring an extra layer even in summer.

Predjama Castle (9 km from Postojna): a medieval castle built inside a cave mouth at 123 meters height — one of the most bizarre and impressive images in Europe. Included free with the combined ticket.

Prices:

Option Adult price
Postojna Cave (individual) ~€28–30
Predjama Castle (individual) ~€14
Combined Cave + Castle ticket ~€38–40
Organised tour from Ljubljana (transport incl.) €55–70

Bus from Ljubljana to Postojna: ~€8 return, 1h. Predjama Castle requires a local taxi or rental car from the cave (9 km).

Triglav National Park — The Slovenian Alps

For more serious hiking, Triglav National Park is 2 hours from Ljubljana — glacial lakes, waterfalls, and trails to Alpine peaks. Lake Bohinj (quieter than Bled, no island but without the summer crowds) is the perfect alternative to Bled.

Soča + Kranjska Gora tour: The Soča river valley with its impossibly turquoise water, Vršič Pass, and the alpine resort of Kranjska Gora. Organised tour from Ljubljana: €65–80. With a rental car: more flexible and similar cost.

Getting around Ljubljana

Ljubljana is completely pedestrian in the center — Dragon Bridge, Prešeren Square, the riverbank, and castle access are all within 20 minutes on foot.

Kavalir — the free electric shuttle in the pedestrian zone. No ticket needed.

LPP buses — public transport network, €1.30/ticket (slightly cheaper with Urbana card). Rarely needed for the center.

Bolt/Uber — available, cheap by Western European standards.


Travel Insurance for Slovenia

Slovenia is in the EU and Schengen. The EHIC works for emergencies at public hospitals. It does not cover repatriation, dental care, or cancellations. Comprehensive insurance for a week: €12–18.

Conclusion: Ljubljana is the ideal destination for those who want something different — a capital that doesn't boast and doesn't overwhelm, with day trips that are among the most spectacular in Europe (Bled, Postojna, Soča), and a scale that lets you genuinely feel a place, not just check it off.


Insider Tips — What Locals Know

1. Kavalir is free and few visitors know it. The small electric shuttle in the center costs nothing. If your feet hurt after the castle, wave it down and it takes you back to the square.

2. The kremšnita should be eaten at Bled, not Ljubljana. The cream cake from 1953 exists in versions everywhere, but the original at Hotel Park Bled (€6.50) is noticeably different — lighter, more airy. Worth eating at the source.

3. Friday Open Kitchen beats any restaurant. The best street food in Ljubljana, produced by serious restaurants, served informally on the riverbank. If you're in Ljubljana on a Friday, that's dinner.

4. Pumpkin seed oil on ice cream. Sounds impossible. It's an experience. Vanilla ice cream with black-green bučno oil is a must at any serious café in Ljubljana or Bled.

5. Metelkova at night is completely different from daytime. If you go during the day, it's an interesting arts district. If you go Thursday–Saturday after 11 PM, it's one of the most authentic alternative music scenes in Eastern Europe. Decide based on what you're looking for.

6. Slovenia is smaller than you think. 20,000 km² — smaller than many European regions. With a rental car, you can see Bled in the morning, Postojna Cave after lunch, and be back in Ljubljana for dinner. The density of spectacular scenery per square kilometer is improbable.

7. Slovenian wine is unknown and excellent. Malvasia from Primorska is a white wine with saline and floral notes, superior to many Italian Pinot Grigios at the same price. Šipon from Podravje is an aromatic gem. No tourist knows them — meaning the wine bars in Ljubljana are never crowded.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How many days do you need in Ljubljana?
R: 2 days comfortably cover the entire center: the Castle, Dragon Bridge, Prešeren Square, the riverbank, Metelkova, Tivoli Park. 3 days add a day trip to Lake Bled or Postojna Cave. 4 days allow both excursions plus Triglav National Park. Ljubljana is small — the advantage is that you're not rushing, you have time to stop at a riverside café.

Î: Is Lake Bled worth the day trip from Ljubljana?
R: Yes, absolutely — it's one of the most photogenic views in Europe. 1h15 by bus from Ljubljana (€6 return), Lake Bled has a small island with a white church in the center, a medieval castle on a cliff above the water, and the Slovenian Alps as backdrop. The original kremšnita cream cake (since 1953) is mandatory. In summer it gets crowded — arrive early.

Î: Is Ljubljana expensive?
R: No — it is 30–50% cheaper than Western European capitals. A main course at a local restaurant: €10–16. Ljubljana Castle (full ticket): ~€16. Public transport: free in the center with the Kavalir electric shuttle. Lake Bled by bus: €6. Ljubljana is cheaper than Vienna or Prague, but more expensive than Kraków or Sofia.

Î: What is Metelkova and is it worth visiting?
R: Metelkova is the former Yugoslav Army barracks, occupied in 1993 by artists and activists and transformed into the largest urban autonomous art zone in Europe. Buildings covered entirely with graffiti and art installations, alternative clubs, galleries, and a completely different energy from the tourist center. Daytime visit is free and interesting. Evenings (Thu–Sat) it becomes alternative nightlife. Not for everyone, but genuinely authentic.

Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Ljubljana?
R: No regular direct flight. The most efficient routes: fly to Venice (2h, Wizz Air/Ryanair) + bus or train to Ljubljana (2h30, ~€15–25). Or fly to Vienna (1h40) + Railjet train Vienna–Ljubljana (5h, €20–40). Or fly to Zagreb (1h) + bus Zagreb–Ljubljana (2h30, €8–15). Most accessible via Venice or Zagreb.

## Things to Do in Munich: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Oktoberfest & Neuschwanstein

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-munich
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-06
Actualizat: 2026-08-06
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-munchen

Descriere: Complete Munich 2026 guide — Marienplatz, English Garden with surfers, Nymphenburg Palace, Deutsches Museum, Bavarian beer gardens, Oktoberfest, and Neuschwanstein Castle day trip.

Răspuns scurt: Munich deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Marienplatz with the Glockenspiel (free), English Garden with the Eisbach surfers (free), Nymphenburg Palace (€15 full ticket), Deutsches Museum (€15), an evening at a local beer garden (€8–10 a litre), and the Neuschwanstein Castle day trip (€21 entry + train). Munich is expensive but has dozens of free attractions. Oktoberfest (September–October) transforms the city completely — book your hotel a year in advance.

Munich knows exactly what it is — and makes no apology for it. It is the capital of Bavaria, it is wealthy, it is proud, and it serves the world's best weisswurst before noon, with wheat beer, in a wooden hall with painted ceilings. Hofbräuhaus is not a tourist trap — it is a 400-year-old institution that has served people from every social stratum under the same roof. The English Garden is larger than Central Park and has surfers riding an artificial wave in the middle of an urban river. Neuschwanstein Castle 130 km to the south inspired Disney's Cinderella castle and is visible from a mountain ridge against a complete Alpine backdrop.

Munich is expensive. It is among Europe's priciest cities, with hotels starting at €100 a night and beer costing €9–10 at a local beer garden and €12–13 at Hofbräuhaus. But it has dozens of free attractions, world-class museums at €1 on Sundays, and a quality of experience that justifies every euro.

Marienplatz and the Old Town — the Heart of Munich

Marienplatz is the city's central square — built in 1158, it is as much a functioning civic space as a tourist attraction. The Frauenkirche with its twin onion-domed towers is the skyline symbol, while the Neues Rathaus (New Town Hall) with its Glockenspiel provides the daily spectacle.

The Glockenspiel: Daily at 11:00 AM (and noon + 5:00 PM in season), 43 bells and 32 mechanical figures re-enact two stories from Munich's history — the 1568 wedding of Duke Wilhelm V and the Schäfflertanz (coopers' dance) from 1517. Free — stand in the square and watch. Duration: 12–15 minutes. Crowds form — arrive 10 minutes early for a good spot.

Viktualienmarkt — Munich's food market, in operation since 1807, 2 minutes from Marienplatz. Fresh pretzels, Bavarian sausages, cheeses, honey, exotic fruit, and a beer garden at the center. Entry is free; food and drink are paid.

Asamkirche — Munich's most spectacular Baroque church, built in 1746 by the Asam brothers as a private chapel. The small dimensions (28m length) concentrate a density of ornaments, marble, gilded stucco, and frescoes that completely overwhelm. Free entry.

St. Peter's Tower (Alter Peter): Munich's oldest tower, 306 steps, complete panorama over Marienplatz and the Frauenkirche. ~€4 adults — one of the best accessible views in the center.


English Garden — Bigger Than Central Park, With Surfers

The English Garden is freely accessible and is one of the world's largest urban parks — 370 hectares (versus 341 for Central Park in New York), with lakes, a Japanese garden, Chinese Tower (a wooden pagoda surrounded by a beer garden), and vast meadows where thousands of Munich residents come to read, walk, or swim in the Eisbach.

Eisbach Surfers — the artificial wave created by the fast-flowing Eisbach river current is the world's only permanent urban surf spot. One surfer rides the wave at a time, 30–60 seconds each. Spectators gather on the bridge above. Free, permanent (more animated in summer). Location: southern entrance of the English Garden, near Haus der Kunst.

Chinese Tower Beer Garden — the beer garden around the Chinese pagoda at the center of the park. A litre of beer (Masskrug): €8–10, giant pretzels €5–7, traditional meals €8–15. You can bring your own food — it is completely normal and accepted.

Insider tip: One of Munich's best-known money-saving traditions: you are legally allowed to bring your own food to beer gardens, as long as you buy your drinks from the venue. This is widely observed by locals and completely accepted. A supermarket picnic eaten at a beer garden table, with a €9 Masskrug of Augustiner, is one of the best value experiences in Munich.


Nymphenburg Palace — the Wittelsbachs' Summer Residence

6 km west of the center (tram 17 direct), Nymphenburg Palace is the Wittelsbach royal family's summer residence — a vast Baroque construction from the 17th century, with a central canal, 490-hectare park, and impressive satellite pavilions.

What not to miss:


Gallery of Beauties — 36 portraits of women who fascinated King Ludwig I, including Helene Sedlmayr (a cobbler's daughter) alongside nobility and actress Lola Montez (who also brought about his abdication)

Amalienburg — hunting pavilion with a Hall of Mirrors, considered the gem of German Rococo

The Park — free strolling through canals, gardens, and pavilions


2026 Prices:

Option Price
Main palace (interior) €8
Full ticket (palace + pavilions) ~€15
Park Free
Under 18s Free

Hours: 9:00–18:00 (April–October); 10:00–16:00 (November–March). Pavilions open April–15 October only.


Deutsches Museum — the World's Largest Science and Technology Museum

On an island in the Isar river, the Deutsches Museum is the world's largest science and technology museum — with a real submarine (U-Boot), Otto Lilienthal's pioneering glider, a full-scale underground mine reconstruction, the original 1965 Apollo lunar lander mockup, and a working Tesla coil. €15 entry, allow at least 3 hours.

Note: The museum is undergoing partial renovation — check deutsches-museum.de for which sections are open at your visit date.


Munich Residenz — the Wittelsbach Palace in the City Center

The Residenz is the palace complex in central Munich, the principal residence of the Bavarian royal family from 1508 to 1918 — 130 rooms, the Treasury collection of decorative arts (one of the world's richest), and the Cuvilliés-Theater, one of Europe's most beautiful Rococo theater spaces.

Prices: ~€13 (palace + treasury).

Tip: Cuvilliés-Theater has opera and chamber music performances — check the program at residenz-muenchen.de for the complete experience.


Beer Gardens — the Authentic Bavarian Experience

Munich has 30+ beer gardens (Biergarten) — a tradition dating from the 19th century when brewers dug cellars under chestnut trees to keep beer cold in summer. Locals sat down in the shade and asked to drink there. The Bavarian government legalised the tradition in 1812 and added the right to bring your own food — a law that still stands today.

Recommended beer gardens:

Hirschgarten — the world's largest beer garden (8,000 seats), outside the tourist center. A litre of beer: €8–10 versus €12–13 at Hofbräuhaus. Authentic local atmosphere.

Chinese Tower (English Garden) — central and accessible, inside the park. Lively and touristy but pleasant.

Augustiner Keller — near the central station, one of Munich's oldest breweries, with Augustiner beer served directly from wooden barrels.

Biergarten am Viktualienmarkt — central, in the heart of the market, perfect for a lunch break.

Hofbräuhaus — the 400-Year-Old Institution

Visit Hofbräuhaus once for the atmosphere — long benches, brass band music, tourists from everywhere, and beer at €12–13 a litre. It is an experience in itself, but not where you drink every evening. Go once, stay 2 hours, drink one Masskrug. Ticked off.


Bavarian Food — What to Order

Essential dishes

Weisswurst (white sausage) — white veal sausage seasoned with parsley and lemon, always boiled (never fried), served with sweet Bavarian mustard and a Brezn (pretzel). Munich tradition: eaten before noon, with wheat beer (Weissbier). €3–5 each at any traditional brewery. Local rule: you don't eat weisswurst after noon — it's a Bavarian breakfast or brunch.

Schweinshaxe (pork knuckle) — roasted in beer, with crispy skin and juicy meat, served with red sauerkraut and Knödel (bread dumplings). €22–32 at a good restaurant — a complete meal for one or a large portion for two.

Obatzda — camembert cheese paste with butter, beer, and spices, served with Brezn. The definitive beer garden appetizer. €4–6.

Brezn (Bavarian pretzels) — large, soft, with chunky salt, completely different from industrial pretzels. €3–5 at a street stand, €5–8 at a restaurant.

Leberkäsesemmel — sandwich with leberkäse (baked meatloaf, thick slices), mustard, in a bread roll. ~€4.50 — the best quick lunch in Munich, from any butcher (Metzgerei).

Apfelstrudel — apple strudel with icing sugar and cream or vanilla ice cream. €5–8. The definitive Bavarian dessert.

Approximate food budget

Meal type Cost per person
Weisswurst + Brezn + Weissbier (breakfast) €10–15
Leberkäsesemmel at a butcher (quick lunch) €4–6
Full meal at a traditional brewery €20–35
Complete Schweinshaxe €22–32
Litre of beer at a local beer garden €8–10
Litre of beer at Hofbräuhaus €12–13

Golden rule: Two streets away from Marienplatz, Hofbräuhaus, and the central shopping streets, the same meal costs 30–40% less.
