Tip about €1 Sunday museums: State museum entry is reduced to €1 on Sundays — including Alte Pinakothek, Neue Pinakothek, Pinakothek der Moderne, and Bayerisches Nationalmuseum. If you're in Munich for a weekend, plan the museums for Sunday.

BMW Welt: The BMW showroom next to the Olympic Park was designed by Coop Himmelb(l)au (cost €500 million) and presents all BMW, MINI, and Rolls-Royce models. Completely free. Adjacent BMW Museum costs €12 and traces the brand's history from 1916.


Oktoberfest — the 6-Million-Visitor Phenomenon

Oktoberfest is the world's largest folk festival — September 19 – October 4, 2026 , on the Theresienwiese, 10 minutes on foot from Munich's center.

Entry to the grounds: FREE. You pay for food and drink.

2026 prices inside the tents:

Item Price
Masskrug (1 litre beer) €13.60–15.80
Rotisserie chicken (Halbes Hendl) €16–20
Pork knuckle (Schweinshaxe) €22–32
Pretzel (Brezn) €5–8
Bratwurst on the street (cheaper) €5–8

The tents (Zelte): 14 major tents (Spaten, Augustiner, Hofbräu, Paulaner, Löwenbräu etc.) + smaller tents. Each has a distinct personality. Table reservations for the tents are mandatory for weekends and evenings — they generally open in spring on the tents' official websites.

Essential Oktoberfest tips:


Arrive at 9:00 AM for unreserved seats (tents open at 9:00–10:00 AM, free tables disappear fast)

Accommodation: Munich hotels during Oktoberfest cost 3–5x the normal rate — book at least 6–12 months ahead or stay in S-Bahn accessible suburbs

Tracht: Lederhosen or Dirndl are not compulsory, but 80% of attendees wear them — if you want to fit in, buy in advance (€50–150 for decent versions, €300–500+ for authentic leather)

Avoid the scam: At busy beer gardens, people may offer to return your heavy glass mug — and pocket the €2–3 deposit (Pfand) that is rightfully yours.


Book an Oktoberfest guided experience on GetYourGuide


Neuschwanstein Castle — the Alpine Fairy Tale

130 km south of Munich in the Bavarian Alps, Neuschwanstein Castle is Germany's most visited monument and the direct inspiration for the Disney Cinderella castle. Built by King Ludwig II of Bavaria (nicknamed the "Mad King") between 1869–1886, it was never completed — Ludwig died mysteriously in 1886 at age 40.

How to get there:

Option Price Duration
Train Munich–Füssen (Bayern Ticket, group) €29/group (1–5 people) ~2h
Train Munich–Füssen (individual return) ~€21 ~2h
Bus Füssen–castle (73/78) €4–6 10 min
Organised tour from Munich €50–70/person Full day

Castle ticket: €21 adults. Online booking mandatory 2–3 months ahead in summer — daily visitor quotas fill completely.

Tip: The smart visitor walks or takes a carriage to the castle (not the crowded bus) and also visits Hohenschwangau Castle (Ludwig's childhood home, €21) in the valley — the combination is richer than Neuschwanstein alone.

Book a Neuschwanstein Castle day trip on GetYourGuide


Other Day Trips from Munich

Salzburg (Austria) — 1h30 by train, covered by Bayern Ticket (yes, Bayern Ticket works into northern Austria). Mozart, Hohensalzburg Fortress, UNESCO Baroque center. A complete day.

Dachau Concentration Camp Memorial — 30 minutes by S-Bahn + bus. The first Nazi concentration camp (1933), with a documented permanent exhibition. Free entry , audio guide €6. Allow 3–4 hours.

Lake Chiemsee — "Bavaria's Sea," 1h by train, with Herrenchiemsee Castle on an island (Ludwig II's copy of Versailles). Bayern Ticket valid.

Munich Christmas Markets (late November – December 24) are among the world's oldest — Marienplatz with the giant Christmas tree, craft stalls, Glühwein (spiced mulled wine), and Lebkuchen (decorated gingerbread). Authentic atmosphere.

Insider Tips — What Locals Know

1. Weisswurst is not eaten after noon. Bavarian tradition says weisswurst is breakfast or brunch — eaten before noon with wheat beer. Ordering it at dinner makes locals raise an eyebrow.

2. You can bring your own food to beer gardens. As long as you buy drinks from the venue, you can eat your own picnic at the table — a Bavarian law from 1812, still valid today. An Edeka or Rewe supermarket has everything you need.

3. The Pfand deposit is yours. The beer mug has a deposit (Pfand) of €2–3 — when you return it to the bar, you get the money back. Don't let anyone "helpfully" return it for you.

4. Supermarkets are closed on Sundays. Buy everything you need on Saturday — German supermarkets don't open on Sundays. Petrol stations and small bakeries are open.

5. Always validate your transport ticket. Germany has no turnstiles on the metro, but inspectors (in plain clothes) appear frequently. A fine costs €60. Always stamp your ticket at the validator machine.

6. Bayern Ticket works after 9:00 AM on weekdays. Bayern Ticket is valid Monday–Friday after 9:00 AM (to avoid competing with commuters). Saturday and Sunday — valid from the first train of the day. If you catch a train before 9:00 AM on a weekday, you need a different ticket.

7. Pinakotheken on Sundays = €1 each. The major state museums cost €1 on Sundays — Alte Pinakothek (old European masters: Rubens, Rembrandt, Dürer), Neue Pinakothek (19th century), Pinakothek der Moderne (contemporary + design + architecture). All three on the same street — a full day of art for €3 total.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is Munich expensive?
R: Yes — Munich is one of Germany's most expensive cities and among Europe's priciest. 3-star hotel: €100–180/night, beer at Hofbräuhaus: €12–13/litre, traditional meal: €20–35. But it has dozens of free attractions (English Garden, Marienplatz, Viktualienmarkt, state museums at €1 on Sundays) and beer gardens where you can bring your own food and only pay for drinks. Realistic budget: €100–150/person/day.

Î: Is Oktoberfest worth it if you don't drink beer?
R: Surprisingly yes. Oktoberfest is more than beer — it's a folk festival with carousels, live music, authentic Bavarian food (rotisserie chicken, pork knuckle, giant pretzels), and a globally unique atmosphere. Entry to the festival grounds is free. You only pay for food and drink inside the tents. Without beer, your daily budget drops to €25–40 versus €60–100+ with drinks.

Î: How do I get to Neuschwanstein Castle from Munich?
R: Regional train (Regionalbahn) Munich–Füssen: ~2h, €21 return, or €29 with Bayern Ticket (covers up to 5 people — best value for groups). From Füssen, bus 73/78 to the castle (€4–6). Castle ticket: €21 adults — online booking mandatory months in advance in summer. Alternatively, an organised tour from Munich with transport included: €50–70.

Î: When is Oktoberfest 2026?
R: Oktoberfest 2026: September 19 – October 4, 2026. Dates vary annually — the first Saturday after September 15 is always opening day. Munich hotels during this period cost 3–5x the normal rate (€200–600/night for a 3-star). Book accommodation at least 6–12 months in advance.

Î: What is the Bayern Ticket and how do I use it?
R: Bayern Ticket is a regional train pass for Bavaria, valid for one day for 1–5 people at the same fixed price: €29/group (€26 digital). Covers all regional trains (not ICE/IC) in Bavaria Monday–Friday after 9:00 AM, all day on weekends. Perfect for Neuschwanstein (Füssen), Salzburg (Austria), or anywhere in Bavaria. One person pays €29, but 5 people also pay €29 — extremely efficient for groups.

## Things to Do in Paris 2026: Complete Guide with Prices, Insider Tips & Itineraries

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-paris
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-07-15
Actualizat: 2026-08-20
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-paris

Descriere: Complete Paris guide 2026 — Eiffel Tower, Louvre, Montmartre, Versailles, Seine cruises, food tours, secret neighbourhoods, real prices and how to experience Paris like a local.

Răspuns scurt: Paris must-dos in 2026: Eiffel Tower (€14.80-€36.70, book 60 days ahead), Louvre (€32, free first Sunday Oct-Mar), Notre-Dame (reopened 2024, free), Sacré-Cœur + Montmartre (free), Musée d'Orsay (€16, free first Sunday year-round), Sainte-Chapelle (€16-22), Versailles day trip (€21-35), and a Seine cruise at sunset (€15-20). Budget: €75-170/day. Key tip: Eiffel Tower and Louvre tickets sell out weeks ahead — advance booking is mandatory in summer. Coffee at the bar: €1.50-2. Sit-down terrace coffee: €4-6. A morning croissant: €1.20. Paris is expensive at tourist restaurants, but the free experiences (Notre-Dame, parks, Seine walks, Sacré-Cœur) are world-class.

Why Paris is still Paris

Every first-time visitor has the same worry: "Is Paris overhyped?" And every first-time visitor has the same reaction when they turn a corner and see the Eiffel Tower framed between Haussmann buildings at dusk — a reaction that has nothing to do with hype and everything to do with a city that is simply, relentlessly beautiful.

Paris earns its reputation not through any single attraction but through accumulation: the way light falls on limestone, the smell of fresh bread at 7 AM from a boulangerie where locals emerge with baguettes under their arms, the scale of the Louvre's galleries that makes you feel small, the casual perfection of a €1.20 croissant, and the Seine flowing through all of it. It's a city that rewards both meticulous planning and aimless wandering.

But Paris also punishes the unprepared. Ticket prices at major attractions have risen sharply in 2024–2026 (Louvre from €22 to €32, Sainte-Chapelle from €11 to €22), timed-entry online tickets are mandatory nearly everywhere, and the gap between an informed visitor's experience and a "wing it" visitor's experience is wider than ever.

This guide has everything: updated 2026 prices, insider tips, what's free, where to eat well without paying €30 for a mediocre croque-monsieur, and how to see Paris the way Parisians see it.

The Eiffel Tower — the hardest ticket in Europe

The Eiffel Tower isn't just Paris's symbol — it's the most difficult attraction to access in all of Europe. Seven million visitors per year trying to climb a tower that can accommodate roughly 25,000/day. The result: tickets on the official site (tour-eiffel.fr) open 60 days in advance and sell out within minutes. If you don't have a ticket, your alternative is a 2-3 hour queue for the stairs (when available) or a guided tour with priority access.

2026 official prices

Option Adult Youth (12–24) Child (4–11)
Stairs — 2nd floor €14.80 €7.40 €3.70
Elevator — 2nd floor €23.50 €11.80 €5.90
Stairs 2nd floor + elevator summit €28.00 €14.00 €7.00
Elevator — summit €36.70 €18.40 €9.20
Children under 4 Free — —

Hours: 9:00 AM – midnight (last ascent 11:00 PM for summit, 11:30 PM for 2nd floor). Operates continuously until midnight in summer.

Which option to choose

Stairs to 2nd + elevator to summit (€28) — best value. You climb 674 steps (20-30 minutes, manageable if you're moderately fit), see the iron structure up close, feel the tower sway slightly under your feet, then take the elevator to the summit. The complete experience.

Stairs to 2nd floor only (€14.80) — minimum budget, excellent experience. The view from the 2nd floor (115m) is in many ways better than from the summit (276m) — you see the city's details, not just the panorama. And Le Jules Verne restaurant (1 Michelin star) is on this floor.

Elevator direct to summit (€36.70) — most expensive, fastest, but you miss the experience of the climb. Recommended only if you have mobility issues.

Guided tours with priority access — the practical alternative

When official tickets are sold out (which is 90% of the time in summer), guided tours with priority access are the workaround: €50-70/person, includes skip-the-line, English-speaking guide, and guaranteed access. Agencies like GetYourGuide have separately allocated quotas, so they can offer tickets even when the official site shows unavailable.

Book Eiffel Tower guided tour on GetYourGuide

Best time to visit

Evening, at sunset — the city turns golden, and after dark, the tower's lights sparkle for 5 minutes every hour on the hour. The 7:00-8:00 PM summer tickets are the most coveted.

First thing in the morning (9:00 AM) — shortest queue, perfect light for photos, the tower nearly empty.

Avoid: weekends (Saturday is the busiest day of the week) and the 11:00 AM – 3:00 PM window.

The free alternative

Trocadéro (across the Seine) offers the most iconic view of the Eiffel Tower — the photo you know from every poster. Free, 24/7. Champ de Mars (the park below the tower) is perfect for a wine + cheese + baguette picnic with the tower as backdrop — one of the most romantic free experiences in the world.


The Louvre — the world's largest museum, with a strategy

380,000 objects, 35,000 on display, 72,000 sq metres of galleries, 15 km of corridors. The Louvre is not a museum you "visit" — it's a museum where you get lost, literally. Without a strategy, you leave after 4 hours exhausted, disoriented, and with the vague feeling you missed something. With a strategy, you leave after 2-3 hours with a few artistic experiences that stay with you.

2026 prices and logistics

Detail Info
Online ticket (mandatory) €32
Free Under 18, EU 18-25, first Sunday Oct-Mar
Hours Mon, Wed, Thu, Sat, Sun: 9:00-18:00
Friday 9:00-21:45 (late opening — best time )
Closed Tuesday + Jan 1, May 1, Dec 25
Last entry 30 min before closing

Important 2026 note: The price has risen from €22 to €32 (a 45% increase). Timed-entry online tickets are mandatory — you cannot show up at the ticket office without a reservation. Friday evenings (18:00-21:45) are the best time: the museum is half-empty, the artificial light is beautiful on sculptures, and there's a special energy to a nocturnal museum.

What to see in 2-3 hours (the essential route)

If time is limited, focus on three pieces that define Western art:

Mona Lisa (La Gioconda) — Denon wing, 1st floor. Yes, it's smaller than you expect (77x53 cm). Yes, it's behind bulletproof glass. Yes, there are 200 people in front of it. But it's impossible not to be struck by what a 520-year-old painting can generate in human attention. Tip: go at opening (9:00 AM) or Friday after 7:00 PM — you'll reduce the crowd by 70%.

Venus de Milo — Sully wing, ground floor. The Greek sculpture from ~100 BC that defines the classical ideal of beauty. Far less crowded than the Mona Lisa, and far more impressive at real scale than in photographs.

Winged Victory of Samothrace — top of the Daru staircase, Denon wing. A 2.75m Hellenistic sculpture that appears to be taking flight. Its placement on the monumental staircase is the finest art "display" in any museum in the world — see it from below coming up the stairs, then up close.

Bonus: Napoleon III Apartments (Richelieu wing) — extravagant imperial furnishings, almost nobody finds their way here; Apollo Gallery — the French Crown Jewels; and the Code of Hammurabi (the oldest known legal code in history, ~1750 BC).

Guided tour or self-guided?

A 2-3 hour guided tour (€40-60, GetYourGuide) includes skip-the-line, an expert guide who takes you straight to the pieces, and context the information panels don't give you. Worth it especially on a first visit — the Louvre without a guide is like a library of a million books without a catalogue.

Insider tip: The entrance through Passage Richelieu (Rue de Rivoli side) or Carrousel du Louvre (underground mall) has 3-5 minute queues. The main entrance through the pyramid has 30-60 minute queues. Everyone goes to the pyramid. Don't be everyone.


Notre-Dame — the restored cathedral (reopened December 2024)

After the devastating fire of April 2019 that destroyed the roof and flèche (central spire), Notre-Dame was restored over 5 years and solemnly reopened in December 2024. The interior is spectacular — brighter and cleaner than before the fire, with cleaned stained glass windows that let light in a way that hadn't been seen for centuries.

Entry: Free. Queues can be long — go early morning (8:00-9:00 AM) or evening.

What's new: The rebuilt flèche (faithful to the 1860 original), completely restored roof, new liturgical furniture in bronze and wood, and a redesigned visitor circuit that improves flow.

Don't miss: The rose windows — north, south, and west — are from the 13th century and survived the fire intact. They're among the oldest original stained glass windows in Europe.

Île de la Cité — the island Notre-Dame sits on is the geographic and historic centre of Paris. From Pont Saint-Louis, you can see the cathedral's side facade reflected in the Seine — one of the most beautiful perspectives in the city.


Musée d'Orsay — where Impressionism lives

If the Louvre is art history from antiquity to 1848, Orsay is the explosion from 1848 to 1914 — Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, Art Nouveau. Monet, Renoir, Degas, Van Gogh, Cézanne, Toulouse-Lautrec, Gauguin, Manet — they're all here, and the building itself (a converted 1900 railway station) is spectacular.

2026 prices

Category Price
Online ticket €16
At the door €14
Thursday evening (after 6 PM) €12 (cheapest)
Combo Orsay + Orangerie €20
Under 18 / EU 18-25 Free
First Sunday of the month Free (reservation required)

Hours: Tuesday-Sunday 9:30-18:00, Thursday until 21:45. Closed Mondays.

The secret: Thursday evening is Paris's best-kept museum secret — half-empty, €12 ticket, and the artificial light gives the Impressionist paintings a particular intensity. After 7:00 PM it's nearly empty.

Must-sees: Bal au Moulin de la Galette (Renoir) — the happiest painting in art history; Van Gogh's Self-Portrait (1889) — painted at the Saint-Rémy asylum; Monet's Water Lilies (preparatory series for Orangerie); and the station's giant glass clock through which you can see Sacré-Cœur on the Montmartre hill.


Sainte-Chapelle — the stained glass that takes your breath away

Paris's most underrated attraction. Built in 1248 by King Louis IX to house Passion relics (the Crown of Thorns, a fragment of the True Cross), Sainte-Chapelle has 1,113 stained glass panels covering 600 sq metres — the oldest and most complete medieval stained glass in the world to survive intact.

The effect: you step into a box of light. When the sun hits the glass (ideally morning or midday), the interior explodes in colour. It's one of the most intense visual experiences in Europe.

2026 prices

Individual ticket (EU/EEA citizens) €16
Combo Sainte-Chapelle + Conciergerie (non-EU) €30
Combo Sainte-Chapelle + Conciergerie (EU) €23
Under 18 / EU 18-25 Free
Included in Paris Museum Pass Yes

Hours: April-September 9:00-19:00, October-March 9:00-17:00.

Tip: Go early morning (9:00-10:00 AM) for the best light through the glass. The queue is short (15-20 min). Combine with the Conciergerie next door (the medieval prison where Marie Antoinette was held).


Montmartre and Sacré-Cœur — the artists' quarter

The hill of Montmartre is the Paris from the movies — cobblestone streets, artists painting in Place du Tertre, the white dome of Sacré-Cœur gleaming at the top, café terraces on pedestrian lanes, and a panoramic view of all of Paris from the basilica steps.

Sacré-Cœur

Entry: Free (basilica). Dome (360° panorama): ~€7.

The white travertine basilica (the stone self-cleans in rain, which is why it stays permanently white) was built between 1875 and 1914 on the highest point in Paris (130m). From the steps in front of the entrance, you can see from the Eiffel Tower to Tour Montparnasse — the best free view in the city.

What to do in Montmartre

Guided walking tour (€20-35, 2h) takes you through the streets where Picasso (at the Bateau-Lavoir), Renoir, Van Gogh, Toulouse-Lautrec, and Dalí lived. Context is everything — without a guide, you walk past the buildings that changed art history without noticing them.

Place du Tertre — the artists' square, where painters have been working on portraits and landscapes for over 100 years. Touristy? Yes. Still magical? Yes. A custom portrait costs €30-80 and is the most Parisian souvenir possible.

Moulin Rouge — cancan shows since 1889. Tickets: €90-200 (show without dinner) or €180-400 (with dinner). Book at least 2 weeks ahead.

La Maison Rose — the most photographed house in Montmartre (pink, on the corner of Rue de l'Abreuvoir). Free as a backdrop, but coffee at its terrace costs €6 and comes with the feeling of being inside an Impressionist painting.

Warning: At the base of the Sacré-Cœur steps, bracelet scammers operate — they stop you, tie a bracelet to your wrist, then demand money. Hands in pockets, firm "no thanks," keep walking. Don't stop.


Seine cruise — Paris from the water

One of the most pleasant experiences in Paris — and one of the most accessible. From the water, you see the Eiffel Tower, Notre-Dame, the Louvre, Musée d'Orsay, Conciergerie, Pont Alexandre III (Paris's most beautiful bridge), and Île de la Cité — all in one hour, relaxed, with audio commentary.

Options and prices

Option Price Duration When
Standard cruise (Bateaux Mouches / Vedettes de Paris) €15-20 1h Anytime
Sunset cruise with drink €20-35 1-1.5h Sunset (best value)
Dinner cruise €70-120 2-3h Evening
Premium dinner cruise (Bateaux Parisiens) €120-200 3h Evening, dress code

Recommendation: The 1-hour sunset cruise — costs €15-20 and delivers 80% of the experience at 15% of the dinner cruise price. Pont d'Iéna (near the Eiffel Tower) or Pont Neuf are the classic departure points.

Insider tip: Dinner cruises are romantic but the food is mediocre for the price. Better alternative: take a standard sunset cruise (€15), then have dinner at a local brasserie (€20-25 for steak-frites with a glass of wine). Better experience, half the cost.


The neighbourhoods — where the real Paris hides

Paris isn't a city of isolated attractions — it's a city of neighbourhoods (arrondissements, 1-20), each with its own distinct personality. The best experiences aren't at the big monuments, but on the streets between them.

Le Marais (3rd-4th arr.) — the best all-round quarter

Medieval streets between Bastille and Hôtel de Ville. Former aristocratic quarter (17th century), then Jewish quarter, then LGBTQ+ hub, now the most vibrant mix in Paris — galleries, vintage shops, artisan bakeries, Place des Vosges (Paris's oldest planned square, perfect for sitting on a bench), and the best falafel in Europe at L'As du Fallafel (€8, inevitable queue, worth it).

Le Marais on Sunday is when Paris comes here — boutiques are open (the exception to France's Sunday closing rule), the Rue des Rosiers market is buzzing, and the whole quarter has a relaxed energy you won't find elsewhere on a Sunday.

Saint-Germain-des-Prés (6th arr.) — the literary Left Bank

Where Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir held court at Café de Flore (still there, €6 for a coffee — you're paying for the view and the history). Where Hemingway wrote at the terraces along Boulevard Saint-Germain. Elegant, expensive, and effortlessly Parisian. The bookshops, art galleries, and pastry shops here are the finest in the city.

Shakespeare and Company (technically on the opposite bank, in the Latin Quarter, but 2 minutes away) — the most famous English-language bookshop in the world, open since 1951, with beds between the shelves where penniless writers could sleep in exchange for helping in the shop. Free entry. Don't skip the upstairs.

Latin Quarter (5th arr.) — student energy

Around the Sorbonne and the Panthéon. Crêperies on Rue Mouffetard (complete galette with ham, egg, gruyère — €8-12), Jardin du Luxembourg (Paris's most beautiful park, free, perfect for an afternoon), and the Panthéon (€11.50, crypts with Victor Hugo, Voltaire, Marie Curie, Alexandre Dumas).

Bastille / Oberkampf (11th arr.) — where locals eat

No tourists, no inflated prices. Neo-bistro restaurants with €15-18 lunch menus (3 courses), natural wine bars, and the market on Boulevard Richard-Lenoir (Thursday and Sunday mornings) — the most authentic food market in Paris.

Canal Saint-Martin (10th arr.) — young Paris

The canal with locks and iron footbridges where Amélie Poulain skipped stones. On Friday evenings, locals sit on the canal bank with wine and cheese — the most Parisian experience possible, completely free. Indie boutiques and specialty coffee shops have multiplied here.


Versailles — a day trip worth every minute

The Palace of the Sun King is 40 minutes by RER C train from central Paris. The estate is vast — the palace with the Hall of Mirrors, the geometric gardens (800 hectares), Grand Trianon, Petit Trianon, and the Hameau de la Reine (Marie Antoinette's artificial hamlet).

2026 prices

Ticket Price
Palace (interior only) €21 (€19 reduced)
Passport low season (Nov-Mar) €25 (includes everything)
Passport high season (Apr-Oct) €35 (includes everything + fountain show)
Musical Fountain Show (supplement) ~€10.50
Under 18 / EU 18-25 Free
First Sunday Nov-Mar Palace free

Closed Tuesdays. Open 9:00-17:30 (winter) / 9:00-18:30 (summer). Trianon estate opens at noon.

How to get there

Independent: RER C from Saint-Michel, Invalides, or Champ de Mars stations to Versailles-Château-Rive Gauche (€7.50 return, 40 min). Then a 10-minute walk to the palace.

Guided tour (€50-80, GetYourGuide): Includes transport, skip-the-line, guide, 4-5 hours. Recommended for first-timers — queues at Versailles rival those at the Eiffel Tower, and without a guide, the Hall of Mirrors is beautiful but you miss the history behind every detail.

Book Versailles day trip on GetYourGuide

Versailles insider tips

1. Don't go to the palace at 9:00 AM — everyone does that. Go to the gardens first (they're nearly empty in the morning) and the palace after 2:00 PM when crowds thin.

2. The Musical Fountain Show (weekends and Tuesdays, April-October) is spectacular — fountains fire to Baroque music with synchronised water effects. Worth the ~€10.50 supplement.

3. The Hameau de la Reine (Marie Antoinette's hamlet) is a 20-minute walk from the palace and almost nobody makes it there — an artificial village with mills, a farm, and thatched-roof cottages where the queen "played peasant." Included in the Passport ticket.

4. Bring your own food — restaurants inside Versailles grounds are expensive and mediocre. A jambon-beurre baguette from a Paris boulangerie (€4-5) is three times better at a quarter of the price.


Food tours — how to eat like a Parisian, not a tourist

Paris is the gastronomic capital of the world — and a food tour is the investment that transforms your entire culinary experience for the rest of the trip. It teaches you where locals eat, the difference between a good boulangerie and a bad one, and why a €1.20 croissant from a corner shop can be better than a €4 one in a tourist zone.

Popular food tour areas

Le Marais — the most popular zone, includes artisan cheeses, charcuterie, éclairs, Belgian chocolate, French wine, and the best falafel in Paris. Tours of 3-4h, €50-80/person, 5-8 stops.

Montmartre — more authentic, local boulangeries with award-winning baguettes, fromageries with 200+ cheeses, neighbourhood patisseries, wine by the glass. Tours of 2-3h, €45-65.

Saint-Germain — the refined zone. Famous patisseries (Pierre Hermé, macarons at €2.50/piece), artisan chocolatiers, and pastries that are works of art. Tours of 2-3h, €55-80.

What you must eat in Paris

Croissant — from any boulangerie artisanale (look for the "Artisan Boulanger" sign): €1.20-1.80. The quality floor in Paris is higher than the ceiling in most cities. Signs of a good croissant: exterior that shatters at a touch, airy interior with visible "fibres," buttery flavour (not margarine), and a fragrance that stops you in your tracks.

Baguette tradition — the artisan baguette with cracked crust, elastic crumb, and nutty flavour. €1.30-1.50. The French buy baguettes twice a day (morning and evening) because "yesterday's bread is already old." The annual "Meilleure Baguette de Paris" competition crowns the best baguette — the winner supplies the Élysée Palace for a year.

Jambon-beurre — the world's most underrated sandwich: half a baguette with (quality) butter and Parisian ham. €4-5. The French eat 1.2 billion per year. Perfect for a bench lunch in the Tuileries or Jardin du Luxembourg.

Fromage — France produces over 400 types of cheese. At a fromagerie, ask for a tasting platter: Comté (18 months, the most popular), Roquefort (sheep, blue mould), Brie de Meaux (cow, creamy), Chèvre (goat, enormous variety). A cheese platter + baguette + a glass of red wine = €10-12, on a bench on the Seine bank = the most Parisian dinner possible.

Macarons — almonds, sugar, filling. Ladurée (since 1862, on the Champs-Élysées) and Pierre Hermé (the inventor of modern flavours) are the two big names. €2-3/piece, gift box €15-30. The Ispahan flavour (rose, raspberry, lychee) by Pierre Hermé is considered the finest macaron in the world.

Crêpe — Nutella + banana: €4-6 from a street stand. Savoury galette (buckwheat crêpe with ham, cheese, egg): €8-12 at a sit-down crêperie. The best crêperies are in Montparnasse (Rue du Montparnasse), not the tourist zone.

Escargots — snails in garlic-herb butter. €10-15 for 6 at a brasserie. The taste is 90% garlicky butter (delicious) and 10% chewy texture. Worth trying once.

Steak-frites — steak (usually onglet or entrecôte) with French fries. €14-20 at a brasserie. Order "à point" (medium) — the French cook steak rarer than most visitors expect.

Where NOT to eat

Any restaurant on Rue de Rivoli with a menu in 8 languages, photos of the food, and a waiter trying to pull you inside. Any restaurant within 100m of Notre-Dame, the Eiffel Tower, or Sacré-Cœur with a tourist menu at €18-25. General rule: if the menu has photos of food taped to the window, run.

Where to eat well and cheaply

Le Bouillon Chartier (9th arr.) — brasserie since 1896, stunning Belle Époque interior (chandeliers, mirrors, stucco), classic menu at incredibly low prices: French onion soup €3, steak-frites €11, crème brûlée €3. Three courses for €15-20. Queue guaranteed — go at 6:30 PM, not 8:00 PM.

Bouillon Julien (10th arr.) — similar to Chartier, protected Art Nouveau interior, same low prices.

Bouillon Pigalle (18th arr.) — the modern version, near Moulin Rouge, identical prices.

Any bar à vin in the 11th arr. — natural wine by the glass €5-7, charcuterie + cheese board €12-15.

Richard-Lenoir market (Thursday and Sunday) — rotisserie chicken (€8-10, huge portion), cheeses from producers, fruit, bread, and wine — complete picnic for €10-12/person.

Paris is expensive at ticketed attractions, but the free experiences are world-class — and there are enough of them to fill an entire holiday.

Paris Museum Pass — is it worth it?

The Paris Museum Pass 2026 provides access to 50+ museums and monuments without ticket queues (though sometimes with security queues):

2 days €85
4 days €105
6 days €125

What's included (most important)

Louvre (€32), Musée d'Orsay (€16), Versailles (€21), Sainte-Chapelle (€22), Arc de Triomphe (€16), Centre Pompidou (€15), Musée de l'Orangerie (€12.50), Panthéon (€11.50), Conciergerie (€11.50), Musée Rodin (€14), Musée Picasso (€14), and 40+ more.

What's NOT included

Eiffel Tower, Disneyland Paris, Catacombs, Seine cruises, Moulin Rouge, Fondation Louis Vuitton.

Quick calculation

Visit Louvre (€32) + Orsay (€16) + Versailles (€21) + Sainte-Chapelle (€22) = €91 . A 2-day pass costs €85 = saving of €6 plus skip-the-line . Add Arc de Triomphe + Orangerie = €119.50 vs. €85 = saving of €34.50 .

Bottom line: Worth it from 3-4 museums visited in 2 days. If you're only visiting the Louvre plus one small museum, not worth it.

2026 important note: The Louvre requires a separate timed-entry slot even with the Museum Pass — book it on the Louvre's website in advance. The pass eliminates the ticket queue, not the security queue.

Getting around Paris — metro, RER, and walking

Metro

16 lines, covers all of inner Paris. Frequency: every 2-5 minutes at peak, 5-10 minutes in the evening.

Ticket type 2026 price
Single ticket (t+) — metro/RER zone 1 €2.55
Bus/tram ticket €2.05
Navigo Day (full day) €12.30
Navigo Weekly (Monday-Sunday) €32.40
Paris Visite 1 day (zones 1-5, includes airport) €30.60
Paris Visite 5 days (zones 1-5) €78

Tip: For a 3-4 day city break, Navigo Day at €12.30/day or individual tickets are more efficient than Paris Visite. Paris Visite only pays off if you're making daily trips to Versailles, Disneyland, or the airport. Navigo Weekly (€32.40, runs Monday-Sunday) is the best deal if you arrive on a Monday.

Walking

Central Paris is surprisingly small on foot. Notre-Dame → Louvre: 15 minutes. Louvre → Eiffel Tower: 30 minutes. Eiffel Tower → Arc de Triomphe: 20 minutes. Bastille → Le Marais: 10 minutes.

A typical sightseeing day involves 15,000-20,000 steps. Comfortable shoes are more important than any metro ticket.

Orly: RER B + Orlyval (€14.10, 40 min) or Tram T7 + Metro (€2.55, but 60+ min).

Beauvais (budget airlines): Shuttle bus (€17, 75 min). Plan 3 hours of buffer for check-in — Beauvais is far and the shuttle isn't frequent.

CDG tip: RER B is clearly the most efficient — fast, frequent, and cheaper than any alternative. But if you have bulky luggage, Roissybus is more comfortable (dedicated luggage space, no stairs/escalators). Never take a taxi from the people who approach you in the terminal — they're unlicensed and charge double.

Day trips from Paris

Versailles (detailed above)

RER C, 40 min, palace + gardens. Ideal Day 4.

Giverny — Monet's garden

April-October only. Train from Paris Saint-Lazare to Vernon (45 min, €15 return) + shuttle bus. The water lily garden in real life — the one that inspired the most famous paintings in art history. Entry: €11. Organised tours from Paris: €60-90 (includes transport + guide). Some tours combine Giverny + Versailles in one day.

Château de Fontainebleau

Royal residence older than Versailles (12th century), less known, less crowded, equally impressive. Train from Gare de Lyon (40 min, €10 return). Entry: €14. Included in Paris Museum Pass.

Disneyland Paris

RER A, 45 min. Ticket: €60-110 (varies by day and season). Go Tuesday-Thursday — weekends are extremely crowded. Organised tours with central Paris transfers are pricier (€80-130) but more convenient.

Champagne (Reims / Épernay)

TGV from Gare de l'Est to Reims (45 min, €30-50) or train to Épernay. Visit Champagne houses: Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, Taittinger. Tasting + tour: €25-50. Organised tours from Paris: €100-150 (includes transport + 2-3 houses).

Insider tips — what Parisians know

1. Coffee at the bar vs. terrace coffee = double the price. An espresso at the bar (comptoir) costs €1.50-2. The same coffee at the terrace: €4-6. The French drink their first coffee standing at the bar, in 2 minutes. The terrace is for long conversations, not caffeine.

2. Boulangerie vs. pâtisserie — the difference matters. Boulangerie makes bread (baguette, croissant, pain au chocolat). Pâtisserie makes pastries (éclair, tarte, millefeuille). The best croissants come from small artisan boulangeries, not famous pâtisseries. Look for the "Artisan Boulanger" sign — it's legally protected.

3. "L'addition, s'il vous plaît" — in France, the waiter will never bring the bill unprompted. If you sit at your table without asking for the bill, you can sit there all evening without being bothered. The French consider bringing the bill unprompted rude (a suggestion that you should leave). When you're ready, you ask. "L'addition, s'il vous plaît" (the bill, please).

4. Don't tip. Service is included in the price (service compris) by law in France. The French leave at most €1-2 for an exceptional meal, never 15-20% as in the US. This is the most important financial tip in Paris.

5. Monday is the day many museums and restaurants close. The Louvre is open Monday (but closed Tuesday). Orsay is closed Monday. Many local restaurants (bistros, neo-brasseries) are closed Monday. Check beforehand.

6. Sunday is market day. The markets at Bastille, Aligre, and Richard-Lenoir are at their liveliest on Sunday morning — vegetables, fruit, cheeses, flowers, rotisserie chicken. It's the most Parisian experience possible.

7. Transport strikes are normal. Paris has transport strikes periodically (especially RATP/SNCF). Check ratp.fr in the morning — if the metro is disrupted, Uber/taxi or walking are the alternatives. It's not a disaster — it's France.

8. Tap water is free in any restaurant. Ask for "une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît" and you'll get free water. Bottled water (€3-6) is optional, not mandatory. Many tourists don't know this and pay €5 for a bottle of Evian that's no better than Paris's tap water (which is excellent).

9. "Bonjour" is mandatory. Entering a shop? "Bonjour." Addressing someone on the street? "Bonjour." Ordering at a restaurant? "Bonjour." Without "bonjour," Parisians turn cold — not out of malice, but from a deep conviction that it's rude. With "bonjour," they become surprisingly warm and helpful. It's the only French word that truly matters.

10. The best views in Paris are free. Trocadéro for the Eiffel Tower. Sacré-Cœur steps for all of Paris. Galeries Lafayette rooftop for the Opera Quarter. Pont Alexandre III at sunset. The top floor of Centre Pompidou (ticket required, but included in Museum Pass). The paid observation decks (Tour Montparnasse, Arc de Triomphe) are good but not necessary.


Travel insurance for France

France is in the EU and Schengen. The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) works but only covers medical emergencies — it doesn't cover repatriation, dental, flight cancellations, lost luggage, or theft (which is a real issue in Paris, especially on the metro and in tourist areas). A comprehensive policy for one week costs €12-20/person.

Common scams in Paris — how to avoid them

Paris has its specific scams, especially in tourist areas:

Bracelets at Sacré-Cœur: People who "offer" free friendship bracelets. They tie one to your wrist, then demand €10-20. Solution: hands in pockets, firm "no thanks," don't stop.

The fake petition: Young people with clipboards asking you to sign a petition (usually "for the deaf and mute"). While you're signing, someone else checks your pockets. Solution: "Non, merci" without stopping.

The "gold ring": Someone "finds" a gold ring on the ground near you and offers it, then asks for a reward. The ring is brass. Solution: ignore completely.

Fake metro tickets: People at metro entrances selling "tickets" at half price. They're expired or invalid. Solution: buy only from RATP machines or counters.

Unlicensed taxi at CDG: "Taxi drivers" who approach you in the terminal offering rides. They charge double or triple the official rate. Solution: go to the official taxi rank (follow the "Taxi" signs) or order an Uber.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How many days do you need in Paris?
R: 3-4 days for the highlights, 5 days for a complete experience. Day 1: Eiffel Tower + Seine cruise + Trocadéro. Day 2: Louvre (3-4h) + Tuileries + Champs-Élysées. Day 3: Montmartre + Sacré-Cœur + Notre-Dame + Sainte-Chapelle. Day 4: Versailles day trip. Day 5: Le Marais + Musée d'Orsay + food tour. A week is ideal for deeper exploration.

Î: Is Paris really that expensive?
R: The sit-down terrace coffee that costs €5 makes headlines, but the same espresso at the bar counter is €1.50-2. A croissant from any boulangerie: €1.20. A crêpe from a street stand: €4-6. A full brasserie meal (steak-frites + wine): €15-20. Le Bouillon Chartier serves 3-course meals for €15-18 in a stunning Belle Époque dining room since 1896. Paris is expensive at tourist spots and surprisingly affordable everywhere else. The key: eat and drink where Parisians do.

Î: Is the Paris Museum Pass worth it in 2026?
R: Yes, if you visit 3+ museums. Paris Museum Pass 2026: 2-day €85, 4-day €105, 6-day €125. Includes Louvre (€32), Orsay (€16), Versailles (€21), Sainte-Chapelle (€22), Arc de Triomphe (€16), Orangerie (€12.50), Panthéon + 50 more. Does NOT include Eiffel Tower, Disneyland, Catacombs, or Seine cruises. Louvre + Orsay + Versailles + Sainte-Chapelle = €91 without pass — so from 3-4 museums in 2 days, the pass saves money plus skip-the-line.

Î: How do I get from CDG airport to central Paris?
R: RER B train is the best option: €11.45, 35 minutes, runs every 10-15 minutes. Roissybus: €16.60, 60-75 minutes to Opéra (better with bulky luggage). Taxi: fixed fare €55 (right bank) or €62 (left bank). Uber: €45-70 depending on demand. Never accept transport from people who approach you in the terminal — they're unlicensed and charge double.

Î: What's the best neighbourhood for a hotel in Paris?
R: Le Marais (3rd-4th arr.) — central, vibrant, close to Louvre and Notre-Dame. Saint-Germain (6th arr.) — elegant, literary, pricier. Montmartre (18th arr.) — atmospheric, cheaper, hilly. Bastille/Oberkampf (11th arr.) — local vibe, great restaurants, better prices. Avoid: Gare du Nord area at night, and the 1st arrondissement (ultra-touristy, double prices).

Î: How far ahead should I book Eiffel Tower tickets?
R: 60 days ahead minimum in summer for official tickets (they sell out within minutes of release). Guided tours with priority access via GetYourGuide are the practical alternative — tour operators have allocated quotas and can offer tickets even when the official site shows sold out. They cost more (€50-70) but include skip-the-line and a guide. Official 2026 prices: stairs to 2nd floor €14.80, elevator to summit €36.70.

## Things to Do in Porto: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Port Wine, Douro Valley & Tips

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-porto
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-08-05
Actualizat: 2026-08-05
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-porto

Descriere: Complete Porto 2026 guide — Ribeira UNESCO, Livraria Lello, Dom Luís Bridge, Port wine cellars in Gaia, francesinha, Douro Valley day trip. Porto is better than Lisbon and 30% cheaper.

Răspuns scurt: Porto deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Ribeira and Dom Luís I Bridge (free), Livraria Lello (€8, redeemable against a book), Port wine cellars in Vila Nova de Gaia (€15–25 with tasting), Clérigos Tower (€8), and the Douro Valley day trip (€50–80 guided). Francesinha is the mandatory meal. Porto is 30% cheaper than Lisbon and far more authentic — locals haven't left yet.

There is a historical injustice in Portuguese tourism: everyone goes to Lisbon and few reach Porto. And precisely this injustice makes Porto perfect — a city not distorted by excess attention, where locals haven't yet fled the center, where a pastel de nata with espresso costs €2.50, and where Port wine — the product that put Portugal on the world map — is drunk at source, in the lodges on the Gaia hillside, with views across to the city.

Porto doesn't try to impress. It is a working city with a trading and maritime past, houses covered with azulejos (blue ceramic tiles) peeling at varying degrees of picturesque decay, an architecture that alternates Baroque and Brutalism, and a medieval Ribeira UNESCO waterfront that ends directly at the Douro. It is the only major European city where you can drink a glass of tawny at a wine lodge and watch the rooftops of the city across the river.

And it is 30% cheaper than Lisbon.

Ribeira and Dom Luís I Bridge — Porto's River Heart

Ribeira is the medieval riverside district, UNESCO since 1996 — narrow 4–5 storey houses, facades covered in azulejos or painted in colors washing slowly away in Atlantic rain, restaurants with waterside terraces, and rabelo boats (the traditional vessels that once hauled Port wine barrels from the Douro to the Gaia lodges) now moored decoratively along the bank.

Dom Luís I Bridge — built in 1886, designed by a collaborator of Gustave Eiffel, with two levels: the lower for pedestrians and tram, the upper (62 meters above the water) exclusively pedestrian, with the complete panorama of Ribeira, Gaia, and the river. Completely free. At sunset, the light on the azulejo facades is Porto's signature photograph — arrive 30 minutes before sunset for a good position.

Insider tip: Dom Luís I Bridge early morning (7:00–8:30 AM) is nearly empty. The same view, no crowds, with morning mist on the river. This is the moment for the real photograph.


Livraria Lello — One of the World's Most Beautiful Bookshops

Open since 1906, Livraria Lello is consistently ranked among the world's top 3 bookshops — the polychrome carved wooden spiral staircase, stained glass, ornate ceiling, and Victorian library atmosphere have created a legend that now brings 4,000 visitors a day.

The Harry Potter legend — that J.K. Rowling, who lived in Porto in 1991–1993 as an English teacher, was inspired by Livraria Lello for Hogwarts library — is not officially confirmed, but neither denied. Regardless of truth, the staircase is real and it is impressive.

2026 Prices and logistics:

Detail Info
Entry ticket (voucher) €8
Redeemable against purchase Yes — buy a book of €8+, entry is effectively free
Online booking Mandatory in peak season (time slot) — livrarialello.pt
Queue without booking 45+ minutes (11:00–15:00)
Opening hours 9:30–19:00
Best time to visit 9:30 AM at opening or after 17:00

Tip: Buy a book — even a small one at €8–10. You pay for entry and leave with something authentic from Porto. The best souvenir in the city.


Clérigos Tower — the City Panorama

The 1763 Baroque tower, 76 meters tall, is Portugal's tallest tower and the symbol of Porto's skyline. 240 spiral steps, complete panorama of the city, the Douro, and on clear days — the Atlantic Ocean.

Prices:

Category Price
Adult (tower + church) ~€8
Reduced (students, seniors) ~€4
Children under 10 Free

Hours: daily 9:00–19:00 (summer until 20:00).

Tip: Clérigos Tower in the evening, with sunset light, is more beautiful than midday — and less crowded.


São Bento Station — the World's Most Beautiful Station Hall

Opened in 1916, São Bento Station is no longer a main railway terminal (it now serves suburban trains), but the entrance hall is one of the most spectacular public spaces in Europe: 20,000 blue azulejo panels illustrating scenes from Portuguese history and rural life, painted by Jorge Colaço between 1905–1916.

Entry: Free. It's a station, not a museum — walk in, look around, walk out. 15–30 minutes are enough, but many people stay longer.

Tip: Visit early morning (8:00–9:30 AM) or late afternoon (17:00+). At midday it is overcrowded with organised tour groups blocking the view.


Port Wine Cellars in Vila Nova de Gaia — Port Wine at Source

Cross Dom Luís I Bridge (lower level) and you're in Vila Nova de Gaia — the city on the south bank of the Douro where all the major Port wine houses have their lodges. Taylor's, Sandeman, Graham's, Calem, Ferreira, Ramos Pinto — names that have existed for 200–300 years, each with its own story and a wine selection unrivalled in the world.

What Port wine is: A red (or white, or rosé) wine made from native Douro Valley grape varieties, whose fermentation is stopped halfway by adding aguardente (wine brandy) — leaving natural residual sugar and raising alcohol to 19–22%. The result: a complex, dense wine with dried fruit, chocolate, and nut notes, capable of ageing in cask for decades.

Types of Port you'll drink:

Type Character Glass price at lodge
Ruby (young, red) Red fruits, fresh €3–5
Tawny (barrel-aged) Nuts, caramel, dried fruit €5–8
Tawny 10/20/30 year More complex as aged €8–15
LBV (Late Bottled Vintage) Structured, concentrated €7–12
Vintage (declared year) Rarest and most valuable €20–50+
White Port Dry or sweet, served with tonic as aperitif €4–7

Recommended cellar tours:

Taylor's €15–25 Exceptional views, premium tour
Calem €15–20 Includes fado show inside the cellar
Graham's €15–22 One of the oldest houses, historic collection

Book a Port wine cellar tour on GetYourGuide

Gaia Cable Car (Teleférico de Gaia): The gondola descending from the lodge hillside to the riverbank — €5–7 return , 5 minutes, with complete views of Porto and Ribeira. Optional but photogenic.


Palácio da Bolsa — the Arab Room in Porto's Heart

The former Stock Exchange Palace, built between 1842–1910 by Porto's Chamber of Commerce, is Portugal's most impressive Neoclassical interior — with one notable exception: the Arab Room, a Moorish Arab replica with gilded stucco and silver panels that has nothing Neoclassical about it and is completely unexpected given the building's sober exterior.

Prices: ~€10 adults, includes mandatory guided tour (30–45 min, in English or Portuguese). You cannot enter without a guide.

Hours: 9:30–18:30 (Oct–Mar: 9:30–13:00 + 14:00–17:30).

Tip about azulejos: Porto is the world's best open-air azulejo museum. Blue ceramic tile facades — some worth millions of euros, others peeling off abandoned buildings — are distributed randomly across the city. Igreja do Carmo and Igreja das Almas (near Clérigos) have the most spectacular exterior facades, free to view.


Food in Porto — Cheaper and Better Than Lisbon

Porto's cuisine is port city cooking: filling, quality simple ingredients, and one iconic sandwich that exists nowhere else. Locals eat large at lunch (prato do dia) and light in the evening — follow the same rhythm.

The Essential Dishes

Francesinha — Porto's iconic sandwich, incomparable and unrepeatable anywhere else. Layers of cured ham, linguiça sausage, and steak between slices of toast bread, covered with melted cheese and a fried egg on top, flooded with a spicy beer, tomato, and secret spice sauce. With chips, it is a complete meal. €8–12 at any Porto restaurant. Café Santiago (Rua Passos Manuel) is the benchmark — open since 1959.

Pastel de nata — the Portuguese egg custard tart, warm, with cinnamon sprinkled on top. €1.20–1.50 at any pastelaria. With an espresso (€0.80–1), a complete breakfast costs under €3. There is no better version than one still warm, freshly pulled from the oven.

Bacalhau (salt cod) — Portugal's national ingredient, with 365 official recipes (one for each day of the year, according to culinary legend). Bacalhau à Brás (with eggs and matchstick potatoes), bacalhau à Gomes de Sá (with boiled eggs and potatoes), or bacalhau com natas (with cream). €12–18 at a traditional restaurant.

Bifana — pork sandwich marinated in garlic and spices, simple and perfect. €3–4. Conga (Rua do Bonjardim) has been serving Porto's best bifana since 1964.

Tripas à moda do Porto — tripe stew with white beans, sausage, and vegetables. Porto's historical dish — Portuguese from the rest of the country call Porto people "tripeiros" (tripe-eaters) from a 1415 episode when the city gave all its meat for Henry the Navigator's expedition to Ceuta. €12–15.

Vinho verde — the light, low-alcohol (9–11%), slightly sparkling wine produced in northern Portugal. White, red, or rosé. Perfect in summer, incredibly accessible. €2–4 a glass , €5–10 a bottle at restaurants.

Where to Eat Locally

Tascas (traditional taverns) in Cedofeita or Miragaia — 10 minutes from Ribeira, prices 30–50% lower, identical or better food.

Mercado do Bolhão (renovated 2022) — market with vegetables, fish, cheeses, and prepared food stalls. Complete lunch: €8–10.

Matosinhos (20 min by metro) — the fishing neighbourhood with Porto's best fish and seafood restaurants. Rua Heróis de França: whole grilled fish sold by weight, €15–25/person with wine. Locals eat fish at Matosinhos, not at Ribeira.

Prato do dia (daily lunch menu, Mon–Fri, lunchtime): soup + main + drink + sometimes dessert. €7–10. The best value in Porto.

Approximate food budget

Complete francesinha with chips €8–12

Douro Valley Day Trip — UNESCO 2 Hours Away

The Douro Valley is one of the world's most beautiful wine regions — terraces of vines carved into granite on the steep hillsides along the Douro river, UNESCO since 2001. It is where Port wine has come from for 2,000 years.

How to get there:


Scenic train São Bento–Pinhão: €12–15 return , 2h30 — one of Europe's most beautiful railway routes

Organised tour from Porto (with transport, winery, lunch): €50–80/person

Rental car (flexible, EN-322): ~2h


What you do there: Visit one or two wineries, drink wines from local production, eat in a village, and look at a landscape that took 2,000 years of human labour to create.

Book a Douro Valley day trip on GetYourGuide

Tip: If you go by train and like independent adventures, get off at Pinhão (a 700-inhabitant village in the heart of the vineyards, with a station covered in azulejos) and book a local winery tour from there. This is the authentic experience, without coaches.

São João Festival (June 23–24) — Porto's biggest celebration. People hit each other on the head with plastic hammers (a tradition), launch paper balloons, and dance all night in the street. It is organised chaos and absolutely fascinating.

Conclusion: Porto is Southwest Europe's revelation. If you've already been to Lisbon, Porto is the logical next step — smaller, more authentic, cheaper, with Port wine at source and a dish (francesinha) that exists nowhere else on Earth.


Insider Tips — What Locals Know

1. The couvert is NOT free. When you sit down in a Portuguese restaurant, the waiter automatically brings bread, oil, butter, olives, sometimes cheese. They are NOT a gift — they appear on the bill. If you don't want to pay €2–4 extra, politely decline: "Não, obrigado."

2. Francesinha varies enormously between restaurants. There is no standardised recipe — each restaurant has its own secret sauce. Café Santiago is the reference, but Francisco (Rua do Bonjardim) and Zenite have excellent versions. Avoid tourist restaurants with photo menus.

3. Tawny 10 Year is the best value Port. 10-year-aged Tawny has the complexity of a serious dessert wine without the enormous price of vintage. A glass at the lodge: €8–10. At home, a bottle of Taylor's Tawny 10: €15–20.

4. The metro from the airport costs €2.50 with the Andante card. The card itself costs €0.60 at airport machines. The cheapest airport-to-center transfer of any Western European capital — cheaper even than Lisbon.

5. Prato do dia Monday–Friday is Porto's best deal. €7–10 for soup + main + drink at any serious tasca. The best tascas have no English menus — a good sign.

6. Fado in Porto is different from Lisbon. Porto fado (fado portuense) is rawer, more masculine, more melancholic — sung with Portuguese guitar and viola baixo, without Lisbon's lyricism. The best is heard informally in Ribeira or at the Museu do Fado do Porto — not at tourist shows with included dinner.

7. The best sunset is from Dom Luís I Bridge upper level. Not from a hotel rooftop, not from a tower. Stand on the upper bridge railing, look toward Gaia and the Douro catching the orange light — with all of Ribeira below you.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Porto or Lisbon — which is better?
R: It depends what you're looking for. Lisbon is larger, more cosmopolitan, easier to reach. Porto is more authentic, more compact, with a stronger identity, Port wine at the source, and prices 20–30% lower for accommodation and food. Francesinha doesn't exist in Lisbon. If it's your first time in Portugal, Lisbon comes first. If you've already been — Porto is the revelation.

Î: Is Livraria Lello worth it and how do I avoid the queue?
R: Yes, it's worth it — it's one of the most beautiful bookshops in the world, with a polychrome carved wooden spiral staircase that inspired the (unconfirmed) rumor that J.K. Rowling, who lived in Porto in 1991–1993 as an English teacher, drew on it for Hogwarts. Entry costs €8, redeemable against any purchase. The queue is long 11:00–15:00. Arrive at opening (9:30 AM) or book online with a timed entry slot — you avoid 45+ minutes of waiting.

Î: What is a francesinha and why is it mandatory?
R: Francesinha is Porto's iconic sandwich — layers of cured ham, linguiça sausage, and steak between slices of bread, covered with melted cheese and a fried egg, flooded with a spicy beer-and-tomato sauce. It's a complete meal (€8–12), served with chips. It doesn't exist in Lisbon or anywhere else in Portugal — it's specific to Porto. Café Santiago is considered the benchmark.

Î: What is Vila Nova de Gaia and why should I go?
R: Vila Nova de Gaia is the city on the south bank of the Douro, directly across from Porto. All the major Port wine houses (Taylor's, Sandeman, Graham's, Calem) have their lodges there — on the hillside above the riverbank, with views across to Porto and the Ribeira. A tour with tasting costs €15–25. Cable car to the riverside: €5–7. It's the 2–3 hour excursion that justifies a flight to Porto on its own.

Î: What is the couvert in Portuguese restaurants?
R: When you sit down in a Portuguese restaurant, the waiter automatically brings bread, olive oil, butter, olives, sometimes cheese. They are NOT free — they appear on the bill. If you don't want to pay €2–4 extra, politely decline: 'Não, obrigado.' This is standard practice across Portugal, not a scam.

## Things to Do in Prague 2026: Castle, Beer Culture, Hidden Gems & Real Prices

URL: https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-prague
Limbă: English
Verticală: experiente
Publicat: 2026-07-15
Actualizat: 2026-08-23
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-praga

Descriere: Complete Prague guide for 2026 with real prices in CZK and EUR, day-by-day itineraries, best beer halls, authentic Czech food, local neighbourhoods, day trips, and tested practical tips.

Răspuns scurt: Prague essentials 2026: Prague Castle — world's largest castle complex (Main Circuit ~450 CZK/~€18), Charles Bridge at dawn (free, go at 6 AM), Old Town Square + Astronomical Clock (free, hourly show), Czech beer at a local hospoda (55-80 CZK/€2-3 for the best lager on Earth), Vltava cruise (from 350 CZK), Jewish Quarter Josefov (~600 CZK full ticket), and day trip to Český Krumlov (UNESCO). Budget: €50-70/day (budget) or €100-150 (mid-range). 1 EUR ≈ 24.2 CZK (2026).

Prague is the city that makes you believe in fairy tales — except the beer costs €2 and the food is hearty enough to skip the gym. The old town survived World War II virtually untouched (one of the few European capitals not bombed), and the result is an extraordinary concentration of Gothic, Baroque, Art Nouveau, and Cubist architecture, all within a walkable area you can cross in 30 minutes.

Czechs drink more beer per capita than anyone else on Earth (140 litres per year), and that's not just a statistic — it's an entire culture you feel in every pub in the city. Add prices 30-40% lower than Western European capitals, and you have a city that's remarkably hard to leave.

This guide has all prices updated for 2026 (in CZK and EUR at the rate of 1 EUR ≈ 24.2 CZK), concrete itineraries, tested beer halls, and the tips you'd only learn from living there.

Prague Castle — the world's largest castle complex

Prague Castle (Pražský hrad) is Guinness-recognized as the world's largest castle complex: 70,000 m² of palaces, churches, gardens, and towers on a hill above the Vltava river. It has been the seat of Czech rulers for 1,100 years and remains the official residence of the president.

What's inside the Castle

St. Vitus Cathedral (Katedrála sv. Víta) — the Gothic masterpiece that took 600 years to build (1344-1929). Alfons Mucha's Art Nouveau stained glass window (in the third chapel on the left) is worth the visit alone. Climb the south tower (287 steps) for the best panoramic view of Prague — 150 CZK (~€6) separately.

Old Royal Palace (Starý královský palác) — the Vladislav Hall (1502) is so large that jousting tournaments were held inside — the horses climbed a special staircase that still exists.

St. George's Basilica (Bazilika sv. Jiří) — the oldest church in the Castle (920 AD), with a surprisingly vivid red Romanesque façade.

Golden Lane (Zlatá ulička) — tiny colourful houses built into the castle wall, once home to archers and later goldsmiths. Franz Kafka lived at No. 22 (now a bookshop). The houses are furnished as they were — armour displays, alchemists' workshops, artisan studios.

Royal Garden (Královská zahrada) — the gardens on the north side are free and stunning in spring when the tulips bloom. Includes the Queen Anne's Summer Palace, the purest Renaissance structure north of the Alps.

Tickets and prices 2026

Option What's included Adult price Reduced (6-16)
Main Circuit (former B) St. Vitus Cathedral + Old Palace + Basilica + Golden Lane 450 CZK ( €18) 225 CZK ( €9)
Extended Circuit (former A) Everything in Main + Castle Gallery + Daliborka Tower + permanent exhibition 600 CZK ( €24) 300 CZK ( €12)
Cathedral Tower (separate) 287 steps, panoramic view 150 CZK (~€6) 80 CZK (~€3)
GYG guided tour Skip-the-line + guide 2.5-3.5h 500-1,450 CZK (€20-60) Varies
Castle grounds + gardens Walking without interiors Free Free

Book a skip-the-line guided tour on GetYourGuide — includes a guide who brings the history alive (without context, the castle feels like a lot of rooms), skip-the-line access, and usually includes the walk down through Malá Strana.

Practical tips for Prague Castle

When to go: enter at 9:00 AM when interiors open — by 10:30 the tour buses arrive and queues triple. The courtyard and gardens open at 6:00 AM and are magical in the early hours, virtually empty.

Changing of the Guard: every hour, but the most elaborate is at noon (with a brass band). Photogenic but extremely crowded — if you don't insist, the 11:00 AM ceremony is nearly identical but with far fewer people.

Entrances: there are two — the First Courtyard (from Hradčanské náměstí, the main entrance with security check) and the east gate (from Golden Lane side, much less crowded). Pro tip: enter from the east and visit in reverse order.

Duration: 2-3 hours self-guided, 3-4 hours with a guided tour. Add gardens + lunch at a terrace with a view and it's a half-day.

The descent: don't take the metro back — walk down through Malá Strana (15-20 min) via Nerudova street or through Seminářská park (lesser-known route, fewer tourists, spectacular views). You arrive directly at Charles Bridge.

Old Town (Staré Město) — Prague's medieval heart

Old Town Square (Staroměstské náměstí)

Prague's centre for 1,000 years. The square is surrounded by Gothic, Baroque, and Renaissance architecture, dominated by the Church of Our Lady before Týn (the two Gothic spires that define Prague's skyline) and St. Nicholas Church (Czech Baroque at its most exuberant).

Astronomical Clock (Orloj) — the world's oldest functioning astronomical clock (1410). Every hour (9:00 AM-11:00 PM), the apostles appear in small windows above the dial. The show lasts 45 seconds — everyone watches, then disperses. The dial simultaneously shows three things: time, the position of the sun and moon, and the calendar. Legend: master clockmaker Hanuš was blinded by the city council to prevent him from reproducing the clock elsewhere.

Old Town Hall Tower — the best viewpoint in the Old Town. Lift + stairs, 250 CZK (~€10). The 360° view from 65m covers the entire square, the Týn towers, the Castle on its hill, and red rooftops as far as the eye can see.

Clementinum — the library the internet envies

The second-largest architectural complex in Prague (after the Castle), a former Jesuit college turned National Library. The Baroque Library Hall (1722) is one of the most beautiful rooms in the world — painted ceiling, historical terrestrial globes, leather-bound books on walnut shelves.

Mandatory guided tour (45 min): 300 CZK ( €12). Includes the Library Hall, the Mirror Chapel (classical music concerts in the evening — 500-800 CZK), and the Astronomical Tower with views.

Insider: the classical music concerts in the Mirror Chapel (evening, 8:00 PM) are an extraordinary experience — perfect acoustics, Baroque setting, 45-60 minutes. Tickets 500-800 CZK (€20-33) on GetYourGuide or at the door.

Charles Bridge (Karlův most) — 600 years of history on 621 metres

30 Baroque statues lining a 621-metre stone bridge across the Vltava. It's Prague's signature image — and its most crowded spot. In summer, 30,000 people cross daily.

When to cross: at 6:00 AM . The bridge is empty, morning mist rises from the river, the light on the Old Town towers is golden, and you'll take photos that look like they belong in another century. By 8:00 AM, street artists and the first tourists arrive. By 10:00 AM, it's shoulder-to-shoulder.

Alternative: see the bridge FROM the river. Rent a paddleboard or pedal boat on the Vltava (250-400 CZK/hour from Žluté Lázně or Slovanka) — unique perspective, zero crowds.

Bridge towers: you can climb both. The Old Town Bridge Tower (250-step ascent) offers a view straight down the length of the bridge toward the Castle — one of the most iconic perspectives in Europe. 100 CZK ( €4).

St. Nepomuk statue — the 8th sculptural group on the right (coming from Old Town). Legend: touch the bronze plaque at the base and your wish will come true. The plaque is polished smooth by millions of hands. It's kitschy, but it's tradition.

Powder Tower (Prašná brána)

The Gothic gate from 1475 marking the entrance to Old Town. 186 steps, 100 CZK (~€4). A different view from the Town Hall Tower — here you see along Celetná street toward the square.

Jewish Quarter (Josefov) — Europe's best preserved

Prague's Jewish Quarter is unique in Europe — it survived for a grim reason: Hitler deliberately preserved it as a "museum of an extinct race." The result: Gothic and Renaissance synagogues, the Old Cemetery (tombstones stacked on 12 levels), and an extraordinary collection of Jewish artefacts.

What to see in Josefov

Sight What you see Details
Old Jewish Cemetery 12,000 tombstones stacked on 12 levels (1439-1787) Oldest Jewish cemetery in Europe
Old-New Synagogue (Staronová) Oldest active synagogue in Europe (1270) The Golem legend — the attic is inaccessible
Spanish Synagogue Spectacular Moorish interior (1868), permanent exhibition Prague's most beautiful synagogue
Pinkas Synagogue Holocaust memorial with 77,297 names on the walls Profoundly moving
Maisel Synagogue History of Jews in Bohemia Religious silverware collection
Klaus Synagogue Jewish rituals and traditions Adjacent to the cemetery

Josefov tickets 2026

Option What's included Price
Full ticket (all Josefov) All synagogues + cemetery + Ceremonial Hall 600 CZK ( €24)
Without Old-New Synagogue Everything except the active synagogue 400 CZK ( €16)
Guided tour (GYG/local) Everything + guide 2-2.5h + historical context 600-1,000 CZK (€25-40)

Insider: go on a Monday-Thursday morning. Josefov is CLOSED on Saturday (Shabbat) and extremely crowded on Friday and Sunday. Tuesday morning at 9:00 AM is ideal.

Context matters: Josefov is worth visiting with a guide — the historical context transforms the visit from a series of buildings into a profound experience. The guide explains why the cemetery has 12 levels (Jews weren't allowed to expand it), why the synagogue is called "Old-New" (Staronová — a Hebrew wordplay), and the story of the Golem created by Rabbi Löw.

Czech beer — the national religion

Czechia invented the pilsner (in Plzeň, 1842). Czechs drink more beer per capita than anyone else in the world — 140 litres per year (roughly a glass a day, weekends included). Czech beer isn't just good — it's an art form, and Prague is the main gallery.

Essential Prague beer halls

U Fleků — brewing since 1499 (yes, over 500 years). They make a single beer — a dark lager available nowhere else on Earth. Served in a medieval hall with long wooden benches. Touristy but historically essential. 130 CZK/beer ( €5.40). Waiters bring beer to your table without asking — if you don't want another, put a coaster on your glass.

Lokál — modern Czech pub chain with Pilsner Urquell tankové pivo (unpasteurised beer served from pressurised tanks delivered weekly from Plzeň). 65 CZK/half-litre ( €2.70). The food is equally excellent — svíčková, vepřo-knedlo-zelo at 180-280 CZK. Three locations: Lokál Dlouhááá (Old Town), Lokál U Bílé kuželky (Malá Strana), Lokál Hamburk (Karlín). The Dlouhá one is the most atmospheric.

Letná Beer Garden — open-air terrace in Letná Park with THE best panoramic view of Prague. Bridges, river, Old Town, Castle — everything from one spot. 60-80 CZK/beer (~€2.50-3.30). Best at sunset. Fun fact: the terrace sits where the world's largest Stalin statue once stood (demolished in 1962 with 800 kg of dynamite), and the current metronome marks the spot.

U Sudu — underground maze of rooms, each with a different atmosphere. Student prices (55-70 CZK/beer). Comes alive after 10 PM. You enter through an unremarkable door on Vodičkova — you'd never guess what's inside.

Strahov Monastery Brewery (Klášterní pivovar Strahov) — monastic beer brewed by Premonstratensian monks since 1628. Terrace with views of the Castle and city. Sv. Norbert beer (their own) — amber, dark, IPA. 80-110 CZK/beer (~€3.30-4.50). Visit after Prague Castle — it's a 5-minute walk.

BeerGeek — Prague's craft beer bar. 32 rotating taps, Czech and international craft beers. For connoisseurs. 80-150 CZK/beer. Two locations (Vinohradská and Seifertova).

Czech beers to know

Beer Style From Why it's special
Pilsner Urquell Pilsner (the original!) Plzeň The first pilsner in history (1842), every pilsner derives from it
Budějovický Budvar Lager České Budějovice The real Czech Budweiser — 100+ year legal dispute with the Americans
Staropramen Lager Smíchov, Prague Prague's quintessential brewery
Kozel Dark lager Velké Popovice "The Goat" — accessible and excellent dark lager
Bernard Unpasteurised Humpolec Premium, no preservatives, one of the world's best beers
Gambrinus Desetítka (10°) Plzeň The Czech everyday beer, light and drinkable
Svijany Multiple Svijany Independent brewery, local favourite
Únětický pivovar 10° / 12° Únětice (near Prague) Award-winning microbrewery, 15 min from the centre

Tankové pivo (tank beer) — this is the secret you need to know. Tank beer is unpasteurised and unfiltered, delivered in pressurised tanks directly from the brewery. It has a freshness and complexity that bottled beer will never match. Lokál, Kozlovna, and most local hospodas serve tankové pivo. Ask "Máte tankové?" — if the answer is yes, order that.

Beer tasting tours

A beer tasting tour is probably the most fun experience in Prague — 3-4 hours, 4-6 pubs, with a guide who explains Czech beer history, brewing processes, and style differences. Usually includes traditional snacks.

Budget: 850-1,500 CZK (€35-60), 3-4 hours, 4-6 stops. The best ones run in the evening. Check beer tours on GetYourGuide

Czech food — hearty, authentic, surprisingly varied

Czech cuisine is winter food, hearty and based on meat, potatoes, cabbage, and knedlíky (bread dumplings that soak up the sauce). It's comfort food at maximum level — the kind of meal after which you want to lie down on a park bench.

Essential Czech dishes

Svíčková na smetaně — the national dish. Slow-braised beef sirloin in creamy vegetable sauce, served with bread dumplings (knedlíky) and cranberry compote. 180-280 CZK (€7.50-11.50). The ultimate test of any hospoda — if the svíčková is good, everything is good.

Vepřo-knedlo-zelo — roast pork + dumplings + sauerkraut. The Czech holy trinity. 160-250 CZK (€6.60-10.30). Simple, but when done right, overwhelmingly satisfying.

Smažený sýr — deep-fried Eidam cheese, served with fries and tartar sauce. Maximum comfort food, accidentally vegetarian. 130-200 CZK (€5.40-8.30). Street version (in bread, takeaway): 70-100 CZK.

Guláš — the Czech version is thicker than the Hungarian one, with more meat and less broth, served in a bread bowl (chlebový koláč) at street stands. 120-200 CZK at a restaurant, 80-130 CZK at a stand.

Svíčková vs. guláš: both are must-tries, but svíčková is more refined, guláš is more rustic. If you only have time for one, choose svíčková — it's the most Czech thing you can eat.

Trdelník — the cylindrical pastry you see at every corner in the centre. The uncomfortable truth: trdelník is NOT traditional Czech — it's Slovak/Hungarian and only became popular in Prague in the 2000s as a "tourist tradition." That doesn't mean it's not delicious — but locals don't eat it. Price: 70-90 CZK plain, 130-210 CZK with ice cream/Nutella/fruit.

Chlebíčky — open-faced mini-sandwiches from traditional delis. Egg, salami, cheese, fish paste, vegetables — endless combinations. 30-60 CZK each (€1.20-2.50). The most authentic Czech snack. Sisters Bistro (near Old Town Square) does excellent modern versions.

Palacinky — Czech pancakes (thicker than French crêpes), with jam, chocolate, fruit, or sweet curd cheese (tvaroh). 80-140 CZK. The traditional dessert.

Where to eat — from local to gastronomic

Category Recommendation What to eat Price/person
