## Croatia Road Trip 2026: Split to Dubrovnik in 5 Days Along the Dalmatian Coast

URL: https://plecari.com/en/inchirieri-auto/croatia-road-trip-split-dubrovnik-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: inchirieri-auto
Publicat: 2026-07-14
Actualizat: 2026-07-14
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/inchirieri-auto/road-trip-croatia-split-dubrovnik

Descriere: Day-by-day road trip itinerary from Split to Dubrovnik along the Dalmatian Magistrala. Stops, hidden beaches, Game of Thrones locations, costs, and driving tips.

Răspuns scurt: A 5-day road trip from Split to Dubrovnik covers 350 km along the Dalmatian Magistrala — one of Europe's most beautiful coastal roads. Key stops: Omiš (canyon rafting), Brela (Croatia's most beautiful beach), Makarska Riviera, Biokovo Skywalk (glass platform at 1,228 m), Ston (oysters + second-longest wall in the world), and Dubrovnik (Game of Thrones). Total cost: €450-750 per person including car rental (from €20/day), fuel (~€45), accommodation, food, and activities.

Why this is one of Europe's greatest drives

The Dalmatian Magistrala (road D8) is 350 km of limestone cliffs, turquoise coves, red-roofed fishing villages, and the Adriatic stretching to the horizon. It's not the fastest route from Split to Dubrovnik — but speed isn't the point. With 5 days and a rental car , you transform a 3.5-hour drive into one of the most memorable holidays you can have in Europe.

Croatia uses the euro (since January 2023), so no currency confusion. Card payments are accepted everywhere.



Day 1: Split — Roman palace, waterfront, food

Driving: 0 km (pick up car, explore the city)

Pick up your rental car at Split airport. First stop: Diocletian's Palace — not a museum behind ropes, but an actual living city inside a 4th-century Roman emperor's retirement home. People live, eat, and shop INSIDE the palace walls.

Walk through the underground halls (€8, Game of Thrones filming location ), climb the cathedral bell tower (best Split views, €7), and lose yourself in the narrow streets. Evening: the Riva waterfront promenade — where locals spend hours over a single coffee.

Dinner: peka (meat or octopus slow-cooked under an iron bell) at Konoba Fetivi. Full meal: €15-20.

Accommodation: Split centre or Bačvice (urban beach, 10-minute walk). From €60/night.

Book Split experiences on GetYourGuide — walking tours, food tours, and Game of Thrones tours are available.

Day 2: Split → Omiš → Brela → Makarska (90 km)

Driving: 2 hours with stops

Omiš (30 km) — medieval pirate town at the mouth of the Cetina canyon. If you want adrenaline, Cetina River rafting (3 hours, €35-45) is one of Croatia's best outdoor experiences.

Brela (60 km) — Punta Rata beach, repeatedly voted Croatia's most beautiful: fine pebbles, pine shade, and an iconic rock formation in turquoise water. Stop here for 2-3 hours.

Makarska (90 km) — your evening base. The Makarska Riviera sits between the Adriatic and the Biokovo mountains (1,762 m) — the backdrop is dramatic. Stroll the palm-lined promenade, eat seafood on the harbour.

Accommodation: Makarska or Brela, from €55/night.



Day 3: Makarska → Biokovo Skywalk → Pelješac Peninsula (120 km)

Driving: 2.5 hours with stops

Biokovo Skywalk (20 km from Makarska) — glass viewing platform at 1,228 m with 60 km of coastline visible below. Entry: €6 + parking €8. Go early morning — queues form from 10:00.

Pelješac Peninsula — Croatia's best-kept secret. Stop at:

Ston — the second-longest defensive wall in the world (after the Great Wall of China), 5.5 km across hills. Walk the walls (€12) and then descend for fresh oysters directly from the producer — 12 oysters + a glass of Plavac Mali wine: €15. This is genuinely one of the best food experiences in Croatia.

Dingač wine region — Croatia's finest red wine. Many cellars offer tastings (€10-15, 3-5 wines).

Accommodation: Ston or Orebić, from €50/night.

Day 4: Pelješac → Trsteno → Dubrovnik (70 km)

Driving: 1.5 hours

Trsteno Arboretum (20 km north of Dubrovnik) — Renaissance botanical garden (1502) with 500-year-old plane trees and the Neptune fountain — another Game of Thrones filming location (King's Landing gardens). Entry: €7. A perfect 1-hour stop.

Dubrovnik — arrival. Park at Ilijaš garage (near the cable car, €4/hour or €30/day — no cars in the Old Town). Take the cable car up Mount Srđ (€27 return) for your first aerial view of the city. The sunset from up here is staggering.

Accommodation: Dubrovnik, 2 nights, from €70/night. Stay in Ploče (5 minutes from Old Town, sea views) or Lapad (beach area, 15 minutes by bus).



Day 5: Dubrovnik — walls, GoT, island

Full day in Dubrovnik. The suggested schedule:

8:00 — City walls (€35). Go at opening — by 10:00 it's packed and brutally hot. The complete circuit: 1.5-2 hours, 1,940 metres of medieval fortification above the sea.

10:30 — Game of Thrones walking tour (2 hours, from €25). Filming locations with side-by-side scene comparisons, even if you haven't watched the show.

13:00 — Lunch at Pizzeria Tabasco (locals' favourite, pizza from €7) or Proto (fine dining, fish, €30/person).

14:30 — Ferry to Lokrum Island (€15 return, 15 minutes). Iron Throne replica (donated by HBO), botanical garden, "Dead Sea" (salt lake for swimming), and rocky beaches with crystal water.

18:00 — Buža Bar (cliff-edge platform outside the walls). Beer with the best view in Dubrovnik.

Read the complete Dubrovnik city break guide for more details.

Car rental tips

Choose full insurance (CDW + TP + Super CDW). Croatian coastal roads have tight curves and occasional loose gravel. A scratch on the door costs €200-500 without insurance. With Super CDW (€5-10/day extra), excess is zero. Compare prices on DiscoverCars .

Photograph the car at pickup. Every scratch, every side, including roof and wheels. Email the photos to yourself as timestamped proof.

Diesel or hybrid. Fuel costs €1.40-1.50/litre. On 350 km with a small diesel: ~25 litres = ~€37.

One-way fee. Pick up in Split, drop off in Dubrovnik: €30-80 extra. Worth it — saves a day of driving back and fuel.

Don't park in Dubrovnik Old Town. It's pedestrianised. Ilijaš garage (near cable car) or Pile Gate parking (€7/hour) are your options. Both are walking distance from the Old Town gates.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How long does it take to drive from Split to Dubrovnik?
R: Non-stop: 3.5 hours via the coastal Magistrala (D8). But driving it without stopping would be a crime — the road passes through some of the most beautiful coastal scenery in Europe. With stops (beaches, villages, viewpoints), plan 5-7 hours. With a 5-day itinerary, you drive just 1-2 hours per day and explore the rest.

Î: Can I rent a car in Split and return it in Dubrovnik?
R: Yes. Most major companies (Sixt, Europcar, Enterprise) offer one-way rental with a fee of €30-80. This saves a day of driving back. Book via [DiscoverCars](https://discovercars.tpo.mx/rR73qao3) and filter for one-way availability.

Î: Is the Dalmatian Magistrala safe to drive?
R: Yes — the road is well-maintained (recently upgraded on major sections). Be aware of: tight curves between Omiš and Makarska, heavy summer traffic in tourist zones, fast-moving motorcyclists. Speed limit: 90 km/h on national roads, 50 km/h in towns. Croatian police issue on-the-spot fines.

Î: Do I need a toll vignette for Croatia?
R: Croatia doesn't use vignettes — tolls are paid at barriers on motorways. Split→Dubrovnik via motorway + Magistrala costs about €15 in tolls. The Pelješac Bridge (opened 2022) is toll-free and bypasses the Bosnian Neum corridor entirely.

## Car Rental in Greece 2026: Documents, Prices, Rules and Island-by-Island Guide

URL: https://plecari.com/en/inchirieri-auto/inchiriere-masina-grecia-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: inchirieri-auto
Publicat: 2026-07-25
Actualizat: 2026-07-25

Descriere: Everything you need to know before renting a car in Greece: required documents, 2026 traffic law changes, real prices by season, which islands need a car and which traps to avoid.

Răspuns scurt: EU citizens can rent a car in Greece with their EU driving licence — no international permit required. Minimum age is 21, with a young driver surcharge for under-25s. A credit card is required for the deposit. Key 2026 change: speed limits in urban areas have dropped to 30 km/h with stricter enforcement and higher fines. On large islands (Crete, Rhodes), a rental car is practically essential to reach the best beaches and villages.

On the large Greek islands, a rental car transforms a holiday entirely. Instead of being tied to your resort or the limited local bus network, you reach hidden beaches, mountain villages, and attractions that most tourists never see. On Crete or Rhodes, this is not a luxury — it is the difference between a standard beach holiday and a genuinely interesting one. Here is everything you need to know for 2026.

Documents required at the counter

EU citizens need three things:

Valid EU driving licence (category B). Your national licence is sufficient — no international driving permit needed. Greece is in the EU and EU licences are mutually recognised.

Passport or national ID card. Most rental companies prefer a passport. Some specifically require it rather than an ID card, especially for international chains. Bring both to be safe.

Credit card in the driver's name. The company will place a hold (pre-authorisation) on your card for the security deposit — typically €200–1,500 depending on the car category and the excess level on your insurance. This is not charged; it is blocked and released when you return the car in good condition.

Bring the booking confirmation (email or print) and arrive with time to inspect the car before driving away.

What changed in 2026 — new traffic rules

Greece introduced significant changes to its road traffic laws effective January 2026. The most important for drivers:

Urban speed limit reduced to 30 km/h. In most town and village zones, residential areas, and pedestrian-heavy areas, the limit is now 30 km/h rather than 50 km/h. This applies to the majority of built-up areas across the islands. Enforcement is stricter and fines are higher than before.

Other rules in force:


Outside built-up areas: 90 km/h on national roads, 130 km/h on motorways

Seat belts mandatory on all seats

Mobile phone use prohibited without hands-free

Blood alcohol limit: 0.5‰ (0.2‰ for drivers with less than 2 years of licence)

Children under 12 must use an appropriate child seat


The 30 km/h zones are the change most likely to affect tourists — they are not always clearly signposted at the entry to every village. When in doubt on a narrow island road passing through a settlement, slow to 30.

Island-by-island: where a car is essential, useful, or unnecessary

Crete — essential. Greece's largest island at 250 km long. Without a car, you are effectively confined to your resort and its immediate area. The best beaches — Elafonisi (pink sand, turquoise water), Balos (lagoon accessible only by boat or 4WD road), Preveli (palm-lined gorge), and Falassarna — are only reachable by car or expensive organised tours. The Samaria Gorge hike requires driving to the trailhead. Rent a car.

Rhodes — very useful. The medieval old town of Rhodes City and Lindos can be reached by bus, but the western and southern beaches, the Valley of the Butterflies, and the inland villages require a car. A rental for 3–4 days of your week gives you access to a completely different island.

Corfu — useful with caution. Corfu's roads are narrow and heavily used in summer. A small car (not an SUV) is genuinely easier to park and manoeuvre. The north of the island — Kassiopi, Sidari, Paleokastritsa — is most worth exploring by car. The old town of Corfu City is best on foot.

Zakynthos — recommended. The famous Navagio Beach (Shipwreck Beach) is only accessible by boat, but the rest of the island's best spots (Keri Lake, Marathonisi Island viewpoint, the blue caves coast road) require a car. Buses are infrequent.

Lefkada — recommended. Connected to the mainland by a bridge, so you can drive your own car. The beaches on the west coast (Porto Katsiki, Egremni) are spectacular but only reachable by car on steep, winding roads.

Thassos — optional. Small enough to be circled by scooter. A car helps but is not essential if you are based near the main towns. Accessible by ferry from Kavala (mainland), so you can bring your own car.

Mykonos — unnecessary. Parking in Mykonos Town is effectively impossible in summer. ATV and scooter rentals are the island's transport system. The island is small enough that everything is reachable by the local bus or a short ATV ride.

Santorini — unnecessary. The caldera villages (Oia, Fira, Imerovigli) are connected by foot paths along the cliff edge. Cars are used by locals but tourists find parking close to impossible. The local bus (KTEL) is adequate and cheap.

Prices: what to expect in 2026

Prices vary significantly by season, island, and category:

Category May–June / September July–August
Small (Hyundai i10, Fiat 500) €25–40/day €40–70/day
Compact (VW Golf, Toyota Corolla) €35–55/day €55–90/day
Small SUV €50–80/day €80–130/day
Automatic (add to above) +€15–25/day +€15–25/day

Airport surcharge: Collecting from the airport adds 10–15% to the total. If you are willing to take a short taxi to a city-centre location, you save this fee.

Young driver surcharge (under 25): €5–15/day extra on top of the base rate.

Book 4–6 weeks ahead for the best prices. On popular islands in July–August, cars genuinely sell out — not as a sales tactic but as a physical reality. Walk-up prices at island airports in peak season are consistently 40–60% higher than pre-booked rates.

The CDW excess problem — the most expensive "included" feature

Almost every rental includes CDW (Collision Damage Waiver) in the base price. This sounds like full protection but it is not — CDW comes with an excess : the amount you personally pay if the car is damaged, regardless of fault. This excess is pre-authorised (blocked) on your credit card at collection.

Rental company insurance level Your excess
Basic CDW (standard included) €500–1,500
Super CDW (counter upsell, €15–25/day) €0
Third-party excess waiver (pre-purchased online) €0

The counter Super CDW at €15–25/day for a week costs €105–175 extra. A third-party excess waiver from a specialist (insurance4carhire.com, RentalCover, iCarhireinsurance) covers the same thing for €5–8/day, or €35–56 for the week. Always buy the third-party version before arriving — the counter staff will push their product but you are not obligated to buy it.

For a complete explanation of all rental fees and how to avoid them, read: Hidden fees in car rental — how to avoid paying double .

At collection: the photograph routine

This single habit prevents the majority of damage disputes:


Before touching the car, walk around it and photograph every panel — all four sides, the roof, the bonnet, the boot, and both wing mirrors

Photograph the interior (any stains on seats, condition of dashboard)

Photograph the fuel gauge showing it is full

Email all photos to yourself immediately — the timestamp is your legal proof

Have the agent note any existing damage on the contract before you sign


On Greek islands in summer, rental cars are used intensively. Pre-existing scratches and scrapes are common. Without your own timestamped photos, you cannot prove which damage was there before you drove away.

Parking on Greek islands — the colour code

Greek road markings determine parking rules:


White markings: free parking (sometimes with a time limit — check signs)

Blue markings: paid parking (pay at a nearby meter or kiosk)

Yellow markings: no parking at any time


In village centres and old towns, parking is often scarce and the streets are too narrow for anything larger than a small hatchback. Plan to park at the edge of town and walk in — most Greek village centres are pedestrianised or effectively so.

Fuel policy — always choose full-to-full

You will encounter two main policies:

Full-to-full: You collect the car with a full tank and return it full. You pay only for what you used, at petrol station prices. This is the correct and transparent option — always choose it.

Pre-purchase fuel: You pay upfront for a full tank at the company's price (higher than the petrol station), and return the car empty. You never manage to return it exactly empty, so you always lose paid fuel. Avoid this.

Find a petrol station within 2–3 km of the drop-off point as you navigate back to return the car. Returning with a full tank from a proper petrol station rather than the company's surcharge is always cheaper.

Which islands have the best local rental companies

On larger islands, local Greek companies often offer significantly lower prices than the international chains, with comparable car quality:

Crete: Look for companies based in Heraklion, Chania, or Rethymno city centres — not the airport. Local companies like Auto Motor Sport, Alegria, or Simply Crete regularly offer rates 20–30% below Hertz or Europcar for the same category.

Rhodes: The city centre has dozens of local operators along Ierou Lohou street. Negotiate in low season (May, October) — prices are genuinely flexible.

Corfu: Airport road companies are mostly international chains. Town-based companies around Corfu Town (Kerkyra) are cheaper.

Whichever company you use — local or international — the documentation rules and the photograph routine remain exactly the same.

Getting to Greece and travel logistics

Flights from Bucharest to Heraklion (Crete), Rhodes, or Corfu run throughout summer — direct charters from May to October. For the best fares, read how to find cheap flights .

Greece is in the EU — EU roaming applies, no eSIM needed. Your Romanian mobile plan works without extra charges.

Travel insurance is not legally mandatory for Greece, but highly recommended. The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) covers emergency treatment at public hospitals, but not repatriation, private clinics, or trip cancellation. A full travel insurance policy costs €12–18 for a week and covers what the EHIC does not. Compare options: travel insurance guide 2026 .

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Do I need an international driving permit for Greece?
R: No, if you hold an EU driving licence. EU licences are recognised directly across all member states. An international driving permit is only required for drivers from outside the EU (USA, UK, Australia, etc.) or when the licence is not written in Latin characters.

Î: What credit cards do Greek rental companies accept?
R: Typically Visa or Mastercard credit cards in the driver's name, used for the security deposit hold. Debit cards are accepted less frequently and with additional conditions. Revolut can work if you have the credit card version (not prepaid or debit). Always verify before booking — especially with small local companies on smaller islands, which sometimes insist on a traditional credit card.

Î: Should I bring my own car or rent locally?
R: Depends on the destination. For Halkidiki or Thassos (reachable by road), your own car works well. For Crete, Rhodes, Corfu, or Zakynthos (reached by flight), rent locally — it is far cheaper and simpler than paying €100–200 each way to ship your car on a ferry.

Î: What is the average car rental price in Greece in peak season?
R: A small hatchback (Hyundai i10, VW Polo) costs €35–70/day in July–August on the islands. Prices drop 20–30% in May–June and September. Booking 4–6 weeks ahead typically saves 25–40% compared to walk-up prices at the island airport.

Î: What happens if I scratch the car?
R: If CDW (Collision Damage Waiver) is included, the company covers the damage minus the excess (which can be €500–1,500). If you have not reduced the excess to zero, you pay that amount. Always photograph the car thoroughly at collection — every existing scratch, on all four sides, roof included — and email the photos to yourself immediately as timestamped proof.

Î: Can I drive between Greek islands with a rental car?
R: No. Rental contracts in Greece are almost always restricted to the island or region where you collected the car. Taking the vehicle on a ferry to another island is specifically prohibited by most rental agreements. If you want to visit multiple islands, you return the car, take a ferry or flight, and rent again at the next island.

Î: Is a GPS or a phone sufficient for navigation in Greece?
R: Your phone with Google Maps is completely sufficient. Download the offline map for the island before departure. The counter GPS (€8–15/day) is an unnecessary expense. Road signs in Greece are bilingual (Greek and Latin alphabet) on main roads, so navigation is manageable even without a device — but GPS helps on the narrow backroads of Crete or Corfu.

## Romania Road Trip 2026: Bucharest to Transylvania in 7 Days — Complete Itinerary

URL: https://plecari.com/en/inchirieri-auto/romania-road-trip-transylvania
Limbă: English
Verticală: inchirieri-auto
Publicat: 2026-07-12
Actualizat: 2026-07-12
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/inchirieri-auto/road-trip-transilvania

Descriere: The ultimate Romania road trip itinerary: 7 days from Bucharest through Transylvania and back. Castles, medieval towns, Carpathian mountains, fortified churches, and the best food in Eastern Europe.

Răspuns scurt: A 7-day Romania road trip from Bucharest through Transylvania covers roughly 1,200 km and costs €500-900 per person (car rental from €20/day, fuel €80-100 total, accommodation €30-60/night, food €15-25/day). The ideal route: Bucharest → Sinaia (Peleș Castle) → Brașov → Sighișoara → Sibiu → Transfăgărășan Highway → Bucharest. You'll see medieval towns, fairy-tale castles, Carpathian mountain passes, fortified Saxon churches, and eat some of the best traditional food in Europe — all for a fraction of what Western Europe costs.

Why Romania is Europe's best-kept road trip secret

Romania has everything a great road trip needs: dramatic mountain passes, fairy-tale castles, medieval walled towns that look like they haven't changed in 500 years, and some of the best traditional food in Europe. All of this at roughly half the cost of a similar trip in Austria, Italy, or France.

The country sits on the Carpathian arc — a horseshoe of mountains that cuts through the heart of the country and creates some of Europe's most spectacular driving roads, including the Transfăgărășan (famously called "the best road in the world" by Top Gear).

And then there's the food. Romanian cuisine doesn't get the international recognition it deserves: slow-cooked stews, grilled minced meat rolls ( mici ), fresh sheep cheese, and the best soups you'll eat anywhere. A full traditional meal costs €8-15 in most restaurants outside Bucharest.



The route: 1,200 km loop from Bucharest

Bucharest → Sinaia (120 km) → Brașov (50 km) → Bran (30 km) → Sighișoara (185 km) → Sibiu (95 km) → Transfăgărășan → Curtea de Argeș (150 km) → Bucharest (170 km)

Total distance: ~1,200 km. Total driving time: ~18 hours. Spread over 7 days, that's 2-3 hours of driving per day — the rest is exploring.

Day 1: Bucharest — pick up car, explore the capital

Pick up your rental car at Henri Coandă Airport. Spend the day in Bucharest: Palace of Parliament (the world's heaviest building, guided tour €10), Old Town walking (free), lunch at Lacrimi și Sfinți (best traditional restaurant, €12-15 for a full meal), and evening drinks in the Old Town (beer €2.50, cocktails €5-7).

Accommodation: Hotel near Calea Victoriei, €40-70/night.

👉 Full Bucharest guide: Bucharest in 3 Days — Ultimate City Break Guide

Day 2: Bucharest → Sinaia → Brașov (170 km, 2.5 hours)

Sinaia — the Pearl of the Carpathians

Peleș Castle is the highlight of the entire trip. A Neo-Renaissance masterpiece with 160 rooms, Murano glass, and hand-carved woodwork — it's often called the most beautiful castle in Europe, and it lives up to it. Standard tour: €10, extended tour: €20. Closed Mondays/Tuesdays.

Walk through the surrounding pine forest to Pelișor Castle (Art Nouveau, Queen Marie's residence, €5) and stop at Sinaia Monastery (1695, free).

Brașov — medieval Transylvania

Arrive in Brașov by afternoon. Walk through Council Square (one of the best-preserved medieval squares in Eastern Europe), visit the Black Church (largest Gothic church between Vienna and Istanbul, €5), and if you have energy, hike or cable car up Tâmpa Mountain (€10 cable car, panoramic views of the city and surrounding mountains).

Dinner: Sergiana restaurant — enormous portions of traditional Transylvanian food. Full meal: €8-12.

Accommodation: Brașov Old Town, €35-60/night.



Day 3: Bran Castle + Brașov region (60 km total)

Bran Castle (30 minutes from Brașov)

The so-called "Dracula's Castle." The Vlad the Impaler connection is tenuous, but the 14th-century fortress perched on a cliff is atmospheric, well-preserved, and genuinely interesting as a museum of Romanian royal history. Entry: €12. Buy tickets online to skip the summer queue (30-45 minutes).

Option A: Rașnov Fortress

15 minutes from Bran, the hilltop Rașnov Citadel is less famous but arguably more dramatic — a massive peasant fortress on a limestone cliff with 360° mountain views. €5 entry, rarely crowded.

Option B: Poiana Brașov

Romania's most popular ski resort is equally beautiful in summer. Take the cable car to Postăvaru Peak (1,799 m) for hiking with alpine views. Cable car: €8 return.

Return to Brașov for a second evening exploring the narrow streets, medieval towers, and the Strada Sforii (one of the narrowest streets in Europe).

Day 4: Brașov → Viscri → Sighișoara (185 km, 3 hours)

Viscri — Charles III's favourite village

The road from Brașov to Sighișoara passes through some of Transylvania's most beautiful Saxon villages. Detour to Viscri (30 km off the main road) — a village so well-preserved that King Charles III bought a house here. The Viscri Fortified Church (UNESCO World Heritage) sits on a hill surrounded by whitewashed houses with blue-green shutters. Entry: €3.

Stop at the village shop for homemade jam, sheep cheese, and sourdough bread. This is rural Transylvania at its most authentic.

Sighișoara — Dracula's birthplace

Sighișoara is the best-preserved medieval citadel in Eastern Europe, and it's still inhabited — people live inside the 12th-century walls. The Clock Tower (€5, museum + panoramic view), the Covered Stairway (176 wooden steps built in 1642), and the Church on the Hill are all walkable in 2-3 hours.

This is also where Vlad the Impaler was actually born (1431) — his birthplace is now a restaurant (Casa Vlad Dracul, touristy but fun). Have dinner there for the novelty — the food is average, the atmosphere is everything.

Accommodation: Inside the citadel walls, €30-50/night. Falling asleep inside a 12th-century fortress is an experience in itself.



Day 5: Sighișoara → Biertan → Sibiu (95 km, 1.5 hours)

Biertan Fortified Church (30 km detour)

Another UNESCO Saxon fortified church, but grander than Viscri. The triple ring of walls, the massive Gothic altar, and the "marriage lock" (couples seeking divorce were locked in a room for 2 weeks with one bed, one plate, one fork — almost no one divorced) make it worth the stop. Entry: €3.

Sibiu — Romania's most elegant city

Sibiu was European Capital of Culture in 2007, and it shows. The Grand Square ( Piața Mare ), the Brukenthal Palace (national art museum, €5), the Bridge of Lies (legend says it collapses if you lie on it), and the iconic "eyes of Sibiu" (dormer windows on rooftops that look like watching eyes) create one of the most photogenic cityscapes in Romania.

Walk along Strada Nicolae Bălcescu for cafés and bookshops, then explore the Lower Town (craftsmen's quarter, more local, less touristy).

Dinner: Crama Sibiu Vechi — traditional Transylvanian restaurant in a medieval cellar. Try bulz (polenta with melted cheese and sour cream) and local wines from Jidvei. Full meal: €10-15.

Accommodation: Sibiu Old Town, €35-60/night. Stay two nights — Sibiu deserves an unhurried visit.

Day 6: Transfăgărășan Highway (150 km, 4-5 hours with stops)

This is the driving day. The Transfăgărășan is a 90 km mountain road climbing to 2,042 metres through the Făgăraș Mountains, with hairpin turns, tunnels, and views that will make you stop every kilometre. Built by Ceaușescu in the 1970s as a military road, it's now one of the world's most famous driving roads.

Important: the road is only open mid-June to late October (weather dependent). Check the status before planning. Start early — the road gets busy after 10:00 in summer.

Key stops:

Bâlea Waterfall — pull over at the marked viewpoint. 15-minute walk to the base of a 60-metre waterfall.

Bâlea Lake (2,034 m) — glacial lake at the summit. Cold even in August. Have a coffee at the chalet (€2), walk around the lake, and take in the 360° Carpathian panorama.

Curtea de Argeș — on the descent, stop at the Episcopal Cathedral (1517) — one of Romania's most beautiful churches, with twisted stone columns and intricate carvings.

Accommodation: Curtea de Argeș, €25-40/night.

Day 7: Return to Bucharest (170 km, 2.5 hours)

Relaxed morning. Drive back to Bucharest on the A1 motorway (fastest) or via Pitești on national roads (more scenic). Return the car at the airport or drop it off in the city.

If your flight is in the evening, spend the afternoon at Therme Bucharest (30 minutes from the airport, €25 entry) — thermal pools, slides, and relaxation. Perfect end to a road trip.

Budget — 7 days, 2 people sharing

Category Budget Mid-range
Car rental 7 days (full insurance) €180 €280
Fuel (1,200 km) €85 €85
Tolls / vignette €15 €15
Accommodation 7 nights €250 €400
Food (7 days × 2 people) €210 €350
Attractions / entries €60 €100
Travel insurance (2 people) €30 €30
eSIM (2 people) €10 €10

Per person ~€420 ~€635

Add flights to Bucharest (varies by origin): £50-150 from UK, €100-300 from Western Europe, $400-700 from US.

Driving tips for Romania

Road quality: main roads (DN1, E81) and motorways are good. Mountain roads (Transfăgărășan, village detours) can be narrow with no guardrails. Village roads occasionally have potholes.

Speed limits: 50 km/h in towns, 90 km/h on national roads, 130 km/h on motorways. Speed cameras are common and fines are instant.

Vignette (Rovinieta): required for motorways. Buy online at roviniete.ro (€3 for 7 days). Without it: €130 fine.

Winter tyres: mandatory November 1 — March 31 (but not relevant for summer trips).

Horse carts: yes, really. In rural Transylvania you'll share the road with horse-drawn carts. They're slow-moving and don't always have lights. Drive carefully at dusk.

Fuel: petrol stations are plentiful on main roads. In remote areas (Viscri, mountain passes), fill up before you leave the last town.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is Romania good for a road trip?
R: Romania is one of the best road trip countries in Europe. The roads are well-maintained on main routes, fuel is cheap (€1.40/litre), traffic outside Bucharest is light, and the scenery — Carpathian mountains, medieval villages, rolling hills — is spectacular. The country is large enough to feel like a real adventure but compact enough to cover in a week.

Î: How much does it cost to rent a car in Romania?
R: Car rental starts at €20-25/day for a small car (Dacia Sandero, VW Polo) from international companies at Bucharest airport. A week rental with full insurance (CDW + TP + Super CDW) costs €180-300 total. Manual transmission is cheaper than automatic. Book 4-6 weeks ahead for best prices.

Î: Is the Transfăgărășan Highway really that good?
R: Yes. Jeremy Clarkson called it 'the best road in the world' on Top Gear, and he wasn't exaggerating. It's a 90 km mountain road climbing to 2,042 metres with hairpin turns, glacial lakes, and views that make you pull over every 500 metres. It's only open June-October (weather dependent). Check road status before planning.

Î: Is Romania safe for tourists?
R: Very safe. Romania has lower crime rates than most Western European countries. Standard precautions apply in Bucharest (watch for pickpockets in Old Town, use ride-hailing apps instead of street taxis). Rural Romania is extremely safe and locals are famously hospitable.

Î: Do I need an international driving permit?
R: If you have a driving licence from an EU/EEA country, your regular licence works. US, UK, Canadian, and Australian licence holders should carry an International Driving Permit (IDP) alongside their regular licence, though in practice most car rental companies accept English-language licences.

## Hidden Fees in Car Rental: How to Avoid Paying Double

URL: https://plecari.com/en/inchirieri-auto/taxe-ascunse-inchiriere-auto
Limbă: English
Verticală: inchirieri-auto
Publicat: 2026-07-09

Descriere: CDW, excess, fuel policy, airport surcharges, GPS fees — what awaits you at the counter and how to avoid every extra cost. A practical guide with real numbers.

Răspuns scurt: The most common hidden fees in car rental are: the excess on CDW insurance (you may pay €500–2,000 if you damage the car, even with basic insurance included), the airport surcharge (10–15% added when collecting from an airport), the young driver fee (under 25 years), overpriced GPS (€10–15/day) and the fuel policy trap ('full-to-empty' versus 'full-to-full'). You avoid them by reading the terms before booking and refusing add-ons at the collection counter.

The price you see online for a car rental is not the price you will pay. The difference comes from fees, insurance products and add-ons that appear only at the counter — or buried in the fine print of the contract. Here are the most common ones, with the numbers, and how to avoid each.

CDW and the excess (the industry's most expensive "free" thing)

Almost every rental includes CDW (Collision Damage Waiver) — the basic damage insurance. It sounds good, but it comes with an excess : the amount you pay out of pocket if the car is damaged. This can be anywhere between €500 and €2,000, and it is blocked on your card as a deposit at collection.

What happens in practice: you scratch the bumper in a car park → you pay €800 from your card → the company repairs the bumper for €150 → the difference stays with them. This is legal, because you signed the contract with the excess clause.

How to avoid it: buy a third-party excess waiver (insurance4carhire, iCarhireinsurance, or RentalCover) before collecting the car. It costs €3–8 per day instead of €15–30 at the counter, and it reduces your excess to zero. The counter staff will push their own product — politely decline.

The airport surcharge (10–15% extra)

Rental companies pay a concession fee to the airport for access to the terminal. You end up paying it, labelled as an "airport surcharge" — 10–15% added to the total, typically not shown prominently in the initial search results.

How to avoid it: collect from a city-centre location instead of the airport. Get there by Uber or taxi (€10–20) and save €50–100+ on the surcharge for a week's rental. Some companies even offer a free shuttle from the terminal to their off-airport lot.

The maths: if your rental is €300 for a week, the airport surcharge adds €30–45. The Uber to the city location costs €12. You save €18–33 net, plus you avoid the often chaotic airport car-rental queue.

Young driver fee (under 25)

Under 25 years old? Add €5–15 per day. On a 10-day rental, that is €50–150 purely for being the "wrong" age.

How to avoid it: realistically, you cannot with most major chains. Some smaller or local companies do not charge it — worth comparing on a platform that shows the true total price (including the young driver fee) rather than just the base rate.

Some credit cards with car rental benefits waive the young driver fee — check your card's terms.

GPS: €70–105 per week for something your phone already does

The in-car GPS at the counter costs €10–15 per day. On a 7-day rental, that is €70–105. Your phone does exactly the same thing, for free.

How to avoid it: use Google Maps or Waze on your phone. If you are travelling outside the EU and do not want to use roaming data, get a local eSIM with data for €5–10 (see best eSIM by destination ), or download offline maps for your destination before you leave.

If you genuinely want a physical mount, a phone holder costs €10 on Amazon. That is your one-time investment.

The fuel policy trap

There are two main fuel policies. Understand the difference before signing:

Policy How it works What you actually pay
Full-to-full Collect full, return full Only what you used, at petrol station prices
Pre-purchase fuel Pay for a full tank upfront (at company prices), return empty More than you use — you can never empty it exactly
Full-to-empty Collect full, return empty — fuel included in price Built into the rental price, usually expensive

Always choose full-to-full. The pre-purchase option sounds convenient but you always lose fuel you paid for — nobody returns a car with a perfectly empty tank. The company keeps the surplus.

A practical note on returning full: find a petrol station within 2–3 km of the drop-off point when you are navigating to the return location. Returning the car even 10% below full with a full-to-full contract can result in a surcharge of €20–40 at the company's higher per-litre rate.

Additional charges to watch for

Beyond the major ones, a full contract can include:

One-way fee: Collecting in Split, returning in Dubrovnik, or collecting at Heathrow and returning at Gatwick — many companies charge €30–80+ for this. Some include one-way within the same country for free. Always check at booking, not at the counter.

Cross-border fee: Driving from Italy into Slovenia, or from Greece into Albania — many rental contracts prohibit this or charge €10–30 per country, plus a requirement for additional insurance. If your trip involves multiple countries, declare this at booking and verify it is allowed.

Mileage limits: Some cheap tariffs include a cap of 200–300 km per day, with excess charged at €0.20–0.50 per km. This is rarely an issue for city rentals but becomes significant on road trips. Check the daily mileage allowance before you book.

Child seats and accessories: €5–15 per day each. If you need a child seat for a 10-day trip, that is €50–150 — worth buying a lightweight travel seat (€25–50) if you travel with young children regularly.

Toll charges: some companies rent a toll transponder for €5–15/day rather than you paying individually. On routes with few tolls it is not worth it. On routes like the French péage system or Croatian motorways, check the maths.

Insurance for tyres, windscreen and undercarriage: these are often not covered by basic CDW and are sold separately at €3–8/day each. A third-party excess waiver from a specialist (mentioned above) often covers these automatically — another reason the specialist product beats the counter product.

The counter script (and how to respond)

Here is what the counter agent will say, and the appropriate response:

"I see your booking includes basic insurance only — for just €X per day I can upgrade you to our Full Protection."
→ "No thank you, I have my own excess insurance arranged."

"We are low on your car category — would you like to upgrade for €Y per day?"
→ "I will take what I booked. If you need to upgrade me because of unavailability, there is no additional charge."

"Would you like to pre-purchase your fuel? Then you can return the car empty and not worry."
→ "No, I will use full-to-full. Can you confirm the tank is full now?"

"Our GPS is very useful in this region — just €Z per day."
→ "No thank you, I will use my phone."

Being prepared for these questions takes the pressure off. The counter agent is not your enemy — they have upsell targets — but you are not obliged to buy anything beyond what you booked.

How to compare car rental prices properly

The price shown in the initial search results on most platforms is the base rate — before airport surcharges, taxes, young driver fees, and mandatory insurance add-ons. Here is how to compare properly:


Search on a comparison platform (GetRentacar, DiscoverCars, Rentalcars) that shows the total price including mandatory fees

Set your age correctly — this triggers the young driver fee where applicable

Enter the correct collection location — airport vs. city centre gives you different prices

Check the fuel policy before comparing — two prices can only be compared if the fuel policy is the same

Read the included insurance — is CDW included? What is the excess?

Factor in your own excess insurance (€3–8/day from a specialist) to get the true comparison


The cheapest initial price is very rarely the cheapest final cost.

Before you collect: a practical checklist


Print or download the confirmation with booking reference

Have your third-party excess insurance confirmation ready

Bring the credit card used at booking (most companies require the same card)

At collection: photograph every panel of the car, all four sides, plus roof and wheels

Send the photos to yourself by email immediately — timestamped proof

Verify the fuel level on the contract matches actual (full or noted level)

Confirm the mileage shown on the odometer matches the contract

Get the direct number for the rental company's roadside assistance before driving away


Photographing the car thoroughly at collection is the single most important protection you have. Damage disputes happen — having timestamped photos from before you drove eliminates them.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: What is the CDW excess and why does it matter?
R: CDW (Collision Damage Waiver) is the basic insurance included in the price, but it comes with an excess — the amount you pay out of pocket if you damage the car. The excess can be €500–2,000, blocked on your card as a deposit at collection. You can reduce the excess to zero with a third-party excess insurance (far cheaper than what the counter offers).

Î: Is the extra insurance at the counter worth it?
R: Almost never. Counter insurance costs €15–30 per day and is the rental industry's biggest upsell. A third-party excess waiver from a specialist (e.g. insurance4carhire, iCarhireinsurance, RentalCover) costs 3–5 times less for the same cover and the same period.

Î: What is the 'full-to-full' fuel policy?
R: You collect the car with a full tank and return it full. It is the fairest option — you pay only for what you use, at petrol station prices. The alternative 'pre-purchase fuel' means you pay for a full tank at collection (at the company's price, higher than a petrol station) and return the car empty — but you never manage to empty it exactly, so you always lose paid fuel.

Î: Why is collecting at the airport more expensive?
R: Airports charge rental companies a concession fee for access to the terminal, parking and counter space. Companies pass this cost directly to you — as an 'airport surcharge' of 10–15% added to the total. Collecting from a city-centre location avoids the surcharge, but you need to get there from the airport.

Î: What does a one-way fee mean?
R: A one-way fee applies when you collect the car in one city and return it in another. It can be anywhere from €30 to over €100, depending on the company and distance. Some companies include one-way within the same country for free — check at booking, not at the counter.

Î: Can I use my credit card insurance instead of buying CDW cover?
R: Some premium credit cards (Visa Signature, Mastercard World Elite, Amex Gold) include car rental insurance as a benefit. However, you typically need to pay the full rental on that card, decline the rental company's CDW, and the cover is secondary (it kicks in after other insurance). Check your card's terms carefully — exclusions vary and not all rental companies accept card insurance.

## 15 Budget Travel Tips for Europe That Actually Work in 2026

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/budget-travel-tips-europe-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-15
Actualizat: 2026-07-15

Descriere: The most effective ways to save money on a European holiday without sacrificing the experience. Flights, accommodation, food, transport, and the hidden fees nobody warns you about.

Răspuns scurt: The 8 most impactful money-saving tips for European travel: 1) Book flights 6-8 weeks ahead, on Tuesdays. 2) Stay in Zone 2-3, not city centre (30-50% cheaper). 3) Use an eSIM instead of carrier roaming (saves €5-15/day). 4) Pay with Revolut/Wise (0% foreign exchange fee vs 1-3% on bank cards). 5) Eat one street away from tourist attractions (30-50% cheaper). 6) Use Bolt/Uber not taxis (saves €20-40 per trip). 7) Choose shoulder season (20-30% cheaper than July-August). 8) Get travel insurance (€15-25 prevents €500-5,000 emergency costs).

The philosophy: same experience, less money

This isn't about surviving on €10/day, sleeping in train stations, and eating bread. This is about having the exact same holiday experience for 30-50% less — through smart decisions that uninformed tourists don't make.

Every tip here has been tested across European destinations. Total potential savings: €150-400 per person per trip.

Flights — pay less for the same seat

1. Book 6-8 weeks ahead, on Tuesday morning

Airlines release promotions Monday evening. Tuesday morning has the most options at reduced prices. Under 6 weeks: prices climb steadily. Over 3 months: prices are standard (not cheap, not expensive).

Real example: London → Barcelona , same date: £55 at 7 weeks, £95 at 3 weeks, £180 at 5 days.

2. Use a flight comparison engine, not the airline's website

Ryanair and easyJet don't show each other's flights. A comparison engine shows both, plus Wizz Air, Vueling, and legacy carriers. Sometimes a connecting flight on Turkish Airlines is cheaper than a direct on Ryanair.

3. Be flexible ±3 days

Same route, same week: Friday departure might cost £120 while Wednesday costs £55. If you can shift your trip by a day or two, the savings are dramatic.

4. Don't pay for checked luggage if you don't need it

A 3-4 night city break fits in a free personal item (40×30×20 cm at Ryanair/easyJet). Checked luggage costs £25-50 per direction. That's £50-100 saved by packing smarter .

👉 Destinations under €100 return: many of the cheapest European destinations have direct budget flights.

Accommodation — same comfort, lower price

5. Stay in Zone 2-3, not the tourist centre

The price difference between a hotel in the historic centre and one 10-15 minutes away by metro is 30-50%. The experience difference: almost zero.

In London : Earl's Court is 40% cheaper than Westminster. In Barcelona : Eixample saves 30% over Gothic Quarter. In Rome : Trastevere is more atmospheric AND cheaper than the centro storico.

6. Apartment with kitchen beats hotel for 5+ nights

An apartment at €50/night with a kitchen vs a hotel at €70/night without breakfast. The apartment saves €20/night on the room AND €15/day on breakfast and lunch (you prep simple meals). Over 7 nights: €245 saved.

7. Shoulder season = 20-30% off everything

May-June and September-October in the Mediterranean: warm weather, empty beaches, lower prices. Our overtourism guide explains why this also means avoiding the new tourist taxes and visitor caps.

Transport — stop overpaying for taxis

8. Bolt/Uber instead of street taxis

Street taxis are the #1 tourist scam — rigged meters, "broken" meters, scenic routes. Bolt and Uber: fixed price, GPS-tracked route, card payment. Savings: 30-50% per ride and zero arguments.

9. Contactless payment beats paper tickets

In London , a single paper metro ticket costs £7. Contactless payment caps at £8.90/day for unlimited Zone 1-2 travel. Same logic in Barcelona, Milan, Vienna — contactless or local apps are always cheaper than paper tickets.

10. Walking is free and finds the best places

Most European city centres are walkable in 20-30 minutes. The best discoveries — hidden restaurants, quiet squares, street art — are found on foot, not from a taxi window. Don't take the metro for 2 stops.

By train across Europe: Interrail 2026 Complete Guide — from €212 for unlimited travel.

Data and payments — invisible savings that add up

11. eSIM instead of carrier roaming

Roaming in Turkey : €3-15/day. eSIM from Airalo : €5 for 7 days. Savings: €16-100 per week. In the EU roaming is free, but if your plan has data limits, a €5 eSIM backup prevents overage charges.

12. Revolut/Wise = 0% foreign exchange fee

Your bank card adds 1-3% to every foreign currency payment. On €500 spent abroad: €5-15 lost to conversion. Revolut and Wise: 0%. Plus free ATM withdrawals (€200/month on Revolut free plan).

And always choose local currency at ATMs and POS terminals. "Would you like to pay in pounds?" = Dynamic Currency Conversion = 3-8% loss. Full scam explanation .

Food — eat better for less

13. One street away from the attraction

Restaurants on Piazza Navona in Rome , on La Rambla in Barcelona , or on Stradun in Dubrovnik charge 40-60% more than identical-quality places one block back. Walk one street parallel and save €5-10 per meal.

14. Lunch at the market, dinner at the restaurant

Borough Market in London: lunch for £7-10. La Boquería in Barcelona: fresh fruit and jamón for €8. Central Market Hall in Budapest : full meal for €6-8. Markets are cheaper, fresher, and more fun than sit-down lunch restaurants.

15. All-inclusive is sometimes the cheapest option

Paradoxically, for Antalya , Greek Islands , or a Mediterranean cruise , all-inclusive is cheaper than paying separately for meals. An AI hotel at €50/night includes 3 meals + snacks + drinks. The same food à la carte: €30-50/day.

Protection — the cheapest "expense"

Bonus: Travel insurance = the cheapest thing you'll buy

£15-25 for a week of complete protection : medical emergencies (£2-5 million), repatriation, lost baggage, trip cancellation. Without it, a single hospital night costs €500-3,000 . And if your flight gets cancelled , EU261 entitles you to €250-600 — but insurance covers what EU261 doesn't (your hotel, missed connections, personal costs).

That's a free flight, or a hotel upgrade, or 3 extra GetYourGuide experiences — just from making smarter choices.

### Întrebări frecvente

R: The combination: budget flights (Ryanair, easyJet, Wizz Air — from £20 one-way) + accommodation in Zone 2-3 (30-50% cheaper than centre) + eSIM instead of roaming (€5 vs €5-15/day) + eating at local restaurants (not tourist traps) + Revolut/Wise for payments (0% FX fee). ## Cabin Baggage Rules 2026: Wizz Air, Ryanair, British Airways and the New Liquids Rule

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/cabin-baggage-rules-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-29
Actualizat: 2026-07-29
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/bagaj-mana-dimensiuni-reguli-2026

Descriere: Exact cabin baggage dimensions for major airlines in 2026, the new liquids rule at UK and EU airports, and how to avoid €50–100 gate fees for oversized bags.

Răspuns scurt: Wizz Air free bag: 40×30×20 cm under the seat. Trolley in overhead bin requires Wizz Priority (extra charge) — without it, trolleys are taken at the gate and charged €50–100. Ryanair free bag: 40×20×25 cm under the seat. Overhead bin requires Priority Boarding. British Airways and full-service carriers: one cabin bag plus a personal item allowed free for all passengers. New in 2026 at many UK and EU airports: the 100ml liquid restriction has been lifted for airports with new CT scanners — but verify for each airport, as the rule still applies where old scanners remain.

Cabin baggage rules are the most frequently misunderstood area of air travel — and the most penalised. A bag that is 2 cm too wide, or a trolley without the right add-on purchased, can cost €50–100 at the gate. The rules are not complicated once you know them, but they differ meaningfully between airlines and have changed at several airports in 2026. Here is exactly what applies.

The fundamental distinction: personal item vs cabin trolley

Every passenger on every airline is entitled to carry items onto the aircraft. The question is which items and what size:

Personal item (under the seat in front): a small bag — backpack, tote, laptop bag, handbag — that fits under the seat. Included free in every ticket on every airline, including budget carriers.

Cabin trolley (overhead bin): a larger, wheeled bag that goes in the overhead compartment. On full-service carriers (British Airways, Lufthansa, Turkish Airlines), this is included free. On budget carriers (Wizz Air, Ryanair, easyJet), it requires an additional purchase.

Understanding this distinction prevents the most common and most expensive baggage mistake: arriving at a Wizz Air or Ryanair gate with a trolley you assumed was included, and paying €50–100 to have it gate-checked.


Wizz Air: exact rules for 2026

Free allowance (every ticket)

Item Maximum dimensions Maximum weight Storage
Personal item 40 × 30 × 20 cm 10 kg Under seat

This is the only bag included in a standard Wizz Air ticket. The 40×30×20 cm measurement includes wheels, handles, and all protrusions. The bag must fit entirely under the seat in front — not in the overhead bin.

What fits: a medium backpack, a laptop bag, a tote bag. Not a trolley.

With WIZZ Priority

Item Maximum dimensions Maximum weight Storage
Cabin trolley 55 × 40 × 23 cm 10 kg Overhead bin
Personal item 40 × 30 × 20 cm 10 kg Under seat

WIZZ Priority allows you to board first and bring a trolley into the overhead bin. It is purchased at booking or up to 3 hours before departure online (cheapest option). At the airport: significantly more expensive.

WIZZ Priority prices: vary by route and demand — typically €6–15/person/segment online.

What happens without Priority and with a trolley

If you arrive at the gate with an overhead-bin-size bag and no WIZZ Priority, the bag is taken from you and loaded in the aircraft hold. You receive a hold baggage fee of €50–100 depending on the route and when it is applied. This is the most common expensive surprise at Wizz Air gates.

The prevention: if you want to travel with a trolley in the cabin, add WIZZ Priority at booking. If you are travelling on a city break with a small personal bag only, the standard ticket is sufficient.

Hold baggage (checked)

Options added online at booking or later:


10 kg: available on some routes

20 kg: most common, €15–40 depending on route and timing

26 kg or 32 kg: available on longer routes


Key rule: hold baggage added online is always cheaper than at the airport check-in desk.


Ryanair: exact rules for 2026

Free allowance (every ticket)

Item Maximum dimensions Maximum weight Storage
Small personal bag 40 × 20 × 25 cm No stated limit Under seat

Ryanair's free bag is notably narrower than Wizz Air's (20 cm vs 30 cm width). A bag that comfortably fits Wizz Air's allowance may not fit Ryanair's. This catches many travellers who switch between the two airlines.

With Priority Boarding

Item Maximum dimensions Maximum weight Storage
Cabin trolley 55 × 40 × 20 cm 10 kg Overhead bin
Small personal bag 40 × 20 × 25 cm — Under seat

Priority Boarding prices: typically €6–14/person/segment, purchased at booking (cheapest), or online before check-in.

Ryanair's "2 bags" misunderstanding

Many Ryanair passengers believe they can bring a backpack AND a trolley without Priority. They cannot. Without Priority Boarding: one bag only (under the seat). With Priority Boarding: trolley in overhead plus one personal item under the seat. Attempting to board with two bags without Priority results in one being gate-checked at the standard hold baggage fee.


British Airways: rules for 2026

British Airways includes a cabin bag for all passengers without an additional purchase:

Fare type Cabin bag Personal item
Economy (no seat fee) 1 bag, 56 × 45 × 25 cm, 23 kg 1 personal item
Economy (Flexi) Same Same
Business/First 2 bags 1 personal item

No Priority Boarding required for overhead bin access — it is standard for all passengers.

Note: BA's weight limit for cabin baggage (23 kg) is substantially higher than budget carriers' 10 kg limit. However, staff sometimes verify weight on popular routes — the limit is real, not merely notional.


Full-service carriers: general comparison

Airline Free cabin bag Dimensions Weight limit
British Airways ✅ Included 56 × 45 × 25 cm 23 kg
Lufthansa ✅ Included 55 × 40 × 23 cm 8 kg
Turkish Airlines ✅ Included 55 × 40 × 20 cm 8 kg
easyJet ❌ Requires "PLUS" 56 × 45 × 25 cm —
Wizz Air ❌ Requires Priority 55 × 40 × 23 cm 10 kg
Ryanair ❌ Requires Priority 55 × 40 × 20 cm 10 kg
Vueling ❌ Requires upgrade 55 × 35 × 25 cm 10 kg


The 2026 liquid rule changes: what has actually changed and where

The classic 100ml liquid restriction — all liquids in containers of 100ml or less, in a single clear 1-litre bag — has been in place since 2006. In 2026, this is changing at airports that have upgraded to new CT (computed tomography) scanning technology.

Where the 100ml rule has been lifted

Airports with CT scanners can detect liquids and threats in context without requiring passengers to remove them. At these airports:


Container size: up to 2 litres (approximately) permitted

No clear bag required: liquids stay in your bag

Electronics: laptops and tablets can remain in your bag


UK airports with CT scanners (as of mid-2026):


London Heathrow (all terminals)

London Gatwick

Manchester

Birmingham

Edinburgh

Most other major UK airports


EU airports with CT scanners (partial list, expanding):


Amsterdam Schiphol

Frankfurt

Paris CDG (most terminals)

Madrid Barajas

Rome Fiumicino (partially)

Some terminals at other major hubs


Where the 100ml rule still applies

Airports that have not yet upgraded their scanning equipment — including many regional and smaller airports — still enforce the classic 100ml rule. If you are flying from or connecting through one of these airports, the old restrictions apply in full.

Critical point for return journeys: if you buy large bottles of water or toiletries at your destination and return through an airport that still uses old scanners, those items will be confiscated. Always check the security rules at your departure airport for the return leg.

The rule still in force everywhere

Even at CT-equipped airports, the following always apply:


Prohibited items (regardless of liquid status): firearms, knives, flammable materials

Security screening: bags still go through the X-ray machine

Pre-flight checks: passport control, boarding pass verification



Practical packing for carry-on only

Travelling with carry-on only eliminates checked baggage fees (€15–50 each way on budget carriers), eliminates wait time at baggage claim, and eliminates the risk of lost luggage . For city breaks and most holidays of under 7 nights, it is entirely feasible.

What fits in 40×30×20 cm (Wizz Air personal item) for a 4-night trip:


4 sets of clothing (t-shirts roll efficiently, not fold)

1 pair of trousers/jeans + 1 lighter bottom

1 light jacket or knitwear

Underwear and socks

Toiletries bag (within liquid limits or at a CT-equipped airport)

Laptop, chargers, phone accessories

Shoes: wear the bulkiest pair, pack light sandals or fold-flat shoes


The rolling technique: roll clothing rather than folding. A rolled t-shirt takes 60% of the space of a folded one, wrinkles less, and allows you to see all items at a glance without unpacking.

The shoe problem: shoes are the most space-inefficient item. Wear your heaviest pair through security. Pack one pair of light alternatives. Three pairs of shoes for a 7-night trip: too many.


How to avoid gate baggage fees

Weigh your bag at home: use a luggage scale (€5–10, worth every cent). Bathroom scales are not sufficiently accurate for a 10 kg limit. The gate scale at the airport is calibrated precisely — a bag weighing 10.4 kg will be flagged.

Measure including all protrusions: place your bag in the airline's sizer gauge mentally before arriving — include wheels, extended handles, side pockets, and any outer padding. If in doubt, measure physically with a tape measure.

Add upgrades online, not at the airport: WIZZ Priority and Ryanair Priority Boarding purchased at the gate or check-in desk cost 2–4× what they cost online at booking. If you know you want to travel with a trolley, buy the upgrade at booking.

Pack versatile, light clothing: the single most effective strategy for staying within limits. High-quality merino wool (lightweight, odour-resistant, machine washable) compresses better and needs less of it than synthetic alternatives.


What to always carry in your cabin bag, never check

Regardless of which airline you are flying or how much hold baggage you have, these items should always be in your cabin bag:


Passport and travel documents — if your hold bag is delayed, you need these to enter the country

Prescription medication — enough for the trip plus 3 extra days in case of delay

Laptop, tablet, camera — airline liability for electronics in checked baggage is limited; see lost luggage rights

Cash and bank cards — if checked bags are delayed, you need money

Phone and charger

Glasses or contact lenses and solution

Keys — you need to get into your home on return

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Can I bring a trolley on Wizz Air for free?
R: No. Wizz Air's free baggage allowance is a single personal item of 40×30×20 cm that must fit under the seat. Trolleys (overhead bin-size bags) are only permitted with WIZZ Priority, which costs extra. Without Priority, trolleys are confiscated at the gate and sent to the hold for a fee of €50–100. If you plan to take a trolley on board, add WIZZ Priority online when booking — it costs less than the gate fee.

Î: What is the difference between Wizz Air and Ryanair baggage allowances?
R: Both allow one free personal item under the seat: Wizz Air allows 40×30×20 cm (wider), Ryanair allows 40×20×25 cm (narrower but taller). Both require an upgrade (Wizz Priority / Ryanair Priority Boarding) to bring a trolley into the overhead bin. Ryanair's free bag is noticeably narrower — a bag that fits Wizz Air may not fit Ryanair. Always measure before travelling.

Î: Has the 100ml liquid rule changed in 2026?
R: At airports with new CT scanners (including London Heathrow, Manchester, most major UK airports as of 2024, and selected EU airports), the 100ml restriction has been lifted — you can carry larger liquid containers and do not need to remove them from your bag. However, the old 100ml rule still applies at airports that have not yet upgraded their scanning equipment. Always check the specific airport before travelling.

Î: What is the maximum weight for cabin baggage?
R: Wizz Air: 10 kg for the personal item or Priority bag. Ryanair: 10 kg for the Priority trolley (the free item has no specified weight limit but must fit under the seat). British Airways: 23 kg combined for cabin bag plus personal item. Full-service carriers typically allow 7–12 kg. Note that cabin baggage weight limits are enforced less rigorously than hold baggage, but overweight bags at the gate are sent to the hold at standard hold baggage prices.

Î: Can I bring a backpack AND a trolley on a Ryanair flight?
R: Only with Priority Boarding. Without Priority: you can bring one bag only (40×20×25 cm, under the seat). With Priority: one trolley (55×40×20 cm, overhead bin) PLUS one small personal item (under the seat). Attempting to board with both items without Priority Boarding results in one item being gate-checked.

Î: Are wheels and handles included in the bag dimensions?
R: Yes, always. Bag dimensions include wheels, handles, side pockets, and any extension when the handle is retracted. A trolley advertised as '55 cm' may measure 58 cm with the handle base — measure your actual bag before travel. The sizer gauges at check-in use real dimensions including all protrusions.

Î: What items must I always carry in cabin baggage?
R: Passport and travel documents, prescription medication (enough for the trip plus 3 extra days), laptop and valuable electronics, cash, bank cards, keys, irreplaceable items (jewellery, family photos). The airline's liability for items lost from checked luggage is capped — valuables in the hold are lost at the standard Montreal Convention limit of approximately €1,500.

## 10 Cheapest Destinations from Bucharest 2026: Direct Flights Under €100 Return

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/cheapest-destinations-from-bucharest
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-31

Descriere: The best-value European city breaks reachable by direct budget flight from Bucharest Henri Coandă Airport in 2026. Real prices, daily budgets, what to see, and when to book for each destination.

Răspuns scurt: The cheapest destinations reachable by direct flight from Bucharest in 2026 are: Budapest (from €30 return, 1h20), Rome (from €40, 2h30), Bari (from €40, 2h), Milan (from €45, 2h40), Vienna (from €45, 2h10), Athens (from €50, 2h20), London (from €50, 3h30), Istanbul (from €55, 2h), Barcelona (from €55, 3h10), and Paris (from €60, 3h10). The strategy: book Wizz Air or Ryanair 6–8 weeks ahead, on Tuesday, for mid-week departure. All prices are round-trip per person, achievable outside peak season.

Bucharest Henri Coandă Airport is one of the most underrated departure points in Europe for budget travel. Wizz Air alone operates 60+ direct routes; Ryanair has expanded aggressively since 2023. The result: an extraordinary number of European city breaks within reach for under €100 return, and some for as little as €30.

This guide covers the 10 best-value destinations reachable directly from Bucharest in 2026 — with real prices, daily budgets, the essential things to see, and exactly how to book the cheapest fare.

How to Book the Cheapest Flight from Bucharest — The System

Before the destinations, the method. These cheap prices exist, but they're not always visible on the first search.

Book 6–8 weeks in advance: This is the sweet spot. Under 4 weeks, prices rise consistently. Over 3 months, prices are standard — no early booking discount. The promotional fares appear most reliably in the 6–8 week window.

Search on Tuesday or Wednesday: Airlines typically release and update promotional inventory Monday evening. Tuesday morning searches show the most newly available cheap fares. Friday and Saturday are the most expensive days to search and to fly.

Fly mid-week: The same route can vary by €30–70 between a Friday/Sunday departure (premium pricing for weekend travellers) and a Tuesday/Wednesday departure. If your schedule allows any flexibility, mid-week saves significantly.

Use a flight comparison engine: Wizz Air and Ryanair don't show each other's fares. A comparison tool shows all airlines simultaneously — sometimes a Turkish Airlines connection via Istanbul is cheaper than a direct Wizz Air fare for the same dates. The search widget above shows real-time prices and routes from Bucharest.

Be flexible on dates ±3 days: The calendar view on comparison engines often shows dramatically different prices for the same week. Moving departure from Friday to Wednesday can save €40–60 on the same route.


1. Budapest — From €30 Return (1h 20min)

Budapest is the closest thing to a guaranteed cheap flight from Bucharest. Wizz Air operates multiple daily flights; the route is competitive and frequently on promotion. At 1h20, it's shorter than many domestic Romanian train journeys.

Why it's worth it: Budapest has extraordinary density of experiences per euro — thermal baths, a spectacular Parliament building, the best ruin bar scene in Europe, Michelin-starred restaurants at half-Western-European prices, and the Danube. It also has some of the cheapest food and accommodation of any Central European capital.

Daily budget: €40–60 (meal €8–14, coffee €2–3, accommodation from €30/night for good hostels, €55–80 for 3-star hotels)

Don't miss:


Széchenyi Thermal Baths (€22–30, book in advance in summer)

Parliament building guided tour (€15, jaw-dropping neo-Gothic interior)

Ruin bars in the Jewish Quarter (Szimpla Kert — free entry, extraordinary atmosphere)

Fisherman's Bastion at dawn (free, best panoramic view of the city)

Danube cruise with dinner (€20–40 via GetYourGuide)


When to book flights: Budapest flights from Bucharest are cheap year-round. Christmas markets in December are spectacular and accommodation is reasonable.

Insider tip: The Budapest Card (72h, €50) covers unlimited public transport plus free entry to 12 museums and discounts at baths. Worth it if you're visiting 3+ museums.

2. Rome — From €40 Return (2h 30min)

Rome needs no introduction, but the prices might surprise you. Wizz Air and Ryanair both fly direct from Bucharest to Rome Fiumicino (Wizz Air) and Rome Ciampino (Ryanair). Direct flight time: 2h30.

Why it's worth it: The density of world history per square kilometre is unmatched on Earth. The Colosseum, the Vatican, the Pantheon, the Trevi Fountain, Trastevere — all within walking distance of each other. And unlike many European capitals, Rome's street food and neighbourhood restaurants are genuinely affordable.

Daily budget: €50–80 (meals €10–20 at neighbourhood restaurants, coffee €1.50 at the bar standing up, accommodation from €60/night for decent central options)

Trastevere neighbourhood at dinner time (walk and eat where locals eat)

Piazza Navona at dusk (free, beautiful)

3. Bari — From €40 Return (2h)

Bari is the underrated gem on this list. Capital of Puglia, southern Italy — direct flights from Bucharest for as low as €40 return, and a city that rewards the visitor with extraordinary food, a beautiful old town, and beaches.

Why it's the best-value Italian destination: Daily budgets of €35–50 are realistic. A full meal at a trattoria: €10–14. Excellent espresso: €1. Beautiful Baroque architecture, medieval old town (Bari Vecchia with its labyrinthine streets), and Basilica di San Nicola (where St Nicholas — the original Santa Claus — is buried).

Day trips from Bari (all under 1 hour):


Alberobello — UNESCO-listed trulli houses (unique conical-roofed buildings), train €4.50 return

Polignano a Mare — dramatic cliffs over a crystal-blue sea, train €3 return

Matera — UNESCO cave city ("Sassi"), oldest continuously inhabited city in the world, 1h30 by bus


When to go: Bari is perfect in May–June and September–October. July–August is hot (35–40°C) but still beautiful if you're beach-focused.

Flights: Wizz Air and Ryanair both operate direct routes. Bari is also a cruise port — if you're combining with a Mediterranean cruise via GetYourGuide shore excursions, Bari is an excellent base.


4. Milan — From €45 Return (2h 40min)

Milan is Italy's fashion and business capital, which sounds expensive — but flights are competitive and the city has significant budget-friendly layers once you get past the luxury boutiques of Quadrilatero della Moda.

Why it's worth it: Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper (Santa Maria delle Grazie), the extraordinary Gothic cathedral (Duomo di Milano — rooftop access €13), the Brera Gallery (Raphael, Caravaggio, Mantegna), and the Navigli canal district for aperitivo culture (€8–12 for a drink that comes with a full buffet of food — the Milanese "happy hour" tradition).

Daily budget: €55–80 (Milan is pricier than Rome, but the aperitivo tradition — buy one drink, access a full buffet — saves significantly on dinner)

Don't miss:


Duomo di Milano + rooftop terrace (€13 rooftop, cathedral free)

Last Supper by Leonardo da Vinci (€15, Santa Maria delle Grazie — book 2–3 weeks ahead minimum)

Aperitivo in the Navigli district (18:00–21:00, buy a drink, eat for free)

Pinacoteca di Brera (€15, extraordinary Renaissance collection)

Castello Sforzesco (free entry to courtyards, €5 for museums inside)


Day trips: Lake Como (1h by train, €8 return), Bergamo (50 min by train, €6 return — the medieval upper city is stunning), or Verona (1h15, €11 return — Romeo and Juliet's city).


5. Vienna — From €45 Return (2h 10min)

Vienna is Austrian precision meeting Habsburg grandeur. Direct flights on Wizz Air and Austrian Airlines (more expensive) make it easily reachable from Bucharest in 2h10. The city can be expensive but has a strong free-and-cheap layer: the Naschmarkt food market, Schönbrunn Palace gardens (free), and the world's best coffee house culture.

Daily budget: €55–80 (meals €12–20, coffee culture where you can sit for hours for one €4 Melange, accommodation from €70/night)

Don't miss:


Schönbrunn Palace (gardens free, palace interior €16–30 depending on tour)

Belvedere (Upper Belvedere: Klimt's The Kiss, €17)

Naschmarkt (free to browse, lunch from €8)

Vienna State Opera house tour or standing-room tickets (€10–13, available 80 minutes before performance — world-class opera for the price of a coffee)

Kunsthistorisches Museum (€16, extraordinary art collection)

Prater and the Riesenrad Ferris wheel (€13, vintage 1897 Ferris wheel with panoramic views)


The coffee house tradition: Vienna's historic coffee houses (Café Central, Café Landtmann, Café Hawelka) are living institutions where you can sit for 2–3 hours nursing a single coffee and reading newspapers. Nobody will rush you. Budget €4–6 for the experience.

👉 Full guide: Things to Do in Vienna


6. Athens — From €50 Return (2h 20min)

Athens is one of the most underrated capitals in Europe for value. Direct flights from Bucharest on Wizz Air and Aegean Airlines; the city has low daily costs, extraordinary ancient history, and the best seafood you'll eat anywhere in the Mediterranean.

Daily budget: €45–65 (meal at a taverna €10–15, excellent gyros €3–4, accommodation from €50/night for good central options)

Don't miss:


Acropolis (€20, Athens Pass available for multiple sites) — go at opening (8:00 AM) to beat heat and crowds

Acropolis Museum (€10, extraordinary, modern, right below the hill)

Monastiraki flea market (free, Saturday is best)

Plaka neighbourhood (walking, free)

Seafood dinner in Piraeus or Mikrolimano harbour (€15–25/person, fresh catch)

Cape Sounion day trip (€14 for the temple of Poseidon on a cliff over the Aegean)


Island hopping from Athens: Athens is the gateway to the Greek islands via Piraeus ferry port. Aegina (1h ferry, €9), Hydra (2h, €30), or Poros (2h, €25) all make extraordinary day trips. For longer island stays, see our Greek Islands guide .

7. London — From €50 Return (3h 30min)

London requires a slightly longer caveat: it's the most expensive city on this list for daily costs, and the UK requires a travel insurance policy and an eSIM (EU roaming doesn't apply post-Brexit). But flights from Bucharest are genuinely cheap (Wizz Air to Luton, Ryanair to Stansted), and London's density of world-class free museums is unmatched globally.

Daily budget: £60–100 (meals £8–25 depending on where you eat, transport £8.90/day contactless cap, free museums = £0 for most major attractions)

Don't miss (all free):


British Museum (Egyptian mummies, Rosetta Stone, Elgin Marbles)

Natural History Museum (blue whale, dinosaur hall)

Victoria & Albert Museum (fashion, design, decorative arts)

Tate Modern (world-class contemporary art, South Bank)

National Gallery (Vermeer, van Gogh, Turner)


Essential London logistics: Use contactless bank card or phone for all Tube and bus travel (daily cap £8.90 zones 1–2). UK ETA required (£10, apply online). Travel insurance with UK cover essential (EHIC not valid post-Brexit). eSIM from Airalo or Saily saves €50–100 vs carrier roaming.

8. Istanbul — From €55 Return (2h)

Istanbul is the closest major city to Romania geographically — just 2 hours by direct flight — and offers extraordinary value combined with some of the most visually dramatic sights in the world. The Blue Mosque, Hagia Sophia, the Bosphorus, the Grand Bazaar — all concentrated within walking distance of each other.

Daily budget: €35–55 (Istanbul is excellent value — full restaurant meal €6–12, accommodation from €30/night for decent hotels in Sultanahmet, Turkish tea everywhere for €0.50)

Don't miss:


Hagia Sophia (now a mosque, free entry, remove shoes, cover hair — extraordinary architecture)

Blue Mosque (free, active mosque, requires appropriate dress)

Topkapi Palace (€20, 600 years of Ottoman history, extraordinary treasury)

Grand Bazaar (free to browse, 60 covered streets, 4,000 shops)

Bosphorus cruise (€10–15 for public ferry TK Tours, or evening dinner cruise via GetYourGuide)

Galata Tower (€10, views over both the European and Asian sides)


Essential Istanbul logistics: Travel insurance is essential — Turkey is non-EU, EHIC doesn't apply, and private hospital costs are high. eSIM is critical — buy before arriving in Turkey, as eSIM provider websites are blocked from within the country since 2025.

9. Barcelona — From €55 Return (3h 10min)

Barcelona combines beach access, extraordinary architecture, world-class food, and a vibrant urban culture. Direct flights on Wizz Air and Ryanair. The city is more expensive than Eastern European capitals but comparable to Rome.

Daily budget: €55–80 (meals €12–20 at neighbourhood spots, coffee €2–3, accommodation from €65/night)

Don't miss:


Sagrada Família (€26–36, Gaudí's unfinished masterpiece — book weeks ahead)

Park Güell (€10, Gaudí park with views; free areas in surrounding park)

Gothic Quarter (free, walking)

La Boqueria market (free to browse, lunch from €8)

Barceloneta Beach (free)

Montjuïc cable car + castle (€15 return cable car, €5 castle)


Gaudí package: Barcelona's major Gaudí sites (Sagrada Família, Casa Batlló, Casa Milà/La Pedrera, Park Güell) each sell out independently. Book all of them through GetYourGuide as skip-the-line when official sites show limited availability.

10. Paris — From €60 Return (3h 10min)

Paris is the most expensive destination on this list but consistently one of the most searched routes from Bucharest. Wizz Air flies to Beauvais (90 km from Paris — note the bus transfer adds £17 and 75 minutes); other options to Orly or CDG via code-shares are pricier but more central.

Daily budget: €60–95 (meals €12–20 at neighbourhood bistros, transport €16.90/day Navigo, accommodation from €80/night for decent central hotels)

Don't miss:


Eiffel Tower (€26–35 to summit, or free to stand underneath)

Louvre (€22 — first Sunday of the month is FREE, but expect 2-hour queues)

Notre-Dame Cathedral (undergoing final phases of renovation from 2019 fire — exterior viewing is possible)

Montmartre and Sacré-Cœur (free, extraordinary neighbourhood)

Musée d'Orsay (€16, Impressionists — Monet, Renoir, Degas, Van Gogh)

Galleries Lafayette rooftop (free, panoramic views)


Paris budget tip: The first Sunday of each month, the Louvre is free (€0 instead of €22). But queues form from early morning and can reach 2 hours. Alternatively, book a skip-the-line Louvre ticket through GetYourGuide to combine morning entry with a guide.
