### Întrebări frecvente

Î: What is the cheapest destination from Bucharest by plane?
R: Budapest consistently ranks as the cheapest: Wizz Air flies direct in 1h20 from €30 return. Rome and Bari are close behind (from €40 return). The key to these prices is booking 6–8 weeks ahead, Tuesday–Thursday departures, and avoiding July–August school holiday peak.

Î: Which airline has the most direct routes from Bucharest?
R: Wizz Air operates the most routes from Bucharest Henri Coandă (OTP), with 60+ direct destinations across Europe and the Middle East. Ryanair has significantly expanded from Bucharest since 2023 and now offers 35+ direct routes, often competing directly with Wizz Air on price. Tarom serves Western European capitals but at higher prices. Blue Air went bankrupt in 2022 — any Blue Air route is now served by Wizz or Ryanair.

Î: When are the cheapest flights from Bucharest?
R: January–March and November offer the lowest prices (avoiding Christmas/New Year). Best value with good weather: May–June and September–October. Peak prices: July–August and school holiday weeks (Easter, 1 May, Christmas). Book Tuesday or Wednesday mornings 6–8 weeks before departure for the best combination of price and availability.

Î: Do I need a travel visa for these destinations?
R: No. All 10 destinations in this guide are accessible to Romanian citizens (EU nationals) without a visa. The UK now requires an Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA, £10, takes 10 minutes) — apply online at least 72 hours before flying. Turkey requires no visa for stays under 90 days. All other destinations are standard EU freedom of movement.

Î: Do I need travel insurance for European city breaks?
R: The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) covers medical emergencies at public hospitals within the EU — but not repatriation, trip cancellation, lost luggage, or non-EU destinations (UK, Turkey). For UK and Turkey in particular, travel insurance is essential. A week's policy covering Europe costs €12–25 — less than a restaurant dinner.

Î: Do I need an eSIM for these destinations?
R: For EU destinations (Rome, Vienna, Budapest, Athens, Barcelona, Paris, Bari, Milan), your Romanian SIM has free EU roaming — no eSIM needed unless your data plan has low limits. For the UK (post-Brexit) and Turkey, your Romanian carrier charges €3–12/day roaming. An eSIM from Airalo costs €5–12 for 7 days and saves €16–70 per trip. Buy before departure — especially for Turkey, where eSIM provider sites are blocked from within the country.

Î: Which is better — Wizz Air or Ryanair from Bucharest?
R: Depends on the route. Compare both every time — they don't show each other's prices. Wizz Air is typically cheaper on Eastern European routes (Budapest, Warsaw, Vilnius) and has more direct routes overall. Ryanair often undercuts on Western routes (London Stansted, Barcelona, Madrid, Lisbon) since their Bucharest expansion. Always use a flight comparison tool to see both simultaneously.

Î: How much does a 3-night city break from Bucharest cost in total?
R: Budget breakdown for a typical 3-night city break from Bucharest: Flights return: €40–100. Accommodation (3 nights, mid-range hotel): €90–200. Local transport (3 days): €10–30. Food and drink: €60–150. Attractions: €0–60. Total realistic range: €200–540 per person. Budapest, Bari, and Athens offer the best value at the lower end; London and Paris sit at the higher end.

## How to Find Cheap Flights: Complete 2026 Guide

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/cum-gasesti-bilete-avion-ieftine
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-10
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/cum-gasesti-bilete-avion-ieftine

Descriere: Date flexibility, price alerts, alternative airports, real baggage comparisons and the mistakes that make you overpay. With 2026 prices and data.

Răspuns scurt: The most effective methods for cheap flights are: be flexible on dates (Tuesday–Wednesday departures are 13–14% cheaper than Sunday), set price alerts on Google Flights or Kiwi, book 4–8 weeks ahead for European flights, compare alternative airports (differences of 30–50% are common), and always compare the TOTAL price with baggage included — a Wizz Air ticket at €40 can become €95 after bags. Prices for the same route can vary by 200–300%.

The price of a flight can vary by 200–300% for the same route depending on when and how you search. A Bucharest → Barcelona can cost €55 at 7 weeks out, €95 at 3 weeks, and €180 with 5 days to go. Same plane, same seat — completely different price.

It is not luck or magic. There are specific, documented methods — tested against real 2026 data — that consistently reduce what you pay by 20–50%. This guide covers all of them, from the fundamentals (date flexibility, alerts) to advanced techniques (virtual interlining, error fares, real baggage comparisons). With concrete prices and examples for European travellers.

1. Be flexible on dates — the single biggest saving

If you could choose only one method, this is it. The price difference between days of the week is not 5–10% — it is 30–50% on the same routes.

Which days are cheapest

According to KAYAK's analysis of 917 million fares (January 2025 – March 2026):

Departure day Price level Why
Tuesday Cheapest Minimum demand — neither business nor leisure
Wednesday Very cheap Same pattern, avoided by most travellers
Saturday morning Cheap Early departure = avoided by families
Monday Medium-expensive Business travel (start of work week)
Thursday Expensive Early departure for long weekends
Friday evening Expensive Maximum demand — weekend + business
Sunday Most expensive Everyone returning home

The concrete difference: Tuesday departures are 13–14% cheaper than Sunday. On a €150 route, that is €20–21 saved. On a €400 intercontinental route, €52–56.

How to use flexibility in practice

Google Flights — calendar view:


Search your route (e.g. London → Barcelona)

For dates, select "Flexible dates" or "Whole month"

The calendar shows daily prices, colour-coded: green = cheap, red = expensive

Moving 1–2 days can save €30–80


Skyscanner — "Cheapest month":


Select your route

For departure date, choose "Cheapest month"

See which months and days have the lowest prices

The "Weekend" vs "Weekday" toggle shows the difference


Kiwi — "± 3 days":


Search your route on Kiwi.com

Enable the "± 3 days" flexibility option on departure and return

Kiwi searches all combinations (49 variants) and sorts by price


Cheapest vs most expensive months

Period Price level Notes
January–February Cheapest Post-holidays, minimum demand
March (first half) Cheap Before Easter holidays
April–May Medium Shoulder season — good value for money
June Expensive Start of summer season
July–August Most expensive Peak season, school holidays
September–October Cheap Shoulder season — best quality-to-price ratio
November Cheap Off-season (exception: Black Friday deals)
December Expensive Winter holidays

Concrete tip: a flight in September costs on average 20–40% less than in July–August, while the weather is still warm in Mediterranean destinations (Greece, Spain, Italy, Croatia). Same hotel, same beach, half-price ticket.

Avoid peak periods

The most expensive times of the year:


Easter holidays (April): prices 30–50% above normal

Early July (school holidays begin): demand explosion

August bank holidays : extended weekends, peak pricing

Christmas and New Year (20 December – 5 January): the most expensive days of the year

Long weekends (May Day, national holidays): increased demand on short routes


If you can depart 3–5 days before or after these periods, you save significantly.

2. Set price alerts — let the algorithm work for you

Flight prices change multiple times per day . A ticket can drop by 30% for a few hours, then return to its previous price. No human can monitor this manually — but alerts can.

Google Flights — the best for price tracking

Google Flights is the strongest monitoring tool in 2026:


Search your route (e.g. London → Athens, 15–22 September)

Click the bell icon or "Track prices"

Google emails you automatically when the price drops significantly

On the results page, you see a price history graph — it shows whether the current price is "typical," "high" or "low" for that route


Why it is the best: Google has access to the most pricing data. Their prediction algorithm shows with high accuracy whether the price will rise or fall in the coming days.

Google Flights Price Guarantee: on flights marked with the "Price Guarantee" badge, if the price drops after you book, Google refunds the difference automatically — no forms, no claims. The limit is approximately $500 per traveller. It works primarily on US domestic flights and selectively on international routes, but when the badge appears, it is a genuine advantage.

Skyscanner — alerts + "Everywhere"

Skyscanner has two unique strengths:

Price alerts: work similarly to Google Flights — set the route, receive notifications on drops. Maximum value on routes where the cheapest ticket comes from a carrier Google does not index perfectly (small low-cost airlines, local agencies).

The "Everywhere" function: you do not know where you want to go, but you want the cheapest flight from your city? Skyscanner is the only engine that does this well. Select your origin, type "Everywhere" as the destination, and see all destinations sorted by price — with prices starting at €19–29 for European routes.

Kiwi — alerts + Nomad

Kiwi has a good alert system, but its standout feature is Nomad : if you want to visit multiple cities and your dates are truly flexible, Nomad finds the cheapest combination of routes. Example: London → Prague → Berlin → Amsterdam → London, with the cheapest flights at each stage.

When to set alerts


3 months before departure: start monitoring

6–8 weeks before : the window when the best prices tend to appear

Act quickly : when you receive a drop alert, check and book — good offers last hours, not days


The core rule: you are not trying to predict the perfect price. Set the alert, wait for a price in the lower range of what you have observed (the Google Flights graph helps), and when it appears — act.

3. Book at the right time — the optimal booking window

There is no magic moment, but there are windows that consistently produce the best prices. CheapAir analysed 917 million fares and identified clear patterns.

Optimal booking windows (2026)

Flight type Optimal window Too early Too late
Short European (2–3 hours) 4–8 weeks ahead 3+ months (prices not yet set) Under 2 weeks (maximum price)
Medium European (3–5 hours) 6–10 weeks ahead 4+ months Under 3 weeks
Intercontinental 2–3 months ahead 6+ months Under 1 month
Peak season (July–August) As early as possible No such thing as too early Everything is too late

Why not "too early"

When you book 4–5 months ahead for a European flight, airlines have not yet started optimising seat fill. The initial price is "standard" — not the highest, but not the lowest either. Discounts come when airlines see the flight is not filling as projected, at 4–8 weeks out.

Why not "too late"

Under 2 weeks, remaining seats are few. The airline's pricing algorithm knows that anyone searching now probably needs to fly (urgency, business) and increases the price. It is supply and demand in its purest form.

The exception: flash sales and exceptional prices

If you see a clearly exceptional price at any point (even 4 months ahead), take it . The rules above are statistical averages — a 50% flash discount at 3 months out beats waiting for the 6-week window.

How to recognise an exceptional price:


Google Flights shows "Low price" on the history graph

It is 30%+ below what you have observed in your alerts

It appears on deal sites (Secret Flying, Fly4Free)


The 28–35 day rule

For standard intra-European flights, the data shows that 28–35 days before departure is the window with the best balance of price and availability. It is not an absolute rule, but it is a solid reference point.

4. Compare alternative airports — differences of 30–50%

Flying from a secondary airport can save 30–50% on the same journey. The trade-off is transfer time, but the calculation often makes sense.

Alternative airports at destination

Going to… The "official" airport Cheaper alternative Typical saving
Paris CDG (Charles de Gaulle) Beauvais (BVA) — Wizz/Ryanair hub 20–40%
London Heathrow (LHR) Stansted (STN), Luton (LTN), Gatwick (LGW) 25–50%
Milan Malpensa (MXP) Bergamo Orio al Serio (BGY) 30–50%
Barcelona El Prat (BCN) Girona (GRO), Reus (REU) 20–40%
Rome Fiumicino (FCO) Ciampino (CIA) 15–30%
Berlin Brandenburg (BER) Wrocław (WRO) — 3.5h by train 20–35%
Brussels Brussels Airport (BRU) Charleroi (CRL) — Ryanair hub 25–45%
Stockholm Arlanda (ARN) Skavsta (NYO) or Västerås (VST) 20–40%

The real calculation: cheap flight + expensive transfer = zero savings?

The alternative airport is cheaper on the ticket, but you still need to reach your actual destination. The correct calculation:

Example: Paris Beauvais vs CDG:


Ticket via Beauvais: €39 (Wizz Air)

Ticket via CDG: €89 (Air France)

Transfer Beauvais → central Paris: bus €17, 75 minutes

Transfer CDG → central Paris: RER €11.80, 35 minutes

Real difference: €89 + €11.80 = €100.80 vs €39 + €17 = €56 → saving of €44.80


Example: London Stansted vs Heathrow:


Ticket via Stansted: €29 (Ryanair)

Ticket via Heathrow: €109 (BA)

Transfer Stansted → central London: Stansted Express £22 (€26), 47 minutes

Transfer Heathrow → central London: Elizabeth Line £12.80 (€15), 35 minutes

Real difference: €109 + €15 = €124 vs €29 + €26 = €55 → saving of €69


Example: Milan Bergamo vs Malpensa:


Ticket via Bergamo: €25 (Ryanair)

Ticket via Malpensa: €75 (easyJet)

Transfer Bergamo → Milano Centrale: bus €7, 60 minutes

Transfer Malpensa → Milano Centrale: Malpensa Express €13, 50 minutes

Real difference: €75 + €13 = €88 vs €25 + €7 = €32 → saving of €56


How to compare airports in Google Flights


In the origin field, click "+"

Add multiple airports (e.g. LHR, STN, LTN, LGW)

Google shows the cheapest ticket from each airport

At the destination, you can do the same — add alternative airports


Always calculate total cost: alternative airport saving minus transfer cost (bus, train, taxi to your actual destination). Sometimes the "cheap" option ends up equal to the direct one. Sometimes it saves €100.

5. Compare the TOTAL price — not the base fare

This is the number one trap for European travellers. A Wizz Air ticket at €29 looks better than a Lufthansa ticket at €99 — until you add the baggage.

Hidden costs at low-cost carriers

Wizz Air — 2026 fees

Element Basic Wizz Go Wizz Plus
Small bag (40×30×20 cm) ✅ Included ✅ Included ✅ Included
Cabin bag (55×40×23 cm, 10 kg) ❌ €10–59 separate ✅ Included ✅ Included
Hold luggage (20 kg) ❌ €13–87 separate ✅ 20 kg included ✅ 32 kg included
Seat selection ❌ €5–40 ✅ Included ✅ Priority seat
Priority boarding ❌ ✅ ✅
Flight change ❌ ✅ (1 free) ✅ (unlimited)
Example ticket price €29–49 €59–99 €89–149

Key note: Wizz Air's hold baggage price varies enormously — from €8.50 (short routes, bought early) to €87 (long routes, bought at the airport). Buying baggage online at the time of booking is almost always cheaper than adding it later.

Excess weight: €13 per kg per flight. A bag at 24 kg instead of 20 kg = €52 extra for a return trip.

Ryanair — 2026 fees

Element Value Regular Plus Flexi Plus

Excess weight Ryanair: €11 per kg — similar to Wizz Air.

Comparison on real scenarios

Scenario 1: City break 3 nights (small bag only)

Carrier Ticket Baggage Extra TOTAL
Wizz Air Basic €35 €0 (small 40×30×20) €0 €35
Ryanair Value €29 €0 (small 40×30×20) €0 €29
easyJet Standard €39 €0 (cabin bag 45×36×20 included) €0 €39
Lufthansa Economy Light €69 €0 (cabin 55×40×23, 8 kg) €0 €69

Winner: low-cost, clearly — but only if everything you need fits in 40×30×20 cm . That means a small backpack, no trolley.

Scenario 2: Holiday 7 days (20 kg hold bag)

Carrier Ticket Hold bag Extra TOTAL
Wizz Air Basic + bag €35 €35 (20 kg, online) €0 €70
Ryanair Value + bag €29 €25 (20 kg, online) €0 €54
Ryanair Regular €49 €0 (20 kg included) €0 €49

Winner: depends on the route. Ryanair Regular is surprisingly competitive. Lufthansa is more expensive, but includes 23 kg (not 20), a larger cabin bag, and a meal.

Scenario 3: Family of four (2 adults + 2 children, 3 hold bags)

Carrier 4 tickets 3 hold bags Seat selection TOTAL
Wizz Air 4 × €35 = €140 3 × €35 = €105 4 × €10 = €40 €285
Ryanair Regular 4 × €49 = €196 3 × €0 (included) ✅ Included €196
Lufthansa Economy Classic 4 × €99 = €396 ✅ 4 × 23 kg included ✅ Included €396

Winner: Ryanair Regular for short European routes with families. The gap to full-service shrinks as baggage needs grow. At Lufthansa ticket prices under €120 per person, the full-service option becomes equal or better value.

The golden rule

Compare tickets at checkout, with everything you need. Open two tabs — low-cost and full-service — and add every element you will actually use: baggage, seat selection, check-in. The final price is the only one that matters.

6. Use flight search engines strategically

Not all search engines are equal. Each has different strengths — using 2–3 in parallel consistently finds better prices than using only one.

When to use each

Start with Google Flights when:


You know your route and want the best price quickly

You want a visual flexible calendar (cleanest UI in the market)

You want price prediction (will it rise or fall?)

You want long-term price tracking


Add Skyscanner when:


You have no fixed destination — the "Everywhere" function is unmatched

You are looking for small low-cost carriers Google does not index

You want to compare prices across a full month quickly


Use Kiwi when:


Your route has no direct flight or the direct option is very expensive

You are willing to combine different airlines (virtual interlining)

You want multi-city or a trip with multiple stops


Check KAYAK when:


You want "Hacker Fares" — KAYAK combines the cheapest outbound one-way from one airline with the cheapest return one-way from another, when separate one-ways are cheaper than a round-trip


What is "virtual interlining" and how it can save hundreds

Kiwi.com does something the others do not: it combines separate flights from different airlines into a single journey.

Real example:


London → Tokyo direct: €900+

London → Istanbul (Pegasus): €60

Istanbul → Tokyo (Turkish Airlines): €380

Total through Kiwi: €440 — half the price


Kiwi connects these flights automatically. But watch the connection risk : if the first flight is delayed and you miss the second, you have two separate bookings — the second airline has no obligation to wait.

Kiwi protection: Kiwi offers "Kiwi Guarantee" (supplementary insurance) that rebooks you on another flight if you miss the connection. It costs extra but provides real protection. From 2026, Kiwi launched "Disruption Protection with Instant Credit" — you receive instant credit for rebooking.

What is a "Hacker Fare" on KAYAK

KAYAK checks whether two separate one-way tickets from different airlines are cheaper than a round-trip from the same airline. Example:


London → Milan round-trip with easyJet: €89

London → Milan one-way Ryanair: €29

Milan → London one-way Wizz Air: €35

KAYAK Hacker Fare: €64 — saving of €25


The risk is minimal (each ticket is a separate booking, but on distinct flights), and the saving is 10–25% on average.

7. Use connecting flights strategically

Direct flights are more convenient, but on longer routes, a well-chosen connection reduces the price by 30–50% .

Layover is typically 2–4 hours — enough without being exhausting

European city → New York via Warsaw: €350–500 round-trip

LOT prices average 20–30% below Lufthansa on the same routes.

Layover safety rules

Layover duration Verdict Why
Under 1 hour ❌ Very risky Nearly impossible if the first flight is delayed by even 10 minutes
1–1.5 hours ⚠️ Risky Works if everything is perfect, but any delay = missed connection
2–3 hours ✅ Sweet spot Enough even with small delays, no wasted time
3–5 hours ✅ Safe Ideal if you want to explore the airport or lounge
5+ hours ⚠️ Tiring Worth it only if savings are substantial or you can leave the airport

Rule: if you have a single booking (through ticket), the airline rebooks you for free if you miss the connection due to a delay. If you have two separate bookings (as happens on Kiwi), the risk is yours.

Free stopover — hidden bonus

Some airlines offer a free stopover — you can stop for 24+ hours (or even several days) in the hub city at no additional cost on the ticket.


Turkish Airlines : stopover in Istanbul up to 24 hours with free "TourIstanbul" programme (includes meal and guided tour)

Qatar Airways : stopover in Doha with reduced hotel rates

Icelandair : free stopover in Reykjavik (up to 7 days at no extra ticket cost)


It is a way to visit two destinations for the price of one.

8. Check the airline's own website — the final price matters

Search engines are excellent for discovery — they find the cheapest flight from 50+ carriers. But the actual booking can sometimes be cheaper directly on the airline's site.

Why prices differ


OTA commission : Skyscanner, Kiwi, Momondo redirect to OTAs (Online Travel Agencies) that add a commission of €5–25 per ticket

Lower direct prices : some low-cost carriers (Ryanair in particular) display higher prices on aggregators to offset commission

Exclusive offers : airlines sometimes run promotions only on their own website or mobile app


The efficient booking routine


Discover on Google Flights or Skyscanner — find the cheapest flight

Note the airline, date, time, exact route

Open a new tab with the airline's direct website

Search the same route directly — compare the total price (including taxes, baggage, seat)

Book on whichever is cheapest — direct or through the OTA


This process adds 3–5 minutes but regularly saves €10–25 per ticket.

Mobile apps — sometimes cheaper

Wizz Air and Ryanair sometimes offer prices €2–5 lower in the mobile app than on the website. Wizz Air also has Wizz Discount Club (€29.99/year) which gives €5–10 off each ticket + priority + cabin bag — worthwhile if you fly Wizz more than 4–5 times per year.

9. Error fares and flash sales — how to catch them

Error fares (mistake fares) are tickets sold at prices far below normal due to a system error — a decimal point in the wrong place, a currency conversion mistake, or a pricing error when launching a new route.

How real are they

Error fares are rare but real . Documented examples:


Intercontinental business class tickets at €200–400 instead of €3,000+

European flights at €1–15 (yes, under fifteen euros) due to a tax error

New routes launched with test prices that remain active for several hours


Average savings on error fares: €300–1,200 per ticket . But do not rely on them — they are a bonus when they appear, not a planning strategy.

Where to find them

Source Type How it works
Secret Flying Free website Lists error fares and deals daily, including from Eastern Europe
Fly4Free Free website European focus, lists flash deals and error fares
Jack's Flight Club Newsletter (free + paid) Sends alerts when exceptional deals appear — premium (£39/year) receives alerts first
Going (formerly Scott's Cheap Flights) Newsletter (free + paid) Similar to Jack's, premium ($49/year) offers error fares and priority access
Google Flights alerts Free Catches error fares indirectly — any sudden price drop appears in your alert

How to act on an error fare


Book immediately — error fares last hours, not days. The airline corrects the error quickly

Do not call the airline to confirm the price — this draws attention to the error

Pay with a card that offers payment protection

Wait 24–48 hours — if the airline cancels the booking, you get your money back

Do not book anything else (hotel, car, activities) until you have final flight confirmation


Can the airline cancel an error fare?

Yes, airlines have the legal right to cancel tickets sold at incorrect prices. Most European airlines rarely do this (it is bad PR), but it is not guaranteed. EU regulation does not oblige airlines to honour obvious pricing errors.

Rule: book error fares, but do not plan a holiday around them until you have a confirmed ticket.

10. Avoid the mistakes that make you overpay

Mistake 1: Panic booking — "Only 3 seats left!"

"Only 3 seats left at this price!" — may be true, but it is also one of the travel industry's oldest tactics. Prices fluctuate daily. A flight showing "3 seats" at €120 today may show 10 seats tomorrow at €95 — or may indeed sell out. The problem is that you cannot know .

What to do: if you have researched the route, you know the price is good (alerts and the Google Flights history confirm it), and the dates work — book it. If not — set an alert and come back. Panic booking without comparison costs 15–25% more on average.

Mistake 2: Searching on only one engine

No search engine has all flights at all prices. If you only check Google Flights, you miss the offers Skyscanner finds (small low-cost carriers). If you only check Skyscanner, you miss the price prediction from Google.

Rule: minimum 2 engines, plus the airline's direct website.

Mistake 3: Ignoring baggage when comparing

Detailed above — a €29 ticket with €45 baggage is not cheaper than a €69 ticket with baggage included. It seems obvious, but most travellers compare only the base fare.

Mistake 4: Buying baggage at the airport

Baggage bought at the airport costs 2–3 times more than online:

When you buy baggage Wizz Air (20 kg) Ryanair (20 kg)
At booking online €13–35 €25
Later, online €25–55 €30
At the airport €60+ €40–50

Mistake 5: Not using a miles card

If you fly regularly, a loyalty card (or a bank card with miles) can accumulate enough miles for a free flight per year. Relevant programmes:


Wizz Air Wizz Discount Club : €29.99/year, €5–10 discount per ticket + priority + cabin bag

Star Alliance (Lufthansa, Turkish, LOT, Austrian) : miles accumulated on every flight, transferable between airlines

SkyTeam (KLM, Air France, ITA Airways) : shared loyalty programme

oneworld (British Airways, Iberia, Finnair) : Avios points, excellent for short-haul redemptions


Mistake 6: Booking by phone instead of online

Airlines (especially low-cost) add a booking fee if you call the call centre instead of booking online: €15–25 per ticket at Wizz Air, €20 at Ryanair. The exception is if you have a technical problem on the website — you can then request a fee waiver.

Mistake 7: Ignoring the multi-city option

If you are visiting multiple cities, do not book separate tickets. The multi-city option in Google Flights or Skyscanner can be 10–25% cheaper than individual tickets, because it optimises routes.

Example:


London → Barcelona (€55) + Barcelona → Rome (€35) + Rome → London (€45) = €135 separate

Multi-city London → Barcelona → Rome → London = €109 (saving of €26)


11. Advanced techniques — for experienced travellers

Hidden city ticketing — legal but risky

Hidden city ticketing means buying a ticket with a connection and getting off at the connection point, without taking the final flight. Example: a ticket London → Munich → Paris may be cheaper than London → Munich direct, if Paris is a cheap destination.

Real risks:


Works only one-way — if you do not show up for a segment, the airline cancels the rest of the booking

No hold luggage — bags go to the final destination, not the connection

Airlines prohibit this in their terms and conditions — repeated use can cost you your loyalty account

Some airlines have sued Skiplagged (the site that facilitates this)


Potential saving: 20–60%. Recommendation: only for experienced travellers, only one-way, only with carry-on.

One-way vs round-trip — when is it cheaper

At low-cost carriers (Wizz, Ryanair, easyJet), there is no difference — each flight is priced separately. You can buy outbound with one airline and return with another without penalty.

At full-service carriers (Lufthansa, BA, Turkish), the round-trip ticket is usually cheaper than two one-ways. But not always — check both options.

KAYAK Hacker Fares do this automatically: combine the cheapest outbound one-way from one carrier with the cheapest return one-way from another.

When flying as a family (2 adults + 1–2 children), the calculation changes — and so does the winner.

14. Pre-booking checklist

Before you press "Book," check these points:

Pre-booking checklist


Compared on at least 2 search engines (Google Flights + Skyscanner/Kiwi)

Checked the price on the airline's own website

Compared the TOTAL price (ticket + baggage + seat), not just the base fare

Checked alternative airports (origin and destination)

Checked whether shifting 1–2 days on dates drops the price

Checked whether a connecting flight is significantly cheaper

Checked cancellation and change conditions

Bought baggage online (not at the airport)

Checked travel documents needed (passport, visa, ETIAS if applicable)


Travel documents — what to check


EU/Schengen: national ID card or passport

UK (post-Brexit): passport required

Turkey: passport or national ID card (check validity — minimum 6 months on entry for some nationalities)

USA: passport + ESTA (online application, $21, approved within hours)

ETIAS (from 2026): new authorisation system for EU citizens travelling to non-Schengen countries with visa waiver agreements — check if active for your destination


15. Do not be manipulated by artificial urgency

"Only 3 seats left at this price!" — may be true, but it is often a pressure tactic. Prices change, but they do not disappear.

How urgency messaging works

Airlines and OTAs use several tactics:


Scarcity ("3 seats left"): may be true, but "at this price" — the price changes anyway

Countdown timer : creates artificial pressure — the price does not expire, the timer does

"X people looking now" : often exaggerated or irrelevant

Price increase on second search : less common in 2026, but some OTAs still do it


The right response


If you have already researched the route and the price is good — book it. That is not panic, it is an informed decision.

If you have not researched — set an alert and come back. A good price that disappears today may return tomorrow.

Never book hotel/car/activities before you have a confirmed ticket — especially on error fares.


Putting it together: a realistic booking process


Set your destination and rough travel window (± 3 days on each end)

Search on Google Flights and Skyscanner with flexible dates enabled — look at the cheapest-day calendar

Set a price alert on Google Flights for your route

Check Kiwi if the route has no direct flight or the direct is expensive

When a price appears that is in the bottom 25% of what you have been seeing — book it

Before confirming, open the airline's direct website and compare the total price

If booking well in advance, also search for alternative airports at both ends


This process takes one active hour and then passive monitoring via email alerts. Most people who consistently pay less for flights are not doing anything magical — they are just not booking in a rush.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is there a single cheapest day to buy flights?
R: Not a fixed day — the 'Tuesday is cheapest to buy' myth is debunked by 2026 data. Prices change multiple times daily based on demand, not the day of the week. What matters is the DEPARTURE day: flights departing Tuesday, Wednesday and early Saturday morning are 13–14% cheaper than Sunday evening or Friday, according to KAYAK's analysis of 917 million fares.

Î: How far in advance should I book a European flight?
R: The sweet spot for European flights is 4–8 weeks ahead. Too early (3+ months) means prices are not yet optimised — airlines have not started filling seats. Too late (under 2 weeks) means high demand, few seats, and rising prices. For intercontinental: 2–3 months ahead, especially in peak season (July–August).

Î: Is last-minute cheaper?
R: Very rarely, and only for unpopular destinations or off-peak periods. For popular routes (Greece, Spain, Italy in summer), last-minute is almost always more expensive — remaining seats are few and priced at maximum. The exception: Wizz Air sometimes discounts flights with low occupancy at 48–72 hours before departure, but that is luck, not strategy.

Î: Do cookies or browser history affect flight prices?
R: The myth that 'prices rise if you search multiple times' is debunked by 2026 data — there is no measurable price difference between incognito and normal browsing. Airlines and search engines use dynamic pricing based on general demand, not your personal search history. Searching in incognito does not hurt, but do not expect different prices.

Î: Wizz Air or Ryanair — which is cheaper?
R: It depends on the route and what baggage you need. The base fare may be lower with one, but a large cabin bag costs €10–59 at Wizz Air and €6–20 at Ryanair. A 20 kg hold bag costs €13–87 at Wizz Air and €25 at Ryanair (online). Always compare the TOTAL price (ticket + baggage + seat), not just the headline fare.

Î: What is the best flight search engine?
R: There is no single best — each excels at something different. Google Flights is best for flexible-date calendars and price tracking. Skyscanner is best for 'Everywhere' search and low-cost carrier coverage. Kiwi combines flights from different airlines (virtual interlining) and can find routes 15–35% cheaper. Use at least two, then check the airline's own website for the final price.

Î: Does Google Flights Price Guarantee work?
R: Yes, but with limitations. On eligible flights (marked with a badge), Google refunds the difference if the price drops after you book — automatically, no claim needed. The limit is approximately $500 per traveller. It works primarily on US domestic flights and selectively on international routes. When the badge appears, it is a real advantage.

Î: Are connecting flights worth it?
R: Yes, for long routes (intercontinental). Flights connecting through Istanbul (Turkish Airlines), Warsaw (LOT) or Frankfurt (Lufthansa) can be 30–50% cheaper than direct options. The condition: a minimum layover of 2 hours (under 1.5 hours = risk of missing the connection if the first flight is delayed).

Î: What is 'virtual interlining' on Kiwi?
R: Kiwi.com combines separate flights from different airlines into a single journey — routes that do not officially exist. Example: Bucharest → Amsterdam (Wizz Air, €60) + Amsterdam → San Francisco (United, €420) = €480 instead of €900 direct. The risk: if you miss the connection, you have two separate bookings. Kiwi offers Kiwi Guarantee (supplementary insurance) for protection.

## Extreme Weather & European Holidays 2026: When to Go, Where to Go, and How to Stay Safe

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/extreme-weather-europe-holidays-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-31
Actualizat: 2026-07-31
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/clima-extrema-vacante-europa-2026

Descriere: Extreme heat, wildfires and storms in Europe 2026. Which destinations are safe in summer, when to travel, and how to protect your holiday booking.

Răspuns scurt: Extreme heat is rewriting the rules of European summer travel. Greece, Spain, Italy, and Turkey regularly exceeded 45°C in summer 2025, with wildfires affecting Rhodes, Attica, Tenerife, and the Turkish coast. The solution: travel in May–June or September–October (perfect temperatures, zero extreme risk, 20–30% cheaper), or shift northward to Croatia, Portugal, or Northern Europe. August in the Mediterranean is increasingly uncomfortable and occasionally dangerous — not just inconvenient.

Something fundamental changed about Mediterranean summer holidays between 2022 and 2025. Four consecutive years of temperature records. Rhodes evacuated in 2023. Tenerife burning. Greek islands with smoke-filled skies in July. Alert systems that didn't exist a decade ago now sending notifications every other day during August.

This guide is about understanding what's actually happening — the climate reality behind the headlines — and making practical holiday decisions that account for it. Not alarmism, but adaptation.

What's Actually Happening — The Climate Data

The Mediterranean is warming approximately 20% faster than the global average, according to World Meteorological Organization data. For travellers, this translates to concrete changes in the experience of summer in Southern Europe:

Temperature records: Greece, Spain, Italy, and Turkey each recorded their highest-ever temperatures in 2023 or 2024. Multiple stations across the region exceeded 47–48°C. These weren't anomalies — they're the new baseline for July–August.

Wildfire risk: The fire season has extended from June–September to May–October in many Mediterranean areas. The combination of higher temperatures, earlier and longer droughts, and dry vegetation creates conditions where a single spark can escalate rapidly. Rhodes (2023), Tenerife (2023), Attica/Marathon area (2021, 2023), and the Turkish Turquoise Coast have all seen significant tourist-area fires.

Infrastructure strain: Extreme heat strains electrical grids (air conditioning demand), water supply (droughts reduce reservoir levels), and human capacity — outdoor workers including hotel and restaurant staff face real health risks, which affects service quality.

What hasn't changed: The sea is beautiful, the food is extraordinary, the history is there, and the sunsets haven't been cancelled. What's changed is the risk profile of visiting in the peak of summer, and the intelligence of doing so.

Destination-by-Destination Climate Assessment

Greece

Safest islands for summer heat: Ionian Islands (Corfu, Zakynthos, Lefkada) — greener, more moisture, less extreme than the Cyclades. Crete's north coast — sea breezes moderate temperatures. Northern Greece (Halkidiki, Thessaloniki area) — 3–5°C cooler than Athens in summer.

Higher risk: Attica (Athens surrounds), Cyclades (Santorini, Mykonos, Paros in July–August), Eastern Aegean (Rhodes, Kos in peak heat).

Smart timing: June and September–October are excellent for Greece. Sea temperature in September can exceed 26°C — warmer than June but with autumn's lower air temperatures and crowd levels.

Wildfire alert: Download the European Emergency Number (112) app and/or the Greek 112 app which sends push notifications for wildfire alerts in your area. This is practical, not paranoid.

Athens: Visit the Acropolis at 8:00–9:00 AM, not 11:00–14:00. The difference is 10–15°C and 70% fewer people. This is the single most impactful schedule change you can make if visiting Athens in summer.

👉 Full guide: Things to Do in Athens | Best Greek Islands 2026

Spain

The north is a different country in summer: Galicia, Asturias, the Basque Country, and Cantabria have temperatures of 20–25°C in July–August, green landscapes, excellent food, and almost no foreign tourists. San Sebastián, Bilbao, and Santiago de Compostela are extraordinary cities — and genuinely comfortable in summer.

Southern Spain (Andalucía, Valencia, Murcia): Seville averages 38–40°C in July–August, frequently exceeding 43–45°C. Almería and Murcia are even hotter. These are still visited but require extreme scheduling discipline — everything before 12:00, everything after 18:00, nothing in between.

Barcelona and Catalonia: More moderate than the south (28–33°C typically) but with significant heat spikes. May–June and September are excellent for Barcelona.

Canary Islands paradox: Long marketed as "perfect climate year-round," the Canaries experienced devastating wildfires in 2023 (Tenerife, La Palma) that challenged this narrative. The climate is genuinely milder than mainland Spain — but not invulnerable. November–April remains the most reliable period.

👉 Full guide: Things to Do in Barcelona

Italy

The north vs south divide is stark: Northern Italy — Lake Como, the Dolomites, Venice (with breezes), Milan (urban heat but manageable), Tuscany hills — is dramatically more comfortable than southern Italy in summer. The Alps and Dolomites offer extraordinary hiking and scenery at 15–22°C when Rome is 38°C.

Rome in August: Hot (35–40°C), somewhat emptier than June (many Romans leave), but still very busy with tourists. Visiting Rome in August is still viable — the Colosseum at 9:00 AM before the heat builds, evening dinners in Trastevere — but requires a different rhythm than spring visits.

Sicily and Calabria: Can exceed 45°C in July–August. Beautiful but not comfortable for extended outdoor exploration. April–May and September–October are the right times.

Puglia (Bari, Lecce, Alberobello): More wind than Sicily, slightly cooler, and extraordinary value. Still warm but manageable in July if you follow the morning/evening scheduling discipline.

👉 Full guide: Vatican & Colosseum Tickets Sold Out — How to Get In | Things to Do in Rome

Turkey

Antalya, Bodrum, Marmaris (July–August): 38–42°C with significant humidity on the coast. All-inclusive resorts with pools and air conditioning become refuges rather than bases for exploration. If your plan is beach + pool + hotel food, this is actually fine — the resort bubble is climate-controlled. If your plan is excursions, day trips, and cultural exploration, July–August Antalya is exhausting.

Istanbul: More moderate than the coast (28–35°C in summer) and benefits from breezes off the Bosphorus. May–June and September are ideal; July–August is manageable with smart scheduling.

Cappadocia: Higher elevation (1,000+ metres) makes it significantly cooler than the coast in summer. The famous hot air balloons fly at 5:00–6:00 AM — you're back in the hotel before the worst heat. Cappadocia actually works well in summer for this reason.

Turkey eSIM note: eSIM provider sites are blocked within Turkey since 2025 . Buy and install your Turkey eSIM before departure.

Climate-Safe Alternatives — Destinations That Work Year-Round

Croatia's Dalmatian Coast — The Mediterranean's Best Summer Value

Croatia runs 5–7°C cooler than Greece in peak season, benefits from the Adriatic's consistent afternoon breeze, and is significantly less prone to wildfires than the Cyclades. Split, Dubrovnik, the islands of Brač, Hvar, and Vis — all of it is beautiful and reliably comfortable even in July.

June and September are particularly exceptional — warm enough for beach days, quiet enough for the coastal villages to feel authentic rather than overwhelmed.

👉 Read: Croatia Road Trip — Split to Dubrovnik 2026

Portugal — Atlantic Climate Makes the Difference

The Atlantic Ocean is Portugal's secret weapon. Even in August, Lisbon rarely exceeds 33–35°C (versus Rome's 38–40°C or Seville's 42°C), Porto stays at 25–30°C, and the Algarve coast gets constant Atlantic breeze that makes 30°C feel like 24°C. The risk of wildfires exists in interior Portugal, but coastal areas are far less exposed than Greek or Spanish islands.

Portugal also hasn't yet implemented the aggressive tourist caps and taxes that Barcelona, Venice, and Amsterdam have — making it an increasingly smart choice as those cities restrict access.

👉 Read: Portugal Holiday Guide 2026

Northern Europe — London, Amsterdam, Copenhagen, Dublin

An obvious alternative: go north. London averages 22–25°C in July–August. Amsterdam 20–23°C. Copenhagen 20–22°C. Dublin 18–20°C. No heat warnings, no wildfire risk, long daylight hours (20:00 sunset in London in July), and world-class city experiences.

The trade-off is no beach holiday. But if you're planning a city break, Northern Europe in summer is comfortable in a way Southern European capitals increasingly aren't.

👉 Read: London City Break from Bucharest 2026

Bulgaria's Black Sea Coast

Underrated and undervisited by Western Europeans, Bulgaria's Black Sea coast is an excellent summer choice. Varna and Burgas are the main resort areas — 28–32°C summer temperatures, Black Sea water that's cooler and calmer than the Mediterranean (great for families), and prices significantly below comparable Greek or Croatian options.

The Black Sea's lower salinity makes it easier to swim in. The surrounding landscape — rolling hills, pine forests down to the beach — means temperature feels more manageable than exposed Cyclades beaches.

Budapest — City Break + Thermal Baths

If you want a city holiday that's warm but not brutal, Budapest in summer (28–33°C) is genuinely pleasant. The thermal baths (Széchenyi outdoor pools) become the entire point of the trip — you're supposed to be in hot water surrounded by cooling air. It works perfectly.

Protecting Your Holiday Financially — Insurance in a Weather-Volatile World

Extreme weather has made travel insurance more important than it's ever been — specifically, the right kind of travel insurance.

What you need from your policy

Trip cancellation — natural disaster clause: If an official natural disaster warning or evacuation order is issued before your departure, and you cancel your trip, you should recover non-refundable costs. Standard policies include this; check the policy wording for "natural disaster," "force majeure," or "civil emergency."

Trip interruption: If a wildfire, flood, or extreme heat emergency forces you to cut your holiday short and return home early, the policy covers the unspent hotel nights and the rebooking cost of an earlier flight.

Emergency evacuation: If your hotel or resort is evacuated and you need to move to alternative accommodation in a different area, the policy covers the cost difference.

Medical — heat-related illness: A good travel insurance policy covers emergency medical treatment, which includes hospitalisation for heat stroke or heat exhaustion. At €2,000–10,000 for a hospital stay in Germany, Italy, or France, this is the most financially important cover.

What standard insurance usually does NOT cover:


You deciding not to travel because it's too hot but no official warning/disaster has been declared

Gradual weather deterioration (it was just unpleasantly hot, no emergency event)

Choosing to leave early because you were uncomfortable, without an official reason


A comprehensive policy from EKTA for a week in Europe costs €12–25 and includes all of the above. This is the minimum sensible protection for any Mediterranean trip in summer 2026.

👉 Full guide: Travel Insurance 2026 — What It Covers & How to Choose

EU261 and Extreme Weather — the Compensation Gap

If your flight is cancelled due to extreme weather (volcanic ash, severe storms, airport closure from a wildfire), this qualifies as "extraordinary circumstances" under EU261 — meaning the airline does NOT owe you the standard €250–€600 compensation.

You still have rights: the airline must offer a full refund or rebooking, and provide meals and accommodation while you wait. But the financial compensation element doesn't apply.

This is precisely the gap that trip cancellation and interruption insurance fills. The airline gives you back the ticket price; the insurance covers the hotel you can't use, the non-refundable excursions, and the cost of rearranging your trip.

Practical Preparation — What to Do Before Any Mediterranean Summer Trip

Check the weather forecast 10 days out: Mediterranean forecasts become reliable about 7–10 days ahead. If you see a significant heatwave forecast (40°C+), adjust your itinerary — schedule outdoor sites for very early morning and late afternoon, fill midday with air-conditioned museums, galleries, and restaurants.

Download weather and emergency alert apps:


Weather: Météo-France (France), AEMET (Spain), EMY (Greece), ECMWF (pan-European) — all have alert systems

Emergency: 112 app (EU-wide), Greek 112 app, Spanish Emergency app — send push notifications for active fires, heatwave red alerts, and evacuations in your location


Book accommodation with verified air conditioning: In 2026, "air conditioning" on a hotel listing is not negotiable for summer Mediterranean travel. Read recent reviews specifically mentioning AC effectiveness — older buildings with poor insulation often have units that can't keep pace with 42°C external temperatures.

Schedule outdoor sites for morning: Every major Mediterranean attraction (Acropolis, Colosseum, Alhambra, Topkapi, Dubrovnik walls) is visited best at 8:00–10:00 AM. The temperature difference between 8:00 AM and noon is 8–15°C. You also avoid 70% of the crowds.

Hydration: More than you think. In 40°C heat with physical activity, you lose 1–1.5 litres per hour. Most European cities have excellent free drinking water (Rome's nasoni street fountains, Vienna's Viennese tap water from the Alps, Barcelona's public fountains). Bring a refillable bottle and use it constantly.

Know your hotel's evacuation plan: This sounds extreme but is practical — if you're in a wildfire-risk area (Corfu hills, Peloponnese coast, Tenerife), spend 2 minutes at check-in asking about the evacuation protocol. Most hotels have one; knowing it is just responsible.


The Long-Term Picture — What's Coming for European Summer Travel

The trend is structural, not cyclical. Climate scientists project that by 2035, July–August heat in southern Spain, Greece, Turkey, and Italy will routinely be 2–4°C higher than current records. The "comfortable" summer window in the Mediterranean is contracting.

The tourism industry is adapting slowly:


Venice, Barcelona, and Amsterdam have already introduced visitor caps and taxes to manage overtourism pressure that's increasingly concentrated in shorter "comfortable" seasons

Some Greek islands are actively promoting September–October as the new peak season

Airlines are seeing shifting demand patterns, with earlier and later booking patterns as travellers try to escape peak summer heat


For travellers, the adaptation is straightforward: shoulder season is the new peak season . May–June and September–October offer everything summer used to promise — warm weather, sea swimming, full opening of attractions and restaurants — without the extreme heat, wildfire risk, and premium pricing of July–August.

The places that have always been beautiful in May and September will be beautiful there for years to come. The places that were borderline in August are becoming genuinely difficult. Adjust accordingly, protect your trip financially, and the Mediterranean remains one of the world's great travel destinations.

Not because they're impossible, but because extreme heat advisories are frequent, wildfires are a real possibility, beaches are extremely crowded, and prices are at their highest. ## Flight Cancelled or Delayed? Your EU261 Rights & Up to €600 Compensation in 2026

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/flight-cancelled-delayed-eu261-compensation
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-31
Actualizat: 2026-07-31
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/zbor-anulat-intarziat-drepturi-compensatii

Descriere: Complete guide to EU Regulation 261/2004 passenger rights. How much compensation you're owed, when airlines can refuse, and the fastest way to claim your money — including AirHelp and Compensair.

Răspuns scurt: If your flight was cancelled or delayed by 3+ hours at your final destination, you are entitled to compensation of €250–€600 per passenger under EU Regulation 261/2004. The amount depends on flight distance: €250 (under 1,500 km), €400 (1,500–3,500 km), €600 (over 3,500 km). The airline does NOT have to pay only if the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances (severe weather, ATC strikes, security threats). You have 3 years to file a claim. You can do it yourself for free, or use services like AirHelp or Compensair (commission only if you win).

You land at the departure board. Your flight says DELAYED or CANCELLED. The first instinct is to queue at the airline desk and accept whatever they offer. Before you do anything, read this: you may be owed up to €600 per person — and most passengers never claim it.

EU Regulation 261/2004 has been law since February 2005, yet airlines routinely ignore it, and passengers rarely know their rights. This guide covers everything: what you're owed, when you qualify, what airlines can legitimately avoid paying, and the two fastest ways to get your money in 2026.

What Is EU Regulation 261/2004?

EU Regulation 261/2004 (often called "EU261") is European law that gives air passengers fixed compensation rights when:


Their flight is delayed by 3+ hours at the final destination

Their flight is cancelled with less than 14 days' notice

They are denied boarding due to overbooking


The compensation is automatic — it doesn't depend on the airline's goodwill, your ticket type, or whether you complained. It's a legal obligation.

Updated for 2026: The European Parliament voted in January 2026 on proposed amendments to EU261, including clearer definitions of "extraordinary circumstances" and updated distance thresholds. Until the final adoption (expected late 2026 or 2027), the current rules remain fully in force.

Where Does EU261 Apply?

The regulation covers:


Any flight departing from an EU airport , regardless of which airline operates it (including non-EU carriers like Emirates, Turkish Airlines, American Airlines)

Flights arriving at an EU airport , if operated by an EU-based airline (Wizz Air, Ryanair, Lufthansa, Tarom, Air France, etc.)


UK: After Brexit, the UK adopted its own equivalent — UK Regulation 261 — with almost identical rules. Claims for UK departures or UK-operated flights arriving in the UK follow the same logic and compensation amounts (paid in GBP equivalent).

Norway, Iceland, Switzerland: All three have adopted EU261 as part of their EEA/bilateral agreements.

What's NOT covered: A Delta Airlines flight from New York to Bucharest delayed at JFK — non-EU airline, non-EU departure. But Lufthansa Frankfurt–New York delayed at FRA — covered (EU carrier departing EU airport).

Compensation Amounts — The Full Table

Flight Distance Minimum Delay Compensation Example Routes from Bucharest
Under 1,500 km 3 hours €250 Vienna, Budapest, Sofia, Athens, Istanbul
1,500–3,500 km 3 hours €400 London, Paris, Barcelona, Rome, Tel Aviv
Over 3,500 km 4 hours €600 New York, Dubai, Bangkok, Tokyo

Critical: The amounts are per passenger . A family of four on a delayed Bucharest–London flight can claim €1,600 total (4 × €400).

The compensation is completely independent of your ticket price. A €25 Ryanair promo fare on a 2,000 km route delayed 4 hours = €400. Same as a €400 flexible business fare.

When Airlines DON'T Have to Pay — Extraordinary Circumstances

The one legitimate escape clause for airlines is "extraordinary circumstances" — events genuinely outside their control that couldn't have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken.

Qualifies as extraordinary circumstances:


Severe weather conditions (major storms, fog, volcanic ash like Eyjafjallajökull)

Air Traffic Control (ATC) strikes — not airline staff strikes

Confirmed security threats (bomb threats, terrorism)

Airport infrastructure failures outside airline control

Medical emergencies on board causing diversion


Does NOT qualify (airlines frequently try this — courts disagree):


Technical aircraft faults and mechanical failures

Airline staff strikes (pilots, cabin crew, ground handling)

Crew scheduling failures and rostering errors

Overbooking

Late arrival of the aircraft from a previous flight ("knock-on delays")


The European Court of Justice has ruled repeatedly that technical faults are part of the normal operation of an airline and cannot constitute extraordinary circumstances. When airlines claim this, they often lose — but you have to challenge them.

Practical tip: When an airline says "technical issue — no compensation," challenge it. Statistics from AirHelp show that 70–80% of initially rejected claims based on "technical faults" are later successful when properly challenged.

Your Care Rights — Even Below the 3-Hour Threshold

Even if your delay is under 3 hours, you have legally mandated care rights the moment your flight is delayed:

After 2 hours of delay (short flights under 1,500 km):


Meals and refreshments proportionate to the waiting time

2 free telephone calls, emails, or faxes


After 3 hours of delay (flights 1,500–3,500 km):


Same meals and refreshments


After 4 hours of delay (long-haul flights):


Same meals and refreshments


If the delay goes overnight:


Hotel accommodation

Transport between the airport and hotel (both ways)


After 5 hours of delay — if you choose not to travel:


Full refund of your ticket price (including return journey if you're already at the destination and the delay makes the outbound pointless)


If the airline fails to provide these and you purchase food/accommodation yourself, keep all receipts — you can claim these costs back in addition to the financial compensation.

What to Do at the Airport — Step by Step

If your flight is delayed or cancelled, the order of your actions matters:

Step 1: Document immediately. Photograph the departures board showing your flight status, the time, and any reason stated. Note the exact scheduled departure and the announced delay/cancellation time.

Step 2: Get written confirmation from the airline. Ask at the desk for written confirmation of the reason for delay or cancellation. They're legally required to provide it. If they refuse, the photograph of the board is your evidence.

Step 3: Request your care rights. Ask for meal vouchers. If the airline doesn't offer them and you're waiting 2+ hours, buy food and keep the receipts.

Step 4: Accept a replacement flight — but DON'T waive your compensation. If the airline offers an alternative flight, you can accept it. Accepting the alternative does NOT cancel your right to €250–€600 compensation — these are legally separate entitlements.

Step 5: Do NOT sign compensation waivers. Airlines sometimes offer vouchers "in exchange for" compensation rights. Read everything carefully. If a document says you're accepting a voucher "in full and final settlement," you may be signing away your legal right to cash.

Step 6: File your claim within a reasonable time. Technically you have 3 years (in Romania), but the sooner the better. Details are fresher, evidence is intact.

How to Claim — Three Options

Option 1: Directly to the Airline (Free, Takes Effort)

Every EU airline is required to have a complaint form. Send a written claim via email or their online form, including:


Flight number

Scheduled date and time

Actual arrival time at final destination

Reason communicated by the airline

Explicit request for compensation under EU Regulation 261/2004


Airlines must respond within 6 weeks. If they don't, or they refuse without a valid extraordinary circumstances defence, you escalate.

Pros: You keep 100% of the compensation.

Cons: Airlines routinely ignore, delay, or issue automatic refusals on the first claim. The process can take 3–12 months and may require additional correspondence, complaints to national aviation authorities (ANPC in Romania, CAA in the UK), and potentially small claims court.

Success rate on first attempt: approximately 20–30%. After challenge: 70–80%.

Option 2: AirHelp (Recommended for Hassle-Free Claims)

AirHelp is the largest passenger rights company globally, operating in 35+ countries. You enter your flight details, they assess your claim instantly (free), and if you qualify, they handle everything — negotiation, legal letters, and if necessary, court action.

Commission: 25–35% of the compensation, deducted from what they recover. You pay nothing if they don't win.

Example: Bucharest–Barcelona flight cancelled (approx. 1,900 km) = €400 compensation. With AirHelp: you receive ~€260 net, with zero paperwork, zero follow-up, zero stress.

Best for: Flights delayed/cancelled 3–24 months ago, cases where the airline has already rejected you once, and situations where you don't have time for a 6–12 month correspondence battle.

Option 3: Compensair (Fast for Straightforward Cases)

Compensair focuses on faster resolution for simpler EU261 cases. Similar no-win-no-fee model. Good alternative if you want a second opinion or a different approach.

Comparison table:

DIY (Direct) AirHelp Compensair
Cost Free 25–35% commission Varies
Effort High Zero Minimal
Time to resolution 3–12 months 3–6 months 2–4 months
Court action if needed You handle it Yes, included Limited
Best for Simple cases, patient claimants Complex cases, busy travellers Straightforward recent claims

Special Cases That Catch Passengers Off Guard

Missed Connections on a Single Booking

If you had Bucharest → Frankfurt → Los Angeles on one ticket, and your first leg delayed caused you to miss the Frankfurt connection, compensation is calculated on the total journey distance (Bucharest–Los Angeles = ~10,000 km = €600 per passenger).

The condition: it must be a single booking/PNR. If you bought two separate tickets and missed your connection, EU261 doesn't apply between the two separate contracts.

Return Flights

Your outbound and return flights are treated as separate journeys , each with independent compensation rights. A cancelled return flight from London to Bucharest is a separate claim from your outbound journey.

Flights Operated by a Different Airline Than Who You Booked With

If you booked with Lufthansa but the flight was operated by Brussels Airlines (code-share), the operating carrier is the one liable under EU261 — even though you have a Lufthansa booking reference. The marketing carrier (who sold you the ticket) shares secondary liability.

Overnight Delay Turning Into Next-Day Flight

If your flight is delayed until the next day, you're entitled to hotel accommodation AND the full financial compensation (if total delay at destination is 3+ hours). Both rights apply simultaneously.

Compensation Statistics Worth Knowing

These figures, compiled from airline and consumer authority data, put the scale in perspective:


Approximately 250 million passengers are affected by significant flight disruptions annually across the EU (European Commission estimates)

Only 2–5% of eligible passengers ever file a compensation claim — the vast majority don't know their rights or give up after the first rejection

70–80% of first-time claims rejected by airlines are later successful when properly appealed (source: AirHelp industry data)

Average compensation recovered through AirHelp: approximately €380 per case

Romania statute of limitations: 3 years — meaning you can claim retroactively for flights disrupted in 2023, 2024, or 2025 right now


Quick Checklist — What To Do When Your Flight Is Disrupted

Print or screenshot this before your next trip:


Photograph the departures board with your flight status and time

Request written reason for delay/cancellation from airline staff

Request meal vouchers (after 2 hours)

Keep all receipts for food, transport, or accommodation you pay for

Accept replacement flight if offered — but don't waive compensation rights

Do NOT sign any voucher that uses "full and final settlement" language

Note your actual arrival time at final destination (not departure)

File your claim within 3 years (Romania) / 6 years (UK)

Use AirHelp if the airline rejects you


Protect Future Trips Too

EU261 compensates you for disruptions — but it doesn't cover cancelled hotels, non-refundable excursions, or the personal costs of a ruined holiday when the disruption is your airline's fault in extraordinary circumstances. That's what travel insurance is for.

A good travel insurance policy (from around €12–25 for a week in Europe) covers trip cancellation, medical emergencies, lost luggage, and in some cases, flight delay costs above what EU261 covers.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How much compensation am I owed for a cancelled flight?
R: Compensation is fixed by distance, NOT by ticket price: €250 for flights under 1,500 km (e.g. Bucharest–Vienna), €400 for 1,500–3,500 km (e.g. Bucharest–London), €600 for over 3,500 km (e.g. Bucharest–New York). A €30 Wizz Air promo ticket gives you the same €400 as a €300 business fare on the same route.

Î: Can the airline refuse to pay compensation?
R: Yes, only if they prove 'extraordinary circumstances' — events outside their control: severe weather (storms, volcanic ash), air traffic control strikes (NOT airline staff strikes — those don't qualify), confirmed security threats, or political instability. Technical aircraft faults do NOT count as extraordinary circumstances — the EU Court of Justice confirmed this in multiple rulings. Airlines frequently claim extraordinary circumstances and lose in court.

Î: How long do I have to file a claim?
R: It depends on the country where your flight departed. In Romania, the general statute of limitations is 3 years. In the UK (UK261), it's 6 years. Don't wait — evidence disappears and airlines make reconstruction harder. File as soon as you have the flight details.

Î: Do EU261 rights apply to low-cost airlines like Wizz Air or Ryanair?
R: Yes. EU Regulation 261/2004 applies to ALL airlines operating flights departing from an EU airport, regardless of ticket type. Wizz Air, Ryanair, Blue Air, easyJet — all are legally obligated to pay. Your ticket price (promo, standard, business) doesn't affect the compensation amount.

Î: What's the difference between AirHelp and Compensair?
R: Both handle the claim process on your behalf. AirHelp is larger, operates in 35+ countries, and takes cases to court if the airline refuses — commission 25–35% of the compensation. Compensair is faster for straightforward cases. Both work on a no-win-no-fee basis: if you don't get paid, you pay nothing. For a €400 claim with AirHelp: you receive ~€260 net with zero effort.

Î: My flight was delayed but less than 3 hours — do I get anything?
R: Below 3 hours at your final destination, you're not entitled to the €250–€600 financial compensation. BUT you still have care rights: after 2 hours of waiting, the airline must provide meals, drinks, and 2 free phone calls or emails. If they don't, you can claim these costs back later.

Î: The airline offered me a voucher — should I accept it?
R: You're entitled to cash (bank transfer). Airlines frequently offer vouchers — sometimes higher than the cash amount — to avoid paying money. You are NOT legally obligated to accept a voucher. If you sign a voucher acceptance, check the wording carefully: you may be waiving your right to cash compensation.

Î: Does EU261 apply to connecting flights where I missed my connection?
R: Yes, if it was a single booking. If your Bucharest–Munich–New York itinerary was one ticket and you missed the connection in Munich due to a delayed first leg, the compensation is calculated on the TOTAL distance (Bucharest–New York = 3,500+ km = €600). If you booked two separate tickets, this rule doesn't apply.

## Flight Delayed or Cancelled 2026: complete EU 261 compensation guide — how much you get & how to claim

Descriere: Complete EU 261/2004 guide: get 250-600 EUR per passenger for flights delayed 3h+, cancelled, or overbooked. How to claim, AirHelp vs Compensair, and what changes in 2026.

Răspuns scurt: When your flight is delayed by 3+ hours at the final destination or cancelled with less than 14 days' notice, you're entitled to compensation between 250 and 600 EUR per passenger under EU Regulation 261/2004. The amount depends on flight distance: 250 EUR under 1,500 km, 400 EUR between 1,500-3,500 km, 600 EUR over 3,500 km. The rule applies to any flight departing from an EU airport regardless of airline, and to flights into the EU operated by European carriers. Airlines often invoke extraordinary circumstances to avoid paying, but only 47% of their challenges succeed — meaning most passengers who push back win.

A flight delayed 3 hours on a route like London to Barcelona entitles you to 400 EUR — per passenger. A family of 4 gets 1,600 EUR. The tickets might have cost 200 EUR total. The compensation is 8 times the ticket price.

Most passengers don't know this. Fewer still claim the money. EU Regulation 261/2004 has been in force since 2004 and applies automatically — it doesn't depend on the airline, the ticket price, or the class of travel. It's a right, not a favor. And yet, millions of European passengers lose hundreds of millions of euros every year that they could legally claim.

This guide explains everything: when you're entitled, exactly how much you get, how to claim step by step, what to do when the airline refuses, when you're NOT entitled, what changes with the 2026 reform, and how to maximize your chances of success.

EU Regulation 261/2004 — what the law says

The 3 situations where you get compensation

1. Flight delayed 3+ hours at the final destination
It doesn't matter how long the delay was at departure — what matters is the time you arrive at your final destination. If the flight departs 2 hours late but lands only 2 hours 50 minutes late, you do NOT qualify. If it departs 1 hour late but due to conditions arrives 3 hours 10 minutes late, you qualify.

Important: arrival time is calculated from the moment the aircraft doors open at the gate, NOT from the moment of touchdown on the runway. The difference can be 10-20 minutes at major airports.

2. Flight cancelled with less than 14 days' notice
If the airline cancels the flight and informs you less than 14 days before departure, you're entitled to compensation. Exception: if the airline offers an alternative flight arriving at a time close to the original (±1-2 hours, depending on how early they informed you).

Exact rules for cancellation:


14+ days before: no compensation (only rerouting or refund)

7-13 days before: compensation if the alternative departs 2+ hours earlier OR arrives 4+ hours later

Under 7 days before: compensation if the alternative departs 1+ hour earlier OR arrives 2+ hours later


3. Denied boarding (overbooking)
The airline sold more tickets than seats on the aircraft, and you're the one who doesn't fit. Compensation is automatic, with no extraordinary circumstances exception. This is the only case where the airline cannot make any excuses.

Important: airlines will ask for "volunteers" to give up their seat, usually offering vouchers or upgrades. You're not obligated to accept — but if you accept voluntarily, you waive your right to compensation. Accept only if the offer is better than the legal compensation.

How much you get — exact amounts by distance

Flight distance Minimum delay Compensation Example routes
Under 1,500 km 3 hours €250 London-Paris, Berlin-Vienna, Rome-Barcelona
1,500-3,500 km 3 hours €400 London-Athens, Paris-Istanbul, Berlin-Lisbon
Over 3,500 km 4 hours €600 London-New York, Paris-Dubai, Frankfurt-Bangkok
Over 3,500 km 3-4 hours €300 (50% of €600) Same routes, but with delay between 3-4 hours

Amounts are per passenger. Not per booking, not per family — per individual passenger. Concrete examples:

Situation Total compensation
1 passenger, London-Rome, 3h30 delay €400
Couple, Paris-Athens, flight cancelled €800 (2 × €400)
Family of 4, Berlin-Lisbon, 4h delay €1,600 (4 × €400)
Family of 4, London-New York, 5h delay €2,400 (4 × €600)
1 passenger, Munich-Vienna, 3h15 delay €250

Note: distance is calculated as great circle distance (straight line) between the departure and arrival airports, not the actual flight path. You can check the distance on gcmap.com or airmilescalculator.com .

The amount does NOT depend on the ticket price

This is the point most travelers miss. A €19.99 Ryanair ticket on a London-Milan route delayed 3 hours qualifies you for €250 — 12.5 times the ticket price. A €45 easyJet ticket on London-Barcelona qualifies for €400 — almost 9 times the price.

Low-cost airlines have no legal excuse to offer less. EU 261 applies identically to all carriers: Ryanair, easyJet, Wizz Air, Lufthansa, British Airways, Air France.

Where EU 261 applies

Flights covered

Departure Arrival Airline Covered?
EU airport Anywhere Any airline YES
Non-EU airport EU airport EU airline (Lufthansa, Ryanair, etc.) YES
Non-EU airport EU airport Non-EU airline (Emirates, Delta, etc.) NO
Non-EU airport Non-EU airport Any NO

Simple rule: if the flight departs from the EU, you're covered regardless of airline. If it arrives in the EU but doesn't depart from the EU, you're covered only if the airline is European.

Countries included (beyond the EU)

EU 261 also applies in:


Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein (European Economic Area)

Switzerland (bilateral agreement)

United Kingdom — UK 261, a nearly identical rule post-Brexit

French overseas territories (Guadeloupe, Réunion, etc.)


Concrete examples — covered or not?

Flight Covered? Why
easyJet London → Rome, 4h delay YES EU departure
Turkish Airlines Istanbul → London, 3h delay NO Non-EU airline, non-EU departure
Lufthansa Frankfurt → New York, 5h delay YES EU departure
Delta New York → Paris, 4h delay NO Non-EU airline, non-EU departure
Ryanair London → Barcelona, cancelled YES UK departure (UK 261) + EU airline
Emirates Dubai → London, cancelled NO Non-EU airline, non-EU departure
Wizz Air Abu Dhabi → Vienna, 4h delay YES EU airline, arriving in EU

Connecting flights — special rules

When you qualify on connections

If you have a connecting ticket (flight A → B → C) purchased as a single booking, the delay is calculated at the final destination (C), not at the intermediate stop (B).

Example: flight London → Frankfurt → New York. The London-Frankfurt leg is delayed 1h30, you miss the connection, and arrive in New York 5 hours late. Compensation: €600 (total distance London-New York is over 3,500 km).

Key rule: if both segments are on the same booking (one PNR/booking reference), the rule applies. If you bought the tickets separately (different bookings), each segment is evaluated individually — and you lose the right on the second segment if you arrived at the connection on time but missed the flight for your own reasons.

Connection with different airlines

If the ticket is on a single booking but segments are operated by different airlines (codeshare), the responsible airline is the one that actually operated the segment that caused the delay.

Missed connection due to security queues

If you arrived at the airport on time but missed your flight due to security queues, the responsibility lies with the airport, not the airline. EU 261 doesn't apply — but you can file a complaint with the airport.

Extraordinary circumstances — when the airline does NOT pay

What counts as extraordinary circumstances (airline doesn't have to pay)

Circumstance Details
Severe weather Major storms, blizzards, volcanic ash, hurricanes — conditions making flying unsafe
External strikes Air traffic controller strikes, airport staff strikes, border police strikes
Security risks Bomb threats, terrorist alerts, airspace closures
Natural disasters Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, floods affecting the airport
Political instability War situations, civil unrest near the airport
Unruly passengers Flight diverted/delayed due to a disruptive passenger
Bird strikes If causing significant damage requiring inspection/repairs

What does NOT count as extraordinary circumstances (airline MUST pay)

This is where airlines lose in court, and where informed passengers win:

Situation Why it's NOT extraordinary Reference ruling
Aircraft technical problems Part of normal operations; airline must maintain the fleet CJEU Wallentin-Hermann (C-549/07)
Engine defects found at check Maintenance is the airline's responsibility CJEU van der Lans (C-257/14)
Pilot/crew strikes (airline's own) The airline has control over its labor relations CJEU TUIfly (C-195/17)
Crew shortages (illness) Airlines must maintain standby crew Multiple national rulings
Bad weather at a previous airport The delay isn't related to your direct flight Restrictive CJEU interpretation
Bird strike WITHOUT significant damage If inspection confirms no damage, the flight must operate CJEU Pešková (C-315/15)

The trick airlines use

Statistically, airlines succeed in contesting only 47% of claims (2024 data). This means over half of their challenges fail. The most common strategy: invoke "technical issues" and hope the passenger gives up. The Lufthansa Group is considered the most aggressive in contesting claims on technical grounds.

Tip: if the airline invokes extraordinary circumstances, ask them for the specific reason in writing. Then verify whether it actually qualifies — or use AirHelp/Compensair who know exactly what holds up in court.

Beyond compensation — your care rights

Even when you do NOT have the right to financial compensation (extraordinary circumstances), you ALWAYS have the right to care. The airline must provide:

Right to Care

Delay duration What you must receive FREE
2+ hours (under 1,500 km) or 3+ hours (1,500-3,500 km) or 4+ hours (over 3,500 km) Food and drinks, 2 phone calls or emails
Over 5 hours Right to abandon the journey + full ticket refund
Overnight Hotel + airport-hotel transport (round trip)

What to do if the airline doesn't provide care


Keep all receipts — meals, drinks, hotel, taxi

Spend reasonably (not a 5-star hotel for an economy flight)

Request reimbursement after the trip, with receipts as proof

If they refuse, include the costs in your compensation claim


Right to refund or rerouting

When the flight is cancelled, you choose:


Full refund of the ticket (within 7 days, per the regulation)

Rerouting on another flight, at the earliest available date, even on a different airline

Rerouting at a later date that suits you (if the airline offers)


Important: the airline must reroute you on another carrier if they don't have an available flight. Many airlines "forget" to mention this option — ask for it explicitly.

Downgrade rights

If you're involuntarily moved to a lower class (e.g., from Business to Economy), you're entitled to a fare refund:


30% of the ticket price for flights under 1,500 km

50% of the ticket price for flights 1,500-3,500 km

75% of the ticket price for flights over 3,500 km
