Voucher or cash? What to accept

The basic rule: you're entitled to CASH

Under EU 261, compensation is paid in money — cash, bank transfer, or cheque. Airlines prefer offering vouchers (flight credit, service vouchers) because it's cheaper for them. You're not obligated to accept vouchers.

When it's worth accepting a voucher


If the airline offers a voucher of significantly higher value than the compensation (e.g., €500 voucher vs €250 compensation) AND you're certain you'll fly with them within the validity period

If you urgently need an alternative flight and the airline offers an upgrade + additional voucher


When to refuse a voucher


If the voucher value equals or is less than the legal compensation

If the voucher has a short validity period

If you're not sure you'll fly with that airline

If you need money, not flight credit


15 common passenger mistakes



Not knowing they have the right. Most passengers have no idea about EU 261. If you're reading this, you're already ahead.


Accepting a voucher instead of cash. The airline is happy — you have flight credit instead of real money.


Throwing away the boarding pass. It's the primary proof. Photograph it before discarding.


Not photographing the delay board. Crucial visual evidence — take photos.


Not asking for the reason in writing. Without the official reason, the airline can invent extraordinary circumstances retroactively.


Giving up at the first refusal. Airlines routinely refuse hoping you'll give up. Don't.


Not keeping expense receipts. Meals, hotel, taxi — everything is reimbursable, but only with receipts.


Filing the claim too late. 3 years in many EU countries, but the sooner you file, the more evidence you have.


Confusing departure delay with arrival delay. What matters is when you arrive, not when you depart.


Not checking the correct distance. The difference between under 1,500 km and over 1,500 km is €150 (€250 vs €400).


Assuming low-cost means no rights. EU 261 applies identically to Ryanair, easyJet, Wizz Air, Lufthansa, British Airways.


Not asking for rerouting on another airline. You have the right to rerouting on any airline if theirs has no available flight.


Accepting "bad weather" without verification. Airlines invoke bad weather even when conditions are acceptable. Check on FlightRadar24 whether other planes flew from the same airport.


Not claiming care rights in extraordinary circumstances. Even when you don't get compensation, food/drinks/hotel are mandatory.


Thinking the claim process is too complicated. With AirHelp or Compensair, it takes 3 minutes to check and submit.

Questions people Google

Do I get compensation if I bought the ticket through an agency?
Yes. EU 261 applies to passengers, not to ticket purchasers. It doesn't matter where you bought the ticket — from the airline, Skyscanner, Kiwi, or a travel agency. You file the claim with the airline, not the agency.

Do children get compensation?
Yes, each passenger with their own ticket qualifies. Children with a ticket (even infants with a reduced fare on a parent's lap) qualify. Children under 2 WITHOUT a ticket (€0 fare) do not qualify.

Does it matter if I was late to the airport?
Yes — if you arrived late to the gate and missed the flight, you do NOT have the right to compensation. EU 261 applies only when the airline causes the delay/cancellation. But if you missed a connection due to the delay of the first flight (on the same booking), you qualify.

Do I get compensation for charter flights?
Yes, EU 261 applies to charter flights departing from the EU as well. Including charter flights in package holidays.

Can I claim compensation for a flight from 2 years ago?
Yes, if the claim deadline hasn't passed (varies by country: 3 years in Germany/Romania, 5 years in France/Spain, 6 years in the UK/Ireland). Many passengers successfully claim compensation for flights 1-2 years old.

The airline offered me an upgrade to Business. Do I still get compensation?
Yes! The upgrade is a bonus, not a replacement for compensation. You can have both the upgrade and the compensation — they're separate things.

If I received a ticket refund, do I also get compensation?
Yes. The ticket refund and EU 261 compensation are separate rights. The refund is your money back for the service not received. The compensation is for the inconvenience.

Does EU 261 work if I don't live in the EU?
Yes. EU 261 applies based on the flight route, not the passenger's citizenship or residence. An American citizen on a flight from Frankfurt to New York has the same rights as a European citizen.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is EU 261 compensation mandatory or at the airline's discretion?
R: It's mandatory by law — EU Regulation 261/2004 applies directly and automatically in all EU countries. The airline has no choice whether to pay; if the flight is delayed 3+ hours and it's not due to extraordinary circumstances, compensation is a legal right, not a gesture of goodwill. If they refuse, you can go to court or use AirHelp/Compensair.

Î: How long do I have to claim compensation?
R: It varies by country: 1 year in Poland and Belgium, 2 years in Croatia and the Netherlands, 3 years in Germany/Austria/Portugal/Romania, 5 years in France/Spain/Greece, 6 years in Ireland and the UK. The 2026 EU 261 reform will introduce a uniform 9-month deadline EU-wide, but it's not yet in force.

Î: What are extraordinary circumstances and when don't I get compensation?
R: These are situations beyond the airline's control: severe weather (storms, volcanic ash), air traffic control strikes, security risks, natural disasters, unruly passengers. NOT included: aircraft technical issues (part of normal operations), strikes by airline employees, crew shortages. Airlines frequently invoke this exception, but European courts interpret it strictly — in many cases they lose.

Î: Do I get compensation on low-cost flights (Wizz Air, Ryanair)?
R: Yes, EU 261 applies to all airlines, including low-cost carriers. A 30 EUR Wizz Air ticket on a route like Bucharest-Rome qualifies you for 250 EUR compensation if the flight is delayed 3+ hours. The amount doesn't depend on the ticket price — only on flight distance and delay duration.

Î: What's the difference between AirHelp and Compensair?
R: Both handle the recovery process for you. AirHelp charges a 35% commission (so from 600 EUR you receive 390 EUR) but has the largest platform, court support, and a mobile app. Compensair charges 25% (from 600 EUR you receive 450 EUR) — 60 EUR more. Both work on a no win, no fee basis — if they don't win, you pay nothing.

Î: What if the airline refuses or doesn't respond?
R: If the airline refuses or doesn't respond within 6-8 weeks: 1) File a complaint with your national aviation authority. 2) Use a recovery service (AirHelp, Compensair) that will go to court for you. 3) Go to court directly — the competent court is at your home address or at the departure/arrival airport. Court costs are minimal and the success rate is over 90%.

## Hidden Holiday Fees 2026: Every Cost Nobody Tells You About Before You Book

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/hidden-holiday-fees-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-31
Actualizat: 2026-07-31
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/taxe-ascunse-vacanta-2026

Descriere: The complete guide to hidden fees in European travel — low-cost airline surcharges, hotel tourist taxes, DCC at ATMs, resort fees, car rental extras, and how to avoid or budget for each one.

Răspuns scurt: Hidden costs can add €100–400 to a holiday budget you thought was settled. The main culprits: low-cost airline baggage supplements (€25–100 per direction), hotel tourist tax not shown on Booking.com (€2–7/night), Dynamic Currency Conversion at ATMs and card terminals (3–8% loss on every transaction), car rental counter extras (CDW excess, insurance upgrades: €70–175/week), data roaming outside the EU (€3–12/day), and service charges added automatically to restaurant bills. The rule: always add 15–20% above the headline price.

You've planned the holiday carefully. Flights: €120 return. Hotel: €360 for 7 nights. Budget: €600 all-in. You arrive home and check your bank statement: €815.

The €215 gap isn't incompetence. It's a combination of fees that are designed to be invisible at the point of booking and unavoidable at the point of holiday. This guide maps every one of them — and tells you which to avoid, which to reduce, and which to simply budget for correctly.

The Airline Fees — Where "From €25" Becomes €120

Low-cost airlines have built their business model on advertised base fares that are achievable only by passengers with no baggage, pre-selected seats, and nerves of steel. Understanding the fee structure before you search means the comparison becomes accurate.

Baggage — the Biggest Single Hidden Cost

Every major European low-cost airline includes only a small personal item in the base fare:

Fee Type Wizz Air Ryanair easyJet
Personal item (free) 40×30×20 cm 40×20×25 cm 45×36×20 cm
Cabin bag (large) €15–45/direction €8–35/direction Included in Plus fares
Hold bag (20 kg) €20–55/direction €25–55/direction €13–50/direction
Hold bag (32 kg) €25–65/direction €35–75/direction €30–70/direction
Seat selection €5–45 €4–38 €3–30
Priority boarding €6–16 €6–16 Included with cabin bag

Real example: A Wizz Air "from €30" return flight from Bucharest to Rome becomes:


Base fare: €30 return

Large cabin bag (both directions): €60

Seat selection (2 people, return): €40

Actual cost per person: €130


The solution: For a 3–4 night city break, the personal item (40×30×20 cm) is sufficient for most travellers who pack efficiently. This alone saves €60–100 per direction per person. See our cabin baggage rules guide for exactly what fits and how to pack it.

For holidays requiring more luggage (7+ nights, families): buy the hold bag at booking, not at the airport. Airport purchase prices are 40–100% higher than online prices. Set a calendar reminder 60 days before travel to check if prices have dropped (they sometimes do for advance online purchase).

The Airport Check-In Trap

Wizz Air and Ryanair charge €55 per person for check-in at the airport counter instead of online. Online check-in opens 24–48 hours before departure (48h for Wizz Air, 24h for Ryanair).

The rule: set a phone alarm for online check-in. Download the airline app. If you're travelling in a group, put one person in charge of checking everyone in simultaneously. This is €55 per person completely avoidable.

Seat Selection — When It Matters

On Wizz Air and Ryanair, travellers who don't pay for seat selection are allocated seats randomly. For a couple or family, this means you might sit separately. For solo travellers, the random allocation is fine.

What to do: If you're a couple and don't mind a 50/50 chance of being separated, skip seat selection. If you need to sit together (family with children, accessibility reasons), buy the cheapest available seats online. The cheapest allocated seats (back of the plane, middle seats) are €4–8 — far less than the prominently advertised window and front seats at €20–45.

Airline Upgrade Emails — Ignore Most

After booking, you'll receive emails promoting: priority boarding (sometimes worth it if you have a cabin bag and want overhead locker space), seat upgrades (rarely worth it for short flights), and various insurance products (buy from a specialist insurer instead — it's cheaper and better cover).


Hotel Fees — What Booking.com Doesn't Show at Search Time

Tourist Tax — Compulsory, Often Invisible Until Check-In

The tourist tax (also called "city tax," "accommodation tax," or "taxe de séjour") is a compulsory per-night fee charged by cities and regions to fund tourism infrastructure. It is almost universally EXCLUDED from the prices shown on Booking.com, Hotels.com, and Airbnb at search time — you see it only in the fine print of the booking confirmation, or when you arrive at the hotel.

Current 2026 tourist taxes by city:

City Tourist tax Applied per Maximum nights Impact (2 people, 7 nights)
Amsterdam 16% of room rate Per night Unlimited €60–140 (on €60–100/night room)
Barcelona €4–6.75 Per person per night Unlimited €56–95
Rome €3.50–7 Per person per night 10 nights €49–98
Venice €5–10 Per person per night (hotels) + €5–10 day visitor fee 10 nights €70–140
Paris €1–5 Per person per night Unlimited €14–70
Lisbon €2 Per person per night 7 nights €28
Dubrovnik €2 Per person per night Unlimited €28
Istanbul ~€2 Per person per night Unlimited ~€28
Florence €3.50–5.50 Per person per night 7 nights €49–77
London None — — €0
Budapest 4% of room rate Per night Unlimited €15–35 (on €45–100/night room)

You cannot avoid these. They're mandatory and legally enforceable. What you can do: add them to your holiday budget at planning stage. Add €3–7/night/person as a standard line item for any European city hotel booking.

Booking.com tip: On the room confirmation page (after selecting dates), scroll down to find "Essential information" or "Fine print" — tourist taxes are usually mentioned there in small text. Read it before confirming.

Resort Fees

Common at all-inclusive hotels in Turkey and Egypt, less common in Europe: a daily "resort fee" (€5–15/person/day) for "facilities" or "entertainment" that appears at check-in, not on the booking. On a 7-night, 2-person holiday: €70–210 extra.

How to avoid: Check TripAdvisor reviews for the specific hotel and search for mentions of "resort fee" or "check-in fee." Google the hotel name + "resort fee" before booking. If in doubt, email the hotel directly and ask for a written list of all charges due at check-in before your booking confirmation.

Cleaning Fees (Airbnb and Self-Catering)

Airbnb and Vrbo/HomeAway listings display nightly prices prominently and cleaning fees separately. On a 3-night stay, a €60 cleaning fee adds €20 to each night's effective cost. On a 7-night stay, the same cleaning fee represents €8.50/night — much more reasonable.

The rule: always check the total price (all fees included) for your specific dates before comparing Airbnb to hotels. The sort by "price" on Airbnb uses nightly rate; "total price" is the only meaningful comparison.


ATM and Card Fees — The Invisible Drain

Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) — The Single Most Common Tourist Trap

Dynamic Currency Conversion is a mechanism where a foreign ATM or payment terminal offers to convert your transaction into your home currency at the point of payment. The exchange rate applied is set by the acquiring bank — typically 3–8% worse than the interbank rate your card would have used.

The scenario: You withdraw €200 from an ATM in Rome. The screen asks: "Do you want to proceed in EUR or GBP?" You choose GBP because it seems familiar. The ATM charges you £182 instead of what your bank would have charged (£172 at the interbank rate). You've paid £10 for the convenience of seeing GBP on the screen.

The rule, permanently: ALWAYS choose the LOCAL CURRENCY. At ATMs and payment terminals everywhere:


"Charge in EUR" or "Charge in local currency" → choose this

"Charge in GBP/RON/USD" → never choose this

"Conversion by merchant" → never choose this; choose "conversion by my bank"


Sometimes the DCC screens are designed to make the home currency option look like the helpful or recommended one. It never is.

Impact on a holiday: A family spending €1,500 across 2 weeks, consistently choosing their home currency when prompted, loses €45–120 to DCC. Using Revolut or Wise (which bypass currency conversion fees entirely) and always choosing local currency reduces this to zero.

Bank Card Foreign Transaction Fees

Even without DCC, most traditional bank cards charge 1–3% on every foreign currency transaction. On a holiday with €800 of card spending:


Standard bank card: €8–24 in fees

Revolut or Wise: €0


For high-value travel spending (flights, hotels booked in foreign currency, restaurants over a week), the difference compounds. Open a Revolut or Wise account before your next trip — both are free to open and offer the interbank exchange rate.

ATM Withdrawal Fees

Your bank's own ATM fee for international withdrawals: typically €2–5 per withdrawal, plus the foreign transaction percentage. Strategy: make fewer, larger withdrawals rather than multiple small ones. Revolut free plan: €200/month free ATM withdrawals, then 2%.


Restaurant Bills — Charges That Appear After You've Eaten

Service Charge

Country Standard Practice What It Means
UK 12.5% added automatically You can legally ask for it to be removed; tipping additionally is optional and unusual
USA 18–22% expected Not automatic but effectively mandatory at sit-down restaurants
Italy "Coperto" €1–3/person Cover charge for bread and table setting; legal and traditional
France Service compris (included) Already in the price by law; additional tip is discretionary
Germany Not automatic Round up by 5–10% as custom
Greece Not automatic in most cases Some tourist restaurants add 10% — check the bill
Spain Not standard Rounding up is customary

UK-specific note: The 12.5% service charge added to London restaurant bills is automatic but not legally mandatory. If service was poor, you can ask for it to be removed. If you're happy with service, the 12.5% is the tip — you don't need to add more.

The "Coperto" in Italy

The coperto (cover charge) of €1–3 per person is charged at virtually all Italian sit-down restaurants as a table-setting fee. It covers bread and your place setting. It's legal, traditional, and non-negotiable. Budget for it — it's not a scam, just a different billing convention from most other countries.

Menus Without Prices

At tourist-heavy areas (Piazza Navona in Rome, La Rambla in Barcelona, Old Town squares in Prague and Krakow), some restaurants display menus without prices, or with menu items listed that aren't the items actually served (the "specials" or "today's catch" have prices that are quoted verbally and often much higher than the listed items).

The rule: if there are no prices, ask before ordering. "What is the price of the sea bass?" is a completely normal question. If the waiter seems evasive, leave. See our travel scams guide for more on this pattern.


Car Rental — The Counter Upsell Script

Car rental has the most sophisticated hidden fee structure in travel. The counter upsell is so standard that rental staff are trained to present all of the following as normal and expected:

CDW Excess — The Biggest One

Collision Damage Waiver (CDW) is typically included in online rental prices, but with an "excess" — the amount you pay in case of damage before the insurance kicks in. This excess is commonly €800–2,500.

At the counter, staff will offer to reduce this excess to zero for €10–15/day — "Super CDW" or "Excess Reduction." On a 7-day rental: €70–105 extra.

Solution: Buy excess reduction insurance through a third party (InsureandGo, RentalCover.com, your annual travel insurance) before you arrive at the counter. Third-party policies typically cost €3–6/day and cover the full excess. This costs €21–42 for 7 days vs €70–105 at the counter.

Alternatively, check if your credit card or travel insurance includes car rental excess cover (some do). Call and confirm before relying on this.

Full List of Counter Extras

Fee Typical Cost Notes
CDW excess reduction €10–15/day Buy from third party instead
Tyre and windscreen protection €3–6/day Check if included in your policy
Roof and undercarriage protection €3–5/day Often not covered by standard CDW
Additional driver €5–15/day Sometimes free for spouses/partners
Young driver surcharge €10–20/day Under 25 in most companies
Airport surcharge €5–20 flat Unavoidable if collecting at airport
GPS/navigation €5–10/day Use your phone instead
Child seat €5–10/day Often cheaper to bring your own
Fuel pre-purchase Full tank price Avoid — you usually return more fuel than you need

Total potential counter extras on a 7-day rental: €70–175+ above the online price.

The comprehensive strategy: book a rental with full coverage (CDW zero excess, tyres, glass) included in the online price from the start. It costs more upfront but eliminates counter stress and often works out equal to or cheaper than base price + counter extras.

For car rental in Greece, Croatia, and Turkey specifically — where road conditions and driving norms are different from Northern Europe — full zero-excess coverage is worth it.

Data Roaming — Completely Avoidable

EU Roaming (Free, With Limits)

Within the EU/EEA, your Romanian SIM provides free data roaming — you use your domestic plan in any EU country. BUT: fair use limits apply. If your domestic plan includes 10 GB/month in Romania, your carrier may limit EU roaming to 5–7 GB before throttling or charging extra.

Check your carrier's EU roaming limit before departure. If your plan has generous limits (20 GB+), you're fine. If it's limited (5 GB or less), consider a top-up or a temporary eSIM.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: What fees are NOT included in hotel prices on Booking.com?
R: The local tourist tax (€2–7/night depending on city and hotel category) is NOT included in the displayed price on Booking.com. You pay it at check-in, in cash or by card. Barcelona, Amsterdam, Rome, Venice, Paris, Lisbon — all have compulsory tourist taxes that appear only in the fine print or at check-in. Some hotels also charge resort fees (especially in Turkey and Egypt) at check-in that weren't visible at booking.

Î: How do I avoid losing money at ATMs abroad?
R: Always choose to pay in the LOCAL CURRENCY, never in your home currency. Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) is a mechanism where the ATM or payment terminal makes the conversion at an exchange rate 3–8% worse than your bank's rate. If the screen asks 'pay in pounds or euros?' — choose euros. If it asks 'conversion by ATM or your bank?' — choose your bank.

Î: Why is my actual holiday spend always more than what I planned?
R: Because headline prices exclude most of the real costs: the Ryanair 'from €25' doesn't include your bag; the hotel 'from €60' doesn't include the tourist tax; the 'free' city WiFi doesn't cover your roaming in Turkey; and that nice restaurant lunch came with a 12.5% service charge and a €2/person cover charge. Adding 15–20% to every headline price before booking gives a realistic picture.

Î: How much does Dynamic Currency Conversion actually cost?
R: 3–8% on every transaction where you choose your home currency instead of the local one. On a holiday with €800 of card spending, DCC costs €24–64. On €2,000 (a family holiday), it's €60–160. Use Revolut or Wise (0% exchange fee) and always choose local currency, and this cost drops to zero.

Î: What car rental fees appear at the counter that aren't in the online price?
R: The most common surprise fees at the rental counter: CDW excess reduction (€10–15/day, sometimes mandatory), additional driver fee (€5–15/day), young driver surcharge (under 25), airport collection surcharge (€5–20), fuel policy pre-purchase (often non-refundable), tyre/glass/roof protection (€3–8/day each). Total: €70–175 for a 7-day rental. Buy comprehensive insurance when booking online — it's cheaper and prevents most of this.

Î: What tourist taxes are applied in Europe's top destinations in 2026?
R: The biggest tourist taxes in 2026: Amsterdam (16% on room rate — the highest), Barcelona (€4–6.75/night), Rome (€3.50–7/night), Venice (€5–10/day for day visitors plus per-night hotel tax), Paris (€1–5/night), Lisbon (€2/night), Dubrovnik (€2/night). These are all mandatory, non-avoidable, and frequently not shown on Booking.com at search time.

Î: Is the 'airport tax' included in flight prices shown on comparison engines?
R: Usually yes — EU regulations require that the final price including taxes and charges be shown in search results. But 'optional' charges (baggage, seat selection, priority boarding) are added separately. The advertised base fare and the realistic all-in price for a passenger with a bag can differ by €50–150 per direction on low-cost airlines.

## How to Plan a European Holiday from Scratch: Step-by-Step Guide 2026

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/how-to-plan-european-holiday-2026
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-15
Actualizat: 2026-07-15
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/cum-planifici-vacanta-ghid-pas-cu-pas

Descriere: The complete planning checklist for a European holiday in 2026. From choosing a destination to packing your bag — flights, accommodation, insurance, eSIM, documents, and timing.

Răspuns scurt: Plan a European holiday in 7 steps: 1) Set budget and destination (3-6 months ahead). 2) Book flights (6-8 weeks ahead for best price). 3) Book accommodation. 4) Get travel insurance (€15-25/week). 5) Buy an eSIM for data (€5-15). 6) Check documents (passport, ETA for UK, EHIC card). 7) Pack. The entire process takes 2-3 hours if you know what you're doing — this guide shows you exactly what and when.

Why planning matters (and why it's not hard)

Every year, millions of travellers overpay for flights (booked too late), miss out on sold-out attractions (Colosseum, Sagrada Familia ), and discover at the airport that their passport expires in 3 months (Turkey and the UK require 6 months validity).

This guide puts everything in order. Seven steps, with exact timing, so you don't waste money or miss anything. Total planning time: 2-3 hours.

Step 1: Set your budget and destination (3-6 months ahead)

The question isn't "where do I want to go?" — it's "how much can I spend?" Budget determines destination, not the other way around.

Under €300/person (3 nights): Budapest , Bucharest , Athens , Prague — city breaks with budget flights.

€300-600/person (7 nights): Croatia road trip , Greek Islands , Dubrovnik .

€600-1,500/person (7 nights): Mediterranean cruise , Santorini, Interrail adventure .

👉 Destination ideas: 10 Cheapest European Destinations

👉 Avoiding crowds: Overtourism Guide 2026 — know which cities charge extra fees

Step 2: Book flights (6-8 weeks ahead)

The golden rule: 6-8 weeks before departure is the sweet spot for European flights. Earlier = standard prices. Later = prices climb.

Where to search: use a flight comparison engine that shows ALL airlines (budget and legacy) on one screen. Never search on just one airline's website — you'll miss cheaper alternatives on competitors.

Money-saving tactics:


Search on Tuesday mornings (promotions drop Monday evening)

Be flexible ±3 days (same route can vary €40-60 between days)

Mid-week departures (Tue-Thu) are cheapest

Set price alerts for your route


Baggage trap: budget airlines (Ryanair, easyJet, Wizz Air) include only a small personal item free (40×30×20 cm). Cabin bag and checked luggage cost €15-50 per segment. A 3-4 night city break fits in the free bag if you pack efficiently.

👉 Flight cancelled? Know your EU261 compensation rights — up to €600

Step 3: Book accommodation (2-3 months ahead)

Hotel (B&B) — best for city breaks. Breakfast included, central location, independence for lunch and dinner.

All-inclusive resort — best for beach holidays (Turkey, Greek islands, Spain). Everything included, zero decisions needed.

Apartment/Airbnb — best for stays of 5+ nights and families. Kitchen saves €15-30/day on food.

Key tip: stay in Zone 2-3, not the absolute centre. The price difference is 30-50%; the commute is 10-15 minutes by metro. In London , Earl's Court beats Westminster. In Barcelona , Eixample beats Gothic Quarter. Same experience, significantly less money.

Watch for hidden fees : tourist taxes (€2-7/night in Barcelona, Rome, Amsterdam, Venice) are often NOT included in the price shown on Booking.com. Budget for them.

Step 4: Get travel insurance (immediately after first booking)

This is the step everyone skips and later regrets. A travel insurance policy costs £15-30 for a week and covers:


Medical emergencies (£2-5 million cover)

Emergency repatriation (worth £10,000-50,000 alone)

Lost or stolen baggage

Trip cancellation

Personal liability


EHIC/GHIC is NOT enough — it only covers public hospitals in the EU, not repatriation, cancellation, or theft. For Turkey , UK, and non-EU destinations, EHIC doesn't work at all.

👉 Full details: Travel Insurance for Europe — Complete Guide

Step 5: Get an eSIM for data (1 week before departure)

Instead of paying your carrier €5-15/day for roaming (or buying a local SIM at destination), install an eSIM on your phone before you leave. €5-15 for your entire trip, covering 33+ European countries.

Why it matters: Google Maps navigation, WhatsApp calls (free vs. roaming charges), Google Translate, Uber/Bolt for taxis, and instant sharing of photos.

Setup: 2-3 minutes on your home WiFi. Install before departure — some eSIMs require internet to activate.

👉 Best eSIM for Europe 2026 — Airalo vs Saily vs Yesim compared

Step 6: Check documents (2 weeks ahead)

This is the 5-minute check that prevents the worst-case airport scenario.

Within the EU/Schengen: passport or national ID card.

UK (post-Brexit): passport (6 months validity) + ETA (£10, apply at gov.uk, 1-3 days processing).

Turkey: passport (6 months validity), no visa needed for most nationalities (90 days).

USA: passport + ESTA ($21, apply online).

EHIC/GHIC card: free, covers EU public hospital emergencies. Apply through your national health service. Takes 1-2 weeks.

👉 Detailed document requirements per destination available in our country-specific guides: Bucharest , Dubrovnik , Greek Islands

Step 7: Pack (1 day before)

The universal rule: take half the clothes and twice the money you think you need.

For a 3-4 night city break (fits in a free personal item 40×30×20 cm):


3-4 t-shirts, 2 bottoms, underwear

1 light jacket or hoodie (plane AC is cold)

Comfortable walking shoes (worn, not packed)

Toiletry bag (liquids under 100ml in clear bag)

Phone charger + power adapter (UK = Type G, 3-pin)

eSIM already installed


Weigh your bag at home. Budget airlines charge €25-50 for bags over the limit. A €10 luggage scale pays for itself on the first trip.

Planning timeline — when to do what

When What to do
3-6 months ahead Decide budget and destination
2-3 months ahead Book accommodation
6-8 weeks ahead Book flights
After first booking Get travel insurance
2-4 weeks ahead Book attraction tickets ( GetYourGuide )

1 week ahead Install eSIM , download offline maps
1 day ahead Pack, print/download boarding pass
Departure day Online check-in (if not done already)

Common mistakes that cost real money

Booking flights too late. The same route costs €55 at 7 weeks, €95 at 3 weeks, €180 at 5 days. Set price alerts and book at the right time.

Skipping insurance. One night in a French hospital costs €1,000-3,000. Insurance costs €15-25/week.

Paying roaming charges. €5-15/day adds up to €35-105/week. An eSIM costs €5-15 total.

Not booking attractions. Colosseum , Sagrada Familia , Vatican — 2-4 hour queues without advance tickets. Free with GetYourGuide skip-the-line booking.

Falling for tourist scams . ATM skimming, taxi tricks, restaurant traps — know them before you go.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How far in advance should I book a European holiday?
R: Flights: 6-8 weeks ahead for the best price. Accommodation: 2-3 months (4-6 months for peak season or popular destinations). Insurance: as soon as you make your first non-refundable booking. Popular attraction tickets (Colosseum, Sagrada Familia): 2-4 weeks ahead.

Î: How much does a European holiday cost per person?
R: Varies enormously. City break (3 nights): £200-650. Beach holiday (7 nights): €400-1,200. Cruise (7 nights): $800-2,500. The cheapest destinations (Budapest, Bucharest, Athens) cost €40-60/day; expensive ones (London, Amsterdam, Paris) cost €80-150/day.

Î: Do I need travel insurance for Europe?
R: EHIC/GHIC covers emergency treatment at public EU hospitals, but NOT repatriation, cancellation, lost baggage, or private hospitals. A dedicated policy costs £15-30/week — less than a single restaurant meal — and covers everything EHIC doesn't. For non-EU destinations (Turkey, UK), insurance is essential.

## Interrail 2026: The Complete Guide to Train Travel Across Europe

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/interrail-europe-2026-complete-guide
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-14
Actualizat: 2026-07-14

Descriere: Everything you need to know about Interrail in 2026. Pass prices, best routes, night trains, seat reservations, and whether a rail pass actually saves you money.

Răspuns scurt: An Interrail Global Pass in 2026 starts at €212 (youth, 4 days/1 month) or €330 (adult). A full month of unlimited travel: €522 adults. The pass covers 33 European countries. Night trains (Nightjet: Vienna-Rome, Munich-Amsterdam) save hotel nights. Key caveat: high-speed trains (TGV, Frecciarossa, AVE) require paid seat reservations (€10-34 per segment) on top of the pass. Best value: 5+ cities in 2-4 weeks, youth pass, shoulder season.

Why train travel is having its moment

In 2026, Interrail isn't just for gap-year backpackers anymore. Europe's rail network is experiencing a genuine renaissance: new high-speed lines, next-generation night trains that turn hotel nights into travel nights, and unprecedented connections between capitals. Flying gets you there; the train shows you what's in between.

And the economics have shifted. A youth pass covering 4 travel days costs €212 — roughly the same as 3-4 budget flights with baggage fees, but with unlimited flexibility to change your route on a whim.

Pass prices — the full picture

Pass type Youth (12-27) Adult (28-59) Senior (60+)
4 days / 1 month (flexi) €212 €330 ~€297
7 days / 1 month (flexi) €268 €414 ~€373
10 days / 2 months (flexi) €326 €502 ~€452

Flexi vs. Continuous: Flexi = you choose WHICH days you travel (e.g., 7 out of 30). Continuous = every day is a travel day. Flexi is better if you stay 2-3 nights in each city. Continuous only makes sense if you're moving almost daily.

Where to buy: interrail.eu (digital pass on phone) or at major train stations.

3 routes that work brilliantly

Route 1: Central Europe Classic (10 days)

Budapest → Vienna → Prague → Berlin → Amsterdam

No mandatory seat reservations on most segments (Germany, Austria, Czech Republic = just board). The perfect introduction to Interrail — thermal baths, imperial palaces, medieval squares, world-class museums, and legendary nightlife. 7 days/1 month flexi: €414 adult.

Book experiences at each stop: GetYourGuide has skip-the-line tickets and walking tours in every city.

Route 2: Mediterranean (14 days)

Barcelona → Marseille → Cinque Terre → Rome → (night train) → Vienna → Munich → Zurich

Includes coastal scenery along the French and Italian Riviera that no flight will ever show you. Two night trains save two hotel nights. Seat reservations on TGV and Frecciarossa: ~€50 total extra. 10 days/2 months flexi: €502 adult.

Route 3: Balkans Adventure (7-10 days)

Belgrade → Sarajevo → Split → Zagreb → Budapest

The cheapest route (countries with low prices, no mandatory reservations). Through dramatic Balkan mountain scenery on some of Europe's most underrated train lines. 4 days/1 month flexi: €330 adult.

Sarajevo, Belgrade, and Split are all featured in our cheapest European destinations guide .

Night trains — sleep on the train, save on hotels

Europe's night train revival is real. Nightjet (ÖBB) operates routes that genuinely make sense:

Vienna → Rome 11.5h €14 €34
Vienna → Venice 9h €14 €34
Munich → Amsterdam 12h €14 €40
Zurich → Hamburg 10h €14 €34
Vienna → Paris 14h €14 €40

The double saving: you save a hotel night (€50-100) AND you travel without losing a day. Fall asleep in Vienna at 21:00, wake up in Rome at 08:30.

Book early: the cheapest couchettes sell out within days on popular routes. Book 2-3 months ahead at nightjet.com .

Not all trains are "just board." Here's where you'll pay extra:

Pro tip: if you want to avoid reservation fees entirely, use regional trains. They take longer but every intermediate station is a potential discovery, and the total cost stays at just the pass price. Germany and Austria are paradise for this approach — ICE reservations are optional, and regional trains connect everything.

Interrail vs. flying — the honest comparison

7 practical tips

1. Download the Rail Planner App. The official Interrail timetable app works offline — essential when you're between cities without an eSIM signal.

2. Get a European eSIM before departure. Station WiFi is unreliable. An eSIM covering 33 countries for €10-15/month means Google Maps, booking, and communication work everywhere.

3. Pack light. No baggage limits on trains (unlike planes), but hauling a 23 kg suitcase up three flights of stairs in an Italian station is miserable. A 40-50L backpack is ideal.

4. Get multi-country travel insurance . With Interrail you cross 3-5 countries — your policy must be Europe-wide, not per-country. Full insurance guide .

5. Book experiences with GetYourGuide in advance. Colosseum , Sagrada Familia , Dubrovnik GoT tour — these sell out 2-4 weeks ahead in summer.

6. Don't over-plan. The magic of Interrail is flexibility. Leave 1-2 days unplanned — the best discoveries come from improvisation.

7. Shoulder season (May-June, September) is the sweet spot. Trains are emptier, reservations easier to get, and the cities you visit are less crowded. Everything we recommend in our overtourism guide applies doubly when you're on a flexible rail pass.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: How much does an Interrail Global Pass cost in 2026?
R: 2nd class prices — Youth (12-27): 4 days/1 month = €212, 7 days = €268, 1 month continuous = €522. Adult (28-59): 4 days = €330, 7 days = €414, 1 month = €713. Senior (60+): ~10% discount. Children under 12: FREE with a paying adult (max 2 children).

Î: Do I need seat reservations with Interrail?
R: Depends on the train. Regional trains (Germany, Austria, Czech Republic, Switzerland): NO, just board. High-speed trains: YES, mandatory — TGV France (€10-20), Frecciarossa Italy (€13), AVE Spain, Eurostar (€34). Night trains (Nightjet): YES — seats from €14, couchettes from €34. Book at interrail.eu or at the station.

Î: Is Interrail cheaper than flying?
R: For 2-3 fixed cities: usually not — budget flights are cheaper. For 5+ cities with flexibility: Interrail wins, especially for under-27s (€212 for 4 travel days = ~€53/day). Plus: no baggage fees, you arrive in city centres (not airports 30-80 km away), and the scenery is spectacular.

Î: Can I use Interrail on night trains?
R: Yes, but you must pay a compulsory berth or seat reservation. Nightjet (ÖBB) is the main operator: Vienna-Rome, Vienna-Venice, Munich-Amsterdam, Zurich-Hamburg, Vienna-Paris. Reservations: seats from ~€14, couchettes from ~€34, private sleepers higher. Book the moment reservations open (typically 3-6 months ahead) — cheap berths sell out in days on popular routes.

## Layover vs Direct Flight 2026: When a Connection Saves Money and When It Does Not

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/layover-vs-direct-flight
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-30
Actualizat: 2026-07-30
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/zbor-cu-escala-vs-direct

Descriere: Layover vs direct flight: real savings on European routes, the risks, reliable hub airports, how to protect yourself if you miss a connection, and turning a layover into a city visit.

Răspuns scurt: On short European routes (under 4 hours direct), direct flights almost always win — savings with a layover are typically €10–30, not enough to justify added time and connection risk. On intercontinental routes (USA, Asia, Africa), a layover can save €200–500 — a difference that justifies 3–5 extra hours of travel. The rules: same booking reference (single PNR) for protection, minimum 90 minutes for intra-EU connections or 2–3 hours for international, and reliable hubs (Istanbul, Vienna, Amsterdam, Dubai). With separate tickets you are on your own if you miss the connection.

You are looking at two options: London to New York direct, €900, 7 hours. Or London to New York via Reykjavik on Icelandair, €540, 10 hours. The difference is €360 and 3 extra hours. How do you decide?

The answer is not universal — it depends on the route, the actual saving, the hub quality, the ticket type, and your personal tolerance for travel complexity. This guide gives you the complete framework for any scenario.


How much you actually save: European vs intercontinental routes

Short European routes — layovers rarely make sense

On European destinations where the direct flight takes 2–4 hours, the price difference with a connection is typically minimal. You add risk and time without meaningful financial benefit.

The conclusion for European routes: saving €10–25 does not compensate for 2–3 extra hours of travel and the real risk of missing a connection. On short routes, direct almost always wins.

Intercontinental routes — layovers can be decisive

On long distances, the price difference becomes substantial — and justifies extra hours.

Personal threshold: if the value of your leisure time during travel is below €40–50/hour, a layover saving €200+ is rational. If you are travelling for business or your time has high value, direct wins even with €200 price differences.


The real risk: what happens when you miss a connection

Scenario 1: Single booking (one PNR) — full protection

If both flights are on the same ticket (one booking reference), the airline is fully responsible for the connection:

What you receive automatically:


Rebooking on the next available flight to your destination — at no extra cost

Meals and drinks if the wait exceeds 2 hours

Hotel accommodation and transfers if an overnight stay becomes necessary

EU261 compensation if you arrive at your final destination 3+ hours late: €250–600 per person , depending on total route distance


How to verify you have a single ticket: your booking confirmation has one alphanumeric booking reference (e.g. ABC123). If you have two different codes for the two flights — you have separate tickets.

Full guide: flight delay and cancellation rights EU261 .

Scenario 2: Separate tickets — risk on you

If you booked London → Istanbul on one ticket and Istanbul → Bangkok on a separate booking (different PNR, possibly different airline), the first airline has zero obligation regarding the second flight:

What happens if you miss the connection:


You must buy a new ticket at the current market price

A last-minute intercontinental one-way: €500–1,500

Hotel at the connection city: your expense

Your return flight may be lost (typically non-refundable)


When separate tickets can make sense:


The layover is very long (6+ hours) — near-zero risk of missing the connection

The saving versus a single ticket is significant (€100+)

You have travel insurance with explicit missed connection coverage

You are travelling with hand luggage only — eliminates the baggage problem

Dubai's terminal distances are long but Emirates is systematic about managing connections



Baggage at layovers: exactly what happens

Single ticket (one PNR):
Bags are checked through to your final destination at the original check-in. At the connection point, you do nothing — ground handlers transfer them automatically. No customs, no re-check-in.

Separate tickets — the full process:


Collect bags at the connection airport arrivals belt

Clear customs and immigration (if an international connection)

Exit the arrivals hall with all bags

Find the check-in desk for the second airline

Re-check-in bags for the second flight

Clear security again


Time required: minimum 2–3 hours. With hand luggage only: 30–45 minutes.

Practical recommendation: if booking separate tickets on an intercontinental route, travel with hand luggage only. This reduces the transfer process to clearing security — manageable even in 90 minutes at efficient airports.


Long layovers: turning transit time into a city visit

A 5–10 hour layover is not wasted time — it is a bonus destination if you manage it right.

Istanbul — 5 to 8 hours

Metro M11 from Istanbul Airport: 38 minutes to Gayrettepe station. From there, M2 to Sultanahmet: 20 minutes. Total door-to-door from plane to Hagia Sophia: under 1 hour.

With 5 hours available: Sultanahmet Square, Hagia Sophia (free during prayer times, ticket required for tourist-hours access), the Grand Bazaar, a proper kebab lunch, and back to the airport with comfortable margin.

Turkish Airlines Stopover Programme: officially extends a connection into 1–3 nights in Istanbul with hotel packages at negotiated rates, included in the overall ticket. Register online at Turkish Airlines' stopover page.

Amsterdam — 4 to 6 hours

Direct train Schiphol → Amsterdam Centraal: 15 minutes, €6. The canal rings of Jordaan and Leidseplein are 10 minutes' walk from Centraal. A warm stroopwafel from the Albert Cuyp Market, a coffee at a canal-side café, and the Rijksmuseum exterior — all feasible in 4 hours with time to spare.

Vienna — 5 to 7 hours

S-Bahn S7 to Wien Hauptbahnhof: 16 minutes, €4.30. The Ringstrasse, Hofburg Palace exterior (free), Naschmarkt (open Monday–Saturday), and the Sachertorte at Café Sacher (€8.50). Vienna is the most elegant transit city in Europe — an hour here feels like it belongs in a different era.

Dubai — 7 to 10 hours

Red Metro Line from Terminal 3: contactless card payment, no need to buy tickets. Dubai Mall, Burj Khalifa exterior (free, the observation deck requires booking), and JBR beach — all reachable within 30 minutes.

Emirates Stopover Programme: similar to Turkish Airlines' offering — hotel and tour packages at special rates for passengers with longer connections. Activatable online before travel.

Reykjavik — 4 to 6 hours (Icelandair)

Icelandair's own stopover programme lets transatlantic passengers spend 1–7 nights in Iceland at no extra airfare cost — a genuine two-destination trip for the price of one transatlantic ticket.


Open-jaw itineraries: the experienced traveller's tool

Open-jaw means flying into one city and returning from another:

European examples:


Fly to Rome, return from Barcelona — see both cities without retracing

Fly to Athens, return from Dubrovnik — the Adriatic and Aegean in one trip

Fly to Lisbon, return from Porto — both cities naturally on one ticket


Intercontinental examples:


Fly to Bangkok, return from Singapore — Southeast Asia without backtracking

Fly to New York, return from Miami — East Coast + Florida on one booking

Fly to Tokyo, return from Osaka — Japan from north to south


Cost: typically similar to a standard return ticket on a single route — sometimes marginally more expensive, sometimes the same. The experience is significantly richer.

Search engines that find open-jaw well: Kiwi.com (specialist in non-standard routing combinations), Google Flights with the Explore function, Skyscanner with "Everywhere" as destination.


Virtual interlining: Kiwi.com's specific advantage

Traditional booking systems only combine flights from airlines with interline agreements. Kiwi.com's virtual interlining combines flights from any two airlines — including low-cost carriers that have no agreement with each other — onto what functions as a single itinerary.

What Kiwi Guarantee adds: if you miss a connection on a virtual interline combination (a flight operated by two airlines with no interline agreement), Kiwi will rebook you or refund the unused leg. This extends some of the protection of a single-ticket booking to combinations that would otherwise be separate tickets.

When virtual interlining is useful: when a combination of two low-cost carriers (Ryanair + Wizz Air, or Ryanair + easyJet) produces a significantly lower price than any single-airline routing — and you want protection beyond raw separate tickets.

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: Is a connecting flight worth it to save money?
R: On European routes under 4 hours direct: rarely. Savings are typically €10–30, not worth the added 2–4 hours and connection risk. On intercontinental routes of 8+ hours: often yes. Savings of €200–500 justify 3–5 extra travel hours. The formula: divide savings by hours added — if the result exceeds €40–50 per hour, the layover is rational.

Î: What happens if I miss my connecting flight?
R: If both flights are on a single booking (same PNR): the airline rebooks you on the next available flight at no charge, provides meals and accommodation if needed, and you may be owed EU261 compensation (€250–600) if you arrive 3+ hours late. With separate tickets: you buy a new ticket at the current price — potentially €500–1,500 for intercontinental routes.

Î: What is the minimum recommended layover time?
R: 90 minutes minimum for intra-EU connections at efficient hubs (Vienna, Amsterdam). 2 hours minimum for international connections. 3 hours minimum if you are changing airports (Heathrow to Gatwick, CDG to Orly). A 45-minute flight delay is common — you need genuine buffer, not just the minimum transfer time.

Î: Are bags automatically transferred at a layover?
R: Yes, if you have a single ticket (same PNR). Bags are checked through to the final destination — you do not collect them at the connection. With separate tickets, you must collect bags, clear customs and immigration, and re-check-in for the second flight — allow minimum 2–3 hours. Travelling with hand luggage only with separate tickets reduces this to 30–45 minutes.

Î: Which airports are best for layovers?
R: Most reliable: Istanbul IST (Turkish Airlines, modern and efficient), Vienna VIE (small, well-organised, Lufthansa Group), Dubai DXB (Emirates, excellent for Asia-Pacific). Solid: Amsterdam AMS, Frankfurt FRA. Problematic: London Heathrow LHR (consistently congested, high delay rates), Paris CDG (slow inter-terminal transfers).

Î: What is an open-jaw itinerary?
R: Open-jaw means flying into one city and returning from a different one — for example, flying to Rome and returning from Barcelona. You explore two destinations without retracing your route. The cost is typically similar to a standard return ticket on a single route. Search engines like Kiwi.com are designed to find these combinations automatically.

Î: Is an 8-hour layover worth leaving the airport?
R: Absolutely. Istanbul with 6 hours: Sultanahmet and the Grand Bazaar are 38 minutes by metro. Amsterdam with 5 hours: the canals and Jordaan are 15 minutes by train. Vienna with 6 hours: the Ringstrasse and a Viennese coffee at Café Sacher, 16 minutes by S-Bahn. Turkish Airlines and Emirates have official stopover programmes with included hotel packages.

Î: Does travel insurance cover a missed connection?
R: Only if the policy explicitly includes 'missed connection' or 'travel delay' coverage. This clause covers the cost of a new ticket if you miss a connection due to an unavoidable cause (delayed inbound flight). Check your policy wording before departure — this is the most important clause for travellers booking separate tickets on long-haul routes.

## Lost Luggage: Your Airline Rights and How to Claim Compensation in 2026

URL: https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/lost-luggage-airline-rights
Limbă: English
Verticală: zboruri
Publicat: 2026-07-29
Actualizat: 2026-07-29
Versiunea RO: https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/bagaj-pierdut-companie-aeriana-drepturi

Descriere: What to do when your bag doesn't arrive, how much compensation you're entitled to under the Montreal Convention, what airlines must pay for delayed baggage, and when travel insurance fills the gaps.

Răspuns scurt: If your luggage doesn't appear on the belt, report it to the airline's Lost & Found desk before leaving the airport — you must complete a PIR (Property Irregularity Report) to establish your legal claim. 90% of 'lost' bags are actually delayed and recovered within 24–48 hours. Under the Montreal Convention, the maximum compensation for genuinely lost luggage is approximately €1,500–1,700 per passenger. Airlines must also reimburse 'necessary and reasonable' expenses incurred during a baggage delay — keep every receipt.

The baggage belt slows, then stops. Everyone else has their bags. Yours is not there. The next 30 minutes — what you do and what you say — determine whether you recover your luggage quickly, get fully reimbursed, or lose months fighting for compensation that should be yours by law.

The first 30 minutes: what to do before leaving the airport

The single most important rule: do not leave the airport without reporting. Once you pass through customs and exit the arrivals hall, your options narrow significantly and your legal position weakens.

Step 1 — Confirm the bag is actually missing

Before heading to the Lost & Found desk, check the baggage claim area thoroughly. On busy flights, bags sometimes arrive on a different carousel or are held to one side by airport staff. If your flight had a connection, verify that the baggage claim area is for your final destination.

Step 2 — Find the airline's Lost & Found desk

This is the desk operated by your airline (or handling agent), typically located in the baggage claim hall before customs. It is not the general airport information desk. If you cannot find it, ask airport staff — every airport with commercial flights has one.

Step 3 — Complete the PIR (Property Irregularity Report)

The PIR is the legal foundation of your claim. Without it, you have no documented basis for compensation. At the desk:


Provide your flight details and booking reference

Describe the bag: size, colour, brand, distinctive features

Describe the contents at a general level (do not itemise valuables you should not have checked)

Leave complete contact information: the address where you are staying at your destination, your phone number, and your email


You receive a PIR reference number — write it down and photograph the document. Every subsequent communication will reference this number.

Step 4 — Photograph your baggage tag

The luggage tag attached to your boarding pass (or the receipt stub given at check-in) is proof that your bag was accepted into the airline's custody. Photograph it immediately — this is critical evidence if the airline disputes responsibility.

Step 5 — Note your immediate expenses

If you need to purchase essential items (toiletries, a change of clothes, medication) because your bag has not arrived, keep every receipt from the moment you leave the airport. These are reimbursable.


What actually happened to your bag: the real statistics

Understanding the mechanics reduces panic. The overwhelming majority of "missing" bags are not lost — they are mishandled : they went on the wrong flight, were offloaded at a connection airport due to a tight transfer, were tagged incorrectly, or were held due to a security check.

The numbers (SITA 2025 Baggage Report):


90%+ of mishandled bags are located and returned within 24–48 hours

Transfer mishandling accounts for approximately 40% of all mishandled bags

Only 1–2% of mishandled bags are not recovered within 21 days (the legal threshold for "lost")


The airline's tracking system locates most bags within a few hours. When found, the airline delivers the bag to your accommodation at their expense — you do not go back to the airport.


Your legal rights: the Montreal Convention explained

The Montreal Convention (formally the Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air) is the international treaty governing passenger and luggage rights on international flights. It applies to virtually all international flights between countries that have ratified it — essentially all major aviation markets globally.

Delayed baggage (0–21 days)

If your luggage is delayed (which is what the vast majority of "missing bag" situations actually are), the airline is responsible for reimbursing your necessary and reasonable expenses incurred because of the delay.

What qualifies:


Essential clothing: a couple of days' worth of basics (not designer purchases)

Toiletries: items you could not carry through security (large liquids, razors)

Prescription medication you needed during the delay and could not bring in carry-on

Other demonstrably necessary items specific to your situation


What does not qualify:


Luxury replacements for lost items

Recreational purchases

Items you would have bought regardless of the delay

Expenses not supported by receipts


The important caveat: "necessary and reasonable" is interpreted by airline claims departments in the airline's favour. Submit complete receipts with clear explanations of why each purchase was necessary. Excessive claims are typically reduced or rejected.

How to claim delay expenses: submit receipts to the airline's customer service (most have an online form). Include your PIR reference, flight details, and a brief explanation of why each purchase was necessary. Airlines typically respond within 4–8 weeks.

Lost baggage (after 21 days)

If the airline cannot locate your bag within 21 days of the flight date, it is officially declared lost. At this point, you are entitled to compensation under the Montreal Convention:

Maximum compensation: approximately 1,288 Special Drawing Rights (SDR)

SDR is an IMF monetary unit. At current exchange rates, 1,288 SDR equals approximately €1,500–1,700 per passenger. This rate fluctuates with currency movements — check the current SDR rate when making your claim.

Critical points about the compensation cap:


It applies per passenger, not per bag

It applies regardless of the actual value of the bag's contents

It is the maximum, not an automatic payment — you must document your loss

Airlines will attempt to settle for less; the cap is what you can insist upon


The high-value declaration option: when you check in, you can declare a higher value for your luggage and pay a supplemental fee (typically €1–2 per €100 of declared value above the standard limit). If your bag contains items worth significantly more than €1,500, this is worth considering — particularly for business travellers with laptops and equipment.

Damaged baggage

If your bag arrives damaged:


Report immediately — at the Lost & Found desk, before leaving the airport

Photograph everything — the damaged bag from multiple angles, the contents if relevant

Submit a written claim within 7 days of receiving the bag (crucial — this is a strict legal deadline under the Montreal Convention; missing it typically means the claim is rejected)

The airline is liable for repair or replacement value, subject to the Montreal Convention cap



What airlines must NOT say to you (and often do)

Airlines have financial incentives to minimise luggage claims. Some common tactics:

"We can only offer you €X as goodwill."
Goodwill payments are discretionary and typically lower than legal entitlements. You can accept a goodwill payment OR pursue your legal rights under the Montreal Convention — not both simultaneously. Make clear you are pursuing your legal rights.

"We cannot confirm the bag is lost until [date beyond 21 days]."
21 days is the legal threshold. After 21 days without recovery, you can formally submit a lost luggage claim — you do not need the airline to "confirm" loss separately.

"The delay was caused by [reason] which is outside our control."
The force majeure defence that airlines use for EU261 flight delays does NOT apply to baggage under the Montreal Convention. The Convention is strict liability for baggage — the airline is responsible regardless of cause (with very limited exceptions for inherent defect in the baggage itself).

"Your bag contents are not covered because they are electronics/valuables."
The Montreal Convention cap covers the total claim. However, general conditions of carriage for most airlines specifically exclude or limit liability for electronics, jewellery, cash, and other high-value items placed in checked baggage. This is why these items should never be checked.


Travel insurance vs Montreal Convention: which pays more?

Scenario Montreal Convention (airline) Travel insurance (your policy)
Bag delayed 24 hours Reimbursement of expenses (submit receipts) Fixed daily allowance (€30–80/day, no receipts needed)
Bag delayed 72 hours Reimbursement of expenses Fixed daily allowance × 3
Bag lost (after 21 days) Up to ~€1,600 per passenger Up to policy limit (often €1,500–3,000)
Damaged bag Repair or replacement value (up to €1,600) Replacement value (up to policy limit)
High-value electronics in bag Very limited (excluded in most airline conditions) Covered up to sub-limit (check policy)
Speed of payment Months (airline processes slowly) Weeks (insurer pays you, recovers from airline)
Required documentation PIR + receipts + detailed claims form PIR + simplified insurer claim form

The practical recommendation: file a claim with both the airline AND your travel insurance. Travel insurance pays you quickly and then subrogates (recovers from the airline on your behalf). You are not double-compensated — the total recovery is capped at your actual loss. But you get paid faster.

For full details on what travel insurance covers and how to choose a policy: travel insurance guide 2026 .


Items that should never go in checked luggage

This list is not opinion — it is based on airline liability limitations and practical experience:

Never check:


Passport, national ID, driving licence

Cash, bank cards, cryptocurrency keys

Prescription medication (carry enough in cabin baggage for 3+ days beyond your planned return)

Laptop, tablet, camera equipment

Jewellery, watches, valuable accessories

Keys (home, car)

Small irreplaceable items


The reasoning: the Montreal Convention cap (~€1,600) is unlikely to cover a laptop + camera + jewellery combination. Airline conditions of carriage further limit or exclude liability for these categories. Your travel insurance may have sub-limits for electronics (typically €200–500 per item). No combination of legal rights and insurance fully replaces an irreplaceable item.

The packing rule: if you would be devastated to lose it, it travels in your carry-on bag.


Technology that helps: tracking devices in luggage

Apple AirTag, Tile, and Samsung SmartTag devices can be placed in checked luggage to track location. IATA guidelines permit this, with requirements:


The device must be in Lost Mode (transmit passively, not active search)

Battery must be removable (AirTags meet this)

Inform airline staff if asked about electronics in checked bags


Practical use: if your bag is mishandled, an AirTag location can tell you immediately whether the bag is at your origin airport, your connection point, or your destination — useful information when dealing with the Lost & Found desk and significantly faster than waiting for the airline's tracking system to update.

Limitation: location accuracy varies. AirTag works via the Find My network (other Apple devices detecting it); in airports with high iPhone density, accuracy is good. In less populated areas, updates may be infrequent.


Filing your claim: the full process

For delayed baggage expenses:


Keep all receipts from the moment of leaving the airport with no bag

Within 21 days, submit a written claim to the airline (customer service email, online claim form, or letter to their headquarters)

Include: PIR reference, flight number, date, list of expenses with receipts, bank account details for reimbursement

Follow up after 4 weeks if no response — airlines have no legal deadline to respond but typically process within 4–8 weeks

If rejected or undervalued: contact your national aviation authority or file in small claims court (for amounts under €2,000, typically fast and low-cost)


For lost baggage (after 21 days):


Formally notify the airline in writing that you are making a claim under the Montreal Convention for lost luggage

Submit a detailed inventory of bag contents with estimated replacement values (for regular items, not high-value electronics or jewellery — see above)

The airline will typically offer a settlement — this may be below the Convention maximum; you can negotiate

If you cannot agree: small claims court or your country's aviation dispute resolution body


For damaged baggage:


Report at airport (mandatory — before leaving the arrivals hall)

Photograph damage in detail

Submit written claim within 7 days of bag receipt

Request repair or replacement value for damaged items



Your complete baggage rights at a glance

Situation Your right Deadline to claim
Bag delayed Reimbursement of necessary expenses Submit within 21 days of flight
Bag lost Compensation up to ~€1,600 per passenger Submit after 21 days
Bag damaged Repair or replacement compensation Report within 7 days of receipt
Valuables in cabin bag stolen Airline has no liability (your risk) N/A

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: What is the difference between delayed and lost luggage?
R: Legally, luggage is 'delayed' (temporarily mishandled) for up to 21 days after the flight. It becomes officially 'lost' only after 21 days without being located. 90% of bags reported missing are actually delayed — they went on a different flight, were left at a connection airport, or were loaded incorrectly. The airline is obligated to locate and deliver them to your address, at their expense.

Î: How much compensation do I get for lost luggage?
R: The Montreal Convention caps airline liability at approximately 1,288 Special Drawing Rights (SDR), which translates to roughly €1,500–1,700 per passenger (the rate fluctuates with currency). This applies regardless of the actual value of the contents. If you carry high-value items, you can declare a higher value at check-in and pay a supplemental fee for increased coverage — otherwise the cap applies.

Î: What expenses does the airline reimburse for delayed baggage?
R: Necessary and reasonable expenses incurred because of the delay: essential clothing, toiletries, medication you need and couldn't bring in cabin baggage. The standard is 'necessary and reasonable' — not designer replacements. Keep all receipts. Airlines do not have a fixed daily allowance — they assess submitted receipts against the reasonableness standard.

Î: What if my luggage arrives damaged?
R: Report the damage to the airline's Lost & Found desk immediately — before leaving the airport. Photograph the damage thoroughly. Submit a written claim within 7 days of receiving the bag (not 7 days from the flight — 7 days from when the damaged bag was delivered to you). After 7 days without reporting, airlines typically reject damage claims.

Î: Does travel insurance cover lost luggage better than the Montreal Convention?
R: Often yes, in two ways: higher coverage limits (many policies cover €1,500–3,000 per person for lost bags, plus specific sub-limits for electronics and valuables), and faster, simpler claims processing through the insurer rather than the airline. The key difference: travel insurance pays you directly and quickly, then recovers from the airline if applicable. Airline claims can take months.

Î: What should I never put in checked luggage?
R: Valuables (jewellery, cash, expensive watches), electronics (laptops, cameras, tablets), prescription medication you need on the trip, passports and travel documents, keys to your home or car, and irreplaceable items. Airline liability for these items in checked baggage is limited — the Montreal Convention cap and the airline's general conditions typically exclude or significantly limit coverage for these categories.

Î: Can I track my bag in real time?
R: Most airlines now provide bag tracking through their app (Ryanair, easyJet, British Airways, Lufthansa, Turkish Airlines all have this). Apple AirTags and Tile trackers are allowed by IATA guidelines in checked baggage (set to Lost Mode) — they provide location data that can help locate a mishandled bag. Note: report AirTag presence to the airline if asked; regulations on tracking devices in luggage vary.

Descriere: Flights from Bucharest OTP in 2026: top 15 routes with verified prices, Wizz Air vs Ryanair vs TAROM comparison, best booking windows and how to avoid hidden costs.

Răspuns scurt: The most popular flights from Bucharest are to London, Rome, Istanbul, Barcelona, Paris, Amsterdam, Dublin and Athens. Wizz Air, Ryanair, TAROM and Turkish: real comparison

Wizz Air: the Bucharest market leader

Wizz Air operates from Bucharest Otopeni (OTP) and has the largest direct route network from Romania — 60+ destinations. Its fundamental advantage: low base fares and dense coverage across Europe.

Strengths: 60+ direct destinations, competitive base fares, excellent app, WIZZ Priority adds good value.

Weaknesses: hold baggage always extra (€20–45/segment), seats not allocated without additional payment, changes are costly.

Real cost calculation for Wizz Air:


Base fare (ticket + small hand luggage 40×30×20 cm): €X



WIZZ Priority (cabin bag in overhead + priority boarding): +€6–15/segment





Hold baggage 20 kg: +€20–45/segment





Seat selection: +€5–15/segment




A ticket displayed at €45 return with hold baggage and a seat = €115–155 total. Always calculate the complete price.

Ryanair: fast expansion at OTP

Ryanair has significantly grown its Bucharest presence from 2023–2025, now operating 35+ direct routes. It is frequently cheaper than Wizz Air on Rome Ciampino, Milan Bergamo, and London Stansted/Luton.

Watch out for: Ryanair typically uses secondary airports. Add the transfer cost before comparing:

Route Ryanair airport Transfer to centre Cost Time
Rome Ciampino (CIA) Bus → Termini €6 45 min
Milan Bergamo (BGY) Bus → Central €7 60 min
London Stansted (STN) Stansted Express train £25 50 min
London Luton (LTN) Bus + train £18 60 min
Paris Beauvais (BVA) Bus → Porte Maillot €17 75 min

If Ryanair base fare + transfer > Wizz Air to the main airport, Wizz Air wins on total cost.

TAROM: when it makes sense

TAROM is frequently overlooked because the displayed fare appears higher. But TAROM includes checked baggage (23 kg) and an in-flight meal — the total price compared with Wizz Air + baggage is often similar or in TAROM's favour.

TAROM wins when:


You need flexibility (some fare classes allow free changes)

You have hold baggage and the total cost comparison is close

Connecting through major hubs (Frankfurt via Lufthansa codeshare)

You value comfort over the absolute lowest price


Turkish Airlines: gateway to the world

For any destination outside Europe, Turkish Airlines via Istanbul (IST or SAW) is typically the most competitive option from Bucharest. The Istanbul hub has connections to virtually every country on earth, multiple daily Bucharest connections, and competitive pricing.

Typical round-trip prices from Bucharest via Turkish Airlines:


New York (JFK): €600–950

Dubai (DXB): €350–600

Bangkok (BKK): €500–800

Tokyo (NRT): €700–1,100

Johannesburg (JNB): €600–900

Mumbai (BOM): €450–700

London and Dublin

The Romanian diaspora connection keeps prices to London and Dublin more stable year-round than Mediterranean routes — demand stays high all year. Off-season (November–March, excluding Christmas and New Year) produces the most significant discounts.


How to compare correctly: total price, not base fare

The most common mistake: comparing a €40 Wizz Air base fare with a €90 TAROM fare and choosing Wizz. But Wizz with baggage + seat = €90–130; TAROM with baggage included = €90. They are identical or TAROM is cheaper.

The correct formula:

Total cost = Ticket fare + Hold baggage (if needed) + Seat selection (if travelling together) + Secondary airport transfer (if applicable)

Always use a search engine that shows all airlines simultaneously — Kiwi.com or Google Flights. Never search only on the airline's own website, as airlines do not show each other's prices.


Connection flights from Bucharest: when they make sense

When connections are unavoidable

All intercontinental destinations require a connection from Bucharest — no direct long-haul flights exist from OTP.

Best hub connections from Bucharest

Istanbul (Turkish Airlines): most widely used. Multiple daily flights, huge global network, competitive prices. The 1–2 hour connection is typically smooth at IST (well-designed transit zone).

Frankfurt (Lufthansa): premium hub for the USA and Asia. Higher quality connections, slightly higher fares.

Amsterdam (KLM): excellent for North America (New York, Boston, Toronto, Vancouver).

Vienna (Austrian Airlines): close to Bucharest (1h40), frequent, good option for destinations where Austrian has direct services.

Open-jaw routing: the experienced traveller's trick

Fly outbound to Rome and return from Barcelona. This lets you explore two cities without retracing your steps — and costs approximately the same as a standard return on one route. Search engines that support open-jaw routing (Kiwi.com does this well) automatically find these combinations.


Your rights on flights from Bucharest

EU261 compensation

All flights departing from Bucharest are covered by EU Regulation 261/2004, regardless of which airline operates the flight. If your flight is delayed by 3+ hours at your final destination or cancelled with less than 14 days' notice:

Route distance Compensation
Under 1,500 km (Budapest, Rome, Istanbul, Athens) €250
1,500–3,500 km (London, Amsterdam, Madrid, Paris) €400
Over 3,500 km €600

You can claim for past flights up to 3 years after the disruption. AirHelp and Compensair process claims on a success-fee basis.

Full guide: flight delay and cancellation rights EU261 .

Cabin baggage rules

Avoid the €50–100 gate fee by knowing the exact allowances. See: cabin baggage rules 2026 — Wizz Air, Ryanair, and all major airlines operating from Bucharest.

Cheapest European destinations from Bucharest — where to go with the flights you book

### Întrebări frecvente

Î: What is the cheapest destination to fly to from Bucharest?
R: Budapest and Rome are consistently the cheapest: tickets from €35–45 return with Wizz Air. Budapest benefits from the short flight time (1h20) and very low local prices. Rome and Bari compete for second place, especially in off-season. Istanbul is the cheapest non-EU destination (from €50 return).

Î: Is Wizz Air or Ryanair cheaper from Bucharest?
R: It depends on the route and date. Wizz Air has more direct destinations from Bucharest (60+ vs 35+) and typically wins on Eastern Europe and Balkan routes. Ryanair is more competitive on Rome Ciampino, Milan Bergamo, and London Stansted/Luton. Essential: always compare both on a search engine — never directly on airline websites, as they don't show each other's prices.

Î: When is the cheapest time to fly from Bucharest?
R: Cheapest months overall: November, January, February (excluding Christmas/New Year). Spring (March–May) and autumn (September–October) offer good prices combined with excellent weather at Mediterranean destinations. July–August are the most expensive, with sharp peaks during the Romanian school summer holiday.

Î: How much does baggage cost on Wizz Air from Bucharest?
R: Small hand luggage (40×30×20 cm): free on all tickets. Extended hand luggage (cabin bag, with WIZZ Priority): €6–15 added at booking. Hold baggage 20 kg: €20–45 per segment (cheaper added at booking, significantly more expensive at check-in). A ticket showing €40 with hold baggage return can cost €80–130 total — always compare the complete price, not the base fare.

Î: Are there direct flights from Bucharest to the USA or Asia?
R: No direct flights in 2026. All intercontinental routes require a connection. Best options: Turkish Airlines via Istanbul (IST or SAW) for Asia, Africa, and the Middle East; Lufthansa via Frankfurt for the USA and Asia; KLM via Amsterdam for North America; Emirates via Dubai for Asia-Pacific and Africa.

Î: What EU261 compensation can I claim on flights from Bucharest?
R: All flights departing from Bucharest Henri Coandă are covered by EU Regulation 261/2004, regardless of the airline. Compensation for delays of 3+ hours at the final destination: €250 (flights under 1,500 km), €400 (1,500–3,500 km), €600 (over 3,500 km). This applies to Wizz Air, Ryanair, and all carriers operating from Romanian airports.

Î: Is it worth using Wizz Discount Club?
R: Wizz Discount Club (approximately €30–40/year) provides discounts of €10–40 per ticket. It pays for itself after 2–3 flights if you take 3+ Wizz Air trips per year. Not worth it for occasional flyers. Activate from the app or website when purchasing a ticket.
